item.title: High surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions at San Diego beaches this Labor Day weekend
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 4.72
SAN DIEGO (KGTV)- San Diego lifeguards are on high alert this Labor Day weekend as high surf and strong rip currents create dangerous conditions along the coast. San Diego Fire-Rescue officials warn that the biggest risk isn't just the size of the waves — it's the rip currents that aren't always visible. Candace Hadley, public information officer for San Diego Fire-Rescue and Lifeguards, said the department has already had an exceptionally busy summer. "Our lifeguards have performed about 5,500 rescues since June, and typically in an average year you have about 7,000 to 8,000 rescues, so it's been a very busy summer," Hadley said. This Labor Day weekend marks the last weekend of full summer staffing for lifeguards. Officials are urging beachgoers to check in before getting in the water. "Check in with a lifeguard, they'll tell you the safest place to swim, you can learn about conditions in the area specifically, and make sure you know what to do if you get caught in a rip current," Hadley said. Surfers are also taking the conditions seriously. Damien Manzino, a surfer at one of the San Diego beaches, said the incoming swell brings excitement — but also responsibility. "I think everyone gets a little excited when they know some surf is coming. I think making sure all your gear is ready and that you're in shape, and yeah, get out here and have some fun," Manzino said. Manzino also offered a word of caution to anyone heading into the water. "The ocean is very unforgiving; it doesn't care if you're tired or if you're exhausted, it's going to keep going, so I think once you start feeling a little fatigue, I think it's time to come out and take a break," Manzino said. Whether swimming or surfing, officials say beachgoers should know their limits and stay aware of conditions throughout the holiday weekend. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. item.title: Rare orca pod spotted hunting dolphins off the San Diego coast
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 4.52
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — A rare pod of orcas has been spotted multiple times off the coast of San Diego — and they were hunting dolphins. Legacy Whale Watching captured video of the Eastern Tropical Pacific orca pod, which is considered among the least-studied orca pods in the world. "We usually only get to see them about once a year; this time we got to see them three times within the span of about five days," said Evin Rose, a naturalist and alumna of Scripps Institution of Oceanography. Nicole Schriber, a UCSD Scripps Oceanography graduate who works with Gone Whale Watching in San Diego, said the pod was last seen heading toward Mexico. It remains unclear whether the whales will return to Southern California waters, in an email statement. "We are hoping for more sightings this fall and winter because of the El Niño," Schriber said. "But we can't say for sure! If you want to see these Orcas, you can't really make plans for it; it's a situation where you see the sighting report and rush to the boat that same day for a chance." The orcas have been targeting local dolphin populations, not humans. "They've been hunting our common and bottlenose dolphins offshore," said Rose. While experts say there is no cause for alarm, they advise against entering the water near the animals. item.title: Labor Day travel weekend comes amid higher gas prices
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.77
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) – Many people are either calling it a night after arriving or waking up early on Saturday to get to their Labor Day destinations. AAA said people are looking for ways to make travel work despite higher gas prices. “We know just historically what we've seen, even with the travel being more expensive or gas being more expensive, most people still prioritize travel,” Annllyen Venagas, AAA Southern California Here’s where gas prices stand right now in our region. It’s tipping about $5.92 a gallon for regular gas here in San Diego. That’s 16 cents more than a week ago and essentially a month ago. But regular gas was below $5 a gallon this time last year. AAA said you’re still encouraged to hit the road early, before 10 a.m. on Saturday and before noon on Monday, despite this time period not being the busiest of all holiday travel time periods. If you are driving, you’ll clearly be spending more getting to your holiday destination. AAA Southern California said Labor Day travelers can anticipate spending roughly $18 to $24 more to fill up their gas tank compared to last year’s holiday. “They're finding ways to make it work. They're modifying their trips so that they can still prioritize travel but still save money on gas and travel, even though, like you said, gas prices are higher than a year ago,” Venagas said. AAA said that’s still not stopping people from traveling, just maybe shorter distances if they are driving. Still, some are opting to stay home for Labor Day rather than make a trip out of the weekend. “Well, gas is $6 a gallon, which is crazy. Like I can't afford that. I really can’t,” Julia Campbell said. “If this is how much I have to spend on gas, I can't really spend anything else on anything else, you know.” “For me right now, no, because I got like 4 kids, so it's just really expensive right now here in California,” Melissa Diaz said.

item.title: Bodysurfer working to walk again after breaking neck at Carlsbad beach
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.46
Matthew Lee walked into the ocean in Carlsbad on August 28, 2026. He was carried out. The experienced bodysurfer dove headfirst into a sandbar, breaking his neck. He was left temporarily paralyzed, floating face down in the water. "I remember very vividly hitting the sand and hearing underwater, my neck break," Lee said."And I was floating face down in the water, totally awake but couldn't move anything.” Lee's friend Bryce Mihaly was in the water nearby. Mihaly, who works alongside Lee as a paramedic, initially wasn't sure what was happening. "I thought he was just joking for a minute, so I kind of was, I was quickly walking towards him, but once about 30 seconds that, I figured out, probably not joking too much," Mihaly said. His life-saving training quickly took over. "I'm accustomed to working with critical and sick patients, but it's not the same when it's someone you know, when it's a buddy of yours, it's a little bit different," Mihaly said. Nearly two weeks later, Lee is recovering in the hospital from a broken neck, collapsed esophagus, and damaged spinal cord. By focusing his mind on healing, he has regained feeling in his lower body and strength in his upper body. A nurse's words helped drive that determination. "I had a really amazing nurse. She said, the power of your mind can go many places, and she said if you can will it with your mind, you can make it happen. And so after I don't know, 20 or 30 people came in every day, I would spend hours and hours and hours a night willing it to work" Lee said. Lee is hopeful he can return to the ocean one day and is certain he will walk again. "I'll have to call you and then we can go hike Mount Whitney together," Lee said. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Lee on his road to recovery. To donate, click here.

item.title: Chula Vista Charter School students chase IT careers
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.38
CHULA VISTA (KGTV) — Students at a Chula Vista charter school are learning to repair computers and working toward an industry-standard certification that could launch their careers in the technology industry. Inside a computer lab at Learn4Life Chula Vista, about seven high school students are enrolled in a digital technology program built from the ground up by Career Technical Education (CTE) instructor Robert Link. "So my job is to work with students to teach them about career technical education. It's kind of like a modern-day auto shop," Link said. Link works with students four to five hours a day, twice a week, giving them hands-on experience with the hardware and software they will need to know how to repair in the real world. Student Maria Ochoa said the hands-on approach has made a difference in how she learns. "So it was just very fun, very easy. If I didn't get it one way, he would explain it in another way," Ochoa said. Once students complete the course, they can take the CompTIA A+ certification exam, which is an industry-standard credential for entry-level IT jobs. "With that certification, they can find jobs in all kinds of different IT fields, usually things that are structured around IT support or IT help desk," Link said. Link said employers like Apple, Best Buy's Geek Squad, and local tech repair shops like 'I Break You Fix' are among the places where certified graduates could find work. The A+ certification can also serve as a launchpad into a broader IT career, serving as the first of many more certifications the students would have to build on to get into more technical roles. Student Darius Pitts said he is already thinking ahead. "After I graduate from Learn4Life, I was thinking about taking a course or majoring in computer science and possibly a second in business so I could start selling computers," Pitts said. Link said the students have already taken the certification exam once and are preparing to retake it. "So these tests are very much adult-level tests," Link said. "We're expecting them to come through and pass the second time."

item.title: NTSB to release readout from cockpit recorder after deadly Amazon cargo plane crash
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 4.03
Cockpit voice recorder indicates pilot tried to abort landing before Amazon cargo plane crash: NTSB One of the pilots also made comments about the plane's "excessive speed." Cockpit voice recordings from inside the Amazon Air cargo plane that overran a Miami runway crashing into a van and leaving five people dead, indicate one of the pilots called for a "go-around" to abort the landing just seconds before the crash. The NTSB, which is investigating the crash, released a readout of the final minutes before the crash taken from the cockpit voice recorder, which contained more than 2 hours of audio. About 1 minute and 42 seconds before the plane crashed, one of the pilots warned they were going too fast and continued to make comments about the plane's "excessive speed throughout the remainder of the recording," according to the NTSB summary. About 30 seconds before the crash, the NTSB said sounds similar to the aircraft touching down can be heard, but about 15 seconds later, one of the pilots called for the "go-around" to abort the landing. Just five seconds later, the plane had already veered off the runway. The release of the select moments captured on the cockpit voice recordings came the same day the NTSB expected to interview the two pilots, NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy told reporters at an earlier press briefing. In its update on Wednesday, the NTSB did not share any information from the pilot interviews. A preliminary report is expected in the new few weeks. At the press briefing Tuesday, NTSB officials discussed some of the details recovered from the flight data recorder, which indicated that the plane was coming in for landing, but that several seconds before the recording ends, throttles increased consistent with a "go-around thrust," NTSB investigator Chihoon Shin said. A few seconds later, brakes were reapplied and continued to be applied until the end of the recording, but there was no indication that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed, he said. The cargo plane, Amazon Air Flight 7598 arriving from Puerto Rico, was carrying about 32,000 pounds of mostly contact lenses, Homendy said. When it overran the runway, the plane hit a Ford Econoline van owned by a company that cleans aircraft, with seven people inside. The five people who were killed were identified by the Miami-Dade County Sheriff's Office as: Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Narajo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47. The aircraft's two pilots were treated and have been released from the hospital, according to the sheriff's office.

item.title: 25 years later, Michael Strahan recalls days after 9/11
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.73
25 years later, Michael Strahan recalls days after 9/11 The special "9/11: United We Stand -- 25 Years Later" airs Tuesday, Sept. 1. Michael Strahan will never forget looking out his window in Montclair, New Jersey, and seeing the first World Trade Center tower in flames on Sept. 11, 2001. Strahan, a former football star turned "Good Morning America" co-anchor, said he never expected he would end up in New York City but fell in love with it after being drafted to the New York Giants, the team he stayed with for 15 seasons of his career. He's among the athletes, musicians and entertainers who reflected on how their industries worked to bring healing after tragedy for the the ABC News special, "9/11: United We Stand -- 25 Years Later." An ABC News special, "9/11: United We Stand -- 25 Years Later," airs Tuesday, Sept. 1, at 9 p.m. ET on ABC and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu. In the wake of the attacks, Strahan was one of the players who pushed for the cancellation of that weekend's football games out of respect for those lost. He also contributed to an NFL-wide effort to provide disaster relief and support to victims and their families. "What were we gonna do? Sit at home? No, we wanted to collectively get together and offer whatever kind of assistance that we could at Ground Zero," Strahan said. "That's the biggest show that we wanted to give them, was a show of respect." The NFL wasn't the only major sports league to use its platform to foster unity and support victims post-9/11. In fall 2001, the Yankees went to the World Series, and though they ultimately lost the series, commentators say the team's participation in the games that came just over a month after the tragedy unified New Yorkers. "It became more than just playing baseball," Derek Jeter, then Yankees shortstop, said. "Our job was to bring joy, especially to New York at that time." Selena Roberts, then sports columnist at the New York Times, noted that the leagues recognized their role in a difficult time. "After Sept. 11, players and coaches absolutely knew that they had a platform and a responsibility to be there for the public, and I think in so many ways, really did help heal people," she said. That fall, a star-studded concert at Madison Square Garden, organized by singer Paul McCartney, brought some of music's biggest names together for a benefit to honor and raise money for 9/11 victims and first responders. Called The Concert for New York City, the benefit featured singers David Bowie, Mick Jagger, Jon Bon Jovi, Billy Joel and McCartney, among others. Bon Jovi reflected on the meaning of his band's song "Livin' on a Prayer" in that moment. "'We got each other and that's a lot.' That's what it is, right?" the singer said. "In that moment in time, when you felt helpless, to have a lyric that is about just simple unity and faith." Late night talk show hosts also did their part to calm the public's nerves. CBS's David Letterman was the first of the late-night hosts to return on air post-9/11. During his first show back after the attack, Letterman said, "There's only one requirement of all of us, and that is to be courageous." Anthony DeCurtis, an author and music critic, said that immediately after 9/11, there was a moment in which people questioned listening to music or going to the theater. That, though, is precisely why we have art, he said. "At moments like that, you know, you want artists who are going to help us understand and come to terms with the things in our lives that are the most frightening things," Curtis said. "This is what we do, and what better time to do it than now?" Strahan said it was an era where people learned to be more compassionate. "I'd never seen the level of unity that we had during that time."

item.title: Meet the chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.58
Meet the New York City chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks Members of "Operation Chefs With Spirit" reflect on the tragedy 25 years later. Chef Don Pintabona spent years cooking up the finest dishes for celebrities, Wall Street brokers and other VIPs at the Tribeca Grill in downtown Manhattan, but nothing could have prepared him and the rest of the city's restaurant community for their biggest job. In the hours after the World Trade Center was attacked and destroyed on Sept. 11, 2001, Pintabona said he and many other chefs, caters, food service workers and others all yearned to help the city in some capacity with their skills, but didn't immediately know how. But through quick thinking, organizing and the generosity of thousands New Yorkers, Pintabona and the other restaurant members put together a massive operation that fed Ground Zero workers around the clock for two months after the attacks. "Everybody kind of just said, 'Okay, let's jump in,'" Pintabona, 66, told ABC News. He and other volunteers of "Operation Chefs with Spirit" said that even though 25 years have passed since the attacks, the memories of those weeks are still fresh, as is the sense of awe at how they put the operation together. Turning the page on a tragedy Pintabona said he had a desire to do something after the attacks to help the city, but it was a little piece of paper that came to him serendipitously that sparked his idea for the operation. On Sept. 11, he said he watched the destruction of the towers from the roof of his home in Brooklyn, which was so close that pieces of paper debris from the towers were floating in the air near him. One of those was a "P" page from a dictionary and when Pintabona picked it up he said he noticed that one side of the page had words with negative connotations, such as pesky, while the other side had words such as persevere, perseverance, persistence. “9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. "I mean, in my mind, this came straight from heaven, that through the perversion, you gotta persist, you gotta persevere," he said. "So those words were banging around my head for the days and weeks and just trying to figure out how can I live up to this." Pintabona said the next day he was able to get to his restaurant, and he started cooking with what he had in his kitchen. He then brought the food to Stuyvesant High School in lower Manhattan, which was one of the staging areas for first responders. "We had just floods of people coming in to attack the food," he said adding that the meals were gone in a matter of hours. Pintabona said he wanted to continue to feed more people but transporting the meals through the streets, which were damaged and restricted to first responders and the National Guard, would be a challenge. He said he had a eureka moment during a cigarette break while watching the Hudson River. "I saw a barge…And I said, 'Holy s---, this is it. We've got to feed everybody by boat,'" he recalled. A crew assembles, quickly gets into action Pintabona told ABC News he found that that other chefs in the city were also interested in feeding the Ground Zero workers and they all put their heads together. He soon started calling up several contacts within the food industry, the city government and the owner of Spirit Cruises, which operated city sightseeing and party cruises lines, and things quickly began to fall in place. Spirit provided three boats, one at Chelsea Piers that would be used to cook and prepare the meals, another to transport the food to Ground Zero, and a third, a triple decker, stationed in Battery Park City near the pit that was used for the workers to eat and rest. The city's top chefs, such as Charlie Palmer, Danny Meyer and Daniel Boulud, and food workers and volunteers would be doled out with tasks with everything from cutting veggies to organizing forks, spoons and plates. Jim Stewart, a longtime food service coordinator who had experience coordinating food operations at the Meadowlands and other big clients, jumped in when Pintabona made the calls for help. Stewart said he too was compelled to do something after the attacks. "I think at that point, having something to do was sort of helpful, and it gave you some sort of purpose in a very difficult situation," Stewart, 66, a Navy veteran, told ABC News. Stewart used his connections to secure food from the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, which was still in fridges following the end of that year's U.S. Open. Stewart and Pintabona estimated that the food from the tennis center could serve 75,000 meals, but that was all eaten within three days. Fortunately, they weren't the only New Yorkers who were willing to share from their fridges. Stewart recalled how a whole slew of Downtown Manhattan restaurant staff, from small Chinatown restaurants to larger, more elite eateries like the ones under B.R. Guest, were calling him up and ready to offer their food. "So they would be bringing down enormous amounts of food packages to go. All the cooks from down there, they brought meals for like 200 people without question for a month," Stewart said. "I would get a call, and they would go, 'At the airport, there's two pallets of beef from Texas.' It was not just New York," Stewart added. Pintabona said that thousands of New Yorkers arrived at Chelsea Piers ready to volunteer, even those who never cooked a meal in their life. Although Pintabona had to turn many would-be volunteers away because of space and logistics issues, he said he worked out to tailor their skills to fit the operation. "When they would come on, I would try to talk to as many as possible. 'Okay, you work at Smith Barney in the accounting department? You know what? We need you to help us inventory the food that comes in off the trucks,'" he recalled. "A lot of people, obviously servers and whatnot, food service people, I would put them front-facing on the buffets, you know what they're used to." Megan Murphy was a full time bartender at Rue 51 in Manhattan on Sept. 11 and she told ABC News she immediately answered Stewart's call. She helped to serve the food and coordinate with other volunteers right at the pit. "It was my call to duty," Murphy, 51, told ABC News while holding back tears. " I had been doing something because I was helpless. I felt helpless and I just wanted to help. I just want to be…I just needed to be there." 'Nourishing more than their stomachs' By Sept. 14, the operation had kicked off and the volunteers were ready to go and the first set of food was delivered to the pit. The boats would sail from Chelsea Piers nearly 2 1/2 miles south to Ground Zero with a team of volunteers and return back for another round and the operation would continue 24/7. Workers still had soot on them and looked liked they hadn't slept in days but they gladly accepted the meals and cherished the time to step away from the terrible scene. Pintabona said massage therapists joined in on the volunteering and provided the crews with free massages to ease their muscles. He said the meals definitely helped the pit workers have the energy to push through with their work, but the chefs and volunteers all felt that their service meant a lot more than a free lunch. "You'd see the looks on the faces of people that came in, if they'd been on the pile for God knows how many hours and starving and then they got to sit in a clean environment and then talk to other first responders," he said. "So that was the most amazing part of the effort," he added, "[It] kind of nourished a lot more than just stomachs." Murphy, who continued to bartend at night during her volunteer time, said that many who came down to help went beyond just serving food and in many cases offered the pit crews a place to unwind and let out their raw emotions. "I would make an effort just to go to everyone and talk to them, and let them talk to me about the experience," she said. "If after lunch they could walk out and I could walk out with them and they were smiling and getting off their shift and made it a better day, that was what I was there to do," Murphy added. The volunteers and chefs said that while they pushed forward with the operation, with some sleeping on the boats, the stress and hard work did compound. Fortunately, the volunteers had each other's backs, according to Pintabona and Stewart. "It got so ridiculous that one day Jimmy was working the phones and, you know I just had this stupid, selfish craving for a Krispy Kreme doughnut," Pintabona recalled. "I said, 'All right, let's call this guy.' We called them, and the next day a whole truck with like 20 rolling racks of Krispy Kreme donuts showed up," Stewart said. "So [Pintabona] looked at me and was like, I should have known better." Looking back 25 years later The operation ended after roughly two months and roughly a million meals after the Red Cross came in and took care of meals for the Ground Zero pit crew. But Pintabona said that the crew didn't grow apart. He organized a Christmas party at Cipriani in Soho for all of the volunteers and their families and many stayed in touch in the last 25 years. Stewart said he was humbled by the outpouring of support from not only New Yorkers, but people throughout the world who heard about the feeding operation and were moved. "I have these pictures that were sent to me from a class where the children, they drew cartoons," he recalled. "They said like, 'Keep going. You're doing great.' You know, 'thank you for your efforts.'" Murphy said that she is still emotional thinking back to the weeks after the attacks, but the memories of selfless New Yorkers always stand out. "New York is strong, New Yorkers are strong," she said. Pintabona agreed and said for him it all came back to that floating dictionary page and that push to persevere. "You have to turn the page and stay on the positive side. So that's kind of what I've learned through this experience," he said.

item.title: 9/11 firefighter's son spends months bringing steel from World Trade Center across US
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.10
The steel 'embodies his soul': 9/11 family takes World Trade Center beam across US Stephen Siller Jr. was just 9 months old when his firefighter dad died on 9/11. On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, 34-year-old New York City firefighter Stephen Siller had just finished his overnight shift when he heard a call come in on the scanner. "He immediately knew something was awry," so he drove to his firehouse in Brooklyn, his son, Stephen Siller Jr., told ABC News. "When he got there, he realized his whole unit had responded [to the World Trade Center]," Siller Jr. said. "So he grabbed his gear, threw it in his truck and started to make his way to the World Trade Center. But on 9/11, they shut down every entryway into Manhattan." He parked his car by the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller Jr. said, put about 60 pounds of gear on his back, and ran through the tunnel to the South Tower of the World Trade Center. Stephen Siller was among 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11. He was survived by his close-knit siblings, his wife Sally, and his five children, including Stephen Jr., who was 9 months old. Siller Jr., now 25, doesn't have his own memories of his father, but he's poured his energy into honoring those who died on 9/11. And to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, he spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S. in hopes that seeing a piece of history up close will help Americans remember, learn and be inspired. The Steel Across America campaign allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day -- the sacrifice of first responders and their loss, the loss of innocent people who just went to work," Stephen Siller Jr.'s uncle, Frank Siller, told ABC News. 9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. Siller Jr. described the entire tour as "incredibly powerful." At the first stop, ground zero, a firefighter whose entire unit was killed on 9/11 "walked up to the steel and he put his hand on it, and he was overcome with emotion," Siller Jr. recalled. "You could just immediately see tears rushing down his face. And he started to hug the steel like he was hugging his friends he lost 25 years ago." To Siller Jr., the steel represents the more than 1,000 bodies never recovered from the World Trade Center -- including his father's. "Who they are is ingrained in that steel, what they did is ingrained in that steel. It holds the memory of that day," he said. "It's the most overwhelming piece of history I've ever come across." The beam represents "resilience, strength, but also sacrifice," Frank Siller added. "... Ground zero is my brother's burial place, obviously. But the steel has his -- embodies his soul, and the souls of so many." As Siller Jr. spent his summer traveling the U.S., from Oklahoma to California to Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, he said he was surprised by how many people had personal connections to the terror attacks, like the police officer he met in Seattle whose uncle was killed on 9/11. "And we had thousands of people show up to 35 events across the country who may not have had a connection to 9/11," he added, "but for them, they wanted to mourn that day, they wanted to make sure they never forgot." "Everywhere we went was incredible -- the support, it was mind-boggling," Siller Jr. said. "In Texarkana, a small, little town in Texas, we had about 1,000 people show up to an event. It was unbelievable. You know, companies letting all their employees out of work to go see this piece of steel." Siller Jr. found one of the most memorable stops to be Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Florida, where President George W. Bush was reading to students on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, when he learned of the attacks. "We normally have stairs that go up to the steel truck," Siller Jr. explained, but on this May visit to the school, it was pouring rain. Still, the children "were begging the firemen, 'Hey, can we get up? We just want to touch the steel,'" Siller Jr. said. As the kids were lifted up, they began "praying over this steel," he recalled. "Little kids who understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history ... it once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day," he said. "I was really shocked at how interested they were," he said. To Frank Siller and Siller Jr., educating the next generation was a key goal of the Steel Across America campaign. "These kids were incredible; they were patient ... and they consistently showed up," Siller Jr. said. "No matter where we were in the country, there were families there, which was beautiful -- fathers and mothers wanting to teach their kids." "I was 9 months old on 9/11 -- if you were born after me, and not in New York City, you know, there's a high chance that you have no real understanding of that day," he continued. "It's important that that lesson is taught to these kids -- there's so much to be pulled from the sacrifices made." The Steel Across America campaign is part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, started by Frank Siller in honor of his brother's run from the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the World Trade Center. The foundation supports military members, first responders and their families across the U.S. The foundation is currently providing wounded veterans and first responders with mortgage-free, specially-adapted smart homes. "We didn't let Stephen just perish in that rubble and let that story end there. No, we took his act of courage and sacrifice and said, 'We're going to do good with it,'" Frank Siller said. "Would Stephen make that run again through the tunnel, knowing he was gonna die? I think he knew he was gonna die," Frank Siller said. "At the very least, he knew it was a strong possibility that he might not be coming home. And to think that he did that, knowing how much he loved Sally and his kids, people like that are few and far between. ... And it's got to be recognized and never forgotten."

item.title: 9/11 victims hope newly uncovered records will help illuminate Saudis' alleged role
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.77
25 years later, 9/11 victims hope newly uncovered records will help illuminate Saudis' alleged role Victims' families are pressing President Trump to declassify more materials. Twenty-five years after Sept. 11, a trove of newly obtained records is offering what families of the victims characterize in court as compelling evidence of deep Saudi complicity in the attacks. Now, as their decade-old lawsuit against the Saudi kingdom marches toward trial, the families are pressing the Trump administration to declassify more government records they believe could finally deliver justice. The newly revealed records, from a lawsuit involving an alleged Saudi agent, include a video purportedly casing the Capitol two years before the attacks and a sketch that purportedly shows calculations for navigating a plane toward a target on the ground, which one family member called "smoking gun evidence." The decision on whether to declassify additional records ultimately lies with President Donald Trump, whose administration has touted government transparency and who has personally signed executive orders declassifying records ranging from purported UFO sightings to high-profile assassinations. "We've seen him do it for the [President John F. Kennedy] files. Why not the 9/11 files?" Brett Eagleson, whose father Bruce was killed in the World Trade Center's South Tower, said in an interview with ABC News. "Now is the moment, 25 years later, to finally bring resolution," Eagleson said, "and the man that sits in the Oval Office has a historic and a tremendous opportunity to do it." Eagleson has enlisted the support of members of the New York congressional delegation to press the administration to release key records that include phone logs purportedly belonging to Omar al-Bayoumi, who the families allege is a Saudi intelligence asset, as well as two of the hijackers. Among those who cosigned a letter seeking the declassification of those records is Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., a Trump ally who is urging the president take up the matter before the 25th anniversary, less than two weeks away. "This is probably one of the better shots that we have at getting this information out there," Malliotakis said. "And I think that hopefully we'll see this type of transparency coming from this administration." White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told ABC News, "President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, and his team is working diligently to identify records that are responsive to these families' request." 'Smoking gun' The families have waged their legal campaign against the Saudis in one form or another since 2003, but only recently uncovered videos, notes and other records they say offer irrefutable evidence of Saudi government complicity -- claims that the Saudis have long denied. Al-Bayoumi lies at the heart of those records. The Saudi national lived in the U.S. for the better part of a decade -- nominally as a student -- prior to the attacks, and provided "essential support" to two hijackers when they arrived in California in early 2000, according to the families' lawsuit, which claims that al-Bayoumi assisted the men by "finding them an apartment in his complex" and "providing funds just below the suspicious activity reporting threshold to help them open a bank account." According to the families, al-Bayoumi also threw a party for the hijackers and "the hijackers stayed at al-Bayoumi's apartment for 1-2 days, before their apartment was ready." "He was the man," Eagleson told ABC News. "Omar al-Bayoumi is coordinating and directing logistical and financial support to the hijackers." In 1999, al-Bayoumi travelled to Washington, D.C., where he filmed what the families called a "chilling" video of al-Bayoumi "'casing' the U.S. Capitol for an attack," according to the suit. The Capitol is believed to be the target of United Flight 93, the hijacked plane that crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. In the video, according to the suit, al-Bayoumi describes to an unidentified audience the security posture inside and outside the Capitol building, highlights its proximity to the nearby Reagan National Airport, and opaquely references a "plan." The families also presented in court a sketch and math equation from al-Bayoumi's notebook showing what they claim to be a "line of sight calculation for navigating a plane to a target on the ground." The Saudis have repeatedly denied having any role in facilitating the attacks and replied in court that they remain "an ally of the United States [and] a sworn enemy of Al Qaeda." Attorneys for the kingdom also fervently disputed the families' characterizations of that evidence in court, dismissing the Capitol "casing" film as a "tourist video that includes footage of artwork, flowerbeds, and a squirrel on the White House lawn." They say the notepad sketch "appears to be a high school math assignment" belonging to al-Bayoumi's child. Al-Bayoumi, who is believed to now live in Saudi Arabia, "became entangled in the 9/11 investigation because he had helped two fellow Saudis he had no reason to suspect of wrongdoing," the Saudi attorneys said -- a sentiment al-Bayoumi shared in a deposition in the case. Al-Bayoumi has also denied any connection to Saudi intelligence. Last year the judge overseeing the case ruled that the evidence presented by the families was compelling enough to proceed to trial, dealing a major setback to the Saudis and granting the families what they called "the most consequential step yet" in two decades of litigation. The judge noted that the Saudis' exculpatory explanations "are either self-contradictory or [are] not strong enough to overcome the inference that [the Saudis] had employed al-Bayoumi ... to assist the hijackers." And while there remains no evidence that Saudi leaders at the top of its government were likely aware of plans for the attack, "the total evidence creates a high probability as to al-Bayoumi's ... [role] in the hijackers' plans," the judge concluded, "and the related role of [his] employer," the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. An 'extraordinary irony' For Eagleson, the material amounts to "smoking gun evidence" that should not have taken nearly a quarter-century to unearth. "That information never saw the light of day until 25 years later," Eagleson said. "And what was found in those files should blow everyone's mind. Everyone should be outraged." The families presented this new body of evidence in court last year after retrieving it from British authorities, who first gathered it as part of a raid on al-Bayoumi's home in the U.K. just 10 days after the attacks in New York and Washington. The evidence was turned over to the FBI, Eagleson said, but what became of it later remains murky. Crucially, according to attorneys for the families, much of this evidence was not made available to the 9/11 Commission, which released its report in 2004 absolving the Saudi governing of "knowingly" supporting Al Qaeda. Experts suggest this evidence could reshape the public's understanding not only of the attack on Sept. 11, but also the United States' subsequent geopolitical and military decisions in the Middle East. Daniel Benjamin, a counterterrorism official during the Clinton and Obama administrations, said the al-Bayoumi records and other materials "force us to think that our entire theory of what 9-11 was about -- what the whole war on terrorism was about -- was largely mistaken." "The Bush administration insisted that no non-state actor could have done something as complicated as the 9/11 attacks, and that was a major reason that it turned the focus on Iraq and on Saddam Hussein," said Benjamin, now the president of the American Academy in Berlin. "And it is an extraordinary irony that they may have been right about the need for state support -- but they got the state completely wrong." The Saudi lawsuit is far from the last remaining question mark regarding culpability for the attacks. Last week, a military judge ruled that after spending two decades at Guantanamo Bay, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the self-proclaimed "mastermind" of the attack, would finally face trial in June 2028. 'Repeated obstacles' In July, Rep. Malliotakis, the New York Republican, joined Democratic Reps. Dan Goldman and Jerry Nadler in writing a letter to a little-known but powerful advisory panel called the Public Interest Declassification Board, housed within the National Archives, which carries the power to consider requests for sensitive government secrets and make recommendations to the president about whether to declassify them. The lawmakers' request, sent at the behest of the families, bemoaned the "repeated obstacles" attorneys for the families have faced "in obtaining access to these materials from U.S. law enforcement and intelligence agencies." In the letter, lawmakers requested the declassification of "various phone records and analyses directly relevant to al-Bayoumi's role" in 9/11, including records for a cell phone purportedly belonging to al-Bayoumi that he, according to the letter, "lent ... to the hijackers to keep in touch with his associates such as Anwar Aulaqi," the high-profile American al-Qaeda follower who in 2011 was killed by a U.S. drone strike. Attorneys for the families believe those records could help them better understand the timing and nature of al-Bayoumi's and the hijackers' communications and key events in the hijackers' planning of the attacks. The board responded weeks later, writing that it was "actively engaged in interagency consultations to determine what equities, if any, may remain in relation to these records." It urged patience as "those discussions continue." The White House said last week that President Trump would attend a ceremony at the Pentagon to commemorate the 25th anniversary. Vice President JD Vance will travel to New York to be at Ground Zero.

item.title: 9/11 air records released after years of fights against City Hall
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.27
NYC Mayor Mamdani releases thousands of long-sought city documents on 9/11 air quality "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied," the mayor said. For nearly a quarter century, New Yorkers, Ground Zero workers, advocates and elected officials have called on City Hall to reveal the truth about what it knew about the air quality in downtown Manhattan after the 9/11 attacks. On Tuesday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani released tens of thousands of long-guarded city documents related to the air quality that showed how first responders who rushed to the World Trade Center were likely exposed to dangerous toxins. The mayor's office released the first 170,000 pages of records via an online portal. It includes memos from city leaders and agencies going as far back as the Giuliani administration, which ran from 1994 to 2001. Mamdani, who was joined by 9/11 responders and advocates at City Hall, said that New Yorkers needed to know the truth. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," he said. "9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept. 11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. "We are here to release these documents today because for a long time New Yorkers have known the truth, but they have been unable to see the truth in any document presented to them," he added. Among the documents that have been revealed is the "Harding Memo", an October 2001 memo from then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that indicated the city knew of the air quality dangers and the legal liability even through publicly the city declared the air was safe. The memo has been sought by 9/11 victims advocates for decades. Another released document shows the presence of asbestos on the facade ledge of 15 John Street, away from Ground Zero, months after the attacks, in July 2002. In addition to releasing the first throve of city documents, the city announced a settlement of two lawsuits brought by the advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued the city to force publication of the records. Nearly 6,000 people have died of 9/11 related illnesses since the attacks and many are suffering from chronic illnesses, according to the group. Advocacy groups filed several Freedom of Information Act requests for the documents over the years, but it was only last year that 68 boxes of records were found in a city office, according to city officials. "The Daily Show" host Jon Stewart, who has been advocating for health benefits for 9/11 first responders, said at the news conference that many of those victims had to fight for the documents while they were "sick and dying." "I'm not saying the information may have changed the outcomes, unfortunately, for their families, but I guarantee you it would not have been the struggle that it was to get people to recognize what they all knew ... that there was poison in the air," he said. Mamdani declined to directly blame any of his predecessors, saying he would "leave that to New Yorkers," but said, "administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity." The mayor said that the city will continue to use its resources to promote two federal programs established under the Zadroga Act: the World Trade Center Health Program and the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund. They are designed to provide relief to residents and workers who were in downtown Manhattan after the attacks if they experience any related illnesses.

item.title: AI agents are poised to be the next hacking victims, cyber CEO predicts
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 6.81
In a world of AI-enabled cyberattacks , the victims of hacks will no longer just be humans — they'll also be AI agents themselves, Bugcrowd CEO Dave Gerry told Axios. Why it matters: Cyber defenses are tailored toward predicting and defending humans. Now, companies need to start treating the agents roaming their systems as both potential adversaries and the targets. Driving the news: Gerry's prediction during an interview at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last month came after OpenAI disclosed that its agentic system hacked Hugging Face but before the AI lab released its technical deep dive into how its agents carried out that attack. What he's saying: "We're going to see agents as the victim," Gerry told Axios. "You're going to start to see agents getting hacked, not people." The big picture : Gerry's prediction comes as AI labs continue to grapple with the long-tail impact of their agents taking unauthorized actions during pre-deployment security testing. But many of those cases involve AI agents acting in unintended ways, not hacking each other as a way to break into an organization. Zoom in: Gerry fully anticipates that the growing number of hacks against AI agents are going to take place in the enterprise, rather than on consumer-owned and operated agents, since that's where the bulk of AI agents are currently deployed. "It's going to become the No. 1 attack vector that we're going to see," he said. "To make our lives easier as humans, we've given [AI agents] the crown jewels to everything." He noted that many tools that companies have long relied on now also have agents themselves, making it harder to keep track of what's on a company network. "You have all of these enterprise-approved tools that now magically got AI turned on," he said. "Now, there's a backlog of all of this tech debt of things that I approved that I no longer approve." Between the lines: The cybersecurity industry has been trying to raise awareness about securing AI agents' identities for more than a year, warning that AI agents are now the latest example of insider threats. Those insider agents could be leveraged to provide hackers with unfettered access to sensitive systems, exfiltrate data and break into other parts of an organization. "To me, that's inevitable," Gerry said. Zoom out: Even before AI agents started to proliferate in enterprise networks, poor identity controls were one of the top vectors for malicious hackers. Identity-based cyberattacks accounted for 60% of all of Cisco's incident response cases in 2024, for example. The intrigue: Visibility of the actions that AI agents are taking and their chain of thought is becoming more obfuscated as frontier models advance, making it more difficult for security teams to attribute attacks. What we're watching: "It's new attacks. It's moving faster. It's moving at a bigger scale," Gerry said. "But ultimately, this comes back to good cyber hygiene and understanding what exists and how do you put controls around it." Go deeper: AI models are becoming unknowable

item.title: How extreme heat is rewriting the job of state government
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 4.56
As climate change makes extreme heat more frequent and dangerous, states are building systems to manage a hazard they weren't historically built to handle. The big picture: In a growing number of states , officials are appointing heat officers, writing statewide plans, setting worker protections, funding cooling infrastructure, and coordinating responses across agencies. Driving the news: July was the hottest month ever measured in the contiguous U.S., with every Lower 48 state above its 20th-century average. The speed at which states have ramped up their response to extreme heat has been "stunning," V. Kelly Turner, associate director of heat research at the UCLA Luskin Center for Innovation, told Axios. "Heat's everywhere, but it's sort of fallen through the cracks," said Turner, a professor of urban planning at UCLA. "If everyone's responsible, no one's responsible." Part of the problem, she said, is that heat historically hasn't carried the same obvious property damage price tag as disasters such as floods and wildfires, so it can attract less government funding. "Heat's already competing with all these other climate problems, and it doesn't have its own home; it doesn't have its own budget," she said. Context: Massachusetts announced in August that it became the first East Coast state and second in the nation after Arizona to appoint a heat resilience officer. The state has warmed by nearly 3.5°F in the past century. Massachusetts Department of Public Health data shows there were nearly 1,500 heat-related emergency room visits last year. Heat resilience officer Katie Schlick told Axios that 1 in 5 Massachusetts public schools lacks air conditioning. Sending kids home affects their learning, she said. State of play: Arizona's 2024 heat plan created its chief heat officer role to coordinate heat-response efforts across agencies. It also expanded heat-relief resources and deployed mobile solar-powered cooling centers made from shipping containers. Visits to two cooling centers at the Arizona Capitol rose 59% in summer 2025 from a year earlier, according to the state. California has no official with such a title, but Turner said "we do have an office that is dedicated to extreme heat and a dedicated funding program that's putting a lot of money into the hands of communities to work on the problem." California's 2022 Extreme Heat Action Plan established what officials called the state's first "all-of-government framework" for extreme heat. Its updated 2026 plan spans public health, emergency response, housing, infrastructure, energy and worker protections. A separate law will require cities and counties to address extreme heat hazards when they next update certain general plan elements on or after Jan. 1, 2028. Turner said that ultimately means "every single community" will have a clause "that says here's how we're addressing heat." What we're watching: Schlick's initial goals for Massachusetts include reducing heat-related school closures through more cooling, building local heat-planning capacity, creating safer workplaces, and planting more trees. The state has identified "heat equity communities" where less tree cover, shade and green space leave residents particularly exposed, Schlick said. Schlick doesn't know whether she'll have dedicated funding for heat initiatives and expects to draw on broader resilience investments and existing programs and partnerships. She wants to better quantify heat's costs — including lost work and wages, ER visits, and insurance costs — and measure which interventions are cost-effective. The bottom line: "It's very early days in terms of heat governance," Turner said, as states figure out what an effective response looks like. Go deeper: How Phoenix's chief heat officer is combating rising temperatures

item.title: Historic NYT v. OpenAI copyright battle heats up
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 4.18
A landmark copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 moved into a critical new phase Friday, as all three parties presented their official arguments to a judge, with hopes of a favorable ruling ahead of a possible trial. Why it matters: A ruling in favor of the Times could wreak havoc on the lucrative business models underpinning the AI industry. A ruling in favor of OpenAI and Microsoft would serve as a massive blow to the publishing industry, potentially undermining its ability to control and monetize how content is scraped and used by AI giants. Zoom in: In its motion for summary judgment, the Times argued OpenAI and Microsoft copied its works at scale to build commercial substitutes, which it believes violates the law. OpenAI argued existing copyright laws and legal precedents allow tech giants to scrape publicly available works to train their large language models, and that reported facts are not protected by copyright law. It cited studies that suggest outputs to queries via ChatGPT do not create commercial substitutes of the Times' work. Microsoft made similar claims for its Copilot AI product. How it works: In its filing, OpenAI cites two recent California federal court decisions, Kadrey v. Meta and Bartz v. Anthropic, which found using copyrighted works to train AI models constituted as "fair use" in both of those cases because the training was considered transformative. The Times doesn't dispute those findings, but says those cases are different and can't be applied to this suit because those plaintiffs didn't show that AI outputs competed with their products, creating market substitutions for their journalism. The Times also argues that the case, which it filed in a New York federal court, should be evaluated against binding copyright precedents established by higher courts — the Supreme Court and the Second Circuit — rather than those recent lower court rulings. Zoom out: Around the world, the case is being closely watched as a groundbreaking legal precedent that could shape the future of the AI industry. This is especially true for the Trump administration, which has publicly tied its national security and economic goals to the development of AI infrastructure. On Thursday, the Justice Department filed a brief supporting OpenAI in the case, arguing training large language models from millions of digital works delivers a transformative public benefit that offsets any competitive harm to the publishing industry. What to watch: District Judge Sidney Stein is expected to rule in the coming months whether the case, or key portions of it, should move to trial next year. Disclosure: Axios and OpenAI have a licensing and technology agreement that allows OpenAI to access part of Axios' story archives while helping fund the launch of Axios into several local cities and providing some AI tools. Axios has editorial independence.

item.title: America's jobs scare recedes
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.87
The labor market looks considerably healthier than it did at the start of the summer. Why it matters: Friday morning's jobs report recast the last two months as a period of modest job growth rather than of outright deterioration, capped by a gain last month that was more than triple what economists expected. The labor market is weathering the Iran conflict and an AI-driven transformation of the economy with surprisingly little damage, at least for now. For the Federal Reserve, the report puts inflation even more squarely in focus — with less evidence that the labor market is too fragile to hold up in the event of higher interest rates. What they're saying: "August turned the heat back up on the job market," Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao wrote Friday morning. But Zhao noted that "the data has swung hard from month to month, and revisions keep rewriting what we thought we knew, so the underlying trend is tough to read." Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Driving the news: Employers added a surprisingly strong 162,000 jobs in August, the biggest gain since March. The unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.1%. Paired with positive revisions to June and July numbers, the release lifts three-month average job gains to 71,000, from just 20,000. June and July payrolls were revised up by a combined 55,000, a revision that flipped July from a 23,000-job loss to a 21,000-job gain . Between the lines: What looked like a labor market shedding jobs this summer now looks like one that slowed but kept expanding. August's headline was boosted by 42,000 jobs added in local government education, which largely reversed July's decline. That suggests some of the summer's apparent weakness — and August's subsequent rebound — reflected seasonal volatility rather than a sudden shift in labor demand. Zoom in: Bars and restaurants added 59,000 jobs in August, a surprising result considering that the World Cup ended in July and that it seemed plausible there would be a falloff in the sector's employment. Manufacturing added another 16,000 jobs, continuing an upward trend in employment that started late last year. The jobs contraction in the information sector — which includes tech infrastructure, publishing and media jobs — deepened, shedding 23,000 jobs in August and 115,000 over the past year. By the numbers: The unemployment rate held at 4.1% (though the unrounded rate edged up to 4.14% from 4.09%). The details of the household survey were promising. The labor force participation rate rebounded to 61.6%, reversing some of a steep two-month slide in which nearly 1 million people had exited the workforce. Still, participation remains 0.7 point below a year ago. The share of prime-age Americans — those aged between 25 and 54 — with a job held at 80.4% in August, still below its recent high of 80.8% in May. What to watch: August may help clarify whether the recent hiring slowdown reflected fewer workers available or less appetite among employers to hire. About 700,000 people entered the labor force last month and most found work, suggesting that employers were able to absorb a sudden influx of workers. That follows a stretch when a shrinking labor force kept unemployment low, obscuring whether weak hiring reflected limited worker supply or weak labor demand. The risk of a sharp labor market downturn looks considerably smaller than it did a month ago. Still unresolved is whether hiring is accelerating again or simply settling into a slower — though still solid — equilibrium. The solid numbers add ammunition for those Fed officials who see an urgent need to raise interest rates to bring inflation down. The big picture: With the labor market hovering at something near full employment but inflation in its sixth year of exceeding the Fed's 2% target, the decision of whether to raise interest rates in less than two weeks comes down to two key August inflation indicators due out next week. The best that can be said of the robust jobs report is that it affirms the preexisting view of the central bank's leaders that the big question now is around inflation. Nothing in the report would act as a caution flag for those who might seek a rate hike, and indeed the data supports the idea that the job market could even be reaccelerating. "August payrolls were strong across the board, including in cyclical sectors like construction and manufacturing," Sonu Varghese, global macro strategist at Carson Group, wrote in a note. "Add in elevated inflation, and the Fed looks well offsides against an economy that's running hot." Yes, but: The jobs report has often been the most important monthly economic data release for parsing what the Fed will do next. Not now. The August numbers don't so much turn the overall economic narrative as affirm chairman Kevin Warsh's statement in a speech last week that "I believe the labor markets are consistent with full employment." What's next: Next week's releases of the August Producer Price Index on Thursday and the Consumer Price Index on Friday have now taken on greater importance for interest rate decisions. Economists can, by combining elements of the two, come up with a quite accurate estimate of where the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, will land when it is released Sept. 30. The bottom line: The jobs numbers bolstered the case for a rate hike, but next week's inflation numbers are more likely to settle the decision one way or the other.

item.title: AI models are becoming unknowable
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.81
AI models may be getting safer while also getting harder to monitor. Which side of that seesaw prevails could determine whether AI is scaled safely or ruins civilization as we know it. Why it matters: Right now both options are running full steam and no one knows who's in charge of making sure the right one wins. State of play: OpenAI on Thursday released GPT-6 Astra , which president Greg Brockman said could eventually be seen as the start of artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Astra performs better, but it's also better at avoiding monitoring, meaning it could be harder to know what it's thinking or doing. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman separately told Axios this week that models are becoming "superhuman" in some capabilities and that "we are just sailing in unknown waters." Between the lines: The top leaders of AI companies are sounding the alarm on their own technology just as it gets harder to understand a model's actions. OpenAI, Anthropic and more than 100 other companies warned that time is running out to prepare for AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure. Altman told Axios that Congress is struggling to figure out how to regulate such a fast moving technology. "We've been talking to some external organizations about potential concrete standards we could put in place" OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters, adding that OpenAI has also been working to strengthen its own processes. Threat level: While awaiting regulation, AI models are becoming unknowable. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said on a call with reporters that it would continue to get harder to monitor the thoughts of AI models over time. The Information reported this week that the latest OpenAI model used a new technique to boost its performance that may have also made its thoughts less transparent (OpenAI disputes that reporting.) In an analysis of a cyber incident in which an OpenAI model broke into the Hugging Face AI library to get the answers to a benchmark test, one researcher said AI agents generate so much activity that humans can't realistically monitor them without the use of more AI . What they're saying: "This is an even bigger deal than Hugging Face," Sydney Von Arx, an AI Safety researcher and founder of the nonprofit Nightingale told Axios regarding lack of insight into model reasoning. The concern is that, over time, a model's thinking could happen in a hidden layer, which means it could do bad stuff without us knowing. OpenAI says this is not the case with Astra: the model doesn't write out its reasoning as often as prior models do, but that was not done intentionally. Regardless, if models do less thinking out loud some researchers worry their behavior will be harder to monitor. The bottom line: AI is getting sneakier and even the executives driving its growth are asking for help monitoring the risks.

item.title: Anthropic insiders warn AI could kill all humans
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.37
Three Anthropic researchers went public last night with chilling concerns about out-of-control AI , warning it could destroy humans this decade. Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote on X, after resigning Tuesday to sound the alarm: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger." Anthropic alignment-science lead Evan Hubinger responded : "Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to." Samuel Marks, Anthropic scalable-oversight lead, added : "AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes). This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are." Why it matters: They're hardly alone. Their warnings came just days after top OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, said AI is speeding into a scary, uncontrollable phase. Via X Warnings from inside the AI giants point to an epic shared dilemma: Slow down and risk falling behind, or press ahead and risk losing control. The companies are full speed ahead, even as they practically beg for regulation or a global pause, Axios' Maria Curi, Madison Mills and Ina Fried report. The big picture: Calling this unprecedented would be a gross understatement. You basically have the fastest-growing companies in human history warning their products could harm or even destroy humanity. Critics say Anthropic and OpenAI are hyping their products to raise their valuations and invite regulation that would benefit them alone as the dominant incumbents. But we've been talking with dozens of people inside these companies for months, and they've sounded increasingly spooked and concerned. Given they see models not yet released to the public, it seems reckless not to take them seriously. 🏛️ Context for readers from Mike & Jim: This is self-evidently scary stuff — and these vague warnings are impossible to validate or appraise. But we think readers, especially members of Congress and those in relevant federal agencies, need to be aware that the AI creators themselves see potential catastrophic outcomes absent a shift in how America, China and others review and release more powerful AI models. 💡 How to think about this: Nobody is warning AI is an imminent high-level threat. What they're saying is that the technology keeps improving faster than they thought possible and will soon be able to self-improve (recursive self-improvement). Once that happens, it gets even better, faster ... and much harder to predict or control. Go deeper .

item.title: EU tech chief: AI guardrails inevitable for U.S.
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.33
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — The Trump administration used this week's G20 innovation summit to draw a bright line between U.S. and European approaches to AI regulation. The bloc's top tech official says the U.S. is ending up with many of the same guardrails anyway. Why it matters: The U.S. is urging countries to avoid Europe's sweeping approach to AI regulation, but the fight is shifting to which guardrails advanced AI needs and how governments put them in place. What they're saying: European Commission tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Axios that the two sides often end up addressing the same safety concerns, even if U.S. safeguards are starting to emerge through state laws and court cases rather than something broad like the EU AI Act. "We see when it comes to technologies that in the USA the culture is different. So often it's coming via court cases, but often very similar things anyway, very similar concerns." "I don't see that this is so like black and white," Virkkunen said. ChatGPT is officially facing strict rules under the Digital Services Act, for instance, and Virkkunen said it's important for the EU to simplify the bloc's rules and make the region "easier, simpler, faster" for businesses. The big picture: The U.S. hasn't adopted sweeping federal AI rules, but Washington is still shaping how companies develop and deploy advanced models through executive actions, voluntary frameworks, national security restrictions and other policy. Meanwhile, states are moving ahead with varying degrees of AI regulation, and product changes are being forced on companies through lawsuits. Zoom in: The EU is working on a framework for pre-deployment testing and trusted partner access, Virkkunen noted, another area where the EU is working through similar AI policy questions facing the U.S. "So in [the] European Union, we are also working for that blueprint, and we are continuing to discuss also under G7, especially with our partners, how we should work on this topic." The Trump administration has developed a voluntary framework for reviewing some advanced AI models before release, including potentially giving government officials access for up to 30 days. The White House does not plan to publicly release this framework. OpenAI's Sam Altman confirmed this week to Axios that the administration reviewed its Astra model and noted the process is voluntary: "But we of course did it." Industry leaders at the G20 innovation summit knocked the EU approach to regulation in remarks before Virkkunen as well as representatives from Germany, France and Italy. In response to White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios' question about what foreign governments should and should not do, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said an approach that's "relatively free of regulation" is the way to go. It's "pretty straightforward," Musk said. "You have to have an environment that's relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal." "In the EU, for example, we find that the regulation level is extraordinarily high, and things are generally default illegal, and this inhibits progress with new technologies. It slows it down." The bottom line: As AI has grown more powerful, Washington has increasingly gotten involved with model releases.

item.title: The body image battle is real in 2026, but the bodies may not be
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.13
A societal spotlight on extreme thinness is stripping body diversity from screens, just as fashion magazines did in the early aughts, mental health experts tell Axios. The big picture: Fake content creators are introducing unattainable, AI-generated body images that prey on human nature and exacerbate the struggle for many to reach self-acceptance for their bodies. When shrunken celebrities "become the ideal ... because of their status, then the virtual influencers are going to be emulating that," Katy Bruchmann, who leads Santa Clara University's Social Cognition and Comparison Lab, says. "Then, the more really thin, super beautiful virtual influencers you have, the target changes for all the real people again. It's a really scary cycle." Driving the news: Some are posing as influencers selling wellness products or services, while others are sharing body transitions or beauty advice. Axios reviewed dozens of social media posts that include clear AI-generated body transformations or fitness influencers , while online sleuths have uncovered content that appears fake. Zoom in: Some were labeled as AI. Many were not. But research from Brooke Bennett, the director of the Body image, Eating, Access, and Media Lab at the University of Clemson, and her colleagues found that it essentially doesn't matter. Even when people know the image they're viewing is AI, it still hurts their body satisfaction. "I think it's this expectation management piece," Bennett says. "We might... say, 'OK, I know that person's AI, but that doesn't mean that everyone else knows, and people are going to expect me to look like that too.'" Zoom out: The striving for thinness has been fueled by a GLP-1 boom and pushed to extremes with dangerous internet trends. While "SkinnyTok" was banned by TikTok, the messages are still slipping through. Coupled with images of flawless women wearing a size 00, social media can be a body image minefield. "In the clinical space, we're seeing patients coming in really struggling to deal with some of this AI and ... social media pressures in general," Bennett says. Follow the money: Tech and media companies have flooded the zone with a host of cyber stars that are accessible and low-cost . "You can hire an AI influencer for cheap, and they can be in Brazil tonight selling a beverage, and in Tokyo tomorrow selling a T-shirt," Bruchmann says. Our thought bubble: Beyond the completely virtual vixens, it's easier than ever to edit images using AI. I tried it myself, asking ChatGPT to slim me down. I still looked like myself, with no immediate signs that the photo had been altered, like garbled text or extra fingers. The fine print : When organic AI content is posted to Meta products, users can opt in to identify it, or Meta's system may. TikTok "encourage[s]" creators to label content generated or significantly edited by AI. The platform may also label it. But the rules aren't foolproof, and likely AI-generated content still appears unlabeled. Reality check: Zoë Bisbing, founding director of Body-Positive Therapy NYC, tells Axios that body diversity (yes, real bodies) is still online. "It's true — the thin ideal is getting thinner," she says. "At the same time, it's not hard to find size diversity on the street, at the beach and [in] your algorithm." Start simple by searching terms like body acceptance, body positive or body liberation, she says. Go deeper: TikTok glorifies weight loss among teens, young adults: Study

item.title: Scoop: Anthropic whistleblower gave up his equity to leave the company
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 2.68
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job due to concerns about the safety of AI two months before his equity would have vested, he told Axios. Why it matters: The disclosure raises the stakes on Coxon's now mega-viral resignation from the AI lab, which laid out the broad view that the tech could end humanity. What they're saying: "I no longer have anything to gain by juicing up Anthropic's valuation... I left before any of my equity vested," Coxon said in an interview with Axios Wednesday. In his post on X announcing his resignation, which now has over 115 million views, he wrote: " The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt." Other AI researchers, particularly from Google , have resigned over safety. But they did so after years of work, and presumably after their stock vested. Coxon was at Anthropic for just four months, and employees have to be there for six months for their stock to vest, he said. He still has equity in his prior employer, OpenAI. The big picture: Anthropic has traditionally been viewed as more publicly cautious and safety-oriented than other frontier AI labs, making Coxon's departure particularly striking. Coxon said he has not seen Anthropic compromise safety to outlast its competitors, but he is concerned about the future: "If you're under pressure to race, you have to cut corners" or "skip steps in the oversight process," he said. Those concerns can sometimes go too far, he said, describing what "sometimes feels like there's maybe excessive paranoia of OpenAI, excessive paranoia of China" that can help justify pushing ahead. Threat level: As AI models are getting better, faster, they're also becoming harder to monitor. That, combined with the pressure to win on AI, was Coxon's breaking point that led him to quit. What was once science fiction about models knowing they are being tested, for example, is now "just a daily fact of working with these AIs," he said. "They know when they're being tested, and they will think about the fact that they're being tested." "The word doom is kind of silly," he said, adding that serious leaders in the industry are "on record saying they ... expect the potential for human extinction." The danger was evident during the many recent cyber incidents across frontier AI labs, he said. The bottom line: Coxon is one of now several people who have seen AI's peak capabilities up close — and are warning that what they saw could end humanity as we know it.

item.title: U.S. attacks 3 Iranian tankers in tit-for-tat response
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 2.01
U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships, U.S. Central Command said. Why it matters: The strikes continue a tit-for-tat war that just passed the six-month mark . A U.S. official told Axios this week it had a new "tanker-for-tanker" policy approved by President Trump. Driving the news: CENTCOM said it retaliated after a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer evaded missiles fired by Iran. The U.S. attacks "permanently disabled" the M/T Downy and the M/T Stark 1, CENTCOM said in a news release. They also "completely destroyed" the M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman after the crew was warned to abandon ship. CENTCOM posted footage of the strikes on social media. The big picture: On the first day of the war, Trump told Axios he "can go long and take over the whole thing, or end it in two or three days." The next day, he predicted to the Daily Mail the military campaign would "take four weeks — or less." Six months later, the U.S. and Iran are still trading attacks. The latest exchange came a day after Trump called the Iran conflict "small potatoes" and two days after Vice President Vance insisted there was no war and "no active shooting" between the two.
