An Aug. 14–17 Economist/YouGov poll found 65% of Americans want the U.S. to make a deal to end the war as quickly as possible.

item.title: Iran referred to UN Security Council for nuclear non-compliance
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 5.16
- Published The UN nuclear watchdog has referred Iran to the Security Council for "non-compliance" with its obligations under the non-proliferation treaty - the first such move in 20 years. The board of governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) passed a resolution at a meeting in Vienna. It cites a lack of information on Iran's nuclear material such as its stockpile of highly enriched uranium, and the lack of access to nuclear facilities for IAEA inspectors. Tehran condemned the IAEA decision, blaming US and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting inspections. New sanctions are nonetheless unlikely because Iran's allies China and Russia have veto powers in the council. The IAEA resolution - tabled by the UK, France, Germany and the US - was backed by 23 countries, with eight abstentions. China, Russia and Niger voted against. The document , externalasks IAEA chief Rafael Grossi to report Iran to the Security Council. Iran had repeatedly warned the IAEA against passing such a resolution. "They attack Iran's safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal process of verification, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to issue a resolution," Iranian deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi wrote in a post on X. The IAEA has not had access to Iran's nuclear facilities since Israel and the US carried out a number of strikes on those sites during a 12-day conflict in June 2025. The sites were targeted again in the latest war, launched by Israel and the US on 28 February. Iran says the attacks on its facilities, including uranium enrichment plants in Natanz and Fordo, are the reason it does not let IAEA inspectors visit these sites. Tehran also wants such access to be part of a wider settlement with the US and Israel to end the war. Iran has repeatedly stated that its nuclear programme is solely for peaceful purposes. The US, Israel and a number of European countries have questioned this claim, amid concerns that Tehran is trying to build a nuclear weapon. At the start of the latest US-Israel war against Iran, Tehran had roughly 440kg (970lb) of 60% enriched uranium, according to senior US officials. The material can be fairly quickly enriched to the 90% threshold needed for weapons-grade uranium.

item.title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol, motorbikes and other goods
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.96
- Published The US will ban imports of a range of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, some dairy goods and motorbikes, after its neighbour's retaliatory tariffs on American goods came into force. In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said Canada was "discriminating" against the US and outlined the bans, which will begin on 29 September. Officials on both sides have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August. Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's trade minister, said the latest US measures were "unjustified" and that he would work to protect the country's workers, families and businesses. "Our core focus is on what we can control: building strength at home, diversifying our partnerships abroad, and building Canada strong for all Canadians," LeBlanc said. He said he had contacted his US counterpart and promised to work "in good faith" to resolve tensions. Earlier on Tuesday, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that his country's move away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost". The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The two countries have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other. Generally more than two-thirds of Canada's total exports go to the US. In 2025, Canada's exports of alcoholic spirits to the US were worth US$687m (£507m), dairy products were worth $269m and motorbikes were worth $90m, according to UN data compiled by Trading Economics. But Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said the import ban covered just 0.25% of Canada's exports to the US. He said: "Nonetheless, Trump's willingness to impose an import ban is further evidence, if it were needed, that these latest measures are about inflicting economic pain rather than raising revenue." Canada is the second-largest trading partner of the US after Mexico. Its exports are less diversified than those of the US. In recent months, business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall. Last month, the White House imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down. Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as some sporting and fishing equipment businesses. Canada responded with what Carney called "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday. Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting American goods while not doing the same to the same products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday. Some products, like whey and non-alcoholic beer, have been banned from import entirely, while tariffs have been further hiked for others, including for cheeses and cheese substitutes - which were not covered by bans - and for motorboats. The list of Canadian products banned by the White House include: - Some dairy products like whey - Cane molasses - Non-alcoholic beer - A long list of wine, rum and vodka products - Beer made from malt - Motorbikes, including mopeds Those facing higher import taxes include: - Various types of cheese - Raw hides and skins - Paper - Some furniture and mattresses - Some metals, including aluminium and iron - Motorboats - Golf carts - Fishing rod parts and accessories - Switchboards Washington has targeted "significant industries" for Canada, including its politically influential dairy businesses, said economics lecturer Scott French from the University of New South Wales in Australia. Trump has previously argued that Canada's system - which has production quotas, set pricing, and import limits on dairy, eggs, and poultry - is unreasonable to US farmers. The import bans and new tariffs will also put Canada's leaders under more pressure to resist Trump's demands for concessions, French said. The trade war will be "costly for both sides due to the historical level of integration of the North American economy," he said, adding that consumers on both sides will end up as "the biggest losers". On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moved manufacturing there. Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging levies have upset many of the States' traditional allies. Some Canadians have led a massive boycott of US products like alcohol, which have vanished from some store shelves after Trump launched his global tariff campaign last year. Trade expert Deborah Elms, from the Hinrich Foundation, told the BBC the import ban could have a "strong" impact on any Canadian business with US buyers, though early estimates show a "modest impact" affecting around $1bn worth of goods. Canada will likely "hold course for now" and adjust their business support measures to account for the US' latest moves, Elms said. "The bigger question is what it will take for the two sides to sit back down together. The language in these proclamations, as an example, isn't helpful in getting to the negotiating table," she added. Carney said on Tuesday as Canada's counter-tariffs came into effect: "There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still." Tension between the US and Canada has also moved beyond tariffs. In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some in the US.

item.title: LIV files for bankruptcy protection with over $45m owed to players
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.40
- Published LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave. A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, was filed in the United States on Tuesday. The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding. Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m). Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m). The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m). A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts. The court documents show LIV estimates its assets at $100m-$500m (£74m-£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (£370m-£739m). LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future. BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf. Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process. However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours. Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by PIF, with major winners including Rahm and DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money. However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early. LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players to make the new league a reality. DeChambeau said at the conclusion of that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and he believed there was "something fun coming". Speaking on Tuesday before this week's Irish Open, Rahm was tight-lipped when pressed on his future. Asked if he knew what the coming months held, he told BBC Sport: "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis. "There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell." Rahm added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell." The bankruptcy filing was made in the federal district court of New Jersey, where LIV Golf set up a subsidiary earlier in the summer. Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business. PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process. When announcing its decision to withdraw funding, PIF said the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy. Despite its decision to stop bankrolling LIV Golf, PIF added it "remains committed" to its "substantial current and future investments in various sports as a priority sector". On Tuesday, LIV confirmed international investment firm BC Partners as its proposed new investor in a letter to fans outlining its "next phase". "LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality," said the letter. "Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf." O'Neil added in a statement: "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem." In yet another indication the free-spending days of LIV 1.0 are over, the letter said the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model". Players are set to be given equity and individual commercial rights are set to be returned to players, giving them greater earning potential. In terms of prize money, LIV Golf purses are set to be lower than events on the PGA Tour - which has risen in part because of the existence of LIV - but higher than events on the DP World Tour. The letter also outlined proposed changes, with field sizes expanding to 75 players, the introduction of a cut, creating qualifiers and having more teams that "embrace national identities", with the ambitions for teams to "grow into enduring global sports businesses".

item.title: Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.30
- Published Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has attacked energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia with dozens of drones and missiles, injuring 73 people, Saudi authorities say. Tuesday's attacks hit four south-western cities, causing fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said that its forces would respond to the "dangerous escalation". The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi strikes on areas of north-western Yemen that they control. On Monday, they accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of al-Hazm and killing at least 11 people. Twenty inmates are reportedly missing under the rubble. The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the Houthi drone and missile attacks targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, and that women and children were among the injured. An energy ministry statement cited an official source as saying that injuries were also reported after "several energy sector facilities and installations" were targeted. The attacks "caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations," they added. Maliki described Houthi attacks as a "dangerous escalation that confirms the hostile and irresponsible approach of this terrorist militia" and said the Saudi-led coalition would "take all necessary operational measures to deter" the group. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea accused the Saudi military of carrying out more than 120 air strikes on the Yemeni provinces of Marib, al-Bayda, Hudaydah, Taiz and Jawf over the past three days, and of committing "grave crimes". He said the Houthis had responded to this "brutal aggression" with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones", which he claimed caused "significant damage". A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. There has been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The fighting has reportedly left more than 300 people dead and displaced 18,500. The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

item.title: Four Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.16
- Published Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France. Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said. The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight. One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen. CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said. The alarm went off at 05:48 (03:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms. He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed". They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added. Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects. The mayor said that two paintings were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered. The two paintings that are still missing are: - Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) - Jeune fille au puits (1886) And the two pieces that were recovered are: - Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895) - Coco Lisant (1905) "Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," the mayor told reporters at the museum. "It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you cannot sell it like that," he said. The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks. Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters. Last month, four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily. "Beyond Cagnes-sur-Mer, this incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art," the local French mayor warned. Masson called on the French government to provide more financial support to local areas and museums to protect artwork from "increasingly organised and determined criminals".

item.title: Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.17
- Published A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of carrying out a spate of sabotage attacks on Germany's electricity grid after spending several days on the run. The suspect was carrying explosives when he was detained near the Weisweiler power plant in western Germany on Tuesday, police in Cologne said. A tent in nearby undergrowth was also found to be rigged with further explosives, they added. The suspect, named by German media as Daniel V, is believed to have written letters claiming responsibility for the attacks, which have taken place in Brandenburg and Saxony in the east as well North Rhine-Westphalia in the west. Police said explosives found during the arrest were being examined by a bomb disposal expert, while officers were checking to see if any undiscovered devices had been set up in the surrounding area. Prior to the suspect's arrest on Tuesday, police said they had found several launch devices on high-voltage lines near the Weisweiler plant on Monday afternoon, alongside "another confession letter". A series of incidents across the grid in the last week have followed a similar pattern, with rockets used to shoot wires across high-voltage cables in order to cause short circuits. The attacks have led to power-generating units at some plants being temporarily taken off the grid. A statement from the Cologne Public Prosecutor's Office and Cologne Police on Tuesday did not provide further details on the suspect, or on the number and whereabouts of incidents he has been linked to. German media have previously reported receiving two letters from the suspect claiming responsibility for the attacks. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said the handwritten letters contained information that had not yet been made public. The letters were apparently signed with the first name Daniel, while his surname was kept anonymous, in line with German privacy rules. The letters also gave a residential address in the town of Gevelsberg. Cologne Police had previously said it was searching for a 48-year-old suspect from the town in connection with the sabotage of electrical substations in three German states. Investigators had also said explosives were found during a search of the suspect's apartment. In Saxony alone, police found 21 devices near high-voltage power lines last Friday and Saturday. Interior Minister Armin Schuster has admitted it could have led to a regional blackout, but he has warned against jumping to conclusions. "The way this deed was committed makes this case unusual, as well as the manner of the confession," he said.

item.title: Asbestos 'nearly everywhere' after 9/11 - new documents reveal air-quality concerns
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.81
- Published Toxic air quality was being recorded in Manhattan soon after the 9/11 attacks even as officials played down health risks to the public, according to a trove of newly released files. Asbestos was found "nearly everywhere" tested near Ground Zero, where the World Trade Center towers collapsed in 2001, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," he said, announcing the release of 170,000 documents related to the attacks. Illnesses related to the dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have claimed more lives than the nearly 3,000 who died in the attacks, US health officials say. Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants after the Twin Towers collapsed. Speaking alongside Mamdani at Tuesday's news conference, TV host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart said the new files show the city knew by October 2001 - a month after the terrorist attacks - that the air in Manhattan was toxic. "So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically. The records show asbestos was found near Ground Zero for months after the attacks at the same time people were being advised it was safe to go there. The files, which include air-quality reports and communications among city officials, include October 2001 correspondence known as the "Harding Memo". In it, an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks. The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)". City officials also told citizens to clean up dust and debris with "wet mops and rags" despite the presence of asbestos, which is only supposed to be cleaned by licensed professionals, according to another memo documenting the concerns of congressman Jerry Nadler. The memo pointed to testimony from the city's top health official at the time saying a study had found "no elevated levels of asbestos in indoor air", but that tests showed dust had "low levels of asbestos in some samples". The memo, attributed to Ester Fuchs, a special adviser at the time to Mayor Michael Bloomberg, acknowledged "potential problems for City Hall". Days after the attack, city and federal officials - including the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) - declared that the air near the Twin Towers was safe. Christine Todd Whitman, the head of the EPA at the time, later apologised for this declaration, saying the agency "did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had". Tuesday's release of documents resolves a lawsuit brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued after officials said they did not have the records. City officials found 68 boxes of documents last year. The pages of air quality reports and other records were released through an online portal timed for this Friday's 25th anniversary of the attacks. More documents are to be shared over the next year. Karen Klingon, who was involved in the 9/11 Health Watch lawsuit, told the BBC on Tuesday her brother lived five minutes away from Ground Zero. He developed asthma, was later diagnosed with cancer and died at 61 of a related brain tumor. "There's a lot of research, probably, that can be done about what was in the air, and the kind of illnesses that derived of those toxins that were in the air, like what happened to my brother," she said. "Hopefully it helps people that were sick know and in the future." Phil Alvarez, whose brother Luis Alvarez died of cancer in 2019 after exposure to Ground Zero toxins, told the BBC that people "continue to get sick every single day, continue to die".

item.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations worsen
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.20
- Published Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities. "This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details. Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor Orbán for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance. The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful". Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow from the moment his Tisza party was elected in April. He and the foreign minister have both called on Russia to bring an end to the war in Ukraine. In May Anita Orbán summoned the Russian ambassador to protest against a big drone attack on the Transcarpathia region of Ukraine that is home to a large Hungarian minority. Commentators have pointed out that her predecessor had not summoned the ambassador since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion in 2022. Then last month Magyar formally broke with the previous Fidesz government's policies, with new guidelines spelling out that Russia's conduct in Ukraine "poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger". Russia's Ambassador to Budapest, Evgeny Stanislavov, reacted bitterly to Anita Orbán's intention to continue "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules". Budapest's promise of pragmatic co-operation was worth absolutely nothing, he complained, adding that Hungary's "extremely unfriendly step constitutes an unprecedented and ungrounded escalation". Before Magyar was voted into office, Hungary had for years insisted on maintaining close relations with Moscow, partly citing cheap Russian oil imports. Viktor Orbán objected to the EU's supply of aid to Ukraine and repeatedly delayed packages of sanctions on Russia. Ahead of the April elections, independent Russian investigative website Agentsvo reported that 15 of the 47 Russian embassy staff in Budapest were linked to Russian intelligence agencies and six more might be linked. Former Hungarian foreign intelligence deputy head András Telkes told the BBC that even though "Russian spying activity" had been investigated before the election, the Fidesz government had prevented any action being taken. The Russian embassy in Budapest had also rejected as false a report alleging that three Russian military intelligence officers had travelled to Budapest to influence the Hungarian vote. Russia has routinely denied its embassies are used for espionage. However, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled across Europe since 2022, and Russia has responded in kind. Telkes told the BBC that the big question now was how Moscow would respond: "If 10 Hungarian diplomats were to be expelled from Moscow, in a tit-for-tat move, that would effectively close the Hungarian embassy there."

item.title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.10
- Published Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned. Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said. MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action. The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance. MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance. According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year. "War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan. "MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours." This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment. "After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years. Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year. In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said. According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing. It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June. As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city. In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10. According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children. "If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said. At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said. In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide. According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger". The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war. Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.

item.title: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar says ChatGPT's ads should be like 'if Google and Meta had a baby'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 6.54
Congratulations to Google and Meta — they're expecting. OpenAI's chief financial officer, Sarah Friar, was describing her company's ads ambitions on Tuesday when she said that ChatGPT is like "if Google and Meta had a baby." Friar made the remarks before a full room of investors and analysts at Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference in San Francisco. The comment succinctly outlines OpenAI's ambition to turn ChatGPT into a money-printing ads platform, following in the footsteps of its tech giant predecessors. In just seven months of placing ads on the chatbot, OpenAI's ads business is now raking in cash at a rate that Friar said would equal $1 billion in revenue if mapped across a full year. She attributed the "baby" idea to Fidji Simo, the former OpenAI executive who stepped down this year from her role running the company's commercial operations. Friar went on to explain that she thinks ChatGPT can use the data it learns from its users to bring the "intent" of a Google search together with the "context" that Meta has on its social media users. "It's high intent search, you're telling a lot, but with the context — it's not quite people like me, it's me, because it has all the memory of me," Friar said. "So when you put those two things together, the ability to have a really potent ad platform is clearly there." Right now, OpenAI serves basic ads underneath ChatGPT's responses if a user is on the free or Go subscription tiers. Friar expects a more complex, more tailored format in the future. She said her team has shown her "early indications" of what a more AI-native ad format could look like as they develop the platform's basics and scale its availability. "This is all before we've really launched a format that feels truly endemic to AI," Friar said. "That's what I get super excited about." OpenAI's focus on advertising marks a full 180 since 2024, when CEO Sam Altman said he found the idea of combining ads and AI "uniquely unsettling." The ambitions are a break from rival Anthropic, which has skewered the idea of ads in chatbot responses. Each of the companies is preparing to go public in highly anticipated IPOs that will test Wall Street's appetite for AI and serve as referendums on the strength of the companies' finances. Both companies filed their confidential S-1 prospectuses in June, and Anthropic's public version is expected in the coming weeks. OpenAI has not disclosed a specific timeline, but Friar has previously said that the listing will happen by the end of 2027. OpenAI was last valued at a $852 billion in a March fundraise that injected $122 billion into its coffers. The company is trying to parlay that cash, its 1 billion-user ChatGPT app, and its status on the frontier of AI research into a sustainable business. Friar has to balance OpenAI's growing consumer and enterprise businesses with the AI lab's vast expenses on AI inference, data center construction, and research. Friar steered Square through its 2015 IPO as the company's CFO and was Nextdoor's CEO during its transition to the public markets via a 2021 SPAC. Have a tip? item.title: A new TSA program means you can get through security without a plane ticket at some airports
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 6.06
Saying goodbye to a friend who's flying to a new country, or maybe you just really want to do some shopping in an airport terminal? Well, now you can go through security without an airline ticket as the Transportation Security Administration has launched a program called Gateside. Members of TSA PreCheck and other trusted-traveler programs can apply for a Gateside pass at 13 airports across the US, including three of the 10 busiest in the country — Dallas Fort Worth, LAX, and Las Vegas Harry Reid. The TSA says the program is expected to roll out to more airports in the coming months. It added that availability may be limited during peak times, and Gateside visitors are held to the same airport code of conduct rules as ticketed passengers. Saying goodbye or welcoming your loved ones at the gate While airlines occasionally issue gate passes — such as when accompanying a traveling minor — Gateside lets people past security for a variety of reasons. The TSA listed examples like "joining a friend with a long layover for a meal, meeting with a business associate or employee, or visiting dining and retail establishments in the airport." Also, unlike a traditional gatepass, you could use the expedited PreCheck security lanes. Children can also pass through security as visitors on a Gateside pass. Gateside is free, and the TSA says you should apply between one and three days before your planned visit. If approved, you wouldn't get a digital or physical pass. Instead, you would show a TSA officer your ID and the portal dashboard on your mobile device, which shows your approved Gateside status. Passes are valid for one calendar day and allow for re-entry on that date. Here's the full list of airports currently taking part: - Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Little Rock, Arkansas. - Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) in Texas. - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) in Michigan. - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Omaha, Nebraska. - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas, Nevada. - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) in Indiana. - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) in Ohio. - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in California. - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona. - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) in Utah. - San Diego International Airport (SAN) in California. - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas. - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma.

item.title: It's not your imagination: Streaming services are showing you more ads this year
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.33
If you feel like you're watching commercials with TV in between — instead of the other way around — you're not alone. Streaming advertising loads have increased this year as consumers flock to cheaper, ad-supported plans in the face of steady streamflation. Ad minutes per hour rose 18% on top streamers in the US from January to August, according to data from entertainment research firm Ampere Analysis shared exclusively with Business Insider. "Everyone is trying to squeeze more value out of existing subscribers, because it's become so much harder and so much more expensive, in terms of cost of customer acquisition, to keep growing," said Brandon Katz, an analyst at entertainment data firm Greenlight Analytics. Ad loads have increased on all but one of the streamers in Ampere's analysis. Of the nine most-viewed streaming services, as measured by Nielsen's US ratings, only Prime Video showed users fewer minutes of ads per hour last month than it did at the start of the year, Ampere found. Streamers showed audiences just over five minutes of ads per hour on average in August, according to Ampere. (The research firm said it changed how it tracks ad loads at the start of this year, which makes comparisons to prior years difficult.) Netflix had the biggest ad load increase from January to August, though it still shows the fewest ads per hour of any major streamer at less than 2.5 minutes per hour. By contrast, Paramount+ shows the most ads per hour on average, Ampere found. It's showing 9 minutes of ads per hour, which means fans of Taylor Sheridan shows like "Landman" are spending about 15% of their viewing time watching commercials. Disney's streamers are next on the list, showing between 7.5 and 8.5 minutes per hour across Disney+ and Hulu, respectively. There isn't a significant correlation between streamers' ad-tier price and average ad loads, Business Insider found. Ad-vancing streaming profits The additional ads that audiences are seeing on streamers come amid a profit push among Hollywood giants. "Management teams are now being pushed by investors to show how they will capture the largest possible share of streaming retail value and advertising revenue, at the highest defensible long-term margin," Hernan Lopez, the founder of media consultancy Owl & Co., wrote in an early September report. Every major streaming service has raised prices in the past 12 months in hopes of getting subscribers to either pay more or trade down to an ad plan. Streamers with scaled ad businesses can charge higher rates to advertisers than those with few users. And although ad-supported plans cost less, they can generate more revenue per user than pricier tiers. "Once you reach scale, ad-supported tiers are more lucrative than ad-free tiers," Katz said. About 11% of subscribers to ad-supported streamers as of the first quarter had switched from more expensive ad-free plans, according to subscription data firm Antenna, up from 7% in 2024. Ad-supported streamers, including free services, have become increasingly popular as paid services continue to hike prices. Ad plans generated 4 million net sign-ups in the first quarter, while ad-free plans actually had more cancellations than sign-ups, according to Antenna. Nearly 60% of streaming users pick ad plans when signing up, the firm found. Consumers are "more than willing to tolerate ads" if they can watch their favorite shows for less, said Mike Proulx, a research director at Forrester. As streamers have raised prices, TV fans have gone from primarily having ad-free services to mixing in ad-tier subscriptions. "They're balancing out their streaming portfolio," Proulx said.

item.title: Anthropic posted, then swiftly deleted, a $450,000 sales job aimed at its 'mega' customer Meta
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.96
Anthropic posted — and then deleted — a job listing for a salesperson tasked with selling to Meta, its AI rival and one of its largest customers. The listing, titled "Mega Account Executive, Meta," appeared on Anthropic's job board at a delicate moment for the companies' relationship. Meta still spends hundreds of millions of dollars a month as Anthropic's customer, according to a recent New York Times report. But it's also trying to reduce its reliance on Anthropic's AI tools as Anthropic is shoring up its finances ahead of a massive initial public offering. The post suggests Anthropic is betting Meta will remain a major customer even as Meta builds more capable AI models of its own. After Business Insider asked Anthropic about the listing on Wednesday, the company pulled it down. Anthropic and Meta declined to comment. Anthropic's job posting offered an annual salary of $380,000 to $450,000, and didn't mention Meta outside the title. It said the salesperson would "win new business and drive revenue within a book of strategic digital native accounts." The listing stands out for its specificity. Other Anthropic account executive openings target broad regions or sectors, including startups in Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa, or the public sector in Southeast Asia. Anthropic's AI coding tool, Claude Code, became popular across Silicon Valley, including at Meta, this year. One internal projection said Meta could spend $10 billion annually on Anthropic, the Times reported. Meta's head of AI product, Nat Friedman, told employees that if Meta decreased its reliance on Anthropic's tools, it could hit Anthropic's revenue as it approaches its IPO, the report said. item.title: Job seekers are learning a new interview skill: how to sound excited about AI
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.79
College students might think twice before telling their professors how much they use AI. But in a job interview, the incentives can flip: Suddenly, having an AI story to tell is something to brag about. But what if you don't have much experience with AI — or simply aren't sold on it? Felisha Case was laid off as a program manager at LinkedIn in May. Now, she's regularly asked during job interviews how she used AI in her previous role. Case said she has limited experience to draw on because LinkedIn only pushed employees to really adopt the technology soon before she left. "It can feel like we're being asked to go back and get a whole new education in AI," she said. As employers embrace AI and look for workers with experience using it, some job seekers say they're feeling pressure to demonstrate enthusiasm for the technology — even when they have reservations about its limitations and societal impacts. They're learning AI tools in order to have examples to discuss in interviews, playing up their interest in the technology, and trying to read the room to figure out just how much enthusiasm prospective employers want to hear. AI skills are appearing in more job postings, and some of the companies investing most heavily in the technology are also adding the most workers. A recent study by Ramp and Revelio Labs found that companies making the biggest investments in AI tended to see more employment growth than companies with smaller or no AI adoption How enthusiastic about AI do you need to be? A Big Tech employee currently looking for a new job said AI tools have helped him with small coding tasks and reviewing documents, but he's skeptical of the broader hype around the technology. "If it all magically disappeared tomorrow I wouldn't shed a tear," he said. Nevertheless, he believes AI roles are "where the money is" and where much of the tech industry seems to be headed, so he's applied for several of them. He believes his AI skepticism may have worked against him during one interview, where he couldn't feign enthusiasm for a company he thought had an outlandish AI strategy. But if he were more desperate for work, he might have tried harder to do so. "I do have a bit of luxury in that right now I'm job hunting while currently employed, so I don't feel such overwhelming pressure to conform too much," he said. Unemployed job seekers don't always have that luxury. Cristina Estupiñán, a laid-off software developer, previously told Business Insider that she felt pressure to sound enthusiastic about AI during job interviews, despite her concerns about its environmental and social impact, and its use in workplace surveillance. "I have to make up something about what excites me about AI because, frankly, nothing really excites me about AI," she said. Kareem Osman, a vice president at staffing firm Robert Half, previously told Business Insider that hiring managers want to understand how candidates have used AI, including examples of how they used it to overcome challenges or streamline processes. He added that many employers are interested in candidates who can use AI without relying on it entirely, and that asking about a company's approach to AI during an interview can signal curiosity about where the business is headed. "Employers are really trying to see individuals that are adaptable, that are embracing new technologies," Osman said. Job seekers are learning to read the room on AI Figuring out what employers want to hear about AI can also mean keeping tabs on how the broader conversation around the technology is changing. A former communications professional at a Big Tech firm said most companies he interviews with want to know how he can use AI tools for PR roles, so he's experimented with the technology, including ways to use AI to track media coverage and sentiment. "Leadership everywhere seems to think AI is the magic bullet for everything," he said. "It's important to be able to speak like an AI native and dazzle the right folks." In recent months, however, he's noticed growing concerns about the cost of AI and overuse of the technology. So he's tried to change his tune accordingly during interviews, focusing more on identifying where the tools are most useful. Of course, job seekers can't share their thoughts on AI if the subject never comes up. Former Microsoft employee Mody Khan said he earned a certificate in AI and machine learning in hopes of adapting to a changing tech industry. He added it to his résumé, but said interviewers haven't shown much interest in it. Aaron Laniewicz, who's been looking for work after being laid off from his consulting job, believes AI can make someone dramatically more productive if used correctly. But AI doesn't always come up in his interviews. "If they don't mention it, I ask if the position or company supports AI tools such as Claude Code," he said. You can be skeptical of AI — to a point Job seekers don't necessarily need to love AI to discuss it effectively during interviews. Hiring experts interviewed by Business Insider's Madison Hoff and Tim Paradis said candidates can be honest about their reservations while focusing on ways they're comfortable using the technology. Josh Bersin, an HR analyst and consultant, said many companies are still assessing how to best use the technology, so it might be helpful to ask questions about their approaches rather than write them off. But if you tell a recruiter you don't believe in AI, "you may have just lost your opportunity to get a job there," he said. Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at jzinkula@businessinsider.com, or via Signal at jzinkula.29.

item.title: Your old company might want to hire you back
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.30
When Ahmed Mousa wanted to return to the tech firm Deel, he texted CEO Alex Bouaziz a selfie of the two of them with another colleague. "hey! ready and fully committed. when can we recreate this photo?" Mousa wrote to Bouaziz. The cofounder quickly replied, writing in part: "Which team" Roughly 48 hours after that exchange, Mousa, who'd spent about five years at the HR and payroll platform, was talking with a Deel recruiter about the details of his return, nearly four months after he left. He had become a "boomerang" employee. Mousa is not alone. Rehires at Deel more than doubled between 2024 and 2026, the company said. Nationally, 3.4% of new hires in the US were boomerangs by the end of 2025, up from 3.1% two years earlier, according to the latest figures from Revelio Labs, which analyzes employment data. Why some companies want their exes back Finding a job remains tough for many desk workers. Returning to a former employer can offer an advantage: Job seekers already have a history and connections inside the organization. That inside track can be particularly helpful at a company like Deel, which has more than 7,000 employees globally and said it drew 1.3 million job applicants in 2025. The fully remote company projects it will hit 2 million applicants this year. Despite that huge applicant pool, Bouaziz said former employees who were strong performers and left on good terms can be obvious candidates. "They understand the company," he said. "They have the right relationship inside of the company to make some things happen faster." Those workers can also tell Deel why they left and whether the company could make changes to address any issues, Bouaziz said. Not everyone gets a return ticket While many CEOs see value in boomerang employees, they aren't necessarily eager to welcome back anyone who knocks. "What I don't like are job-bouncers," said Fred Voccola, the chairman and CEO of AI software company Simpro Group. Still, he said he's happy to rehire someone who behaved honorably and didn't try to "burn the house down when they left." Simpro Group and Deel aren't the only companies that have made a point of welcoming back former workers. In 2023, Salesforce wooed former employees by handing out stuffed animals wearing T-shirts featuring a boomerang image. That same year, CEO Marc Benioff gave a shout-out to returning workers for helping the company achieve its profit-margin goals sooner than expected. Voccola said people sometimes leave because "the company just can't offer the person what they need for their career." He sees a potential long-term payoff in letting good employees leave, and then circling back. "They're going to go somewhere else, learn some new skills, and you'll be damn sure I'm calling them in a year to come back," Voccola said. "That's the way you build lasting companies." Bouaziz draws lines, too. Someone who left Deel after only a few months or went straight to a competitor might have a harder time returning. "Obviously, we cannot take back everyone. We tend to focus on the highest performers," Bouaziz said. The path back can be harder for former employees who didn't leave by choice. Bouaziz said he's received dozens of messages over the years from people who'd been fired for poor performance or other reasons and wanted another chance. He typically passes those requests along to hiring managers. While a rehire is unlikely, Bouaziz said their willingness to ask is a positive sign about Deel's culture. An added benefit of boomerangs Bouaziz said boomerangs can influence how employees who never left feel about the company. Employees sometimes ask returning colleagues why they came back, he said, and hearing their answers can reinforce their own decision to stay. "Sometimes you don't know what you're missing unless you don't have it anymore," Bouaziz said. Mousa, 34, wasn't looking to leave Deel when a startup that had courted him for months made a compelling offer. He had friends there and could earn far more — an important consideration as the father of two young children. "It felt irresponsible not to go take a look," he said. After a couple of months, Mousa left the startup and completed work trials at a few other companies, though nothing felt right. Eventually, he started thinking about returning to Deel, where his brother also works. For a couple of days, he couldn't bring himself to ask because he felt embarrassed. Then Mousa fired off the selfie to Bouaziz. Mousa's wife, meanwhile, wasn't surprised by the whole episode. When he left Deel, he said she told him, "You know you're going to go back, right?"

item.title: 'There's no accountability': AI startups keep claiming huge revenue. VCs say the math is getting 'murky.'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.60
Few metrics thrill Silicon Valley investors more than surging annual recurring revenue (ARR). In the AI boom, however, VCs are increasingly skeptical of what that number actually represents. "The amount of VC-backed AI companies lying about their ARR publicly is absolutely unsettling," Greg Isenberg, CEO of Late Checkout, wrote in a post that went viral for saying something out loud that has been whispered about, but rarely said publicly in tech circles. ARR was a metric that came into vogue during the software era, intended to estimate the yearly sales a company can expect from paying customers, a quick way for investors to judge a startup's valuation. Now, venture capitalists and founders who spoke with Business Insider said ARR has become so loosely used that it can blur the line between contracted subscriptions, future deals, token consumption, hardware sales, and a single strong month of revenue. In short, recurring revenue is often not recurring. "It's ARR inflation," said Shruti Gandhi, a general partner at Array Ventures. "There's no accountability right now." Gandhi says she has called out founders for exaggerating revenue. Their defense: "Everybody else is doing it." To Alexander Niehenke, a partner at Scale Venture Partners, the current trend of padding ARR reflects a top-of-the-bubble mentality when founders have all the leverage. "It feels like we're at the tail end of 2021 again, given some of the behavior I'm seeing in the venture ecosystem," he said. "Anytime you get deeper into a bull cycle, everybody has more tolerance for risk." Founders know how excited VCs get about ARR, according to Niehenke. "The smart and brilliant entrepreneurs use it like catnip on us," he said. Cluely CEO Roy Lee raised eyebrows earlier this year when he admitted to misstating his startup's ARR to a TechCrunch reporter. But that was very much the exception. With startups under much less regulatory scrutiny than public companies, revenue claims are rarely verified. it’s genuinely crazy tech has so isolated itself from regulatory forces that you can just admit to securities violations on the internet — Will Manidis (@WillManidis) March 5, 2026 More startups are using run rate, but is it better? Before AI, Silicon Valley was in love with software-as-a-service companies, where ARR was much more dependable. SaaS companies like Salesforce or Workday often sell annual or multiyear deals, making it fairly straightforward to tally the value of subscriptions likely to recur. "When you have ARR, you have a signed contract, and you know what you've signed up for for the year," said Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo Ventures. AI has proven less predictable. Many AI companies no longer sell a simple per-seat license that costs the same every month. They charge customers based on how much they use, often measured in tokens. Someone may use a product aggressively, then pull back, or switch to a cheaper model. The startup's own costs vary widely, too, because it may have to pay a model provider or cloud company every time a customer uses its product. AI startups have increasingly shifted to describing run rate, which extrapolates a month of revenue over a full year and does not purport to be recurring, according to Murphy. "Venture does this from time to time, which is that there's a new metric that shows up," he said. Pocket, which makes an AI recording device, is one of those companies, having recently said it crossed the $100 million run rate threshold. Founder Akshay Narisetti said he avoids ARR because tokens make revenue too unpredictable to expect it to be recurring. Run rate can come with its own problem in that a gangbusters month does not necessarily translate to a year, but Narisetti said he avoids doing that. "We never annualize one large month with a spike," Narisetti said. The biggest AI labs have used both metrics. OpenAI has described subscription sales as ARR while calling its newer advertising business an annualized revenue run rate. Anthropic has generally described its overall sales as run-rate revenue. Linear, which is an increasingly rare breed of SaaS startups, recently said it crossed $100 million in ARR. Cofounder and CEO Karri Saarinen said he stands by the metric because Linear sells multiyear contracts and has been in business since 2019. "Since we've been operating longer, we can better forecast the actual ARR," he said, adding that for newer AI startups, it is a different story. "It's gotten really murky," he said.

item.title: We searched for New York's best-dressed lawyers. These 9 stood out.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.29
Law has a dress code. A navy suit is safe. Black is safer. Shoes should be sensible. The message is clear: Blend in. Never give the jury something to talk about. But a new class of lawyers is finding room for a little more zhuzh. Men are badging into Hudson Yards office towers in vintage sport coats and baseball caps. Women are power suiting in Celine pumps. Even jeans have made their way into firms that once treated them like contraband. The softening of the dress code comes at a moment when lawyers are being forced to think harder about what, exactly, makes them indispensable. Artificial intelligence can already draft briefs, research case law, and dig through piles of documents. Yet, software cannot earn a client's trust. It cannot read a room or persuade a judge. Law is still a people business. And at a time when attorneys are being asked to defend the value only they can provide, some lawyers tell us that personal style is more than self-expression. It is part of how they show clients they are worth their hourly rate. Business Insider asked readers and law firms to nominate New York's best-dressed lawyers. Our judging panel included Business Insider's editor in chief of Life, Joi-Marie McKenzie, fashion editor Leah Faye Cooper, who's worked as digital style director for Vogue, and Roberto Concepción Jr., a former Hearst lawyer, who's now an employee relations senior leader at Instacart. They reviewed 46 nominations and whittled the list down to nine honorees. We then invited the lawyers into our newsroom for a photo shoot and interviews about why they wear what they wear. Vanessa Ajagu, Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP Vanessa Ajagu likes her clothes loud. "Nothing feeds me more than a compliment about my outfit," she says. For the Gibson Dunn litigator, Nigerian designers fit the brief. She flies home for the holidays with an empty suitcase and returns with it full of vintage pieces and demi-couture suits from Ohlanna bu Zikora, whose founder won the top prize on Nigeria's version of "Project Runway." For the office, Ajagu builds an outfit around one anchor piece, then adds a printed scarf, statement earrings, or a dash of color. In court, she turns the volume down with a plain black suit so her outfit doesn't become the conversation. "The client comes first," she says. Her hair finishes the look. Ajagu has worn cornrows tipped with beads, blonde braids, and more traditional designs, pushing back on old ideas about what Black hair is supposed to look like in a corporate setting. When her students at Columbia Law School, where she teaches legal writing, ask, "You get to wear that to work?" she answers: "Hell yeah, I wear it to work." Judge's note: "The way Vanessa blends Nigerian and Western fashion is to be admired. And while many think of beauty as an afterthought, it's clear from her hairstyles that she thinks about a look from head to toe." — Joi-Marie McKenzie William A. Brewer III, Brewer, Attorneys & Counselors William A. Brewer III dresses the way Hollywood has trained us to picture a powerful litigator. "I'm probably going to be in a suit unless we've declared it a snow day," he says. Brewer's suits are made by tailors at Oxxford Clothes and Zegna, whose soft shoulders and relaxed drape keep his wardrobe from feeling too stiff. For his shirts, he's relied for 15 years on Bruce Cameron Clark, the English tailor with a Savile Row pedigree and a client list that includes Ringo Starr and Elton John. Brewer also knows how to dress down, preferring tennis whites for a match in the Hamptons and Ralph Lauren jeans for an evening affair. That old-school polish has become a house style at Brewer, Attorneys & Counselors, a firm built for high-stakes commercial fights. Last Christmas, Brewer says he worked with longtime contacts at Ralph Lauren to source more than a dozen vintage watches for his leadership team. "You give somebody a timepiece, you're telling them their time is now," he says. Judge's note: "William's style shines in the details: the tailoring, the ties, and even the watches. He stood out to me, however, for how he can expertly move from a traditional suit to a casual look without feeling like he's trying too hard. He just gets it." — Joi-Marie McKenzie Shermin Lakha, Lvlup Legal Shermin Lakha has heard the joke before: She's the lawyer in the crop top. Dressing like herself is more than an aesthetic choice. Lakha left Freshfields and built a law firm for startups, brands, and content creators, many of whom wanted a lawyer they could actually call. Being personable, she says, has been central to growing Lvlup Legal. Her clients span influencer Serena Kerrigan and beauty tastemaker Violet Grey. "I want to change the perception that in order to be a professional woman or be considered serious, you have to look a certain way," she says. "I dress the way I want." Her tailoring comes with more attitude than the typical corporate-law uniform: a nipped-waist pinstripe jacket from Club L London, or a green sequined suit with a jacket that skims the bottom of her ribcage, paired with an Hermès Birkin bag. Judge's note: "Her style is globally inspired yet unmistakably her own. Her look is both worldly and authentic, demonstrating that great style is a balance between inspiration and individuality." — Roberto Concepción Jr. Alec Soghomonian, Boies Schiller Flexner LLP Alec Soghomonian, a fourth-year lawyer at Boies Schiller Flexner, loves the hunt. His favorite tie is a vintage Polo Ralph Lauren in silk, snagged on eBay for $31. On weekends, he digs through racks at Alfargo's Marketplace, a New York gathering for vintage menswear obsessives, in search of sport coats and sweaters. "You don't need money to dress well," he says. "But you do need time." Soghomonian, who represents plaintiffs in class actions, became a student of menswear in law school when he began following Derek Guy, the voluble writer who lays waste to the ruling class's suits on X. He came to think of style as a language: learn the grammar first, then figure out where you can bend it. At BSF, where the dress code skews casual, that might mean pairing a baseball cap with a relaxed suit or wearing jeans cut to sit neatly beneath a tailored jacket. Judge's note: "This isn't so obvious, but Alec knows exactly which proportions suit him, and that lends itself to most things looking great. He mentioned being a fan of the 1980s (same), and I think it's great that he leans into that, despite how polarizing the decade's fashion can be. He looks like himself, and that's the true mark of great style." — Leah Faye Cooper Elena Fast, The Fast Law Firm Elena Fast's dress code has an unusual requirement: Be ready for federal court at all times. Clients get arrested, and hearings materialize in the middle of the day. The criminal defense attorney has built a wardrobe fit for a millennial Elle Woods, if the "Legally Blonde" heroine traded pink for a creamy crepe-knit jacket paired with Manolo Blahnik pumps. Fast cares about keeping luxury under the radar. A vintage Dior jacket is fine if no one can tell it's Dior; a conspicuous designer bag or six-carat ring is not. Standing beside someone accused of a serious crime, she doesn't want a jury wondering why the lawyer looks "so done up and moneyed," she says. There is one audience that judges Fast's attire pretty intensively: corrections officers. Jail rules prohibit visitors from wearing green, orange, khaki, open-toe shoes, and high slits. Every morning, Fast says, her outfit has to pass two tests: Will it work for the judge, and will the jail let her in? Judge's note: "Her style captures classic New York at its finest: polished and sophisticated for the boardroom, yet effortlessly chic for an evening socializing at Brooklyn Bridge Park. She embodies the versatility and confidence of a true New York wardrobe." — Roberto Concepción Jr. Michael Kosowski, Amabile & Erman Michael Kosowski knows menswear doesn't need to be boring. A berry-jam suit and dotted ascot command attention without becoming a distraction. A chocolate-brown checked jacket opens to reveal a silk tapestry sewn into the lining. Before law school, Kosowski recalls, he was riding in an Uber when his boss, public relations pro Juda Engelmayer, turned to him and said, "Everything we do is presentation." Years later, he still takes that edict to heart in the courtroom, where he defends clinicians in medical malpractice cases. His wardrobe mixes custom suits by Ammar Belal, vintage pieces, and retail finds he often personalizes himself. Kosowski learned to sew in high school from his Italian American grandmother, who taught him to make costumes for the drama club. These days, he gives old jackets a second life by restitching them or swapping in family heirloom buttons. "If something off the rack doesn't look like it's me enough," he says, "those buttons are coming off." Judge's note: "Michael has a singular, innate sense of personal style, which I really appreciate. He deftly mixes prints and textures in a way that makes his work wardrobe quite interesting, and gravitates toward great vintage pieces. I really respect the thought, care, and attention to detail that seemingly goes into his self-expression through fashion." — Leah Faye Cooper HY Kim, Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld LLP Hyun Young "HY" Kim shops in the one boutique no one else can access: her mother's closet. She favors crisp lines, padded shoulders, and unusual cuts — many of them first spotted by her mother, whose '90s suits and pristine Gucci bag have steadily migrated into Kim's wardrobe. "Whenever I visit South Korea, we go shopping together," Kim says. Back in New York, she favors Cos for its minimalist, architectural silhouettes. At Akin, she helps lawyers in the investment management group work faster and smarter, organizing the resources they rely on and introducing legal technology. The same instinct extends to getting dressed. When the pandemic sent lawyers home, Kim still dressed for work every morning, then documented each look on Instagram. Years later, she still scrolls through the archive when she needs inspiration. Call it knowledge management for the closet. Judge's note: "When I think of a wildly successful woman who lives and works in New York, she dresses like HY. Her looks are incredibly chic, understated but powerful, and include an incredible mix of accessible fashion brands and aspirational IYKYK designer pieces." — Leah Faye Cooper Ankit Kapoor, Cohen Stine Kapoor LLP Ankit Kapoor has a standing brief for his tailor: Make him look like Harvey Specter. The matrimonial lawyer, who has represented Tom Brady in a family matter, snaps photos of suits he spots on television, including "Suits," then sends them to his tailor in New York or India to recreate the look, down to the peak lapels and double vents. Divorce law runs on referrals, and Kapoor, who nabbed the @newyorkdivorcelawyer handle on Instagram, knows a first impression forms before he says a word. "When you walk into a room, people should feel your presence," he says. A sharply cut suit does some of that work for him, paired with Santoni loafers and an 18-karat yellow-gold Rolex Day-Date. "It's the Tony Soprano Rolex," he beams. There is, however, a catch to bespoke tailoring: Kapoor figures his wardrobe has a roughly seven-pound margin of error. A few pounds gained or lost, and his custom suits stop fitting quite so perfectly. To stay his fighting weight, Kapoor, a former New York police officer, trains for Hyrox races. Judge's note: "When it comes to suiting, nothing is more important than fit, and Ankit clearly understands that. His suits are impeccably tailored, as they should be." — Leah Faye Cooper Nancy Chemtob, Chemtob Moss Forman & Beyda LLP Nancy Chemtob has helped enough celebrities get divorced to fill a Met Gala table. Mary-Kate Olsen and Tory Burch are among them. While negotiating for her high-net-worth clients, she wants to look polished without looking like she's billing the client to bankroll a shopping spree. Her love affair with fashion began in high school, when Chemtob worked at Infinity, the Long Island boutique she still remembers as the place. She also spent summers studying at Parsons. Fashion was the dream. Law was the family business, and eventually she traded sketchbooks for legal pads. She has always loved Chanel, but wears it selectively to court, steering clear of conspicuous logos. Dior feels quieter; a Pucci print might peek out from under a blazer. The common thread is longevity. Chemtob still reaches for pieces she bought almost two decades ago and rewards herself for big wins with jewelry she expects to keep just as long. "Chanel never goes out of style," she says. Judge's note: "With so much of fashion relying on trends, the fact that Nancy leans into classic styles and silhouettes speaks to her eye. And she's not afraid to add a 'surprise and delight' moment, such as a bold print or fishnet stockings." — Joi-Marie McKenzie

item.title: Anthropic has a cute graphic showing how its AI spread 'malicious' code
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.13
Anthropic has a new blog post that shows yet another way its AI model, Claude, misbehaved in ways that the company didn't anticipate. And to help condense its nearly 16,000-word report, the company created a cute little robot figurine to help visualize Claude's so-called "recklessness." In the blog post published Wednesday, Anthropic recounted four incidents — one previously unreported — in which Claude models gained access to the open internet during cybersecurity exercises that were supposed to be closed simulations. The company said the models then acted beyond the tests' scope, including by uploading "malicious packages" to PyPI, a public library for Python code, and accessing credentials tied to real outside organizations. "Our investigation identified two recurring alignment issues, present at varying levels of severity across the incidents: biased reasoning, in which Claude tended to disregard or misinterpret evidence that it was operating on the real internet, and recklessness, or a willingness to take harmful actions in the narrow pursuit of a task," Anthropic said. The post used a laundry list of technical terms to describe the cybersecurity incidents — "misconfiguration," "reward hacking," and "sandbox escape" — but there's an animated graphic that helps boil down one of the most serious episodes so we normies can follow what happened. A Claude model, depicted as a boxy cartoon robot, was conducting a closed cybersecurity exercise known as a "capture the flag" task. The task is shown as a tiny flag inside a clear bubble that Claude is supposed to find. Anthropic said the model was told "it has no internet access" for the exercise, but a "misconfiguration in the environment" — represented by a loose screw rolling away from the bubble — gave Claude a path to the "real internet." The cartoon Claude then holds a red box representing the "malicious package" that was uploaded to PyPI, a public repository that developers use to access prewritten code. Anthropic said in its blog that it was "most concerned" by this incident involving Claude Mythos 5 and that the package was installed on by "15 third-party hosts" that the company does not identify. "We believe that all 15 of these third parties were security vendors deliberately scanning for new packages and installing them in sandboxed environments to assess the package for security concerns," Anthropic said. "One vendor's scanner leaked its access credentials to the model while installing the package, which the model then used to access the vendor's live database." Anthropic said PyPI removed the package after about 90 minutes. The other three incidents involved a model altering records at a real company, an internal research model breaking into "unrelated third-party accounts," and Opus 4.6 accessing a third party's maching after failing to "abort its task." The company said it has since asked METR, an independent AI evaluation group, to investigate the incidents. Anthropic's post comes as frontier AI companies reckon with their models making unauthorized moves outside their controlled environments. In July, OpenAI said that autonomous agents in its cybersecurity tests accessed the internet and broke into parts of Hugging Face's systems. AI researchers have sounded the alarm that self-improving AI could pose a risk to humanity. On Tuesday, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said on X that he quit over concerns that AI companies were "gambling" with people's lives and that "neither company is acting responsibly."
