item.title: Interior designers reveal the 8 decorating rules you should (almost) never break
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.09
The way you decorate your home is entirely up to you — but there are a few guidelines and design suggestions you may want to keep in mind as you're decorating. Although there are rare exceptions, here are a few decorating rules that the pros say you should almost never break. Having curtains that are too short can make your space feel incomplete. Lauren White, owner and principal designer at Ellen W. Interior Concepts, said curtains should always hit the floor. This generally helps a space look larger and more polished. "Curtains that are too short are like wearing high-water pants," she said. "It does not look good and makes your space look unfinished." There are rare exceptions to this — for example, if you're dealing with a window above a sink or bathtub. A rug that's too small can throw off an entire room. A high-quality rug isn't cheap — and the bigger you go, the more expensive they become. Because of this, you may be tempted to choose a smaller, more affordable option, even if it means sacrificing aesthetics. If that's the case, and your rug won't be properly scaled to your space, you're probably better off skipping a rug altogether, White said. "A rug that is too small takes away from the space, although you would hope it adds visual value," she told BI. The "right" size of a rug varies depending on the room. However, at the very least, White said, your rug should at least be able to sit under the front legs of your furniture pieces, Ordering furniture without measuring your space can lead to expensive mistakes. It may seem like a no-brainer, but taking the time to measure your space is a crucial first step to creating a successful design, White said. Even better, try envisioning how an item will sit in your space by using a bit of tape. "Get the dimensions of the furniture you're interested in, grab some blue painter's tape, and create the shape of the furniture with the painter's tape and dimensions," she said. "This will give you a visual guide to ensure your furniture will be functional in your space." Choosing stylish pieces without thinking about their function can cause your space to look cluttered. "When choosing furniture for your home, it is important to not only incorporate pieces you love, but to ensure these pieces work for your lifestyle," Gena Kirk, vice president of design at KB Home, said. Because of this, you want to avoid buying stylish pieces that aren't functional and instead opt for pieces that have a lot of storage space. Doing so helps to "keep your home looking beautiful without the clutter," Kirk said. Having only one source of light in a room can make a space fall flat. Windows aside, having only one source of light (such as recessed lights) could make a room's ambiance fall flat, Kirk said. "It's important to layer the lighting in your home by incorporating pendant lighting, chandeliers, or trendy wall sconces to soften the light sources," Kirk said. "This creates a calm and welcoming environment throughout your home and can complement your design style." When it comes to expensive, tough-to-replace pieces, you might want to stick to timeless colors and designs. Kirk said she always tells her clients to "play it safe" with items that aren't easy to replace, such as countertops, cabinets, and built-in furniture pieces. "You can incorporate current trends through accessories and easy-to-replace pieces such as backsplashes, cabinet hardware, or small pieces of furniture," she said, adding that this can help you keep up with trends in an easier, more affordable way. Your space might feel awkward if you hang artwork too high. "Art is commonly hung too high and looks best at eye-level," Sara Ray, owner of Sara Ray Interior Design in Nashville, said. She said the sweet spot tends to be about 57 to 60 inches above the floor. "There are exceptions to every 'rule,' but this one holds true most of the time," she said. Buying all your furniture from the same collection can make your home look like a showroom. It can be tempting — and certainly convenient — to purchase all your furniture, rugs, and accessories from one store. However, Ray said, you should mix your pieces unless you want the space to feel like a furniture showroom. "It's better to buy from a variety of sources, as well as from different eras, so you can mix vintage and new pieces," she said. "The space feels more collected when older pieces are used, and it adds to the 'story' of your home. This story was originally published on November 16, 2019, and most recently updated on September 8, 2026.

item.title: I planned my wedding in 10 weeks — and it helped me land a Big Tech job. Years later, I'm navigating my first layoff.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.77
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Felisha Case, a former technical program manager at LinkedIn who was laid off in May. She's 40 and lives in the Denver area. The following has been edited for length and clarity. A week before I was laid off from LinkedIn, a colleague told me he'd heard something was coming. So I waited. One morning in May, I logged into my computer and went to grab a cup of coffee while it was booting up. When I came back, there was a meeting on my calendar that hadn't been there 30 seconds earlier. I checked my email. That's when I realized: If you have this meeting, you don't have a job. For the first time in my career, after roughly 13 years working at companies including Amazon, Oracle, Twitter, and LinkedIn, I'd been laid off. There had been layoffs at LinkedIn before, but I thought other roles were more likely to be affected. So the news came as a shock. As I began looking for work, I found myself reflecting on how I'd landed jobs in the past. My first tech job came about in an unusual way: through my wedding. My wedding unexpectedly helped launch my tech career In 2013, my husband and I got engaged, and we knew we didn't want a big wedding. I loved our anniversary date of September 26, which was 11 weeks after our engagement. So, we decided to put the wedding together quickly and get married on our anniversary. My in-laws had connected us with one of their former neighbors to take our engagement and wedding photos. The photographer also worked at Amazon. She said she was impressed by how quickly I'd planned the wedding and asked if I'd be interested in a program manager job on her team. She referred me for the role, which I eventually landed. I started at Amazon a couple of months after the wedding. Moving into tech was a huge financial change for my family. Before Amazon, I worked in a project management role outside the tech industry as an hourly employee. My husband and I didn't think I'd be able to continue working if we had children because my paycheck wouldn't have covered day care. Tech changed that. We were able to finally start thinking about having a family. In 2018, I left Amazon for a technical program manager position at Oracle. About a year later, I joined Twitter, where I worked until 2022, and moved with my family to Colorado during that time. I then joined LinkedIn, working remotely as a technical program manager. I stayed there until I was laid off. I took some time to process my layoff Under the terms of my layoff, I was technically still employed by LinkedIn and receiving my regular paycheck for two months, through mid-July. Then I'd receive my severance pay. What surprised me was the range of emotions I went through right after my layoff. It felt almost like a grief process: I was sad, I was angry, and I went through all of those different feelings. I took a week or two after the layoff before starting my job search. But I knew how long tech interview processes could take, so I wanted to get the ball rolling. I've gotten all of my past roles through personal connections Personal connections played a role in every tech job I landed, whether it be learning about an opportunity or a referral. I've tried to rely on my network in my job search, asking for referrals when I can. But I've also been applying to jobs where I don't have a connection. My advice for job seekers looking to leverage personal connections is not to be afraid to reach out. Most people are happy to help, and you're probably not bugging them. Be open about your search with people in your community, too. You never know who might know someone who's hiring or know of an opening that could be a good fit for you. AI has made this job search feel different One thing I've noticed so far is how much AI seems to be part of the job search process. I think companies are using AI recruiting systems to weed out candidates, which means I get fewer chances to actually talk to a recruiter. I've also noticed how much some employers seem to care about how I've used AI in my previous role. I have some examples to share, but at LinkedIn, there was a more serious push for employees to adopt AI tools only shortly before I left. For people like me, AI was just starting to become part of the job, and now it can feel like we're being asked to go back and get a whole new education in AI. Now that my kids are back in school, I've started spending more time experimenting with AI tools. I'm trying to find an upside to being out of work Being out of work has been a big adjustment for me. This is the first time I haven't worked since I was around 16, and the first time I've been home with my kids since I was on maternity leave. While I've been applying to jobs, nothing solid has come through yet. I think there are a lot of technical program managers competing for roles right now, whether they've been laid off or are looking to make a change. My advice to someone going through a layoff is that it's OK to feel however you feel about it. Even though it's not a personal decision, it can still feel personal. But try not to sit in those feelings for too long. Keep yourself busy, whether that means taking a break or starting the job search right away. Figure out what makes sense for you. It's a crappy situation. I don't want to be unemployed. I don't want to be looking for a job and feeling that pressure. But I'm also trying to see the upside. In early August, I took a weeklong break from searching to kind of reset and focus on the last week of summer with my kids. I've had more time with them. That part has been kind of fun. Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at jzinkula@businessinsider.com, or via Signal at jzinkula.29.

item.title: I worked 12-hour days in a corporate job I loved. I wanted my life back, so I quit, and now I'm a waitress.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.47
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lisa Eder. It has been edited for length and clarity. For 10 years, I worked my way up in luxury hospitality, eventually becoming a director at a high-end hotel group. It had always been my dream position, and I loved my job. Everything about it was exciting, and no two days were ever the same. There were important VIP arrivals, high-profile events, and constant challenges. I became consumed by it all. The job was a lifestyle, and for a decade, it was the lifestyle I wanted for myself. I loved working 12-hour days, most days of the week. I loved leading a team of 100 people and six department heads. I loved the responsibility, the pace, and having to be "on" all the time. But I didn't have much of a life outside work. The job was my life. When my husband and I moved from Austria to Australia in January 2024 for his job, however, my mindset about work began to change. I didn't burn out Australians are generally more relaxed about work. I saw how much they enjoyed the different aspects of life outside their jobs, and I found myself wanting the same for my own life. Slowly, I began to wonder whether I had outgrown my career. I hadn't burned out. I didn't hate my job. In fact, I still loved many aspects of it. It just no longer felt like it was for me. I no longer wanted to fit into the corporate box. I wanted something else. I wanted to have dinner with my husband at night and completely switch off from the day. I wanted the autonomy to decide how I spent my time. I wanted to discover new hobbies and interests that made me feel alive again. For months, I sat with these newly emerging desires, trying to work out what to do with them. I asked myself what I wanted from life I had spent years working to get where I was professionally. What would other people think? Was I giving up? Was I throwing away everything I had worked so hard for? At the same time, I was asking myself bigger questions: What did I actually want from my life? Who was I now? What were my values? Throughout the entire process, my husband made it very clear that I could choose whatever I wanted. The decision and drive mainly came from me, but he supported it because he understood that I was serious about it In early January 2026, I quietly decided to resign. In February, I resigned, and I left the company in March. I'd like to say it was easy, but it wasn't. I took a waitressing job I grappled with who I was now that I was no longer a leader in the corporate world. I had spent so long building a professional identity that I wasn't sure who I was without it. I also had to learn how to live with the uncertainty of not knowing what would come next. Financially, I had been preparing for the transition by saving money to support myself. My husband was also incredibly supportive. But I wanted to make my own money, so I took a part-time waitressing job at a café in Sydney. Unexpectedly, that job became about much more than income. It gave me joy. I loved being around people, food, and coffee. I loved finishing work and coming home without the weight of a corporate job on my shoulders. I had the freedom to decide what I wanted to do with my evenings, whether that was something on my own or spending time with my husband. I also started playing volleyball, running, and tennis — sports I had loved before my corporate life took over. Then I started dreaming about becoming a Pilates instructor. I enrolled in a training course, which I'm still completing, with the goal of becoming an instructor. I found myself again. I won't say I have everything planned out. That wouldn't be honest. But having space in my head has given me the ability to keep asking myself whether my life aligns with my values — and to make changes when it doesn't. My journey is my journey, but it won't be right for everyone. If you aren't willing to do the mindset work — to question your identity, understand your values, and rethink what success means to you — to live with uncertainty and wrestle with doubt, then giving up a corporate career may not be the right choice for you. But for me, it feels almost unthinkable how different my life looks now. And I don't regret it.

item.title: An Anthropic researcher just quit, saying OpenAI and Anthropic are 'gambling with our lives'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.21
An Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI just quit. He's the latest insider who's warned that the AI race has become dangerously reckless. Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on Tuesday, saying he had spent the past three years doing pre-training research at the two AI giants. "Neither company is acting responsibly," Coxon wrote on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Coxon was a member of OpenAI's technical staff from 2023 until July 2026, when he moved to Anthropic as a researcher. His research at OpenAI included work on GPT-4o. In Tuesday's post, Coxon said the two labs have not been transparent about their fears regarding AI. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt," he wrote. "If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately." There is one difference between the two companies, he said. "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes," Coxon wrote. "At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk." Evan Hubinger, a current Anthropic employee who leads the alignment stress testing team at the lab, agreed with Coxon in a reply to his post. "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," he wrote. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to." OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Safety has taken a 'backseat to shiny products' Coxon is the latest among staffers walking away from frontier labs while sounding the alarm, a trend that appears peculiar to the AI boom. While the dot-com and smartphone explosion era had their own set of concerns regarding a digital divide and bubbles, they did not draw as much scrutiny about safety from people closest to the action. OpenAI has lost a string of safety researchers in recent years, and Anthropic is increasingly facing the same phenomenon. In February, Anthropic safeguards researcher Mrinank Sharma left the company, writing in a resignation letter that he wants to contribute toward something that fully aligns with his "integrity." "Throughout my time here, I've repeatedly seen how hard it is to truly let our values govern our actions," he wrote in the letter he shared publicly. "I've seen this within myself, within the organization, where we constantly face pressures to set aside what matters most, and throughout broader society too." In February, OpenAI researcher Hieu Pham said that he could "finally feel the existential threat that AI is posing." Later that month, he announced he was leaving the company, citing burnout. In 2024, former alignment chief Jan Leike quit OpenAI after saying he reached a "breaking point" with leadership. "OpenAI is shouldering an enormous responsibility on behalf of all of humanity," he wrote. "But over the past years, safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products." Recent incidents have added fuel to those fears. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models escaped a test environment and hacked into Hugging Face's systems. OpenAI called the incident a "warning shot" and paused its largest planned frontier reinforcement-learning run. Later that month, Anthropic said it found three cases of Claude models gaining unauthorized access to other organizations' systems. The company also amended a key safety pledge this year, dropping a commitment not to train more powerful models without adequate safeguards in place and replacing it with safety roadmaps and risk reports.

item.title: I used to see countries I'd visited as places I'd 'done.' Slow travel changed that.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.02
Earlier this year, as I set foot in country number 50, I expected the milestone to feel significant. Instead, I realized how little the number actually meant. As a teenager, I became obsessed with seeing the world. My first purchase on Amazon was a set of 50 mini flags to study each day. I turned to quiz websites like Sporcle to learn country capitals and populations when I should have been solving math equations for school. At 14, I'd already developed my first major travel goal: visit every country in Europe. Later that year, after a trip to Greece, Italy, and France, I was every bit as enamored with Europe as I'd imagined I'd be. Unfortunately, I wouldn't visit again for seven whole years. By then, I was 21, in college, and finally had the freedom to start traveling on my own. Visiting Paris, Amsterdam, and Barcelona reignited the obsession I'd developed years earlier. I began traveling during every school break These trips were far from relaxing. I planned jam-packed itineraries to see as much as I could within a one- or two-week window. There was one trip in particular that still makes me anxious to think about. In June of 2019, my friend and I crammed Greece, Croatia, Czechia, Hungary, and Germany into 10 days. We didn't have time to visit the Acropolis in Athens. We spent less than 48 hours in each place and were constantly rushing to catch the next flight. After checking off the main attractions, there was little time to experience the culture and history of each place. I remember spending more time in Split's airport than I did exploring the city. It went like this for my first year of traveling. At most, I would spend three days in each country, sticking mostly to capital cities. At one point, I tried to justify a two-hour layover in Keflavik as a trip to Iceland. Social media made travel feel like a competition Seeing people list the number of countries they'd visited in their bios reinforced my own urge to keep score. Looking back, I was using my number in much the same way: as proof that I was well-traveled. At the same time, part of my rushed travel style stemmed from necessity. Between being a busy college student and later a full-time employee, I only had so much time to travel. But when I was laid off at the end of 2023 and decided to spend most of 2024 traveling in Asia and Australia, those time parameters became obsolete. I was able to prioritize slow travel instead of seeing how many countries I could squeeze into a week or two. On that eight-month trip, I generally spent three weeks in each place, sometimes longer. The longer I stayed, the more I felt like I was actually traveling. Instead of only crossing off must-see attractions, I actually had the time to learn local history and customs, visit lesser-known areas, and experience everyday life. In the end, I felt a deeper appreciation for the countries I traveled through slowly than the ones I raced through. Staying longer made room for experiences that would have never fit into my early itineraries. In Malaysian Borneo, I spent three days exploring the Kinabatangan River deep in the jungle, observing orangutans, crocodiles, and native birds along the way. I took a sailing trip through the Komodo Islands in eastern Indonesia and earned my advanced diving certification on Gili Air, a small tropical island near Lombok. Those two months I spent traveling across Indonesia showed me how culturally and geographically diverse a single country could be. From Java to Flores, each island I visited had its own dialect, religious traditions, crafts, and local delicacies. It's not just about the numbers I stopped viewing the countries I had already visited as places I'd "done." The destinations I know best are the ones I've returned to over and over again, and I still discover something new with each visit. I first traveled to Italy at 14 and returned to live there 10 years later. A trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina in the summer of 2025 led me to establish Sarajevo as my current home base. Those returns didn't increase my country count. Still, they have given me things that a number could never reflect — meaningful relationships, new perspectives, language skills, and a genuine connection to each place. Nowadays, I like planning my trips so I begin or end in a familiar location. I'm always just as excited to return to the places I love as I am to visit somewhere new. There's always comfort in being back in a place where I know my way around, have friends and favorite spots, and can pick up where I left off. I haven't completely stopped counting. My goal to visit every country in Europe is still alive and well — there are 12 left on my bucket list. Admittedly, I still get satisfaction from adding a new country to my Been app, and every milestone is still exciting. The biggest difference is that the number is now something I track instead of something I chase.

item.title: 50 years after his death, Mao still shapes China
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.42
On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died. The revolutionary leader who led the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to power and founded the People's Republic of China left behind a profoundly contradictory historical legacy. He shaped the narratives of revolution, nation-building and national independence, but also left behind immense social trauma as a result of successive political campaigns and persecutions. How far has China moved away from Mao? Over the past five decades, China has undergone radical changes. When Mao died, China was still a poor and relatively isolated communist state. Today, it is the world's second-largest economy, deeply embedded in the supply and value chains of global capitalism, with a vast private sector, a large urban middle class and a highly digitalized society. Zhang Lun, a professor at Cergy-Paris University, said Mao left behind four major political legacies: the authoritarian and highly centralized political system; a model of governance that relies on revolution and political campaigns to solve social problems; populist tendencies marked by anti-elitism and anti-rationalism; and utopian visions of egalitarianism and moralism. From the perspective of political legacies, Zhang told DW, the most fundamental change in China over the past five decades has been "de-Maoization" — while its greatest challenge has been that this process was never fully completed. How Mao's legacy still shapes China's Communist Party Mao's name remains written into the CCP's constitution, while his thought remains part of China's official ideology and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Mao helped forge the Chinese Communist Party, and his insistence on the party's supremacy over the state and society has remained a fundamental principle throughout the decades, said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt, professor at the University of Zurich. Veteran journalist and political commentator Chang Ping agrees, adding that what has truly endured is the institutional core of the principle that "the party leads everything," serving a state vision of being able to "concentrate resources to accomplish major tasks." The CCP, he said, can pursue such objectives "at all costs" — meaning the interests of ordinary people can be sacrificed to the maximum extent necessary to preserve the regime. Is Xi Jinping taking China back to the Mao era? Under current leader Xi Jinping, a number of political concepts and methods of governance associated with the Mao era — such as ideological unity and the spirit of "struggle" — have again attracted attention. Xi's actions such as abolishing the presidential term limits, strengthening his personal authority and the incorporation of his political thought into the party and state constitutions have invited comparisons between him and Mao. Chang argues that the very term "return" is misleading, since elements of the Mao era have never fully disappeared. Zhang holds a similar view. Authoritarian rule, political rigidity, weak rule of law and the lack of effective guarantees for citizens' rights, he argues, are not only important elements of Mao's political legacy but also among the most significant continuities between the Mao era and China's current political system, he underscored. And Xi, who personally suffered during the Cultural Revolution, seems even move closer to Mao-era policies. "What Xi learned from the Cultural Revolution was not the lesson of a victim, but the lesson of power," Chang told DW. The lesson was not that "such a system must never exist again," but rather that "whoever loses power is at the mercy of others," he added. Felix Wemheuer, professor of modern China studies at the University of Cologne, echoed this view. "The conclusion Xi appears to have drawn from his own experience of the Cultural Revolution was clearly not that Mao should be completely abandoned," he told DW, "but rather that, for political reasons, Mao's historical status as the founder of the state, the military and the party must be upheld." Wemheuer views the current CCP leadership's approach to Mao as "fundamentally Machiavellian and pragmatic." In economic policy, for instance, there is no sign of a return to the Mao era, he said. Today's China operates a highly dynamic model of state capitalism, with a mix of ownership forms coexisting and maintaining a strong private sector. Nor is there any indication that China intends to return to the Mao-era model of a communist welfare state. The same applies to the idea of "self-reliance." Today's China could hardly afford to withdraw from the global economy and international supply chains. How similar are Xi Jinping and Mao Zedong? Experts say similarities between Mao and Xi can be seen in areas such as the emphasis on the CCP's supremacy, the elevation of a core leader, and populist elements that stress a close connection between the people and the leadership. Wemheuer argues that Xi possesses neither Mao's historical authority nor his personal charisma. The two also exercise power in fundamentally different ways. Mao could bypass party institutions, go for years without convening a party congress and mobilize the masses against the party and state apparatus. Mao himself was a populist with certain anarchic tendencies, Wemheuer said, and even tolerated the temporary collapse of the party-state system at the grassroots level in 1966-67. Xi, by contrast, would never allow such a situation to occur, the expert stressed. Xi places greater emphasis than Mao on control and top-down governance, consolidating power by strengthening institutions and the party apparatus. Mittelstaedt likewise cautions against equating Xi with Mao. First, Mao was a revolutionary who destroyed existing institutions during the Cultural Revolution and was fundamentally anti-bureaucratic in his political orientation. Xi, Mittelstaedt argues, does the opposite. Second, Mao stood above the party. His power came from "being Mao himself" rather than from the party's institutional structures. Xi, by contrast, is "a party man through and through." His authority derives from party institutions, and he governs through those institutions, Mittelstaedt pointed out. "At the end of the day," he told DW, "Xi Jinping remains a product of the system Mao created." Why are some young Chinese nostalgic for Mao? China has also seen recurring waves of Mao nostalgia, with some Chinese citizens invoking Mao online and expressing longing for what they describe as an era without social inequality, when everyone supposedly had enough to eat. Chang argues that what they are longing for is neither Mao himself nor the real Mao era. The actual Mao era, Mittelstaedt said, was marked by rigid hierarchies, pointing to the urban-rural household registration divide, different levels of privileges and supplies for officials, and a system in which one's family background could determine one's fate. It was, in many respects, more unequal than China today — and voicing grievances could be fatal. The imagined vision of a more equal world, he underlined, is therefore actually an indictment of the present situation, with widening inequality, soaring housing prices and persistently limited social mobility. Still, many express the dissatisfaction with contemporary reality through Mao's image and language. In Chang's view, this is connected to the continuing contraction of space for public criticism in China. When forms of political expression such as independent trade unions, street protests, free media and opposition parties are tightly restricted, Mao remains a historical symbol that official ideology cannot entirely exclude. The result is a striking irony, he said, pointing to some people invoking Mao's language of anti-bureaucracy, resistance to oppression and even "rebellion" to criticize what they see as corruption, inequality and abuses of power in Xi's China today. Mittelstaedt said this makes Mao a double-edged sword. He remains an important symbol of the CCP's political legitimacy — but parts of the revolutionary language he left behind can also be turned into standards by which contemporary reality is measured and criticized. Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: Australia targets big tech with algorithm opt-out bill
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.36
The Australian government announced planned new rules for social media platforms on Tuesday that would give users greater control over their social media algorithms. Under the "My Feed, My Way" initiative, social media platforms would have to allow users to opt out of content recommended by an algorithm in their feeds. What is in Australia's social media algorithm bill? Prime Minister Anthony Albanese unveiled draft legislation that would impose a "duty of care" on major social media platforms, including Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram. Users would only see content from accounts they choose to follow. "It's not about giving government control. It's about giving people control," Albanese said. The bill is expected to be approved by the Australian Parliament and introduced later this year. Companies that do not comply could be fined up to AU$100 million ($72 million, €62 million). Social media bans for children Anika Wells, Australia's Minister for Communications, said the measure would help ensure children's safety on social media. Australia became the first country to restrict social media access for under-16s in 2025. Several countries, including Germany, Spain, France, Denmark, and New Zealand, followed Australia's lead and drafted plans to introduce similar age restrictions. Some big tech companies have opposed such new regulations. They argue it could encourage young users to move to unregulated online spaces. Edited by: Rob Turner If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: India news: Hindu group apologizes over Eiffel Tower row
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.34
What you need to know These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us. Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India from Tuesday, September 8. - Hindu group apologizes after Eiffel Tower strike over alleged discrimination - Manipuri musician killed in Delhi - Iran hails longstanding India relationship ahead of Pezeshkian's visit Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. WATCH — Can we turn household gardens into food systems? In the southern Indian state of Kerala, the village of Kanjikuzhy has built a remarkable community-led food system. Nearly all 9,000 families grow their own vegetables organically — turning homes, backyards and small plots into productive gardens. Find out more: eBay to investigate how banned gender-test kits were sold in India — report US e-commerce platform eBay is conducting an internal review of its platform's safeguards after news agency Reuters found that several gender-prediction kits were listed for delivery to India. New Delhi has banned the use of such kits under a law aimed at preventing sex-selective abortion. Reuters identified nine listings, including kits from brands SneakPeek and Peekaboo, which were being offered by third-party sellers with shipping to India. The platform removed the listings after being notified last week. "These listings violated local regulations and eBay's policies, and we are reviewing these controls, including the relevant shipping and checkout experience, to determine whether further enhancements are appropriate," eBay told Reuters in a statement. "eBay has controls in place intended to prevent certain gender-prediction products from being visible in India," it added. While eBay does not have a dedicated Indian shopping site, the company does ship to India, functioning purely as a marketplace for third-party sellers. India has a strict prenatal gender determination law dating back to 1994, which followed a steep decline in the ratio of girls born after ultrasound technology spread. With patrilineal inheritance being the norm, people misused the technology to abort female fetuses. Under the law, violations carry prison terms of up to three years, with repeat offenses being hit with harsher penalties. Separately, India's Health Ministry has pressed Google to remove search results linking to Peekaboo's website, according to notices reviewed by the news agency.
Manipur singer killed after confronting group drinking outside Delhi home A group of men has been apprehended for beating Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh to death outside his apartment in Southeast Delhi, local media reported. The 54-year-old lived in Kilokari village, where he was allegedly assaulted by a group of delivery workers and local eatery staff after he confronted them for drinking and creating a nuisance outside his residence, police said. Seven people have been arrested, and a juvenile has been detained in relation to the assault. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi slammed local authorities and Home Minister Amit Shah, raising concerns over the safety of people from the northeastern states of India in Delhi. "A father, killed outside his own home, in his own country's capital. After many such incidents, every Northeast family in Delhi is asking the same question today - are we safe here?" he wrote on X. Chief Minister of Manipur, N Biren Singh, also offered condolences to his family, urging Delhi Police to take swift action on the matter. He also shared CCTV footage that claimed to show the accused heading downstairs after assaulting Singh. The incident has raised concerns among New Delhi's Northeast community. The area that comes under the Sunlight Colony police station is known to have a sizeable population from the region, the Telegraph newspaper reported. In 2023, a group of men assaulted a Manipuri family in the area. Iran hails 'civilizational' relationship with India ahead of BRICS summit Iran highlighted its "long-standing, historic and civilizational relationship" with India ahead of President Masoud Pezeshkian's visit to New Delhi for the upcoming BRICS summit. Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei emphasized the importance Tehran places on its ties with New Delhi during a press conference. He highlighted President Pezeshkian's bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to reaffirm Iran's plans to engage diplomatically with India to deepen economic collaboration. Referring to the upcoming BRICS summit, he added: "We will certainly make use of the opportunity provided by the BRICS Summit to continue our discussions and consultations with India in areas of mutual interest." The 18th BRICS summit will be held from September 12 to 13 at the Bharat Mandapam convention center in the Indian capital. BAPS apologizes over Eiffel Tower row, denies preventing access A Hindu religious group has apologized after the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, was closed on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the exclusion of female workers during a visit by the organization. The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), however, reiterated that their tour was pre-coordinated with the tower's team, adding that no person was denied access. BAPS also offered apologies to anyone hurt or inconvenienced. "We understand the concerns raised and take them very seriously. Given the size of our delegation, the visit was organised in coordination with the Eiffel Tower team at the beginning of normal opening hours to minimise any inconvenience to other visitors," BAPS said in a statement on social media. "To our knowledge, at no point was anyone denied access to the Eiffel Tower. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation," the statement added. Around 100 men from BAPS were visiting the landmark. The company that operates the Tower, SETE, said that the group had requested a visit as part of which the "interactions with women" would be limited. SETE accepted that the decision was a mistake: "These conditions should not have been accepted." On Sunday, BAPS conducted the consecration ceremony of France’s first traditional Hindu temple in Bussy-Saint-Georges, near Paris. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi virtually addressed the inauguration gathering, adding that "India and France’s relations have reached new heights." Read more about the controversy here. Welcome to our coverage Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from across India. If you tried to go up the Eiffel Tower in Paris yesterday, you may have been in for a rude shock, as the tourist hotspot was closed over alleged discrimination during a visit by a Hindu group. The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) has apologized for any inconvenience caused, but with a small caveat. In Delhi, a Manipuri musician was killed after he objected to a group of men drinking raucously outside his apartment. Finally, Iran has hailed its longstanding ties with India ahead of President Masoud Pezeshkian's visit to New Delhi for the 18th BRICS Summit from September 11 to 13. For this and more, follow our live blog.

item.title: Hungary orders 10 Russian diplomats to leave
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.33
Hungary has ordered 10 members of Russia's diplomatic mission to leave the country over activities it said were incompatible with their diplomatic status, Foreign Minister Anita Orban said on Tuesday. The move marks a significant step by Budapest against Moscow, with Orban saying it was intended to protect Hungary's "security and sovereignty." Why is Hungary expelling the diplomats? Orban said a Hungarian Foreign Ministry official had informed the Russian ambassador that the 10 individuals had engaged in activities deemed "unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention." She did not specify what the individuals were accused of doing. Hungary's authorities had made the assessment before the government called on them to leave, Orban said. "This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote. Does this mean a break with Russia? Orban stressed that Hungary was not severing diplomatic relations with Moscow. "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia," she said, adding that Budapest intended to maintain "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules." Orban has served as Hungary's foreign minister and deputy prime minister since May, following the change of government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar. The expulsion is nevertheless a notable deterioration in relations with Moscow, particularly given Hungary's previously close relationship with Russia under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban. Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
