item.title: The Real Risk of a Trade War With Canada
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.96
In late October 2025, the automaker Honda had to indefinitely shutter a Mexican plant that manufactures its SUVs, thanks to an unanticipated shortage of parts. More than 2,000 miles away, in Canada, it had to slash the production of its popular Civic model in half. The shortage panicked companies across North America. Stellantis created a war room to monitor the availability of critical components, and Ford began to track the run-out dates for its inventory. Hundreds of thousands of Mexican and Canadian jobs were at risk if the impact of the parts shortage spread across supply chains that were highly integrated with those in the United States. Honda would later report production-related losses of roughly $300 million from the incident. The cause was a simple but deliberate Chinese policy. Beijing had suddenly banned global exports of semiconductors made by Nexperia, a little-known Chinese company whose parts go into airbags, braking systems, and other automotive essentials. Chinese President Xi Jinping made the move as retaliation against actions taken by the Dutch government and by U.S. President Donald Trump. Xi reversed the throttling of Nexperia’s exports only when Trump agreed, later that month, to delay the implementation of a new U.S. export control regime. This episode bluntly revealed just how integrated North American supply chains have become—and how exposed they now are to Chinese economic coercion. An auto component can cross the U.S.-Canadian or U.S.-Mexican border seven or eight times before it ends up in a fully assembled vehicle. If Beijing targets even one country, the entire North American supply chain could shut down. Yet all three North American governments are looking the other way. Trump’s tariffs on Canada and Mexico in 2025 and his escalating trade war with Canada this year have turned the countries’ attentions inward, onto disputes among the three partners, at precisely the moment when the threat is coming from the outside. Washington’s refusal to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) on July 1 has set up an implicit renegotiation of the pact. The debate must not focus on the terms the three countries impose on one another; rather, it should focus on the terms they set to help one another counter China. China’s monopoly power across a variety of sectors fundamental to the North American economy is growing fast—and the more it expands, the more Mexico City, Ottawa, and Washington each become vulnerable to the relationships the other two have with Beijing. On a continent that is already tightly integrated, Washington cannot fix its own exposure to Chinese coercion unless Mexico City and Ottawa fix theirs, too. Since 2018, Washington has begun experimenting aggressively with a mix of policies to fight back against China’s growing market dominance. Canada and Mexico will need to make a more coherent and concerted effort to join these campaigns—and the United States will need to work much harder to invite them along. The USMCA renegotiation is the place to start. MISSING THE FOREST In his 1992 presidential campaign, the American entrepreneur Ross Perot famously warned that the North American Free Trade Agreement would create a “giant sucking sound” as U.S. industries relocated south of the border to take advantage of Mexican workers’ lower wages. Although the pact did depress the earnings of U.S. blue-collar workers in areas with industries most exposed to new import competition from Mexico, the antipathy was mostly misplaced. One comprehensive 2015 study that added up NAFTA’s impact on consumers, workers, and industries found that it increased the United States’ economic well-being, albeit modestly, by 0.08 percent. (The impact on Mexico was slightly more positive, at 1.30 percent, and slightly negative for Canada, at negative 0.06 percent.) NAFTA nonetheless became a political vulnerability for Democrats. After Trump entered the White House in 2017, he made renegotiating it an immediate priority. When the USMCA officially replaced NAFTA in 2020, Trump declared that its improvements constituted a “colossal victory.” The reality, however, is that the two agreements differed very little. Both mainly reduced trade barriers and committed all three governments to avoid policies that inhibited commercial flows with one another. (The second Trump administration, with its tariffs on Canada and Mexico, has subsequently proved that commitment to be meaningless.) Both agreements, in other words, were designed to encourage trade among the three countries—not to deal with the risks posed by Chinese monopoly power. But that threat is now pressing. Xi’s 2025 semiconductor ban was his second attack on North American auto supply chains in less than six months. His first responded to Trump’s April 2025 imposition of a 145 percent tariff on imports from China; Beijing then halted global exports of rare-earth permanent magnets, another essential input for car seats, windshield wipers, motors, and cameras. Because China controls 90 percent of the world’s supply of rare-earth magnets, the shortage required Ford, among other companies, to temporarily shut down its Explorer SUV plant in Chicago—and forced Trump to reverse his tariff. Beijing’s effective use of export restrictions in 2025 was the culmination of its so-called dual circulation strategy, which aims to make China less dependent on North American and European supply chains and simultaneously make foreign economies more dependent on China. The restrictions proved that Beijing, as Xi put it in 2020, can implement “powerful countermeasures and deterrent capabilities based on artificially cutting off supply to foreigners.” Europe’s experience with Chinese investment reveals risks for North America. If left unchecked, China’s monopoly power—and its value as a weapon—is likely to grow in the years ahead. The country already possesses 85 percent of the world’s battery manufacturing capacity. It accounts for over 90 percent of global refining for rare earths and graphite and more than 60 percent for cobalt, lithium, and nickel. And China has an ever-increasing global presence in other foundational sectors, including steel, aluminum, chemicals, and telecommunications equipment. Chinese leaders have acknowledged that the country’s statist economy leads to involution, or excessive domestic competition and superfluous production—a situation that is unlikely to change any time soon. That means China’s monopoly power, and its ability to weaponize it, will expand as its surpluses force more and more foreign companies out of business. But China’s economic juggernaut goes beyond exports. In high-tech sectors, Chinese multinational companies such as BYD, CATL, and Ming Yang are now global leaders in electric vehicles, batteries, and wind turbines, investing abroad to acquire or build up manufacturing capacity in foreign countries. Consider the growth of Chinese companies in Europe, the target of nearly a quarter of all Chinese outbound investment in 2025. Hungary has received the largest of those investments to date, with the Chinese automotive industry establishing not only a new center of gravity for European supply chains but also additional competitiveness concern for legacy French, German, and Italian carmakers. The European experience with Chinese investment reveals multiple additional risks. Chinese subsidiaries manufacturing electric vehicles, security inspection equipment, and wind turbines in Europe have all been accused of competing unfairly with local firms by benefiting from Beijing’s subsidies. Hungary’s reliance on Chinese investment has increasingly put it at odds with the EU on other priorities, including efforts to sanction Chinese firms for their support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. ONE market, ONE RISK Washington knows it cannot unilaterally change Beijing’s economic approach. After China acceded, in 2001, to the World Trade Organization, the United States initially focused on containing the threat of unfair Chinese trade practices by imposing narrowly targeted import restrictions. When those had little effect, the first Trump administration launched a trade war; by the administration’s end, new tariffs covered roughly two-thirds of what the United States imported from China. The Biden administration maintained and made modest additions to those tariffs. But tariffs alone proved insufficient to tackle the security risks that come with Chinese monopoly power, and Washington has begun to experiment with many more tools of industrial policy. Like the Biden administration, the second Trump administration has used government support to incentivize U.S. and allied companies to build new sources of supply outside China, including for critical minerals, chips, and batteries. Washington has discouraged Chinese firms from investing in the United States and expanded the list of American products that cannot be exported to China. It has also renewed an American interest in stockpiling. Although the USMCA was negotiated relatively recently, it was not designed to counter the threat of Chinese market dominance. Beijing’s 2025 export restrictions showed how vulnerable each country now is to an attack on another—and revealed how much more resilient all three could be if their economies and policies were more in sync. Coordinating their efforts effectively requires some alignment of the three countries’ tariff regimes toward China, an issue on which the USMCA is mostly silent. The negotiators of the original pact did not need to contemplate how the three countries would implement complementary subsidies, investment restrictions, or export controls, as such policies were not then in vogue. Now they are. North America’s economic integration is worth trying to save. The more the United States undertakes comprehensive efforts to reduce its vulnerability to Chinese economic coercion, the more important it becomes for Canada and Mexico to align their own policies. Misaligned tariff rates across the three countries incentivize the transshipment of Chinese goods to U.S. consumers. They also create concerns that industries may unfairly locate in one country because it allows access to cheaper Chinese inputs not available to firms operating in the other two. Indeed, it may be impossible to retain an integrated North American market without policy alignment. And North American integration is worth trying to save: the greater scale offered by one large USMCA consumer market permits companies to spread their fixed costs over more units of production. Fundamental differences among the three countries allow for specialization based on what workers and companies in each do best. Diversifying sourcing across a wider geography mitigates threats from climate change and public health crises, not only geopolitical risk. Policy alignment to create alternative sources of supply outside China will entail costs. In addition to the fiscal burden of subsidies, North American consumers will have to give up some access to cheaper Chinese products today to curtail excessive dependence in the future. And all three countries will need to prepare for the unavoidable costs of Chinese retaliation. THREE-PART HARMONY Trump’s 2025 and 2026 tariffs pursued too many contradictory objectives. Beijing’s economic coercion clarified the most important task: to quickly create new sources of supply outside China. The ongoing USMCA negotiations present a political opportunity to pursue that objective by better aligning the countries’ tariff policies along three dimensions. First, Washington needs to reduce tariffs on imports from Canada and Mexico back to their January 2025 levels. If Ottawa and Mexico City are to bear some costs for jointly strengthening non-Chinese supply chains, they must be able to share in the jobs, profits, and other benefits that come from some North American production. Then, Canada and Mexico need to raise some of their tariffs on China. In 2024, Canada had already matched most of the tariff increases that the United States had imposed on Chinese steel, aluminum, and electric vehicles during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration. Mexico, too, has taken steps toward tariff alignment over the past few years, including a major hike in December 2025 that covered Chinese steel, autos, and auto parts. The United States, Canada, and Mexico may need to work together to raise tariffs strategically in the future to address other vulnerabilities. Future downward tariff adjustments with China will also need to be done in concert, lest they undermine collective North American interests. For example, Trump has proposed that the United States and China reduce their tariffs on each other on a limited set of “non-sensitive” products under a so-called U.S.-China Board of Trade. But unilaterally increasing U.S. clothing imports from China, for instance, would come at the expense of Mexico’s export opportunities. Expanding U.S. agricultural exports to China would be unhelpful if it displaces Canadian sales to China. If managed trade proves necessary to deal with China’s statist model, solidarity requires something more akin to a North America–China Board of Trade. Aligning subsidies is also critical, because maintaining fair competition among North American companies and scaling up entire cross-border supply chains will be difficult without harmonizing how each country’s government supports its industry. Lining up industrial policies across countries is an even harder task than coordinating tariffs. Canada has a smaller economy than the United States, and Mexico is poorer, affording each a smaller budget. And asking taxpayers to fund subsidies that could end up benefiting another country’s workers is not a winner on the campaign trail. Some progress has already been made on aligning subsidies in North America. In 2020, the first Trump administration established a Canada-U.S. Joint Action Plan on Critical Minerals Collaboration, which allowed Ottawa and Washington to co-fund some small-scale Canadian cobalt, graphite, tungsten, and rare-earth projects. Or consider the bipartisan U.S. CHIPS Act of 2022. Although it focused on creating more U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, the program also supported developing workforces in Mexico for the final supply chain step of finishing chips. Beijing’s 2025 export restrictions worked only because chip factories outside China had to ship wafers back to Nexperia’s plants in China for finishing. Some subsidies built into the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 reinforced a North American agenda. For example, its consumer tax credits for electric vehicles required those vehicles to be assembled in North America, not simply in the United States. (Canada subsequently offered Volkswagen support to manufacture batteries in Ontario to better align with the IRA’s generous tax credits.) The IRA’s subsidies for critical minerals were also not limited to mining and processing within the United States. The act effectively sought to create a North American and allied supply chain preference, rather than a purely “Buy American” rule, by offering subsidies to companies that mined or refined critical minerals in Canada, Mexico, and other free-trade-agreement partners or recovered critical minerals through recycling within North America. Trump has forced Canada to divert resources away from the China challenge. So far, however, the second Trump administration’s approach to subsidies has been mostly national. In response to the 2025 rare-earth magnet crisis that its own China tariffs triggered, the administration moved quickly to fund alternative supply chains for numerous critical minerals—deploying money from the Department of Energy and the Department of Defense, including the latter’s Office of Strategic Capital, to grant loans, set up offtake agreements, and guarantee price floors. It has even taken equity stakes in entities such as MP Materials and Lithium Americas’ Nevada mine. But these interventions are aimed at production on U.S. soil and none were coordinated with Ottawa or Mexico City. Canada holds substantial deposits of many of the same minerals and has its own critical minerals strategy; Mexico nationalized its lithium reserves in 2022. Nothing in the USMCA obliges the three governments to work together, let alone keep their subsidy programs from bidding against one another. More recent announcements suggest that the Trump administration may have recognized the speed and cost benefits that come from supporting mining and refining in allied countries. In August, it provided a $400 million loan to an Australian firm to develop a scandium mining project in New South Wales. The administration also announced a U.S.-Mexico Action Plan on Critical Minerals in February, although it has not yet led to any projects. Nevertheless, Trump is simultaneously undermining any such alignment with his trade policy. Ottawa, in particular, has been forced to divert attention and fiscal resources away from the China challenge to address the challenge to its economy from Trump’s tariffs. Instead of escalating a trade war with a longtime ally, Washington should be encouraging Canada to put its considerable critical mineral resources to better collective use. ALIGN OR DIE Canada and Mexico have already shouldered costs from Chinese retaliation because of their policy alignment with the United States. In 2018, after the U.S. Department of Justice asked Canadian authorities to arrest a Huawei executive, China detained two Canadians for nearly two years. In 2024, when Ottawa aligned its import restrictions on electric vehicles, steel, and aluminum with those imposed by Washington, Beijing imposed retaliatory tariffs on Canadian exports of canola, pork, and seafood. And in 2025, when Mexico raised duties on Chinese autos and steel, China put tariffs on Mexican pecans. China’s retaliatory playbook often entails targeting exports from politically powerful industries with few alternative markets—especially farm products with a short shelf life. But North American leaders can better protect their countries against such retaliation. One way is by keeping their import markets open to one another. Another is by directing government funds to further diversify exports away from China to alternative markets. Trump’s deployment of tens of billions of dollars to U.S. farmers hurt by Chinese retaliation during both his first and second terms was politically expedient. Knowing a bailout is coming, however, may inadvertently encourage farmers to sustain their dependence on the risky Chinese export market. Stockpiling critical inputs should also be a tool of alignment. An input that is essential at one stage of a North American supply chain is essential at every stage. Because each country would benefit from more stockpiling, each needs to share in the costs. And if stockpiles grow large enough and their size is adequately advertised, they could even deter China from restricting exports in the first place. In early 2026, the Trump administration launched Project Vault, a multibillion-dollar public-private initiative to stockpile critical minerals for commercial use in the United States. Canada recently announced its own critical minerals stockpiling regime for defense purposes. Each of these efforts needs to go much further and be more North American in scope to contribute to the fight against Chinese market dominance. Canada, Mexico, and the United States cannot afford to become a “Fortress North America.” When it comes to Chinese investment, Washington has thus far mostly worried that Chinese firms could use Mexico as a back door to circumvent U.S. tariffs and regulations. The concerns were driven, in part, by reports in 2024 that BYD and Tesla were scouting Mexican locations for massive new plants and encouraging their Chinese suppliers to follow suit; pushback from Washington undoubtedly contributed to the fact that relatively few such projects have been completed. But the United States, Canada, and Mexico may someday want to attract more Chinese investment that does not pose security risks, especially in high-tech sectors that might benefit North American competitiveness. And at that point, the three countries will need to align their policies to avoid the confusion that has accompanied Chinese investment in Europe and to protect North American economic integration. Each must strengthen its investment screening regulations. Even Washington, for example, will have to expand the scope of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which scrutinizes only the acquisition of existing American companies, not factories foreign investors build from scratch. All three countries will also need to create new regulatory regimes to make sure that Chinese firms operate fairly and do not continue to benefit from Beijing’s subsidies or from its discriminatory allocation of exports of essential inputs. As daunting as it might seem to get all these policies aligned, renegotiating the USMCA is just a first step to tackle China’s market dominance. Even an integrated North America does not have enough scale to compete with China and its 1.4 billion domestic consumers. And so Canada, Mexico, and the United States also cannot afford to become a “Fortress North America,” completely shielded from trade with other like-minded, market-oriented democracies that share their concerns about Chinese monopoly power. Any efforts to align North American policy under a new USMCA must retain an openness to trade with these other countries to facilitate a broader alignment in the future. China’s market dominance demands that all three North American countries work together to take on more activist policies. The most immediate need is for the Trump administration to stop implementing policies and circulating rhetoric that undermine North American unity. If Canada, Mexico, and the United States turn on one another, each will be weakened in the one economic fight that really matters. item.title: The Rise and Fall of Global Jihadism
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.42
Twenty-five years ago, members of the jihadi group al-Qaeda hijacked four American airplanes, flying two of them into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and one into the Pentagon, in Washington, D.C. Passengers attempted to seize control of the fourth plane, and it crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing everyone aboard. The hijackers killed 2,977 people in total—by far the deadliest single terrorist attack in history. To many Americans, the events of September 11, 2001, seemed to come out of nowhere. Few had even heard of al-Qaeda before the attacks. Yet by September 12, the United States had plunged into what President George W. Bush called “a war against terrorism,” a fight that would persist for decades, ensnare multiple jihadi groups, and extend to all corners of the earth. The United States had many setbacks in this war. The ways in which it attempted to prevent another 9/11, or an even larger-scale attack, entailed massive, often inefficient investments as well as troop losses. Some of its efforts, such as the full-scale wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, were brutally destructive. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, in particular, drove a surge in jihadi recruitment. In the years since 2001, various new jihadi groups—some of them connected to al-Qaeda, some opposed to it—have set up shop in the Middle East and across East and West Africa, where they have fueled bloody civil wars, shattered local communities, and launched terrorist attacks both in the region and outside it. But the war on terrorism has not been a complete failure, either. Al-Qaeda itself is devastated. There have been few jihadi attacks on U.S. territory—perhaps the most important measure of success for most American leaders—in the past two and a half decades. According to New America Foundation data, jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people in the United States since 2001, a fraction of what U.S. officials feared in the aftermath of 9/11. And although jihadi groups survive, jihadism has lost much of its ideological salience. Consider what has happened since 2023. On October 7, Hamas, a group that al-Qaeda regularly criticized for compromising on theological principles in the pursuit of its political agenda, launched a bloody terrorist attack on Israel, killing more than 1,100 people. Israel went on to kill tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, many of them civilians, and conduct other attacks in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank. In 2025, the United States joined Israel in bombing Iran, and in 2026 the United States and Israel launched a full-scale war with the initial objective of regime change in Tehran. The Israeli war in Gaza led to mass protests around the world, and all of these events offered fodder for conspiracy theories about the enemies of Islam plotting against Muslims. Yet in contrast to the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq or the onset of the Syrian civil war in 2011, they have triggered no jihadi surge. Indeed, the former jihadis who overthrew the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad, in 2024, quickly sought to make nice with states that have long fought terror organizations, including the United States and Saudi Arabia, upon taking power. A quarter century after Osama bin Laden gave the order for the 9/11 attacks, his successors have not built a durable transnational movement capable of repeatedly attacking the United States and forcing governments to bend to their demands. The sense of historic possibility that once made the jihadi movement so threatening to Western countries has faded. The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost. THE BIRTH OF A MOVEMENT In late 2001, al-Qaeda appeared ascendant. The movement grew out of the armed struggle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, and it attracted Muslim fighters from around the world. Under bin Laden’s leadership, al-Qaeda had many goals, including helping the Taliban secure power in Afghanistan and training its members for terrorist and insurgent campaigns throughout the Muslim world, but ousting the United States from the Middle East was at the top of the list. Other jihadis prioritized fighting governments that they saw as foreign invaders in Chechnya and Kashmir, toppling supposedly apostate Arab regimes, battling Shiite Muslims, or creating a caliphate. The scale of its attack on the United States gave al-Qaeda an aura of momentum and outsize influence within the jihadi movement and beyond. After 9/11, the movement grew in stature, and fighting the United States and its Western allies, which most jihadis had previously considered a relatively low priority, became a more mainstream objective. The fact that the U.S. government would make few distinctions between al-Qaeda-linked groups and jihadis with a more local focus in its subsequent counterterrorism campaign only reinforced that trend. Several factors had made the 2001 attacks possible. Among them were the many shortcomings in Washington’s approach to counterterrorism, including the mistakes identified by the 9/11 Commission, an independent body set up by the U.S. government in 2002, on which I served as a staff member. Those included poor information sharing among U.S. government agencies, a failure to place on watchlists future hijackers who were suspected of links to al-Qaeda and were believed to be traveling to the United States, a lackadaisical effort to find suspected terrorists believed to be in the United States already, and no response to alarming field officer reports that jihadis appeared to be interested in learning how to fly planes. The Islamic State’s overreach was ultimately its undoing. Just as important was al-Qaeda’s own organizing. Most of its leaders were creative, dedicated, and willing to work with other groups, giving the movement a large network from which to recruit the best operatives. Critically, al-Qaeda also had a safe haven in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, from which it could strategize, plot attacks, and coordinate with its international partners without interference. The CIA estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers attended training camps in Afghanistan in the late 1990s, enabling al-Qaeda to build a small army. Recruits from all over the world, but especially the Middle East, learned the basics of insurgent war. The more promising candidates learned advanced counterintelligence and bomb-making techniques. Some of those who received training went to fight alongside the Taliban against the group’s remaining enemies inside Afghanistan, and the Taliban permitted others to leave the country and rejoin local insurgent groups or terrorist cells around the world. Standout recruits among the mass of volunteers were selected for additional training and assigned to high-priority operations. Many of the 9/11 hijackers, for instance, initially went to Afghanistan with the intention to acquire skills and connections before traveling onward to Chechnya to fight alongside Chechen insurgents against Russian security forces. After they were indoctrinated in the camps, al-Qaeda sent them to attack the United States instead. Most governments around the world paid limited attention to this growing danger and did little to prevent members of terrorist organizations from recruiting, generating propaganda, fundraising, and networking on their soil as long as they did not carry out attacks there. Various jihadi leaders and operatives planned operations in Algeria, Bosnia, and elsewhere from London in the 1990s, for example. Even the United States was relatively lax; Ayman al-Zawahiri, who took over al-Qaeda after U.S. forces killed bin Laden in 2011, had come to the country in the 1990s to fundraise. THE TIDE TURNS, EVENTUALLY After 9/11, the United States’ counterterrorism efforts quickly succeeded in dismantling al-Qaeda’s base of operations. As the wreckage of the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers smoldered, the United States commenced military operations in Afghanistan. CIA officers and special operations forces, working with anti-Taliban groups and bolstered by U.S. airpower, quickly overthrew the Taliban. Many al-Qaeda members died in the fight. Those who survived lost their safe haven and, critically, their training camps, and were forced to flee. Most went to Pakistan and Iran and carried on the group’s operations from there; most of al-Qaeda’s most successful post–9/11 attacks, such as the 2005 bombings of London’s transportation system, were orchestrated from Pakistan. But both Islamabad and Tehran were less accommodating hosts than the Taliban were. Neither allowed al-Qaeda to establish new training camps, and Pakistani authorities, in particular, regularly helped the United States arrest and kill the group’s operatives. Without the large-scale training infrastructure that al-Qaeda had set up in Afghanistan, jihadi groups lost much of their ability to mount as sophisticated or distant an attack as 9/11, but they continued to terrorize local populations across the broader Middle East. The United States gave the jihadi cause new energy with its 2003 invasion of Iraq, a war justified in part by the need to confront terrorism. The subsequent U.S. occupation incited anger across the region and fueled the growth of anti-U.S. militant groups in Iraq. The chaos unleashed by the 2011 Arab uprisings gave these and other groups even more room to grow. The eventual outcome was the rise of the so-called Islamic State (or ISIS), which at its height in 2014–15 controlled territory in Iraq and Syria roughly the size of Virginia and home to millions of people. It attracted tens of thousands more recruits from countries in the Middle East, Europe, and Central Asia. Other groups, such as al-Shabab, in Somalia, also came to hold territory where they taxed and menaced the population and planned their operations. Yet persistent American pressure on the remaining jihadi havens bore fruit over time. In Iraq and Syria, the United States steadily eroded the Islamic State’s control until the group lost the last of its territory. Unlike in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which involved tens of thousands of U.S. forces, Washington deployed small special operations teams while local partners, trained by U.S. forces and backed by U.S. airpower and intelligence, did most of the fighting (and the dying). In other places such as Libya and Somalia, Washington supported the national armies and local militias battling jihadi forces and engaged in whack-a-mole with jihadi leaders. The advent of the armed drone aided this effort, enabling the U.S. military to gather more intelligence and strike more quickly, and with less collateral damage, compared with traditional airpower. Increased cooperation with allied intelligence services helped, as well. Much of this work was mechanical and humdrum—for instance, linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there—but it allowed Washington and its partners to uncover and unravel much of the global jihadi web, arresting members of al-Qaeda and other groups and disrupting their operations around the world. No less consequential were massive U.S. investments in homeland security. The Department of Homeland Security, created in 2002, was meant to bring together airport security, border protection, and other parts of the national security apparatus that would be involved in preventing terrorist attacks on U.S. territory. Increased spending at airports, on disaster response, and on improved communication between federal, state, and local officials was meant to ensure that information about new threats would be shared quickly, that terrorists would be prevented from entering the country, and that the response to any future attack would be better coordinated. The FBI made counterterrorism a top priority, and it aggressively investigated individuals suspected of terrorist activity. At times it was too aggressive; civil liberties organizations contend that the bureau detained and questioned large numbers of Muslim men and monitored mosques without evidence of wrongdoing. But overall, the effort was effective at preventing attacks. Each measure bolstered the others. Without training camps, would-be terrorists had no place to gain skills and network. Insufficient training could make them more prone to small mistakes that made their fundraising and recruiting efforts more easily detected. More active U.S. and allied security services would be ready to catch them, and then make the intelligence they gathered from those they arrested available to help target overseas networks and havens. The erosion of jihadis’ havens in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere steadily damaged the groups’ credibility and appeal. At the height of the Islamic State’s power, holding territory demonstrated its prowess and attracted followers who wanted to live in a place governed by the group’s version of Islamic law. But when the Islamic State lost territory, its calls for new fighters to come to defend its self-declared caliphate began to ring hollow. Recruitment became much harder. Fewer and fewer would-be jihadis wanted to join a group that increasingly looked like it was losing. OWN GOALS It was not only U.S. pressure that brought about the decline of jihadism. The jihadis themselves repeatedly made choices that reduced their appeal. For one, they made too many enemies. Al-Qaeda’s foes included not just the United States but also other supposed foreign occupiers, such as India, Israel, and Russia. Some strands within the broader movement also opposed regimes in Muslim countries that they considered impious, including the governments of Egypt, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen. The Islamic State’s list of foes was even longer; it fought most fiercely against Shiites and other non-Sunni Muslims. Declaring so many enemies enabled these groups to attract a wide variety of followers, but it also meant that they diffused their energy. Attacking everyone everywhere all at once made it difficult to put sustained effort into achieving any single goal. Even more damning, it ensured that everyone would attack them. Fighting jihadi terrorism was one of the few causes that united countries around the world, and the United States was able to solicit support for its intelligence and military campaigns from foreign governments that disagreed with Washington on many issues but shared an interest in quashing these groups. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience. Even more consequentially, some jihadi groups turned Muslim publics against them by mistreating Muslim civilians. People who might have been sympathetic to their fights against the United States and other foreign powers did not approve of jihadis’ killing of Saudi police and security officials in 2003 and 2004, for instance, or of an al-Qaeda affiliate’s slaughter of both Sunni and Shiite civilians in Iraq in 2006 and 2007. Such killings diminished the jihadis’ influence. In Saudi Arabia, the government, with the broad support of the public, killed or arrested al-Qaeda members, devastating the group’s operations in the country. In Iraq, the faction earned rebukes from clerics who had previously supported global jihad as well as from more mainstream religious leaders. The Islamic State’s overreach in Iraq and Syria was ultimately its undoing. Its declaration of a caliphate in 2014 was electrifying to many Muslims, coming at a time when the group seemed to be successfully expanding its borders and fighting off enemies. Yet the project created the conditions for the group’s eventual defeat. As bin Laden himself had privately warned another jihadi leader in Yemen years earlier, building a state would give the United States and other countries a place to concentrate their firepower. When the Islamic State declared its caliphate, not only did its territorial control make the group easier to target but its governing also exposed the group’s brutality. Its maximalist claims also made it impossible to work with other jihadis, let alone other countries. By the mid-2020s, the jihadi movement was in no position to capitalize on upheaval in the Middle East. The war in Gaza, the fall of Assad to former jihadis, and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran all supplied the kinds of grievances, images, and narratives that once fueled the movement’s global spread. But with the important exception of Somalia and large parts of West Africa, jihadi groups have not managed a mobilization comparable with the ones after the 2003 Iraq War or during the rise of the Islamic State. At those times, their ideology still had international momentum. Yet after the definitive collapse of the Islamic State’s territorial project, in most places the idea of global jihad lost its former appeal. The past few years might have provided an ideal opportunity to recruit disaffected Muslim youth in Europe and the Middle East, but the jihadis could not seize the moment. THE UNFINISHED FIGHT Despite the decline of jihadism and the relative safety of U.S. territory from attack after 9/11, it is difficult to claim that the United States won its war on terrorism. Neither major war fought under that banner, those in Afghanistan and Iraq, ended well. U.S. forces swiftly removed the Taliban from power in Afghanistan, eliminating the safe haven jihadis had enjoyed, but the campaign turned into a grinding stalemate and then, in 2021, a humiliating defeat when a reconstituted Taliban retook control of the country. The war in Iraq eventually allowed a better government than Saddam Hussein’s dictatorship to emerge, but it also set the groundwork for the rise of the Islamic State. These and other wars in the region came at a huge human cost, too. The Brown University Costs of War project has estimated that almost a million people, nearly half of them civilians, died in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria, and Yemen between 2001 and 2023. The United States lost more than 2,000 soldiers in Afghanistan and more than 4,000 in Iraq, and more than 50,000 were wounded between the two conflicts. Washington spent $8 trillion on its post-9/11 wars through 2021. Counterterrorism efforts did not stop jihadism entirely, either. For years, U.S. military campaigns and effective al-Qaeda and Islamic State propaganda amplifying American and allied abuses kept alive the political conditions that enabled the ideology’s spread. And although no jihadi group was able to carry out another operation on the scale of 9/11, the United States and its allies were the target of numerous plots and attacks by individuals who were inspired by jihadi ideology even if they had never met an al-Qaeda or Islamic State member. Many attempted attacks have been foiled thanks to better countermeasures, but the desire to kill Americans and citizens of other countries on jihadi groups’ lists of enemies has not gone away. Efforts by successive U.S. administrations to take on jihadi propaganda directly—including numerous programs aimed at “countering violent extremism”—were not particularly effective at winning the hearts and minds of people who opposed U.S. policy and were disinclined to trust the United States while Muslim civilians were dying in its wars. It will take constant effort to ensure that jihadis cannot rebuild. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience, however. At their height, jihadi groups proved capable of spectacular violence, forming alliances amid civil wars and even seizing territory. But they failed to translate those achievements into a durable political project or sustained global appeal. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, jihadism no longer offers anything like the same persuasive answer to Muslim grievances or plausible path to political transformation that it did in the first two decades of this century. Jihadis are not flocking to battle Israel or the United States, and the former Syrian jihadis sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers. This leaves Washington with tough decisions about how far it should go to fight the jihadi groups that remain active today. Most of them have survived by getting involved in civil wars that have been highly destructive but have erupted in places that are peripheral to U.S. interests, such as Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. There is a risk that jihadi groups could turn their involvement in these wars into opportunities to create new safe havens from which to organize international attacks. But if the United States attacks them directly, it also risks inviting retaliation and getting bogged down in new conflicts. In places such as Somalia and Yemen, Washington’s solution has been to launch drone attacks on jihadi leaders and operatives and provide limited support to regional governments, warlords, and tribal leaders to keep jihadi groups off balance. Yet as long as the governments in these countries remain weak and security assistance fails to move the needle significantly—or if, as the Trump administration has done in many African countries, Washington cuts its aid entirely—jihadi groups will remain active. The United States must accept that jihadism may never truly vanish. For now, U.S. and allied counterterrorism campaigns and jihadis’ poor track record are keeping these groups relatively contained. But it will take continued, constant effort—intelligence cooperation with allies, drone strikes on jihadi operatives, and military training for local partners—to ensure that they cannot start rebuilding in weak states. All of this is best done behind the scenes, denying jihadis easy propaganda victories and limiting the cost to the United States. If Washington can maintain vigilance without overextending itself, it can keep jihadism a manageable danger rather than letting it once again become a defining threat. item.title: Avoiding the Next Famine
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.32
In a world of great-power standoffs, climatic tipping points, and technological arms races, global hunger may not seem like a particularly significant problem. Yet last year, a total of 2.1 billion people, or more than a quarter of the planet’s population, experienced food insecurity—meaning they either ran out of food over the course of a year or were forced to reduce the quality or quantity of their diet. Over 260 million faced acute food insecurity, meaning their lives or livelihoods were in immediate danger because they could not get enough to eat. Almost a quarter of all children under the age of five were permanently stunted because of malnourishment and will likely reach lower levels of education, earn less over the course of their lives, and live with more chronic health challenges than properly fed kids. And these startling figures do not reflect the food crises that could be unleashed this year by rising energy and fertilizer prices, decreases in grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, and an intensifying El Niño weather pattern. Food insecurity is terrible in and of itself. But it also has disastrous political consequences. It inhibits economic growth, heightens the risk of violent conflict, and destabilizes governments. These problems, in turn, create trouble for the whole world. That means countries that are not overwhelmed by food insecurity still have strong, self-interested reasons to tackle it—the United States included. In fact, a U.S.-led effort to address hunger would do more than create a healthier and more stable planet. Given the waning goodwill toward the United States, Washington needs an agenda through which it can rebuild global confidence in its leadership and demonstrate the value of international cooperation. Addressing global food security could be at the center of such a plan. Different parts of the world, after all, may have different geopolitical ambitions. But almost no government—northern or southern, democratic or autocratic—wants to see so many people go hungry. There may be no better way to rebuild confidence in the liberal world order and in the United States as a committed member of it than for Washington to address this challenge. FOOD, GLORIOUS FOOD It is difficult to overstate just how intertwined food security is with global development, state security, and even international competition. Malnutrition leads to reduced educational attainment, compromised human capital, and lost productivity, costing the world economy $3.5 trillion a year in forgone economic growth and in added health-care costs. Food price spikes can also exacerbate grievances and lead to riots that destabilize governments; anger over hunger, for example, set the conditions for the Arab Spring protests. In rural areas, food insecurity helps armed groups recruit soldiers and causes disputes over scarce land and water resources. And it causes people to migrate to wealthier states. These reasons are, by themselves, enough for Washington to helm a global campaign to reduce hunger. But so should the fact that leading on global food security means helping shape the future of the world’s entire agricultural system—something China is on a path to do. In 2019, Beijing invested significant capital in securing leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, a role with substantial influence over how governments work together on food-related issues. It is also quickly developing other ways to lead the world on matters of food security. China spends double what the United States spends on public agricultural research and development, and its output of agricultural patents and scientific publications has skyrocketed while U.S. output has stagnated. Thankfully for American officials, the United States is still well positioned to lead the world when it comes to food security. The United States is among the world’s largest agricultural exporters. It was instrumental in founding the UN architecture dedicated to food security, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program. And for much of these institutions’ history, Washington has been their largest donor. In fact, for decades, the United States’ international development agenda was the most ambitious in the world, and it was backed by a willing public. Washington retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. The country still has such a public: in early 2026 polling, a strong majority said that the United States should be a moral leader in the world. But a strong majority didn’t believe it was. Perhaps this is because the United States has been walking away from this legacy and this opportunity to lead. In mid-2025, for example, Congress clawed back nearly $8 billion in foreign assistance funds. The United States is now a reluctant international donor and a surly member of key international organizations. Washington, however, still retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. In addition to increasing foreign assistance, it can leverage trade policies, public investment in innovation, and even its impressive data collection systems. Washington, however, will also need to work multilaterally. And to build credibility, it should advance a practical and achievable agenda with clear benefits for all. One overarching goal for collective action should be increasing predictability wherever possible. The global food system is afflicted by uncertainty across many domains—weather, supply chains, labor, trade, and beyond. This wreaks havoc on policymaking, markets, and livelihoods. Being able to better understand these trends and know what tools will be available to manage them could thus do much to shore up food networks and prepare for disasters. Washington should, for example, work with partners to strengthen the world’s fractured early warning systems and the data that enables them. Early warning of shocks to the food system—such as extreme weather, supply disruptions, economic turbulence—buys critical time for preparation and response. The United States should also spearhead the transition of international emergency food assistance funding away from voluntary, ad hoc contributions to preplanned, multiyear commitments. It should simultaneously encourage more donors to contribute in amounts commensurate with their abilities, starting with itself. Food security is one of the few issues that can bring the whole world together. Solving food emergencies requires more than just additional funding. The United States also needs to work to strengthen international norms that protect access to food during conflict. That means making sure humanitarian groups can get into conflict zones, protecting agricultural infrastructure from attacks, and prohibiting the use of starvation as a weapon of war. These concepts have a long-standing basis in international law, but the conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine have demonstrated they need reinforcement. Washington should advance these norms through resolutions and interventions in the UN Security Council and General Assembly and use diplomacy to try to get violators to change their behavior. Food security diplomacy, however, must extend beyond conflict zones. The United States should forge a broad global commitment to avoid unilateral, reactionary policies to agricultural shocks—such as when a grain exporter suddenly bans external shipments in response to price spikes, leaving international buyers in the lurch. Such policies may be politically attractive for governments that want to show citizens they will keep costs down. But they leave other states worse off and often don’t even work at home. Instead, the United States should promote more international financing options that maintain the flow of traded agricultural commodities during periods of price volatility and that fast-track funding to countries facing shocks. Finally, the United States should lead a collective action campaign aimed at protecting agricultural systems from a particularly pernicious challenge: agricultural pests and diseases. Pests and diseases destroy up to 40 percent of global crop production each year, pushing down rural incomes, driving up consumer prices, and wasting natural resources. The existing international surveillance and response systems for these ailments are limited in scope. But Washington can build global support for more comprehensive ones. MORE WITH LESS The world certainly needs better ways of managing food crisis and risk. But it also needs to foster sustainable agricultural productivity growth—or the ability to produce more food with fewer inputs. Such growth is particularly important where populations are rising, as most food consumed is produced domestically. Only certain food commodities can be easily traded across long distances, so international commerce cannot fully solve food and nutritional supply challenges. The most important step countries can collectively take is to promote innovation. To encourage that process, U.S. officials should start by focusing on international agricultural research centers, such as the World Vegetable Center in Taiwan and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico (both of which the United States helped found). These facilities have long been an engine for progress in productivity, food security, and natural resource management, particularly in the developing world. For example, over the last few decades, international centers have developed flood-tolerant rice and drought-tolerant corn that have prevented crop failure for millions of poorer smallholder farmers. In fact, according to studies by a variety of economists, research undertaken by these centers offers an impressive return on investment—for every dollar spent, ten dollars are gained in the form of yield increases, lower production costs, lower consumer prices, and other benefits. But like many institutions, these research centers have suffered from mission creep and bureaucratic accretion. To maximize their effectiveness, the United States should build global support for refocusing their strategy, streamlining their operations, and making new investments in them. The world needs research to keep just ahead of the latest challenges—such as rising temperatures and new strains of old agricultural diseases. But it should also aim higher. Washington thus ought to work with other actors to tackle tough, high-reward problems that have never had the benefit of a truly concerted international effort. This could include, for example, trying to develop high-yielding perennial or nitrogen-fixing grains that would promote healthier landscapes, reduce labor requirements, and need less fertilizer. It might also feature an endeavor to increase photosynthesis efficiency so that plants can produce more from the sunlight they receive. Such inventions would not only change the world, they would also showcase the power of American innovation and deepen Washington’s ties with its partners. But to enable ambitious research, the United States should take steps to reform the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. The agreement was designed to make plant genetic resources, or seeds and tissue, fully and freely available to researchers everywhere. These resources can be used to breed new varieties of crops that are higher yielding, more resilient to climate change, and more nutritious. But the treaty is falling short. Researchers see benefit-sharing provisions as too costly; developing countries see them as offering too little. As a result, fewer researchers seek material that could accelerate innovation, and fewer countries are willing to share it. The United States should thus push everyone to reinterpret the benefit-sharing provisions in a more generous manner. It should also properly fund the Global Crop Diversity Trust’s endowment, which funds the international seed banks that conserve the biological foundation of food crops (particularly since governments, including Washington, are doing an inadequate job of conserving their collections). And if U.S. officials determine that the treaty cannot be saved, they should lead an effort to draft a new one. Lastly, Washington must do whatever it can to make sure that new agricultural and food technologies are quickly adopted. This will require reforms of the international Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is responsible for developing food safety guidelines that protect consumers and facilitate trade. The commission’s guidelines have significant ramifications for technologies that could strengthen global food security, but the body is slow, underfunded, and controversial. The United States should therefore try to enhance its capacity and legitimacy, including by pushing for increased support to the scientific committees that help set Codex standards. REAPING AND SOWING At a time of rising global competition, there are few issues that can bring the whole world together. Food security is one of them. Almost every government knows that hunger is a problem, and almost all of them at least say they want to address it. If the United States can spearhead a strong effort do so, it could bring the planet together under its leadership. That does not mean Washington should instrumentalize food aid or other agricultural endeavors. The United States should not echo its 1970s policies around food power, during which officials boasted of altruism while attempting to exert political strength by alternatively deploying and withholding its grain supply. Instead, the United States must emphasize mutual benefit. It must persuade other actors that it is a constructive and reliable partner. Doing so will strengthen its diplomatic relationships and increase stability around the world—inherently advancing U.S. interests. Rarely do Washington’s strategic imperatives and humanitarian principles align so neatly. It is rarer still for a U.S. foreign policy agenda to clearly reflect what the American people want their country to be: not just strong, but moral. Food security, in other words, is a unique opportunity for the United States. The country cannot afford to waste it. item.title: Why America Can’t Strangle Iran
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.11
For Iran and the United States, August 24 was Groundhog Day. “We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” declared U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime.” It was the same promise he made in April, when he said that the United States was “imposing a financial stranglehold on the Iranian regime” under what the White House called Operation Economic Fury. It was also akin to the May 2018 rollout of the first Trump administration’s “maximum pressure” campaign, in which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced that Iran would be targeted by the “strongest sanctions in history.” And it sounded like U.S. President Barack Obama’s promise, made in 2012, that the Iranian government was to face “even more crippling sanctions.” The Iranian economy has certainly felt the effects of all the successive restrictions. Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, the country has experienced little growth and high inflation. As a result, Iranian firms have built less infrastructure and adopted fewer new technologies compared with peers in other developing economies. Iranian households, once increasingly affluent, are now at risk of falling below the state’s poverty line. Yet for the better part of a decade, Iran has been able to resist U.S. economic coercion. Until the recent blockade, it used sanctions-evasion techniques to continue oil exports to its key customer, China. Its non-oil industries also adapted to the sanctions, as currency devaluation reduced competition from imports and made Iranian products more competitive in regional markets, boosting exports. Iran thereby avoided the kind of runaway economic collapse seen in other sanctioned countries, such as Syria and Venezuela. Today, war is testing the resilience of the Iranian economy in ways that sanctions alone could not. Numerous U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have targeted critical industrial facilities, including some of Iran’s most important steel and petrochemical plants. The damage sustained during these attacks has led to major production outages for key industrial goods. The general decline in maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the specific disruptions caused by the U.S. naval blockade have not only reduced Iran’s exports; they have also throttled imports of much-needed capital and consumer goods. According to a July estimate by the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s GDP is set to contract 5.4 percent this year after shrinking by less than half that over the previous 12 months. Year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent in December 2025 to 88.6 percent by the start of the summer. The value of the country’s currency has hit a record low of over two million rials to the dollar. But even as the country’s economic situation is getting worse, Iran’s leadership remains better able to resist the coercive effects of sanctions than it might appear. The state of the economy is not yet impinging on Iran’s ability to wage war. Stockpiles of various goods remain deep, thanks to years of sanctions experience. And the Iranian state, with its powerful repressive tools, has figured out how to offload much of the economic pain onto ordinary Iranians while making sure its own needs are met. Trump’s approach, in other words, can certainly immiserate most of the country’s people. But it cannot successfully strangle the Islamic Republic itself. ANATOMY OF A CRISIS Iranian officials have acknowledged the country’s economic difficulties. “No matter how strong we are militarily, if the people are hungry and we do not have financial circulation, economic growth and domestic production, we will not endure,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament and a key power broker, on August 21. (Bessent cited this quote as evidence that U.S. economic warfare was having its intended effect.) During a television interview last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian expressed frustration that some of his fellow political leaders continue to deny that sanctions are harming the country. “Some say sanctions have no effect at all; I really don’t know what to say to those people,” he remarked. The statements from Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian reflect genuine concern about Iran’s economic trajectory. The speaker and the president are understandably worried about deteriorating public opinion, given the inherent connections between general economic welfare and political legitimacy. But U.S. officials should be wary of overinterpreting these statements. Contrary to what it might seem, neither leader is suggesting that the country’s economy is on the brink of collapse. American assessments of the Iranian economy and the success of economic coercion fail to account for the ways in which sanctions have transformed Iran’s political economy, altering the distribution of economic resources in ways that reinforce its existing power structure. The Iranian leaders who are most vocal about the suffering of ordinary people are not worried about the country’s imminent economic collapse; they are dissenting against a political consensus that has long enabled Iranian elites to deliberately push the pressure of sanctions onto ordinary people. Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian are complaining about the social costs of a policy response that has worked largely as intended. Perhaps more important, U.S. assessments of the Iranian economy miss important dynamics. Typically, the effects of sanctions are described in terms of macroeconomic indicators, including rates of growth, inflation, and currency depreciation. But these measures mainly capture price levels: the value of goods and services. They provide, in other words, a financial—not a functional—view of the economy. To take a functional view, one must look at the dynamics at the firm and household level; they reveal why deteriorating figures in the headlines have not led to Iran’s capitulation. Iranian officials pushed the pain of sanctions onto households and firms. The fundamental dilemma for policymakers in any comprehensively sanctioned country is how to respond to balance-of-payments vulnerabilities, such as when a country runs out of the foreign currency it needs to pay for imports. There are, broadly speaking, two approaches. Policymakers can use expansionary monetary policy to fuel investment, restoring the trade surplus through a combination of higher exports and increased domestic production. Alternatively, policymakers can use monetary tightening and austerity measures to suppress import demand, restoring the trade surplus at similar export levels. When faced with major sanctions after invading Ukraine, Russian policymakers took the first approach. They increased fiscal stimulus, driving a rapid expansion in industrial activity and manufacturing employment that created a distinct war economy. This spending was necessary to increase military production, but it also had the effect of dramatically tightening the labor market, raising real wages for ordinary Russians. That, in turn, blunted the initial effects of sanctions-related inflation. This approach eventually reached its limits, and inflation is starting to bite, but the economic strategy allowed Russia to persist in its war aims despite U.S. sanctions pressure. Iranian officials, by contrast, chose the second course of action. When major financial and energy sanctions imposed by the Obama administration first pushed Iran into a recession in 2012, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called for Iran to adopt a “resistance economy,” focusing on domestic capacities to counteract the sanctions pressure. But Iranian economic policymakers never managed to implement a new industrial policy or set up a new welfare system. Instead, they tolerated inflation, effectively pushing the pain of the sanctions away from the government and onto households and firms. They ran austerity budgets and refused to rationalize production or consumption through direct administration, such as by instituting quotas or price controls. The worsening economic crisis led to weakness in the labor market, allowing employers to engage in wage repression and leading to further pressure on household incomes. At first, this may seem like a policy failure. But in reality, Iranian authorities appear perfectly content to see economic activity slow. Doing so, they believe, will give them staying power in their confrontation with the United States. GOOD TIMES, BAD TIMES Microeconomic data reveal the effects of U.S. pressure on economic activity at the firm and household level. A review of Purchasing Managers’ Index data compiled by Iran’s Chamber of Commerce makes clear how the country’s economic crisis has intensified. Between 2019 and 2023, Iran’s overall economy was in contraction for two-thirds of the period thanks to Trump’s initial maximum pressure sanctions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and disruptions related to the “Women, Life, Freedom” protests. But throughout this period, Iranian non-oil industries experienced modest growth. At the start of 2023, Iran even began to exit its long recession as the overall economy and the industrial sector grew in tandem. By March 2024, living standards were beginning to rise again, buoyed by a roughly 15 percent increase in real incomes. This recovery was derailed by the April 2024 Israeli airstrikes on Iran. Since then, the economic uncertainty associated with recurring military conflict has triggered a prolonged decline in industrial activity, pushing Iran into an even deeper recession. Industrial firms have reported deteriorating conditions for eight consecutive months. But that does not mean these firms are insolvent. Over the last two decades, Iranian companies have developed a practice of maintaining large inventories. This practice allows firms to mitigate the effects of sanctions on supply chains and helps shore balance sheets in a high-inflation environment in which cash loses its value but goods do not. According to filings made by companies listed on the Tehran Stock Exchange, the average “days inventory outstanding” level among Iranian industries is around three months. In sensitive sectors such as electrical machinery, which has been heavily targeted by U.S. restrictions, firms maintain inventories as high as 200 days. These large inventories have been a source of significant economic resilience during the war. Iranian supply chains came under strain as ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dwindled. A shift toward overland trade could not compensate for the loss of container traffic through Iran’s southern ports. But with an ample inventory of raw materials, semifinished goods, and finished products, Iranian producers could keep customers supplied—or at least customers with the means to pay. Tehran has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. Firms kept raising prices to protect their margins, passing higher input costs onto consumers. And as the war continued, these higher prices led to demand destruction. Iranian households, embattled by years of persistent inflation, began to consume less. When they did buy, they increasingly relied on consumer credit, including new buy-now-pay-later schemes and informal loans. Even in special categories such as food, Iranian retailers reported diminished sales volume. The sharp drop in household consumption is clear evidence that economic welfare in Iran is declining. It is why Iranian officials have been forced to acknowledge the pain felt by ordinary people. But even so, the government has thus far failed to intervene to control rising prices. Not only have officials failed to introduce price controls—a move that successfully blunted the economic pain associated with the Iran-Iraq War 40 years ago—they have also discussed the elimination of cash transfers and energy subsidies for large portions of the population. In this respect, demand destruction has acted as a form of rationing, providing a structured way for Iranian political and economic elites to push the costs of the war and sanctions onto ordinary people. Although the government continues to face significant fiscal pressure, it has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. With a monthly inflation rate of under ten percent, Iran is still a long way from the kind of hyperinflation—typified by monthly inflation of over 50 percent—that will make the government’s strategy untenable. Meanwhile, reduced economic activity has provided buffers for the real economy. In financial terms, the Iranian economy is in a worse position than at the outset of the war, but in functional terms, inventory levels are unchanged from December 2025, and supply and demand may find a new balance at a lower level of overall economic activity. Iran’s foremost vulnerability to sanctions and the blockade remains its persistent need for imports, which totaled $17 billion in the first five months of this Iranian calendar year beginning in March. That means imports will likely total around $40 billion by the end of the year, down significantly from $58 billion in the previous year and $72 billion in the year before that. The fall in import demand, driven by inflation and currency devaluation, is evidence of a deeper economic crisis. But in the near term, it will help Iranian policymakers forestall a wider economic collapse, possibly for several years. LOW POWER MODE When Bessent evoked the imagery of an “economic D-Day” in his August press conference, he failed to consider who is standing on the other side of his planned invasion. Although it may not seem like it, the success of Iranian authorities in transferring the costs of both sanctions and the war onto ordinary people represents a form of wartime mobilization. Ordinary Iranians may not wish to be mobilized in this way, but they do not have a choice. In a recent social media post, Trump asked, “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” But even if ordinary Iranians were to take to the streets again to protest the financial repression they are enduring, they would once again face the brutal violence of the Islamic Republic. With multiple repressive tools at their disposal, many Iranian leaders believe that the country’s population can be made to tolerate more pain, especially if it is necessary to defeat the United States militarily. To prevail in its economic war, the Trump administration will thus need to asphyxiate 25 million households and more than one million firms. But as breathing slows in parts of Iran’s economy, ample oxygen will remain for the country’s elite.
