item.title: Milei Renews Argentina’s Falklands Push
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.96
Milei Renews Argentina’s Falklands Push Buenos Aires is taking advantage of fraying ties between the United States and Britain. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Argentine President Javier Milei’s renewed push for the Falkland Islands, clashes between the Houthis and government forces in Yemen, and international airlines halting flights to Russia. World Brief will be off on Monday, Sept. 7, for the U.S. holiday of Labor Day. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Argentine President Javier Milei’s renewed push for the Falkland Islands, clashes between the Houthis and government forces in Yemen, and international airlines halting flights to Russia. World Brief will be off on Monday, Sept. 7, for the U.S. holiday of Labor Day. Falklands at the Forefront In a nationally televised address on Thursday, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to sanction companies drilling for oil near the Falkland Islands, a British-controlled territory that is also claimed by Argentina. Milei also announced new funding for a naval base in the country’s southernmost province, which would increase Buenos Aires’s military presence near the islands. “Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security,” Milei said, using the Argentine term for the archipelago. The sanctions threat is aimed at halting development on the Sea Lion project, a deep-sea oil field operated by the U.K.’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum. The companies intend to start drilling in the next few months and begin pumping oil in 2028. Rockhopper said in a statement that it doesn’t expect Milei’s announcement to have a “material effect” on those plans. U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, meanwhile, affirmed Britain’s “absolute and unshakeable” commitment to the Falklands on social media. “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” he said, referring to a 2013 referendum in which the islands’ residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining in the United Kingdom. Britain has ruled the islands almost continuously since 1833. In 1982, the Falklands War erupted when Argentina seized the islands. The British military retook the territory after 74 days, but the dispute over the islands’ sovereignty remains contentious. When Argentina and England met on the soccer pitch during the World Cup this summer, Argentina’s players celebrated their victory by holding a banner reading “Las Malvinas Son Argentinas” (“The Falklands Are Argentine”). When he took office in 2023, Milei appeared to de-emphasize the Falklands to prioritize a closer relationship with the United States, which has long maintained neutrality on the issue. However, he has increasingly expressed the traditional Argentine position in recent months in what some analysts see as an effort to counter falling domestic ratings. “Milei’s belated embrace of the Falklands demonstrates why Argentina’s claim to the islands will only grow more insistent going forward: Domestic politicians almost universally use the Falklands to prove their nationalist credentials,” Antonio De Loera-Brust wrote in Foreign Policy in July. Milei’s move to reignite the Falklands issue was also likely influenced by Britain’s fraying ties with the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump hinted earlier on Thursday that he may not support Britain in a conflict over the islands because of the country’s lack of support for the U.S. war against Iran. During his speech, Milei praised Trump and stressed the leaders’ close relationship. “Claiming British territory is no longer the obstacle that it once was for Argentina’s ties with Europe and the United States, which means that Argentine leaders no longer have to choose between issues,” writes De Loera-Brust. Today’s Most Read - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Ukraine’s Mood Swing by Adrian Karatnycky What We’re Following Escalating violence. At least 81 people were killed and thousands displaced in Yemen after the Iran-backed Houthis launched a ground assault on Thursday toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key chokepoint for international shipping at the southern end of the Red Sea. The attack is part of a Houthi effort to sever the government-controlled city of Taiz from the coast, capture the port city of Mokha, and ultimately control all traffic through the strait. Since declaring a blockade on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in July, the Houthis have continued to attack Saudi ships and facilities, raising concerns that a full-blown war with Riyadh could reignite. That would add an additional squeeze on global shipping and energy prices. U.S. diesel prices on Friday hit an all-time high at $5.85 a gallon. Experts say fuel prices are likely to stay high until shipping fully resumes in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance insisted on Thursday that the Trump administration is doing “a lot of things” to pressure Iran to stop shooting at commercial ships in the strait, and on Friday, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions against a minor Turkish investment bank and two subsidiaries that do business with Tehran. “While we hope no more banks will need to be sanctioned, that ultimately depends on how quickly the international community comes to its senses and ceases support of the murderous Iranian regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Yet repeated U.S. military strikes, an oil blockade, and crushing economic sanctions have so far failed to convince Iran’s leadership to back down. Treacherous skies. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that international airlines are beginning to heed his call to suspend flights to Russia. This follows his announcement earlier this week that Ukraine would be expanding drone attacks near Russian airports in an effort to disrupt Moscow’s economy. Ninety-seven flights to Russia were canceled on Thursday, according to data from FlightRadar24, including services operated by Turkish, Emirati, Egyptian, Armenian, Kuwaiti, and Tajik airlines. Air Tanzania announced that flights to Moscow would be suspended until Monday. “[W]e are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said in a Tuesday post on X. Ukraine has intensified its air campaign against Russia in recent months, with a new peak of around 16,000 drones crossing into Russian airspace in August. According to Russia’s Defense Ministry, its forces downed 416 Ukrainian drones between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. Fraught forum. The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), a six-day gathering of officials from 18 countries and territories, came to a close on Friday. The region has emerged as a primary strategic arena in the past decade amid a battle for influence between global powers such as China and the United States. The meetings, which were held in Palau this year—one of only 11 countries worldwide that recognize Taiwan—were marred by geopolitical tensions. Addressing China’s ballistic missile test-launch in the South Pacific in July was at the top of the agenda. But although the forum members agreed on Thursday to register their collective “concern” about the launch, the statement was far from a harsh rebuke, and even then it wasn’t unanimous: Nauru, an island nation that severed its diplomatic ties with Taiwan in 2024, dissented. Nevertheless, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told reporters that he thought the assembly had “got to a very good place,” and that even though Nauru “dissociated itself” from the joint statement, “that shouldn’t be a reason for why we shouldn’t be able to express a PIF position or a consensus position.” Last-minute withdrawals of top leaders from five member nations—Kiribati, Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa, and the Solomon Islands—overshadowed proceedings from the get-go and prompted suggestions that Chinese influence, stemming from its displeasure over the host location, could be to blame. New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters refrained from directly accusing Beijing of interfering, but he said that the collective absence was “highly suspicious.” What in the World? Provisional results on Tuesday showed that voters had approved a referendum on a new constitution in Guinea-Bissau. The new charter would expand presidential authority. Which of the below is not one of the powers it would grant to the president? A. Appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet B. Create and abolish ministries C. Unilaterally determine the military’s annual budget D. Dissolve parliament in a political crisis Odds and Ends It may be that “good things come to those who wait,” especially when it comes to the famously long Guinness pour, which takes 119.5 seconds to complete. But thieves wasted no time pulling off a heist of two truckloads of the stout beer this week from a depot near Liverpool in the United Kingdom. British police are now trying to recover the 70,000 pints, worth $155,000. Here’s hoping the thieves don’t plan to drink it all themselves. And the Answer Is… A. Unilaterally determine the military’s annual budget Coup leaders across Africa have changed strategies to retain power, sometimes extending transitional government windows, delaying elections, or using elections to legitimize their continued grip on power, Salah Ben Hammou and Sydney Dobbins wrote in July 2025. To take the rest of FP’s weekly international news quiz, click here, or sign up to be alerted when a new one is published. Maxine Davey is an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy. item.title: What 6 Different Versions of This Sex Comedy Say About the Countries That Made Them
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.89
Some fears transcend language, transcend cultures. The howl of a wolf, the scream of a hawk, or the doorbell ring of neighbors you invited over but now wish would go away. The uncanny mix of attraction, resentment, jealousy, and annoyance felt toward those we only hear through floorboards and glimpse in elevators is at the center of the droll apartment farce The Invite. The low-budget comedy debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and, thanks to good word of mouth, emerged as an unexpected summer hit alongside special effects blockbusters like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. It is now available to stream in North America, and as you’ll see, it’s a tale that echoes around the world. Some fears transcend language, transcend cultures. The howl of a wolf, the scream of a hawk, or the doorbell ring of neighbors you invited over but now wish would go away. The uncanny mix of attraction, resentment, jealousy, and annoyance felt toward those we only hear through floorboards and glimpse in elevators is at the center of the droll apartment farce The Invite. The low-budget comedy debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and, thanks to good word of mouth, emerged as an unexpected summer hit alongside special effects blockbusters like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. It is now available to stream in North America, and as you’ll see, it’s a tale that echoes around the world. The Invite takes place over one night and is set almost entirely in one location—a desirable-but-not-ostentatious San Francisco apartment in a sonically porous building. The apartment is owned by a jaded music instructor who has abandoned his rock star dreams (we learn he inherited the pad from his parents) played by Seth Rogen, and his deeply unhappy wife played by Olivia Wilde (who is also the director of the film). There’s an early-teens daughter in the mix, but she’s luckily away for the night, so Wilde’s character has sprung a surprise dinner party on her husband. The neighbors, the ones they talk about constantly, are coming over. The ongoing spousal chatter, which is partially a source of shared humor but mostly a wellspring of deeply held animus, comes from the upstairs couple’s regular and thunderous lovemaking sessions—a matrimonial hobby we’ll soon learn the downstairs couple have long since quit. The upstairs duo is played by Edward Norton, a kind but devilish firefighter, and Spanish actor Penélope Cruz, a ravishing, earthy therapist who exudes continental sophistication and excitement. In short time, the downstairs couple reveal themselves to be a bickering, miserable mess, but they briefly put aside their sniping when the upstairs couple shares that they are swingers, and the sleep-depriving sounds come from group sex adventures with a revolving door of participants. As the evening continues, the titular invite comes—would Rogen and Wilde’s characters, neurotic sourpusses though they may be, care to join Norton and Cruz’s for an intimate interlude? The movie is extremely funny, but also insightful and sad, thanks to a sharp screenplay by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones, as well as all four of the performances—especially Wilde, who skitters between debilitating insecurity, marital revulsion, and brazen lust, sometimes all within the same shot. She’s given life-or-death stakes to what could otherwise be a diverting filmed play, aided by rapid editing and a tension-rich original score by Devonté Hynes. The movie is a highwire act, and during the promotional cycle, she regularly cited the influence of Mike Nichols’ adaptation of Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, a key New Hollywood text. Wilde’s references to Nichols are certainly apt, but deviate from a more exact comparison: The Invite is a remake of a recent Spanish film, The People Upstairs (also called Sentimental), which writer-director Cesc Gay adapted from his own play. The People Upstairs came out in 2020 and between then and Wilde’s film’s release, there were four (yes, four) other versions of this story produced—in Switzerland, Italy, South Korea, and France. (A Belgian/Dutch version is en route.) While international remakes are not uncommon, I feel confident in saying that what’s happened with Gay’s work is unprecedented both in its speed and numbers. In the early days of “talking pictures,” one could sometimes find business-minded producers who would crank out alternates of a movie using the same sets and crew but (usually) different actors in different languages for foreign markets. Most of these iterations are now considered lost films, but several are notable. The all-star revue Paramount on Parade from 1930 holds the record with 13 different variants, including ones in Hungarian and Serbian. When Alfred Hitchcock shot Murder! in 1930, he stayed in the director’s chair for the German version, released as Mary in 1931. (He was used to this sort of thing, having filmed both the silent and talking versions of Blackmail in 1929.) Translations went the other way, too. An English version of Josef von Sternberg’s 1930 classic The Blue Angel starring Marlene Dietrich was considered lost for decades until a copy was found in a German archive and presented in 2009. The most celebrated example is George Melford’s Spanish-language Dracula from 1931, which was shot at night (spooky!) after Bela Lugosi and director Tod Browning left Universal’s stages. That English-language Dracula gave us iconic lines like “I never drink … wine,” and was, of course, an instant classic, but if you have hours to kill, I recommend visiting film snob message boards to see how many cinephiles are eager to argue that the Spanish Dracula is greatly superior. (I say they are both good!) But there’s a key difference between then and now. The profusion of versions of The People Upstairs does not represent a production entity looking to maximize profit. It is an organic recognition of a story with legs across different cultures. From a practical standpoint, one can see why local film industries, still wobbly from COVID safety protocols in the early part of this decade, would want to sink their teeth into a one-location movie with just four performers. Quick and easy. But those mechanics aside, what does it say about the world that so many of us are understood to be interested in sex-deprived married couples thunderstruck by their lustful neighbors? Of the six versions of this film that now exist, only the original Spanish and current Hollywood versions are easily found in North America. But leaping across borders is what we at Foreign Policy are all about. After many rounds of emails, Instagram DMs, and the deployment of some translation software, I am proud to say that I have seen each rendition. I immersed myself in this tale of would-be spouse-swapping hoping to learn more about specific cultures. Whether or not my discoveries are truly foundational to a national character is open to discussion, but pages and pages of notes show that this exercise was, if nothing else, fascinating. For starters, I now know that German-speaking Swiss are more into slapstick than I was previously aware, if Die Nachbarn von Oben (The Neighbors From Upstairs) director Sabine Boss is a true representative. Like Brahms interpreting Handel, some scenes of Cesc Gay’s original Spanish film only exist in the bones of each variation, but a few melodic lines remain constant. All six versions retain the reveal that the downstairs woman intentionally crosses her unshaded window while naked, knowing that the upstairs man is likely looking at her. Similarly, she urges her husband not to complain about the lovemaking upstairs because she is happy that the upstairs woman is having such aggressive orgasms—and Wilde is terrified that discussing it will ruin it for her. (This is played as a joke.) There’s also a big laugh across all six versions when the invitation comes, and the downstairs woman starts verbally going through her calendar, causing the downstairs man to complain that it isn’t normal to schedule an orgy. In the Hollywood version, Cruz’s exoticism comes from her Iberian origins, and she even brings over a flan. No other version makes her a foreigner, and in the Spanish, Swiss, and Italian versions, she makes an unspecified Indian dish that is spicy and (the upstairs man jokes) an aphrodisiac. In the French version, she makes “tapas,” and in the South Korean version, some kind of elaborate fried eggplant on a cake stand with a bow on it. Music comes up a lot. In the Hollywood film, the downstairs husband is a frustrated rock musician. In Spain and Switzerland, his repertoire is classical piano; in Italy, it is jazz. In South Korea, he’s not a musician at all, but a film director stuck in years of development on a television project he isn’t that enthusiastic about to begin with. The South Korean film (also called The People Upstairs) is the version with some of the bigger changes. For starters, the downstairs neighbors do not have kids or a pet. (The French version includes not just a daughter, but a pivotal dog.) Moreover, the upstairs sex-positive neighbors are deliberately cast as older and more conservatively dressed. Indeed, the upstairs woman looks like a newscaster and the upstairs man initially comes across as a bit of a dork, wearing a cardigan with ducks on it. Each version shows that the downstairs man has an office, but the South Korean spin strongly suggests that it functions as his nightly bedroom. There’s a gag in each film when the downstairs couple admits how long it has been since they last made love. Most versions, including the Rogen-Wilde version, say “about a year.” But the South Korean couple say four years. (The French version evades the question with, “I can’t even remember the last time.”) Indeed, the two ends of the sexuality spectrum are represented by South Korea and France. In every version, when the upstairs neighbors talk about their group sex encounters, they say they usually limit them to four to six people, except one time when there was 10 for someone’s birthday. (This builds to a variation of a “well, birthdays are special” joke.) The French version keeps this gag but doubles the number: There were 20 participants one New Year’s Eve, apparently. There’s also a funny moment where the upstairs neighbors talk about sexual boundaries and proclivities, with some versions getting more lewd than others. (Quite frankly, the Hollywood version may be the dirtiest of them all.) In multiple versions, the upstairs man declares that his partner is fond of anal sex, and she plain-facedly confirms it. But the South Korean version includes dialogue about enjoying sex “Korean style.” (Here I must tell you, reader, that I have no clue what this means. Furthermore, asking Google “what is Korean-style sex” did nothing but poison my algorithm such that I can no longer use my laptop at the public library. We’re just going to have to accept that not everything translates.) All six versions of the movie build to their conclusion by raising the stakes in different ways. Seth Rogen’s back gives out in the Hollywood version; in the Swiss film, there’s a piano on fire then drunken nakedness. The French version, however, has a wild twist: The off-screen daughter isn’t a preteen at a friend’s sleepover, but a 20-year-old who only comes back from school now and again. It is soon discovered that a particularly noisy night of lovemaking came from the upstairs man seducing her. (To his credit, he didn’t realize who she was.) While this leads to expected anger from the downstairs man, the upstairs woman is also upset—because she wasn’t involved. “We’re supposed to be libertines together!” she cries. (The downstairs woman, the mother of the seduced, isn’t too bothered by the story at all, for what it’s worth.) Across the six films, the story ends with the downstairs couple confronting the fact that their marriage has collapsed, and the next step—separation—is presented as a reasonable, maybe even happy, ending. The big question is whether or not they go through with it or stay in their rut. All versions are ambiguous. The Spanish, Swiss, and Italian versions suggest rapprochement. (I’ve barely mentioned the Italian version, simply called Neighbors, because it’s pretty boring—though it does feature the nicest apartment.) The French and Hollywood versions lean more toward a breakup, but suggest that, in deciding to do so, the couple will grow in maturity and maybe even deepen their friendship. The South Korean version is the true outlier—our younger couple downstairs seems to be quite happy, and maybe, just maybe, has gotten there thanks to their new hobby of swinging. If and when that version (called The People Upstairs, for future reference) ever becomes more widely available, you can watch it and judge for yourself. Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central New Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: The U.S. and China Don’t Need an AI Grand Bargain
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.61
The U.S. and China Don’t Need an AI Grand Bargain The countries can cooperate—even without trust or consensus. The U.S. debate over how to navigate China’s role in developing and governing advanced artificial intelligence is stuck between two extremes. One camp calls for full-blown international treaties even though the two countries cannot yet agree on AI’s most serious risks, let alone how to manage them. The other is deeply skeptical of dialogue, believing progress will only be possible if the Chinese side is desperate. A grand bargain may be too ambitious, yet focusing only on what can be agreed on today could lock both sides into a policy regime that becomes obsolete as technology evolves. Doing nothing is even worse because regardless of whether it was developed in San Francisco or Hangzhou, an AI model that makes it easier for terrorists to synthesize deadly pathogens or hack into the infrastructure that underpins financial markets threatens everyone. These risks are becoming all too real as AI systems demonstrate cyber- and biological capabilities that match or exceed those of human experts on increasingly complex tasks. The U.S. debate over how to navigate China’s role in developing and governing advanced artificial intelligence is stuck between two extremes. One camp calls for full-blown international treaties even though the two countries cannot yet agree on AI’s most serious risks, let alone how to manage them. The other is deeply skeptical of dialogue, believing progress will only be possible if the Chinese side is desperate. A grand bargain may be too ambitious, yet focusing only on what can be agreed on today could lock both sides into a policy regime that becomes obsolete as technology evolves. Doing nothing is even worse because regardless of whether it was developed in San Francisco or Hangzhou, an AI model that makes it easier for terrorists to synthesize deadly pathogens or hack into the infrastructure that underpins financial markets threatens everyone. These risks are becoming all too real as AI systems demonstrate cyber- and biological capabilities that match or exceed those of human experts on increasingly complex tasks. The recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, in which AI agents collaborated to break out of their testing environment and gain access to the internal infrastructure of external organizations, made clear that AI already operates beyond human control in ways that can unwittingly impact third parties. It is only a matter of time before these threats cross borders, and Beijing will certainly want clarity from Washington should one of its companies become the next accidental victim of a U.S. model going rogue—and vice versa. As Tsinghua University’s Xiao Qian recently wrote in Foreign Policy, “Sustained dialogue is a strategic necessity.” She is right. And there is a middle path forward. When U.S. and Chinese delegations gather this month to discuss AI risks, rather than pursuing a comprehensive agreement, they should start with a series of narrower measures focused on preventing extreme risks, managing crises, and investing in verification tools. Each small agreement helps build the understanding and trust needed for more ambitious deals, allowing the two countries to cooperate where they already agree without requiring consensus on everything else. Of course, any bilateral agreement must recognize the powerful incentives for governments and companies on both sides to continue competing against each other. But even within this environment, each country can take steps that advance its own interests while building tools that make reciprocal commitments more credible down the line. One of the biggest obstacles for negotiators is that neither country has developed tools that can confidently evaluate whether AI models are safe, nor safeguards capable of mitigating AI’s most extreme risks. These challenges affect both countries but are particularly acute for China, whose AI safety evaluations are improving but still less mature than the West’s. Given the transnational nature of AI risks, it is in both countries’ interests to have robust safety infrastructure, but governments have been hesitant to participate in technical exchanges, afraid of revealing information that could enhance a rival’s capabilities. But it is possible to have carefully scoped, working-level technical exchanges that discuss best practices without exposing models’ inner workings, vulnerabilities, or advanced capabilities. In general, the two sides should compare broad approaches but withhold tactical details and refrain from granular, riskier discussions of the specific methods they use to elicit unsafe model behavior. They could, for instance, discuss how to scale evaluations to cover more models, behaviors, and potential threats, as well as how to use AI systems themselves to help identify and respond to threats. They could also discuss important, publicly available lessons on monitoring AI models to ensure they don’t escape their sandboxes—a topic that should be of mutual concern following the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. The two sides should also discuss safeguards using the same principles, comparing general approaches to detecting harmful activity, restricting dangerous use, and managing risks once models are deployed without discussing specific techniques for bypassing safeguards or proprietary details about how models are built. U.S. experts might be able to offer insights from how they determined which actors should have access to Mythos, Anthropic’s most advanced model, explaining the broad criteria they used to evaluate safeguard effectiveness. They should also talk about the limitations to their current safeguards, explaining how they decided when dangerous, dual-use capabilities warranted tighter restrictions on model access. Similarly, U.S. third-party evaluators could use the public report from METR and Redwood Research on the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident to examine why safeguards were insufficient. If these discussions go well, a next step could be to create technical working groups to establish voluntary best practices, soliciting input from companies and independent third-party organizations. China would ultimately assess lessons from these exchanges on its own terms, but insights that align with its national security interests could shape decisions that reduce risks for everyone. Even if the United States and China have a mutual understanding of AI risks and do everything they can to mitigate them, serious crises can still unfold. Though China has the world’s most extensive AI regulations, it lacks clear rules for catastrophic risk management. The biggest U.S. AI companies are now subject to California’s SB 53 law, which requires them to disclose safety practices, report certain critical safety incidents, and protect whistleblowers. But these rules have not yet been federally adopted, limiting what the government can do when a serious incident occurs. Thus, the United States and China should discuss how to share key information and communicate effectively in a crisis. On the domestic front, each side should commit to setting up its own reporting systems to track cases where AI caused, or may cause, material harm—for example, if a model escapes a contained sandbox to attack telecommunications infrastructure or gain access to sensitive medical patient data. These incident-reporting systems can vary according to each country’s preferences, but they should collect broadly similar information and have similar categories and thresholds for severity. In parallel, the countries should explore creating a bilateral information-sharing channel, which would be voluntary at first, with the ability to change requirements later on. U.S. companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have already voluntarily shared information on certain safety incidents, but having a private channel can help both sides navigate cross-border incidents and proactively warn counterparts if a model is behaving in unintended ways that might be perceived as malicious. Critically, though, crisis channels must fit how governments actually make decisions. Chinese interlocutors, for example, have explained in Track 2 conversations that they face strong disincentives from answering phone calls on “hotlines” because no individual answering the call has the authority to respond without consulting superiors. Using written communication could circumvent some of those challenges. Even if the United States and China wanted to reach a bilateral AI agreement, they might not trust that the other side will follow through on its commitments. Tools that enable both countries to verify the other’s compliance can allow both sides to feel confident about the other’s safety practices. This mutual confidence, in turn, could enable further agreements and governance applications. The first verification prototypes are just now being developed, and it may take years until they are sufficiently mature and trusted by both countries. That’s why the United States and China need to begin talking about the technology now, explicitly supporting technical research to develop verification tools for bilateral AI agreements. China has been historically hesitant to participate in hardware-based verification regimes. These concerns could be alleviated if the two countries discussed at these early stages what types of verification technologies could be politically acceptable and who should build them to make them credible to both sides. And if specific proposals are brought to the table, the delegations could have a more concrete discussion on a given technology’s strengths and limitations. The United States and China may never need some of these tools, and the agreements they could enable may ultimately not be desirable. But developing credible verification technologies takes both time and institutional capacity, and to be useful, they must be designed and built long before they are needed. The upcoming dialogue should not be evaluated on whether the United States and China reach full agreement on all these issues. It will be a success if it lays the foundation for a serious second meeting and eventually a permanent high-level channel supported by both leaders. If talks break down early, the two sides might not get back to the negotiation table for months or even years. These goals may seem modest, given the urgent need for international cooperation to combat extreme risks. But sequenced strategically, small diplomatic breakthroughs may lead to more ambitious measures, and each minor agreement will open possibilities for the next. The United States and China may be competing to build the potentially defining technology of our time, but rivalry need not foreclose pragmatism. This September, both countries can take the first step in that direction. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: What in the World?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.20
What in the World? Test yourself on the week of Aug. 29: Iceland votes, China threatens Pacific island nations, and Guinea-Bissau approves a new constitution. September arrived without any resolution to several global conflicts. Were you able to look beyond those front-page headlines to keep up with the world’s other developments? Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. September arrived without any resolution to several global conflicts. Were you able to look beyond those front-page headlines to keep up with the world’s other developments? 1. Voters in Iceland on Sunday rejected a government proposal to reopen talks to do what? 2. U.S. President Donald Trump posted an artificial intelligence-generated video on Sunday depicting U.S. military forces doing what? Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran has almost certainly irreparably damaged his foreign-policy toolkit and led to the premature peak of his global influence, FP’s Ravi Agrawal writes in an exclusive prerelease from our latest magazine. 3. Why did China’s Pacific islands envoy on Monday threaten “consequences” for participating members of the Pacific Island Forum, which held a meeting this week? 4. Why did the United Nations’ food agency say on Tuesday that it is halving food assistance to Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank starting this month? 5. Provisional results on Tuesday showed that voters had approved a referendum on a new constitution in Guinea-Bissau. The new charter would expand presidential authority. Which of the below is not one of the powers it would grant to the president? Coup leaders across Africa have changed strategies to retain power, sometimes extending transitional government windows, delaying elections, or using elections to legitimize their continued grip on power, Salah Ben Hammou and Sydney Dobbins wrote in July 2025. 6. Oil giant Chevron confirmed on Wednesday that it planned to expand its operations in which Latin American country? Also this week, Trump announced an agreement with Venezuela’s interim government that will allow the United States to take a partial stake in Venezuela’s oil. The deal won’t lower gas prices anytime soon and is likely illegal, FP’s Keith Johnson reports. 7. Argentine President Javier Milei said on Thursday that he would assert the country’s claims on the Falkland Islands, currently a British overseas territory, by doing what? 8. Finland’s border guard said on Friday that it was investigating whether an object found on its southern shore had violated its territory. What was the object? The discovery comes as Germany and Russia escalate a diplomatic standoff over what is believed to be an attempted Russian drone attack on German territory, FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports in World Brief. 9. Soccer superstar Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international soccer on Monday. Across 21 years as a member of the Argentina national team, Messi scored 125 goals, placing him second in all-time goals scored by men at the international level. Who is in first place? 10. French President Emmanuel Macron joined King Charles III, Queen Camilla, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British Museum in London on Wednesday to view a nearly 1,000-year-old embroidery depicting what event? You scored It’s a big world out there! Brush up on global goings-on by subscribing to World Brief, Foreign Policy’s flagship daily newsletter. Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. Drew Gorman is a deputy copy editor at Foreign Policy. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: What Was the War on Terror?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.55
What Was the War on Terror? A defining period in U.S. foreign policy has ended, but it remains misunderstood. The war on terror is over. It lasted from Sept. 11, 2001, to the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021. As we approach the 25th anniversary of 9/11, it is useful for both historical and policy reasons to define the parameters of this conflict. The war on terror had three primary qualities that define it as a historical period. The first was that policymakers viewed terrorism as a form of war and a high-level strategic threat. The second was that counterterrorism strategy sought not only to protect the U.S. homeland but to change the international system in order to attack the root causes of terrorism. The third was that the war on terror was essentially an attempt to deal with the rise of global jihadism. The war on terror is over. It lasted from Sept. 11, 2001, to the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021. As we approach the 25th anniversary of 9/11, it is useful for both historical and policy reasons to define the parameters of this conflict. The war on terror had three primary qualities that define it as a historical period. The first was that policymakers viewed terrorism as a form of war and a high-level strategic threat. The second was that counterterrorism strategy sought not only to protect the U.S. homeland but to change the international system in order to attack the root causes of terrorism. The third was that the war on terror was essentially an attempt to deal with the rise of global jihadism. These three traits have now faded or been eclipsed by other priorities. The era in which terrorism formed the lodestar for U.S. strategy has ended. Realizing this not only helps policymakers situate themselves in the world but offers them the chance to bury habits that plagued U.S. foreign policy during the war on terror itself. These habits included the tendency to concede too much to countries that assisted in fighting terrorism and turning other countries’ terrorist enemies into U.S. enemies. On a basic level, the war on terror was a response to 9/11, which vaulted terrorism to the top of the strategic hierarchy. On a deeper level, however, it was a response to the vulnerabilities engendered by a globalizing world. The 9/11 attacks marked the culmination of modern international terrorism, an asymmetrical strategy in which small groups seek to take advantage of changes in media, transportation, and weaponry to gain leverage and attention. It prompted a shift to a new bipartisan paradigm for viewing terrorism as war rather than crime. This had been a back-and-forth debate for decades, but 9/11 demonstrated that terrorism had the potential to disrupt modern society and destroy human life on a mass scale. It prompted a shift to an offensive military approach that sought not only to hunt terrorist groups around the world but also to remove or punish the regimes that supported them. The war on terror’s next essential trait was that terrorism needed to be countered on a systemic level through political reform. U.S. President George W. Bush and his administration concluded that the stagnant, autocratic status quo in the Middle East was breeding radicalism and needed to be changed. This was the foundation of the Freedom Agenda, or the idea that democratizing and modernizing the Middle East would resolve terrorism’s root causes. Finally, the war on terror stemmed—on a structural level—from the escalating efforts of radical Islamists to collapse the U.S.-backed order in the Middle East by driving the United States out. While this was not a “clash of civilizations,” the United States conducted military operations almost exclusively against radical Islamists. Terrorism was not the enemy; for U.S. policymakers, the enemy was radical Islamist groups and the regimes that sustained them. These were the war on terror’s defining characteristics: the war paradigm, the linkage of reform and counterterrorism, and the struggle with global jihadism. Still, this was not a homogeneous conflict. The war on terror had three phases, which are defined by changes in objectives, domestic politics, and the perception of the threat’s severity, creating significant overlap between presidencies. The first phase, which I call the radical phase, dates roughly from 2001 to 2006, when the George W. Bush administration launched an ambitious project that included regime change wars and intensive nation-building crusades. It asserted a unilateral right to strike nations that were ostensibly developing weapons of mass destruction and supporting terrorists, even if it could not prove an attack was imminent. The administration also concluded that the world order and Middle Eastern politics must be transformed in order to address terrorism’s origins, which it believed emerged from the despair and anger bred by the Middle East’s deficits of democracy and modernity. This became a critical justification for the Iraq War as well as increased pressure on Arab allies to open their political systems. This phase of the war on terror was radical in both its means and its ends, but it burned out quickly. Iraq’s collapse into civil war fueled the jihadist problem. In Afghanistan, the security and hope of building democracy faded as the Taliban reemerged in the mid-2000s. Finally, efforts to pressure Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to reform fizzled, and Hamas’s victory in the 2006 Gaza elections soured U.S. officials on democracy promotion. The demise of the radical vision prompted a shift to the second phase: consolidation, which dates roughly from 2007 to 2018. Consolidation was defined by efforts to lower strategic expectations, put counterterrorism on a more sustainable basis, and gradually relegate it behind other priorities. This phase began under the George W. Bush administration with the moderation of rhetoric about democracy and the lowering of ambitions. The 2007 troop surge in Iraq, for instance, was aimed not at democratization but at rescuing the country from civil war. U.S. President Barack Obama continued consolidation, although his counterterrorism policies were more limited in scope and objectives. He had opposed the Iraq War, and he did not prioritize global hegemony or democratization. However, terrorism was still a high priority for Obama, and he intensified nation-building efforts in Afghanistan as a means of counterterrorism. In late 2009, he sent an additional 30,000 troops to Afghanistan to wage a counterinsurgency war and expand the central government’s writ into the countryside. However, in keeping with his desire for a more balanced approach, Obama also imposed an 18-month timeline for drawing down the surge. In the early 2010s, Obama devised a more sustainable counterterrorism approach that would still be effective but enable a shift to other concerns. In his light footprint strategy, he limited troop deployments while using special forces, drones, and intelligence resources to kill and capture terrorist leaders and disrupt their operational capacity. He defined this as moving away from “a boundless global war on terror” toward “targeted efforts to dismantle specific networks of violent extremists.” However, Obama’s attempt to level out the war on terror was disrupted in 2014 by the Islamic State’s seizure of swathes of territory in Iraq and Syria. The Islamic State also formed or inspired cells that carried out attacks in Europe and the United States. Obama responded with a “by, with, and through” strategy that provided weapons, intelligence, training, special operations, and air support to forces combatting the Islamic State. Obama also had to reescalate in Afghanistan in response to a series of Taliban offensives in 2015 and 2016. While the number of U.S. troops devoted to counterterrorism declined significantly under Obama, his role in the war on terror was essentially consolidation of terrorism as a major priority of U.S. foreign policy. U.S. President Donald Trump’s first two years in office continued consolidation while taking a further step back from political reform and nation-building. He blasted the Freedom Agenda and counterinsurgency wars as a waste of lives and resources. Instead, he promised a legally unrestrained counterterrorism campaign. As president, he increased the use of drones, loosened targeting restrictions, and embraced autocratic allies in the struggle against terrorism. Nonetheless, Trump’s impulses were modulated by his tendency to let his more conventional advisors handle policy details. Much of the counterterrorism machine that Bush and Obama had created churned onward, especially in the continuing struggle against the Islamic State, wherein Trump essentially continued Obama’s strategy. Trump, however, also planted the seeds for the third and final phase of the war on terror: extraction. Two key developments drove this shift. The first was the defeat of the Islamic State as a territorial entity in 2017-2018. This enabled Trump to declare victory and begin lowering the U.S. troop presence in Iraq and Syria. The second was the stagnant situation in Afghanistan. Trump believed this was a pointless conflict, and he initiated talks with the Taliban that led to the 2020 Doha Agreement. Under this deal, the United States declared that it would withdraw all troops within 14 months if the Taliban agreed to a cease-fire, talks with the Afghan government, and a guarantee to not support terrorist groups like al Qaeda. The agreement was a critical step in ending the war on terror because the United States was extracting itself, however cynically, from the original campaign of this conflict. U.S. President Joe Biden then continued Trump’s policy by beginning the removal of all troops from Afghanistan in April 2021. As the Afghan government disintegrated, he fatefully decided against reinserting U.S. forces, which enabled the Taliban to retake the country. August 2021 marked not only the end of the war in Afghanistan but also the end of the war on terror. Both Biden and Trump in his second term relegated terrorism to a lower place in the strategic hierarchy and avoided major ground deployments in support of counterterrorism. They shifted to a new set of priorities: great-power competition, nuclear proliferation, regional wars, industrial policy, and so on. Terrorism is no longer a central paradigm for U.S. foreign policy as it was during the war on terror. The idea of defeating terrorism through reform, moreover, is dead in both parties. Despite their differences, Biden and Trump finished the extraction phase of the war on terror and effectively ended this conflict. Saying that the war on terror is over does not mean that the United States is no longer conducting counterterrorism operations, as it remains engaged against al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan, and a variety of partner support and training missions. The term “war on terror” would have little value if it simply referred to any counterterrorism operation at any time. This statement also does not mean that the governmental structures and legal regimes created during this conflict have dissolved. No historical period has clean endings, but the legacy of a conflict is not the same as the conflict itself. The Cold War has enduring effects that are still playing out, but as a global competition between communist and democratic-capitalist superpowers, it firmly ended between 1989 and 1991. The same is true for the war on terror, a conflict whose consequences will spin out for decades but has essentially ended. The war on terror created many habits among U.S. policymakers that are best left in the past. One was the willingness to give the benefit of the doubt to countries like Russia and Pakistan, which, while supporting the war on terror, were working cross-purposes to U.S. interests at the same time. Russia, for example, was a critical partner in fighting jihadism in Central Asia and in sustaining logistical networks for the war in Afghanistan. However, cooperation on terrorism not only created the false hope of a better relationship with Russia but also prompted policymakers to downplay increasing signs of Russian authoritarianism and revanchism in the late 2000s and 2010s. Another problematic tendency was making other countries’ terrorist enemies into Washington’s enemies. For example, Bush dramatically expanded U.S. aid to Colombia after 9/11 to combat the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) insurgency, which the country’s leaders sold as part of the war on terror. This was a questionable use of resources to combat a group that did not threaten the U.S. homeland, and it fed the Colombian government’s brutal counterinsurgency war. In the present, the United States should not enter new wars or compromise its principles to combat other countries’ enemies, like Hamas or Hezbollah, that do not pose a significant threat to U.S. territory. Finally, acknowledging that the war on terror is over should push U.S. policymakers to accept that terrorism is a fact of life in a globalized world but not an existential threat. The belief that the United States had to conduct regime change and nation-building campaigns to remain safe from terrorism led to a vast and wasteful overextension of U.S. power that made the initial problem worse. A mix of military, intelligence, and legal tools to combat terrorism can still be effective without letting this menace swallow U.S. grand strategy as it did for the first two decades of the 21st century. Joseph Stieb is an assistant professor of history at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and the author of The Regime Change Consensus: Iraq in American Politics, 1990-2003. item.title: South Korea Should Help Defend Ukraine’s Skies
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.83
South Korea Should Help Defend Ukraine’s Skies Seoul can prove itself a genuine partner to Europe, not just an opportunist. In July, the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, Ukraine intercepted only 29 of Russia’s 195 incoming ballistic missiles, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry. As Russia intensifies its ballistic missile attacks, Ukraine is running dangerously low on the interceptors needed to defend against them. Neither of its major sources of support appears willing and able to fill the gap: European allies have already drawn heavily on their own air defense stocks, and the United States continues to deplete its own missile-defense interceptor inventories in its war against Iran. On Aug. 5, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that supplies of air defense missiles from allies this year have fallen to roughly one-third of their 2025 levels. In July, the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, Ukraine intercepted only 29 of Russia’s 195 incoming ballistic missiles, according to the Ukrainian Defense Ministry. As Russia intensifies its ballistic missile attacks, Ukraine is running dangerously low on the interceptors needed to defend against them. Neither of its major sources of support appears willing and able to fill the gap: European allies have already drawn heavily on their own air defense stocks, and the United States continues to deplete its own missile-defense interceptor inventories in its war against Iran. On Aug. 5, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that supplies of air defense missiles from allies this year have fallen to roughly one-third of their 2025 levels. Ukraine has explored domestic options to replenish supplies, including seeking permission from Washington to manufacture Patriot interceptors and developing its own Freyja ballistic missile interceptor. But Washington has so far rejected the former, and bringing the latter into service would require substantial capital; engineering work; testing; and, crucially, time. With Ukraine’s domestic capacity still years away from meeting its needs and U.S. and European supplies constrained, South Korea is one of the few countries capable of filling the gap. Zelensky has appealed to Seoul, saying: “We would very much like to receive support from South Korea in the form of what we lack—air defense systems.” But Seoul has so far declined. That is a mistake. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, South Korea has emerged as a major arms supplier to Europe. Providing air defense systems to Ukraine would give Seoul an opportunity to prove that it is not merely an arms exporter to Europe but also a genuine security partner. South Korea is particularly well suited to help, because it has developed sophisticated, multilayered missile-defense capabilities to counter North Korea’s nuclear and missile threats, and it has enough surplus to export to other countries. Its homegrown Cheongung-II system has already been battle-tested in the United Arab Emirates with a 96 percent success rate. Its systems are also competitively priced: A Cheongung-II interceptor costs about $1.1 million, roughly one-third the price of a Patriot interceptor. South Korea also produces about 95 percent of the system domestically, reducing its exposure to foreign supply-chain disruptions and export restrictions. Perhaps most importantly, South Korea is also known for its ability to scale production rapidly and deliver systems on time. Although there are concerns that South Korea may lack the capacity to provide these systems to Ukraine quickly due to high demand, its defense industry has noted that existing production facilities are operating below capacity and that factories under construction in Poland and Romania could potentially be utilized to expand production. Yet in response to Zelensky’s request, a South Korean Foreign Ministry official stated, “Our defense supplies … have been provided while complying with relevant domestic laws and policies.” Indeed, South Korea has maintained its long-standing policy of not directly supplying lethal weapons to countries at war, thus far providing Ukraine with humanitarian assistance and nonlethal military equipment and supplying ammunition indirectly through the United States. This, however, is not a categorical legal prohibition, let alone a constitutional ban, as Zelensky has suggested. Some point to Article 5, which stipulates that “The Republic of Korea shall endeavor to maintain international peace and shall renounce all aggressive wars,” as a legal basis for opposing arms transfers to Ukraine. Yet one could argue that assisting a country that has been invaded in violation of international law—and thereby helping to uphold international peace and security—is more consistent with the spirit and purpose of the article. More relevant is South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Act, which allows the government to restrict exports of defense material when necessary to maintain international peace and security, protect national security, or avoid diplomatic friction. The government retains discretion over whether to authorize such exports. The Foreign Trade Act restricts arms exports to “peaceful uses,” but it does not clearly define what constitutes a “peaceful use.” Whether to provide Ukraine with air defense systems is thus, fundamentally, a political choice. If Seoul has the political will, it could approve such transfers on the compelling grounds that they are defensive weapons intended to protect a country subjected to illegal aggression. Seoul’s hesitation is understandable. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has sought to maintain workable relations with Russia, which remains economically and strategically important to South Korea, rather than distance itself on values-based grounds, as his predecessor Yoon Suk-yeol did. Before the war, annual bilateral trade amounted to roughly $27 billion. Russia has also traditionally been an important actor on Korean Peninsula issues because of its leverage over North Korea, although the extent of that influence has ebbed and flowed over time. The relationship became particularly thorny when South Korea imposed economic sanctions against Russia after its invasion of Ukraine; more recently, Moscow has protested South Korea’s humanitarian aid to Ukraine and defense industry cooperation with NATO. Direct arms transfers to Ukraine would likely cross what Russia considers to be a red line—as a South Korean diplomat reportedly noted—and could make it significantly more difficult for Seoul to repair relations with Moscow after the war ends. Moreover, South Korean policymakers worry that directly arming Ukraine could encourage Moscow to deepen military cooperation with North Korea, including transfers of sensitive technologies relating to nuclear-powered submarines, military satellites, or other systems. These technologies would enhance North Korea’s precision-strike capabilities, improve the survivability of its nuclear forces, and strengthen its deterrent against the United States, thereby undermining the credibility of the U.S. security guarantee. Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has also suggested that Russia could provide North Korea with the latest nuclear weapons technology if South Korea were to lend Ukraine military support. However, it is questionable whether South Korea’s efforts to manage its relationship with Russia would ultimately bear fruit. As Russia-North Korea ties have deepened into a treaty-based alliance, it is increasingly unlikely that Seoul will be able to restore its previous relationship with Moscow—or, even if it does, that Moscow would support South Korea’s broader geopolitical objectives. Moreover, Russia is reportedly already providing North Korea with some sensitive technologies, although the nature and extent of these transfers remain difficult to verify. On top of that, whatever value Seoul sees in managing its relationship with Russia should be weighed against what it may lose by doing so—namely, the opportunity to consolidate its security partnership with Europe. Cooperation between South Korea and Europe has expanded considerably in recent years, with Seoul participating in NATO summits and signing a security and defense partnership with the European Union. This relationship has become more important than ever, as both face growing security threats from neighboring powers amid waning confidence in U.S. security commitments. South Korea’s defense industry has already become an important part of Europe’s effort to expand military capacity: From 2021 to 2025, South Korea was the second-largest supplier of major arms to European NATO countries, after the United States. That partnership has been driven most visibly by rapid deliveries of howitzers, tanks, multiple-launch rocket systems, and aircraft to Poland, alongside deals with Romania, Norway, Finland, and Estonia. Yet the political environment in Europe is changing, and the “Buy European” sentiment is gaining momentum as governments seek to revitalize the continent’s defense-industrial base. The European Union’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program has allocated approximately $175 billion to support defense procurement and industrial expansion within Europe but requires at least 65 percent of the component value of funded projects to originate within the European Union. South Korea’s exclusion from SAFE could make its systems less attractive for EU-funded procurement. South Korean policymakers and defense industry leaders increasingly recognize that Europe cannot be treated simply as a destination for Korean weapons. Sustainable cooperation must become more reciprocal cooperation and a broader security partnership. Lee has articulated this ambition, saying that South Korea must “go beyond exporting advanced products” and become “a trusted partner in security cooperation.” In other words, deepening defense cooperation with Europe—whether in the defense-industrial sphere or more broadly—would require Seoul to establish itself symbolically as a trusted security partner, rather than just a business partner. Ukraine presents the clearest opportunity to demonstrate precisely that. Ukraine is the front line of European security, and strengthening its ability to resist Russian aggression directly contributes to Europe’s deterrence and defense at a time when the continent faces its most serious security challenges since the end of the Cold War. South Korea cannot aspire to become one of Europe’s trusted security partners while simultaneously insulating its relations with Moscow from the consequences of that choice. Providing Ukraine with air defense systems would show that South Korea is prepared to contribute to European security when the stakes are highest—not simply profit from European demand. Lami Kim is the Korea chair in advanced technologies, national security, and defense at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. item.title: Iran’s Proxy Strategy Is Never Coming Back
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.73
Iran’s Regional Strategy Is Never Coming Back Iran’s long-running security strategy hasn’t survived the current war. Three years ago, on a clear day, you could stand at the Lebanese border with Israel in the village of Marwahin and see the Baha’i Gardens on Mount Carmel, looking down over the Israeli city of Haifa. The view suited the widespread talk at the time about an Iran-led “axis of resistance” based in Lebanon and Gaza and intent on liberating Palestine. Then Oct. 7 happened. That was when the “axis of resistance” finally met another regional dynamic head-on: an expansionist Israel that was increasingly willing to strike first against its adversaries. What has transpired over the past three intense years of war—in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran—has been the collapse of Iran’s deterrent strategy. The axis was Iran’s first line of defense in its grand strategy against Israel and the United States. But the axis’s forward strongholds were no longer protecting its core; it was no longer possible to keep war away from Iran’s borders. The axis was Iran’s first line of defense in its grand strategy against Israel and the United States. But the axis’s forward strongholds were no longer protecting its core; it was no longer possible to keep war away from Iran’s borders. Iran entered a new era, one that necessitated a rethinking of its grand strategy for confrontation and even survival. Iran’s previous strategy, based on containment and strategic patience, has not survived the current war. Tehran has instead been forced to rely on what had previously been its second and third lines of defense. The second line consisted of its missile and drone arsenal, and the third relied on its geographical superiority: vast expanses of land; mountainous terrain; and, most importantly, the Strait of Hormuz and its significance for global trade. This last line had never previously been tested, and Iran remained wary that its use might fail. But the country has now been testing its ability to fight alone on the battlefield. What has been particularly painful for Iran is that it has been forced to reverse the roles between itself and its allied groups and organizations. Instead of these factions preventing the war from reaching Iran, as the plan had been, Iran rushed to their defense when necessary. Hezbollah was transformed in an instant from a spearhead in the conflict to an organization under pressure, cut off from supplies after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, and besieged by the Lebanese state, which is negotiating with Israel while the militant group strives to maintain its existence, with Iran doing what is necessary to protect it militarily and diplomatically. This profound shift in its function was reflected, in turn, in the arrangement of power tools within the Iranian strategy. The Hezbollah that existed on the eve of the Oct. 7, 2023, events and Hamas’s attack on Israeli settlements surrounding Gaza is no longer the same. Its previously declared objectives are no longer valid, and the role that Hezbollah played on a regional level, from Iraq to Syria and Yemen and decades earlier in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is no longer viable. The war and the fall of Assad in Syria returned Hezbollah to its Lebanese sphere of influence, which in turn altered its function for the axis in general and for Tehran in particular. This shift prompted Iran to explore its latent power, which had remained untested for years in the very confrontation that it had long been talking about. The war appeared simultaneously as a challenge and an opportunity for a nation that, for nearly half a century, had never missed an opportunity to declare its hostility toward the United States and Israel. The activation of the Strait of Hormuz has given the Iranians an unprecedented advantage in the conflict. But Iran has also been confronting two nuclear powers with one of the most advanced air forces in the world, a sophisticated early warning system, and a multilayered air defense system. What has become clear is that U.S. President Donald Trump, confronted with Iran’s new strategy, prefers normalization to a protracted war with Tehran. What complicates this matter is the team that is now in charge in Iran. This team is a product of the war’s unstated fourth objective. From the early days until now, the rhetoric has focused on eliminating the Iranian nuclear threat, destroying its missile infrastructure, and dismantling its regional network. On the sidelines, Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have stated their desire to overthrow the regime. Then, after Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s assassination, Trump repeatedly declared that the regime had fallen. In practice, the regime has indeed changed, but in a direction contrary to what the United States and Israel wanted. The change has produced a more rigid and cohesive system than its predecessor, even if differences have emerged. These differences, however, do not yet appear to be at a level that could divide the country into two opposing camps. This was evident in the recent change that affected the position of the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council in early August. Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr—who succeeded Ali Larijani, who was killed during the war—disagreed with other leaders over how to deal with ships passing through the strait. He threatened to resign after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted them. He was then replaced by former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei, whose appointment coincided with subsequent appointments that filled most of the country’s vacant military leadership positions; Zolghadr himself became an advisor to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who still rules from behind the scenes. The appointment of Rezaei carries a message in more than one direction. He had spent the spring and summer arguing that it was not possible to negotiate and fight at the same time. This is a position that Mojtaba Khamenei had conveyed to other Iranian officials in June, as told to me by an Iranian official who refused to reveal his name. But Rezaei may also be closing the circle on Iran’s evolving strategy, which has seen shifts in its defense priorities. In late August, Rezaei went further than any senior Iranian official had in years. In a television interview, he questioned the entire logic of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, arguing that membership in it had not prevented the United States and Israel from bombing Iranian nuclear sites anyway, and he asked on air: “Why shouldn’t we also seek to acquire nuclear weapons?” Rezaei elaborated extensively on the nuclear issue, more so than any previous secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. This occurred while the Iranian parliament was debating withdrawal from the Nonproliferation Treaty and while the new supreme leader had yet to confirm his adherence to his father’s fatwa prohibiting the use, production, stockpiling, and acquisition of nuclear weapons, but also had not declared anything to the contrary. This leaves the issue open to all possibilities, especially since Iran had stated on numerous occasions before its recent wars against the United States and Israel, through various officials, that it would reconsider its nuclear doctrine if targeted. The nuclear issue brings us back to Iran’s defense strategy. If we combine all the elements that we mentioned earlier and prioritize them, we find that Iran hasn’t changed its strategy but rather reshaped it. The network of allies still exists; although it has been weakened, it hasn’t been eliminated, and Tehran continues to benefit from its existence in various ways. Hezbollah is exhausted after two difficult wars with Israel, but it is preparing. Iran’s allied Iraqi factions are facing pressure at a time when U.S. influence is growing again in Iraqi politics, while its Syrian corridor disappeared with the fall of the Assad regime. The Houthis, however, are still able to exert pressure on Saudi Arabia, which has spent two years trying to avoid this war through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait without fully activating that front. The missile and drone programs have become a higher priority, especially given Iran’s heavy reliance on them. It appears from the past few months that Iran is investing heavily in developing these missiles and drones to increase their effectiveness and the leverage that they can exert in any future confrontation. As for Hormuz, the third layer, this is the card that Tehran has forcefully pushed to the forefront since the cease-fire, and it now uses it in various ways while trying to establish a legal reality for itself. The question that remains unanswered is whether a fourth layer, this time nuclear, will join the three existing layers. From Iran, we return to southern Lebanon, where the areas that a journalist like myself can see from the last point not occupied are shrinking. We can no longer stand in Marwahin to see Haifa, nor even in Naqoura, which is now itself within Israeli-occupied territory. I find myself standing in Haniyeh, observing from there Mansouri and some of the slopes that connect to the sea and lead to Naqoura. This new equation imposed by Israel on Lebanon was the product of a larger battle across the entire region. It is the same battle that brought the Strait of Hormuz to the forefront in a completely opposite equation, an equation in which Iran seeks to establish a new reality in the region—one in which it sees no U.S. presence to challenge it. With this new reality, Iran no longer needs to focus on seeing Haifa. That goal, and the Lebanese front built for it, has quietly become less important. Israel, however, still wants to keep an eye on Tehran, which is why Iran won’t give up its influence in southern Lebanon, no matter the pressure or how weak its hold becomes. At the very least, Iran keeps an early warning system there, staying close enough to Israel to spot any signs of a new war and rebuild its presence however it can. Still, this is now a lower priority for Iran. The main focus is now on rebuilding its missile and drone program, which played a key role in the war and is being rapidly expanded. The old defense line in the south won’t return soon. But what replaces it starts inside Iran’s own borders. Ali Hashem is a journalist and researcher covering wars, diplomacy, and political transformations across the Middle East. He is a correspondent with Al Jazeera and a research fellow at the Centre of Islamic and West Asian Studies, Royal Holloway, University of London.
