item.title: AI Transformation Requires Redesigning Work, Not Cutting Roles
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.72
Summary. AI is beginning to reshape workforce decisions, but many companies are moving faster than the evidence warrants. Early AI-driven layoffs have often failed to deliver expected returns, exposed gaps Precisely how AI will impact the workforce in the short to medium term is unclear. Many layoff announcements are better understood as AI-washing: ordinary restructuring initiatives packaged in AI language to reassure investors that leaders have a grip on the coming technological change. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI reduced monthly U.S. payroll growth by only around 16,000 jobs over the past year, adding roughly 0.1 percentage points to the unemployment rate—a drag that includes slowed hiring as well as outright job elimination. These numbers may well increase, but for now, we are much earlier in the process than the prevailing narrative suggests.

item.title: Are Great Leaders Truly Great—or Just Lucky?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.60
Share Podcast Are Great Leaders Truly Great—or Just Lucky? A conversation with historian and author Jared Diamond on reframing how we think about influential leaders. How much does a leader actually matter to an organization’s success? We tend to credit CEOs, founders, and other powerful figures with shaping the institutions they lead, but historian Jared Diamond argues that we often underestimate the role of timing, circumstance, industry, and plain luck. Diamond explains his “Hamlet test,” which asks whether someone else could have achieved the same outcome or whether the leader was uniquely qualified to do it, and how it applies to many business leaders. He also explains why some leaders are able to seize a fleeting moment of opportunity, why founders can have an outsized influence on institutions, and why boards may overestimate the impact of replacing a struggling CEO. Diamond is author of Prophets, Profits, Coaches, and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Matter? ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ADI IGNATIUS: So Alison, today we’re going to be tackling an age-old question. Are successful leaders people who are uniquely qualified to handle their opportunity or do the context and circumstances they’re in largely dictate how they’ll perform? We’re essentially renewing the great man theory versus the idea that history rises from below. ALISON BEARD: Yes. Great men or great woman. I do like that topic, especially in an era when boards are rewarding CEOs with astronomically large contracts. With astronomically large contracts, you can’t help but wonder whether these leaders really have the differentiated talent to justify that kind of money. ADI IGNATIUS: And while the debate is in many ways unanswerable, Jared Diamond has tried to apply the rigor of research to look at the extent to which an individual leader can truly and deeply influence their institution’s success, and even has advice for leaders who want to increase their chances of doing well. ALISON BEARD: I imagine it has a lot to do with being in the right place at the right time. ADI IGNATIUS: Absolutely. Look, it’s an interesting topic. Diamond is perhaps best known for his 1997 book, Guns, Germs, and Steel: The Fates of Human Societies. And his new book on leadership is called Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Matter. He spoke with me about the secret sauce that makes political, business and sports leaders succeed, and what can and can’t be attributed to the individuals in charge. Here’s our conversation. So in this new book of yours, you’ve reopened the debate about how critical individual leaders are in the unfolding of events. So there’s the great man theory of history where we credit individual leaders in business, in politics, in religion, in sports for uniquely affecting historical developments. And then there’s an opposing view, which is that leaders are constrained by the context and the circumstances they’re in and have little influence on events. My first question is, why dig that up again? JARED DIAMOND: Because the debate still remains unresolved. The traditional way in which historians and biographers have tried to settle the role of the leaders is by writing biographies. But biographies don’t settle things. So I reopened, quotes, the debate, because there are now two new powerful methods, methods of natural experiments that social scientists have pioneered for the vast few decades, and then a method that I introduced called the Hamlet Test. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, so let’s talk about the Hamlet Test. So as I understand it, if you’re going to assess a leader’s greatness, you need to identify, you need to evaluate all the plausible alternatives. JARED DIAMOND: I call it the Hamlet Test because you can ask, was Shakespeare the only person who could have written that great play, Hamlet? Well, in that case, we know who were all the other Elizabethan playwrights at the time. There are about 25 of them. We’ve got their plays, we can judge their plays. Some of them are slightly good, but none of them remotely approach Hamlet. And in addition, Hamlet was Shakespeare’s 22nd play. He had already written Romeo and Juliet and Julius Caesar. He had established himself as a good player. In the case of say, Jeff Bezos, was Jeff Bezos uniquely qualified to found Amazon? Well, the population of the United States is about 340 million and it’s impossible to make an argument that out of those 340 million, the only one who could found Amazon was Jeff Bezos. So Shakespeare passes the Hamlet Test, but Jeff Bezos does not pass the Hamlet Test. But in other cases, you can identify a uniquely qualified person. The founding president of Botswana, Seretse Khama, was uniquely qualified because upon independence, Botswana had only 22 university graduates and Seretse Khama was the chief of the largest tribe, the one on whose land, diamonds were found. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, so in the business world, who does pass the Hamlet? JARED DIAMOND: Few people pass the Hamlet Test in the business world. One of the few is the founder of the pomegranate juice industry in the United States and the world. Until 2002, pomegranates have been investigated for 4,000 years and in some Middle Eastern supermarkets, the markets, you can get someone to squeeze one glass of juice, but there was no industrial production of pomegranate juice because pomegranate juice comes in this hard object which is very difficult to squeeze. As of 2002, there were 22 people in the United States who grew pomegranates and 21 of them didn’t have much money and they had no motivation to make industrial scale pomegranate juice. There was one couple, they had 50% of the pomegranate production in the United States and they were interested in the medical benefits of pomegranates and they didn’t care about the money from it. Those were the Resnicks. They, like Shakespeare with Hamlet, were uniquely qualified to set up the pomegranate juice industry in the U.S. and the world. ADI IGNATIUS: Okay, so there’s a distinction between someone, the Resnick family and pomegranates, who created something, an outcome that probably would not have happened without them. As opposed to leaders like Bezos or other tech titans like Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, where the innovation would’ve happened, but they shaped the outcome and that we have to recognize that. That may not pass the Hamlet Test, but that is one of the definitions of great leadership, which is to seize the moment and shape its outcome. JARED DIAMOND: That’s exactly the point. Leaders can make a difference in several ways. If they pass the Hamlet Test, they can make a difference because they’re the only person who could have done it at all. More often in the business world, there are multiple people who could have done it, but they would’ve done it in different ways. For example, social media, was Mark Zuckerberg uniquely qualified to found social media? No, there were social media before him and there was social media after him, but he did it in a distinct way. And similarly, Jeff Bezos, he made the decision that Amazon should be online and should sell everything. Well, Walmart also has an everything store, but it’s not online. It’s a brick and mortar store. And then eBay preceded Jeff Bezos and operated in a different way. So to use your elegant formulation, there are leaders who make a difference by putting their stamp on how it’s done. But without them it would’ve been done, but in a different way. ADI IGNATIUS: Now, corporate boards tell us that the individuals they select as CEOs must be uniquely qualified to lead their companies because they pay them astronomical salaries and bonuses. Does your research support that approach or does it challenge it? JARED DIAMOND: On the average, my research does not support that approach. On the average, studies show, using the statistical technique of an over analysis of variation. On the average, there are four things that affect the profits of companies. One is the year. 1930 was a bad year for business in general, the Depression. On the average, the year accounts were only about 2% of variation. The other three factors are the CEO and the industry. There are profitable industries like the teenage t-shirt industry, and there are unprofitable industries like public utilities that is highly regulated by government. And then the third thing is the individual company. Procter & Gamble has been very well managed for the last 150 years. The soap industry is a profitable industry, but Procter & Gamble is particularly profitable. On the average, individual leaders account for between 15 to 30% of the variation. Therefore, if a leader says, “Pay me $10 billion because your company made $100 billion,” the fact is that in most cases there are other leaders who could have made that $100 billion, but there are some leaders who really do make a difference. On the average though, the answer is no. ADI IGNATIUS: I think it’s fair to say management literature also tends to assume that leaders matter enormously. I like your skeptical question. Can you say anything about when leaders actually matter? It sounds like we systematically overestimate the importance of CEOs, but can you say anything about when solid leadership really makes a difference? JARED DIAMOND: One case is they’ll have a task in those uncommon situation where only one person is qualified to do it. A second consideration is time and place. There are situations where there’s only a time where anybody can do it. For example, Bill Gates. Bill Gates and Paul Allen had been discussing microcomputers, and Bill Gates kept telling Paul Allen, “The time isn’t right.” And then Bill Gates saw the January, I think it was 1976 cover of Popular Electronics, which showed that Intel had come up with a new chip and Bill said to Paul Allen, “With this new chip, we can finally do it. We got to do it fast because other people will do it.” Steve Jobs saw that same cover. So another thing that makes a difference is, you got to get the right time. A third thing that makes the difference is that some people recognize the right time and seize it, as did Bill Gates. Other people recognize that it’s the right time, but there was nothing they could do to seize it. Winston Churchill was at the perfect time to fulfill his life dream of being British prime minister in a war situation. Winston Churchill did not manufacture World War II. And then finally, Genghis Khan, the largest empire in world history. Genghis Khan had no idea that he was born at the best time in the last 2,000 years to found a land empire in Central Asia because he was born at the wettest time of the last 2,000 years. If Genghis Khan had been born 10 years earlier or 200 miles further away, we wouldn’t know anything about Genghis Khan. Genghis Khan didn’t know that he was born at the perfect time. He didn’t engineer it. Only within the last 10 years, then chronologists figured it out. I will mention two other things. A leader can make a difference if the leader does not have followers almost equally qualified to do it. Clement Attlee made perhaps the biggest changes in the British society in the 20th century, but we don’t think much of Clement Attlee because he had four or five associates who were qualified to do it. And then finally, a leader can make a difference if a leader can get a country to do something that they do not want to do. Franklin Roosevelt got the United States to prepare for World War II when Americans did not want to prepare for World War II. And Charles de Gaulle got the French to accept the independence of Algeria when the French did not want to do it. So those are five things that affect when a leader can make a difference. ADI IGNATIUS: So a lot of this is obviously done with a historian’s perspective in hindsight, but if you were advising a board on choosing between two CEO candidates, what would you want them to ask these candidates, again, to improve the odds that you’re going to bring in a successful leader? JARED DIAMOND: I’m going to frustrate you by saying there is no one thing to look for in a leader. There are different ways that a leader can be successful. In business schools, it’s commonly taught that a leader needs to be charismatic. And yes, there are leaders who are or were charismatic. Hitler, unfortunately, was very charismatic. But there are other ways to be an effective leader. You can be an effective leader by terrorizing your subordinates. Augusto Pinochet, the dictator of Chile. Nobody has ever said that Pinochet was charismatic. He wasn’t. He was successful at terrorizing his subordinates. You can also be successful, not being charismatic, but being a good discussion leader. John Kennedy, who was charismatic, but he was a great discussion leader during the Cuban Missile Crisis. You can be an effective leader by expressing yourself well as Winston Churchill did. So short answer is, there is no magic formula despite what business schools do. ADI IGNATIUS: So a lot of what you’ve talked about is about timing, which seems like it’s about luck, but I want to push you on that a little bit. How much of what we call visionary leadership is really the ability to recognize the moment has arrived? And you mentioned Bill Gates, you mentioned Jeff Bezos doing that to an extent, as opposed to the ability to invent something no one else could do, the Hamlet Test. Is that it? I mean, yes, I’m always looking for a nice, neat, well-wrapped up Malcolm Gladwell-esque explanation of the world, but is that it? Is visionary leadership about maybe it’s about luck, but it’s about seizing that to do interesting, innovative things? JARED DIAMOND: Welcome to interviewing Jared Diamond. There is no simple answer. In some cases, business leadership is luck. Mark Zuckerberg was lucky that he was a sophomore at Harvard at what was at 2002, the perfect time to found a social media. In the previous year or two, the technology just wasn’t adequate. Mark Zuckerberg didn’t know this. Bill Gates did recognize the perfect time, and Jeff Bezos recognized the perfect time. Jeff Bezos saw that the use of the internet had increased by, what, factor at 2.3 in the last 12 months. So he said, “We got to do it now.” Elon Musk was debating going to graduate school at Stanford, and then someone told Elon Musk, “No, this is just the right time to do what you want to do. You better do it now.” So in some cases, people recognize that the time is right. In other cases, the time is right, but they don’t recognize it. And in other cases, they managed to do it, although the time may not have been so critical. ADI IGNATIUS: Business founders seem to occupy a special category in your book, in part because they have extraordinary freedom to establish institutions, norms, past that persist long after they’re gone. Founders are not necessarily successful managers, leaders. Sometimes those skills don’t translate, but talk about founders as leaders and how that differs from leaders of more mature companies. JARED DIAMOND: This gets quadruply interesting because my book is not only about business leaders, but it’s also about political leaders and sports leaders and religious leaders in religion. And in politics as well as in business, founders are important. Founders create institutions that then are likely to carry on. They may create either good institutions or they may create bad institutions. In the political world, we can think of Seretse Khama and other example, Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore, set up the institutions that have carried on with Singapore, made Singapore disproportionately accessible. But there were other founding leaders. The founding leader of Algeria set up bad institutions that have hampered Algeria today, so founders can make a difference either for the good or for the bad. ADI IGNATIUS: We’ve been focusing mainly on business leaders. You’ve looked at leadership across all these disciplines. What were some of the connective threads that you found among those leaders who really did rise to a significant level of success and maybe unique success? JARED DIAMOND: We’ve talked about some of them, the importance of timing, being at the right place at the right time, whether you choose it, whether you recognize it or not. Another connective thread is that there are surprising, to me, surprising generalities cutting across fields. I didn’t realize that much of the studies on outcomes of sports coaches or football coaches, much of the work has been done by business school professors. Sports are a particularly good area to study effective leaders. In the business world, business CEOs, they’re often invisible. They don’t jump up and down on the sidelines. You may see the result in 5 years or 10 years, or you never see the result. Whereas sports coaches jump up and down on the sidelines. There’s a basketball game several times a week. The Boston Red Sox, my beloved Red Sox, play several times a week. There’s a league of several dozen teams and all the teams are organized the same way. That’s not the way in the business world. And so some of the best papers on sports leaders, sports coaches, have been done by business school professors who debug their methods in sports because the database in sports are so neat, and then they applied those methods to the business world. ADI IGNATIUS: So one of the problems with evaluating leaders is that things change. Is there such a thing as enduring success and can you put that in a bottle? Are there people who have the Hamlet effect over and over again, or are these just moments in time? JARED DIAMOND: Good question. Is there enduring success? In the business world, Procter & Gamble has been successful for 150 years. That’s a somewhat rare case. In the political world, Winston Churchill was outstandingly successful as a wartime leader. He was then defeated and he became reelected as a peacetime prime minister. He was considered undistinguished. Then he came back for another term as peacetime prime minister. He was terrible and his associates were eager to get him out and they finally got him out. So there’s a case of a leader who is good in certain circumstances and not in other circumstances. In the sports world, again as an ex-Bostonian, Bill Belichick, great record in Super Bowls. Does that mean that Bill Belichick is a great coach? Well, Tom Brady goes away to another team and Tom Brady is very successful with his other team and Bill Belichick is no longer successful, making one uncertain whether Bill Belichick’s great record goes to the credit of Bill Belichick or how much of it goes to the credit of Tom Brady. ADI IGNATIUS: If I’m an executive and I’m listening to this podcast and I’m thinking, “I would like to be a consequential leader. I would like to pass the Hamlet Test,” this is probably the type of question you hate, but anyway, is there something that an individual can do to increase their possibility for this kind of once in a generation success? JARED DIAMOND: Yes, yes, and yes. In my book, there’s a short section which lists fields in which a CEO can have a big effect and fields in which a CEO cannot have a big effect, but you have your choice. If what you want to do is to have a chance of becoming very rich and being influential, but you’re willing to run the risk of being fired, you pick an industry in which the CEO has what’s called high discretion. Not discretion in the sense of being polite and careful, but discretion in the sense of having a lot of decision-making power. A friend of mine runs a company that makes t-shirts for teenagers. A pattern is good for two weeks and then disappears. My friend is good at recognizing what’s going to be good for the next two weeks, so he’s very successful. But when I had lunch with him the day before yesterday, he’s now in his 60s and he was afraid that he’s going to run out of money for the rest of his life. So if you pick a business like that, like the t-shirt business or the computer business or the soap business or the perfume business, if you get the right perfume, you may be very successful and rich, but if you get the wrong perfume, you may get fired. Alternatively, if you don’t care about being very rich or you want to be moderately rich and you don’t want to get fired, then you go into a business where the CEO has low discretion. For example, blast furnaces. I had never thought much about blast furnaces until I read that CEOs of blast furnace companies, they don’t get fired, but they’re not famous and not wildly successful, because there’s only one way to make a blast furnace. Again, a railroad. Once you have a railroad, the tracks are there for the next 75 years. So CEOs of railroads, nowadays, you don’t hear about them. Or to be the CEO of a public utility company, to be the CEO of the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power, who knows who the head of the DWP is? Why? Because public utilities are tightly regulated. You’re not going to be able to make a killing, but you’re not going to get fired. So I would say to someone who wants to pick a career, if you’re willing to gamble and you want to hope to be rich, but you are willing to risk being fired, become a perfume or t-shirt manufacturer. That you want to have a good living, but you don’t want to get fired, go into public utilities or blast furnaces. ADI IGNATIUS: Well, and I think the management literature might say, if you want to have extraordinary success, differentiated success, you have to have courage. And courage can result in failure and courage can result in great accomplishment if everything works out. JARED DIAMOND: Elon Musk is a good example. There was an occasion in Elon Musk’s business development where in the morning he thought that he was likely to go bankrupt by the evening, and between the morning and the evening, he got more investors, so he did not go bankrupt and he now has his trillion dollars. But yes, it’s risky and you got to have a strong stomach if you want to enter a risky business. ADI IGNATIUS: We talked about success, but I think boards often assume that if the company is struggling, that replacing the CEO is the answer. Your book suggests it’s more complicated than that. Why is that? JARED DIAMOND: Why is it more complicated than that? The business is struggling. Maybe it’s struggling because the CEO is bad and should be fired, but there are many other things that make a business struggle. It may be that it’s a downtime for the industry. It may be that other people in the business made bad decisions. The CEO is not the only reason for a business struggling. And this is a case where business school professors have learned so much from sports. The Red Sox. If a sports team has a losing record, the instinct of the owner is to fire the coach. At UCLA, we had the greatest basketball coach in the 20th century, John Wooden. And following John Wooden, we’ve had a series of, I think, eight basketball coaches. We fired every single one of them. They’ve had winning records, but not as good winning records as John Wooden. And when we fired them, we had to buy out their contracts. The result is that my athletic department at UCLA is $150 million in debt. Well, with $150 million, you could hire an awful lot of classics professors and German professors, but UCLA’s chancellors and their wisdom have not consulted Jared Diamond about firing the coach. And I would’ve told them, business school professors have shown that firing the coach is usually followed by the next coach doing better for random reasons, for throwing the dice reasons, but that usually firing the coach is a bad decision and just does not result in a permanent improvement, but it results in $150 million of debt. ADI IGNATIUS: So any final words for those who are intrigued in this topic of to what extent it’s the great individual, to what extent is the context and how you think about the role of leadership, again, especially in business? JARED DIAMOND: My summary would be in this respect, as in other respects, as in happy marriages, if you would ask me what is the one thing most important for a happy marriage, I would say, “Your asking that question shows that you are going to get divorced in the next year because a happy marriage requires 37 things. You got to agree about sex, money…” And similarly in the business world and the world of politics, there are multiple factors, but at least I boil them down to five factors rather than 37 factors. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, Jared Diamond, thank you for being my guest on the HBR IdeaCast. JARED DIAMOND: Thank you. It’s been a pleasure to talk with you. ADI IGNATIUS: That was Jared Diamond, historian and author of the book Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Matter? Next week, Alison will speak with acclaimed restaurateur, Danny Meyer, about creating and sustaining a great customer service culture. If you found this episode helpful, share it with a colleague and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, please consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to senior producer Mary Dooe and senior production editor, Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Adi Ignatius.

item.title: A Leading Restaurateur on What It Takes to Scale a Winning Culture
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.60
Share Podcast A Leading Restaurateur on What It Takes to Scale a Winning Culture A conversation with Shake Shack founder Danny Meyer on the principles he sticks to when growing an organization. When a company is small, maintaining a strong culture can feel relatively easy. But as organizations grow, layers of management, geographic distance, and pressure for efficiency can make it much harder to preserve what made the company special in the first place. Restaurateur Danny Meyer has spent decades figuring out how to do just that. He founded Union Square Cafe and built Union Square Hospitality Group, then helped scale Shake Shack from a single location in New York City into a global restaurant chain. Along the way, he’s learned that culture isn’t what happens when the CEO is in the room—it’s what happens when they’re not. He explains how he turned his philosophy of “enlightened hospitality” into a set of specific behaviors that employees can understand and practice. He discusses why companies should hire for both technical expertise and emotional skills, how to identify people with a high “hospitality quotient,” and why promotions are one of the most powerful tools leaders have for reinforcing culture. Meyer is the author of What Could Possibly Go Right? The Essential Journey to Scale an Enduring Culture. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard. ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ALISON BEARD: Adi, when a business is small, building a great corporate culture can feel relatively straightforward. Leaders are close to their employees and customers. They can see what’s happening on the front lines and intervene when something feels off, but what happens when the organization gets much, much bigger? ADI IGNATIUS: So yeah, this is a classic business dilemma, and I think a lot of companies get it wrong even though they understand the risk. They make trade-offs for efficiency and profitability. They add layers of management. They forget about what made the business special in the first place. ALISON BEARD: Exactly. So joining me today is Danny Meyer, the restaurateur who founded and scaled Shake Shack, as well as an acclaimed fine dining group, and the author of a new book called What Could Possibly Go Right? The Essential Journey to Scale an Enduring Culture. In an extremely demanding industry—we’re talking about Michelin-starred Manhattan restaurants to a global burger chain—he’s stayed successful for decades, but he’s also really candid about the mistakes that he’s made and corrected along the way. I talked with him about the building blocks of a strong organizational culture, the frameworks he uses to ensure that diverse, dispersed teams stay on the same page, and when a leader should step in versus step back. Here’s our conversation. So when you first started out with your first restaurant, Union Square Cafe, how did you articulate the culture that you wanted to create and get the team to successfully execute on it? DANNY MEYER: I didn’t. I never articulated anything to anybody because I didn’t know the first thing about opening a restaurant, starting a business. I just did what came naturally to me and what was intuitive. I think over time I started to use my words, as we used to teach our kids, instead of just trying to embody the behaviors I wanted to see. I really was trying to let people know what they were, and that’s when things started to get pretty good because it’s not fair to ask your team members to be guessers as to what really matters. ALISON BEARD: You talk about this idea of enlightened hospitality. Explain what you mean by that? DANNY MEYER: So the idea of enlightened hospitality in fact occurred to me when I opened my second restaurant, which was Gramercy Tavern, almost 10 years after opening Union Square Cafe. It didn’t feel right to me in there, and I couldn’t figure out why. For the first time in my career, I was not 100% of the time at the front door in one restaurant. So I was going back and forth, and if I’ve learned one thing about culture all these years later, culture’s what happens when you’re not in the room. And half the time I was not in the room, and I had not done a good job of defining it. There was one awful day, a Union Square Cafe regular dined at Gramercy Tavern, and she came up to me furious after her meal and she said, “What I just experienced never would’ve happened at Union Square Cafe.” And she was really talking about a horrible lapse in hospitality. She went into great detail about what we had done, and I was so upset with myself because I realized I had never really clarified our culture to our team at Gramercy Tavern. And I hosted an all-staff meeting the very next day, and that’s when I coined the expression, enlightened hospitality. And I said, “Guys, from this moment on, we are in the business of hospitality. Yes, we’re going to always try to make our food much better. We’re going to always try to have better wines on our wine list, but when someone pays their bill at the end of a meal here, what they’re paying us for is not the food and wine. You got to pretend all that stuff was free. What they’re paying us for is how we made them feel, hospitality.” Here’s what hospitality means to me: It means that the person on the receiving end of your service truly believes that you were on their side. And I’ll take it a step further, guys. Our first customer is us. And I coined the expression, the virtuous cycle of enlightened hospitality. And I said, “I know for a fact that the way you treat each other is going to directly influence how our guests feel treated. And if you have a lapse in how you care thoughtfully for one another, our guests will feel that. And so enlightened hospitality, I told them, was basically taking all five of our stakeholders and creating a virtuous cycle where the input would be one another, followed by our guests, followed by the community in which we do business, followed by our suppliers, followed by our investors. And if you break this anywhere, you break the whole thing. All of that came to me in a fit of anger over how poorly we had treated a guest the day before. That has been the blueprint for every single restaurant we’ve ever opened since, and people don’t have to guess anymore what matters to me. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. So how do you translate that ethos into values or specific behaviors that you want to see? DANNY MEYER: Well, that’s another thing that I didn’t do a very good job of for many, many years. It was constant learning by doing, and a lot of the doing, I was falling down and getting myself back up. But the first iteration was I said, “I know what I need to do. I need to establish what are our family values.” And somebody really smart said, “Okay, that’s a good idea, Danny. You should really crowdsource those family values from the team. So instead of being a top-down thing, everybody will have some skin in the game.” And so I did that, and this was probably 15 years ago or something. I got probably 60 answers, and we were so smart. We created a word cloud, printed it on coffee mugs and gave it to every leader in the company with 60 words on it. It was everything from enthusiasm, community, spirit, seasonal. And then another consultant came to me and they said, “You can’t do that. You can’t expect people to remember 60 different values.” And so we spent three days locked up in a room bucketing those 60 values into four. And the four family values we came up with, which could be values for anybody’s company, were excellence, doing the thing you do as well as you can do it, a little bit better than you did it yesterday; hospitality, doing it in a way that made other people feel better; entrepreneurial spirit, identifying problems before others identify them and coming up with a fresh solution; and integrity, having the judgment to do the right thing even when no one else is looking and even when it may not be in your own self-interest. So we had these four family values. And then we had a really important aha moment. We had an outside speaker, a guy who’s a friend, his name is Dov Seidman. He’s the founder of The HOW Institute. Dov came to speak to my senior leaders and he said, “Guys, the companies that succeed in this next generation are not going to be the ones that outperform their competition. They’re going to be the ones that outbehave their competition.” I had never thought about that. So with that nugget, I went back with my team, and we said, “You know what? We should really scrap family values, and instead we should replace family values with expected behaviors.” And this was one of the most powerful things we’ve ever done in terms of taking a quantum leap forward for our culture, was that family values is a big problem. We are not a family. We’re a business. It was disingenuous of me to suggest that we were a family. Yes, if you’ve ever worked in a restaurant, there are things that feel good. You sit down and you have something called family meal with everybody else who works on the staff, but you know what? Sometimes you got to fire somebody in a business. You don’t fire a family member. Your crazy uncle still gets invited back to Thanksgiving dinner, but you cannot do that in a business. And so second problem besides it was family is that it’s really hard to hold someone accountable to a value. And then third problem was is that the four family values we had, again, this in terms of advancing culture, could have been any company in the world. Who would argue with wanting your business to be more excellent, more hospitable, better entrepreneurial spirit and exemplifying integrity? So what we did was we took all of the expected behaviors from stories that were actually in my first book, Setting the Table, stories that were uniquely ours, and that’s when we really hit go on this whole thing. ALISON BEARD: So what’s an example of an expected behavior distilled from the enlightened hospitality and the family values? DANNY MEYER: One that I really love is called “center the salt shaker” with an unwavering commitment to excellence, and centering the salt shaker means that you’re doing things the way they are supposed to be done. So that’s one. And if I were to say salt shaker to anyone in our whole company, thousands of people, and then if you add Shake Shack in many, many more thousands of people, they will actually be able to look at a salt shaker and know what that means. ALISON BEARD: So I imagine that finding people who will adhere to those behaviors starts with hiring, right? DANNY MEYER: Yeah. We will never be any better than the quality and the emotional skills in addition to the technical skills of the people who we’ve hired to be on our team, and so our recipe is 49 parts technical prowess and 51 parts hospitality skills. I learned that if we’re just hiring the person who’s the best cook, but they’re not great for the team based on who they are while they’re doing that cooking, it’s a lose. And we’ve all made excuses for people who are great at what they do, even though they’re not great for the culture. So that’s why when we hire somebody, we’re very specific about what the emotional skills are we’re looking for because, quite frankly, we’re much better at identifying those when we interview than we are at changing them once somebody’s actually on the team. ALISON BEARD: This sounds like something that you developed over time. DANNY MEYER: Well, I knew the kind of people who worked really, really well. I knew the kind of people that didn’t work as well or work out as well. And it was really just a matter of, for the first time in my life, saying, “Stop being intuitive about everything, and start being intentional about everything”. “Who are the 10 or 20 most successful servers you’ve ever had at Union Square Cafe? Who are the 10 or 20 most successful cooks you’ve ever had? And what was it about them that made me feel so good? What are the emotional skills that they all have in common?” And when you put them all together, they added up to something that I named the hospitality quotient, and these are people who have a high HQ, are people who are actually happier themselves when they make other people feel better. That doesn’t say a thing about a good bookkeeper, a good sommelier, or do they know how to make pasta? ALISON BEARD: Right. DANNY MEYER: It’s all about their wiring. We started calling those people 51 percenters. Then I realized that that wasn’t even adequate because we got really, really good at hiring 51 percenters, sometimes at the expense of hiring what I now call 100 percenters. It wasn’t doing any good to hire people who were only good at the emotional skills, but didn’t know how to cook very well. But now what we’re really good at is hiring the whole thing because we want to get 100 on our test. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. As someone who frequented the Union Square Cafe from ’99 to 2004, I will say that the one thing I remember the most apart from the delicious tuna is the fact that the servers seemed to love their job and they were really good at it. This hospitality quotient is important not just for people in consumer facing roles, but also for people in the corporate offices who need to be hospitable to their colleagues, right? DANNY MEYER: Yeah, any business on earth is only as good as its team. That’s the real competition is getting the strongest team, and I just don’t know anyone who would rather work with people who, in addition to how good they are at their job, aren’t also good for how it feels to work there. Look, I’m actually a sports fan, and sure, you take a sport like baseball where they measure every statistic of what’s happening on the field and the office staff of baseball teams have gotten really expert at dealing with that data, but the weird thing is that baseball is a game where you spend half the game in the dugout. There’s not one statistic I’m aware of in baseball that measures who are you in the dugout? Meaning who are you for the rest of your team? Are your behaviors actually bringing out the best in everybody else on your team? ALISON BEARD: They do have that in basketball, which is very interesting. It’s like you’re- DANNY MEYER: Really? ALISON BEARD: … plus, minus. Yeah. DANNY MEYER: Well- ALISON BEARD: Absolutely. DANNY MEYER: … I do understand the plus, minus in terms of … Well, I understand in hockey when you’re on the ice, how many goals were scored when you were on the ice versus how many goals were scored on your team? But I don’t think I’ve seen that with respect to what happens when you’re on the bench. So that’s- ALISON BEARD: Yeah, they don’t measure who’s a good locker room guy, right? DANNY MEYER: That’s what I’m talking about. ALISON BEARD: Yeah, exactly. So what are the six elements of HQ? DANNY MEYER: The first one is kind to optimism, and you can look at someone’s eyes and see if they have kind eyes, but I also think optimism, which is a first cousin to hope, you want someone who actually believes that they can impact things for the better. The second emotional skill we look for is curiosity, curious intelligence. We’re not interested in hiring know-it-alls. We love hiring learn-it-alls. The third emotional skill is work ethic. We can teach anybody how to set a table, but we can’t teach most people how to care about doing their job as well as it can be done. The fourth emotional skill we look for is empathy, which is having the unique ability to imagine what it might be like to walk in someone else’s shoes. And I think about the golden rule that I was brought up with growing up in St. Louis was always do unto others as you want others to do unto you. ALISON BEARD: Yes. DANNY MEYER: That’s the golden rule I learned. ALISON BEARD: Right. DANNY MEYER: My golden rule, I call it the golden rule of hospitality, is do unto others as you believe they would want done under them. And it’s very different because we’re all different. So I don’t impose my wants on you. I try to imagine as an empathetic person, what do you need? What do you want? And the next emotional skill is self-awareness, which is what’s making me tick today? What side of the bed did I wake up on? Hospitality is a team sport. So understanding what my personal weather report is and understanding how to make sure that that works for my team and not against my team. And then finally, integrity, which is having the judgment to do the right thing even when no one else is looking and even when it may not be in your own self-interest. ALISON BEARD: So you mentioned your hesitation at wanting to expand, and you expanded not only to sort of more restaurants in New York, but then Shake Shack, which is a international chain now. So why did you or how did you get comfortable making that leap and not being absolutely in touch with every part of your business? DANNY MEYER: I had great leaders who were pushing me to grow, and Shake Shack, we only had one for the first five years. Now there’s over 700 in the world, but I just didn’t really want to grow it because my own father’s bankruptcy. I always associated his two bankruptcies with growth, and it took me several years of therapy actually and also his dying for me to realize that, guess what? There’s a whole lot of businesses that have grown, and that’s not what put them out of business. In fact, they’ve thrived. So it was a combination of my own internal growth and getting over that, but also having the kind of leaders on the team. One in particular, a young man named Randy Garutti, who had been a general manager of our Indian restaurant, Tabla, and then he was the general manager of Union Square Cafe all by the time he was 26 years old, and he wanted to take over Shake Shack. And he saw when we just had this one Shake Shack in Madison Square Park, it was busy all the time, it was making good money, and the only problem we really had at that Shake Shack was the people complained the line was too long. And Randy finally convinced me, he said, “There’s one thing we could do to make the line shorter and that’s open a second Shake Shack.” He probably argued with me to do this for a good three years or so before I finally succumbed. I got to the point and I said, “You know what? Who am I? This business is good for its community. It’s good for its suppliers. The people working there – people were doing really well. We were hiring a lot of people for whom it was their first job ever, teaching them about what it means to be a responsible member of a team. It was a good thing, and I said, “Who am I to hold back more of that?” So we went ahead and opened our second Shake Shack on the Upper West Side five years after the first one, and the only problem with that was that the line at the first one only got longer. So Randy’s primary argument to me had backfired, but that’s when I said, “Uh-oh, we got a tiger by the tail here.” ALISON BEARD: In the position that you’re in now, how do you stay in touch with the culture on the ground? DANNY MEYER: I go. I go to the places and I care. I have an expression, which is that I think a good leader, especially as she’s growing, needs to stop micromanaging, but needs to double down on micro caring. So I don’t travel anywhere in the country or in the world where there’s a Shake Shack without stopping in to say hi. I have a list of all the managers at every single Shake Shack, and I ask for the manager by name, and they are surprised that I do that. They’re surprised that I know them. I just did one this week actually in Boston, and the general manager, whose name is Barbie, was amazed that I asked for her by name. And then I spend time with her. I spend time with her team, and I ask them, “What can we do better?” Everyone loves when you ask them that, and guess what? I get good ideas. And so it starts with caring, it starts with showing up, but I’m not micromanaging. I’m not telling anyone how to do their job. I’m not going there to play a game of gotcha. As a matter of fact, I’m going there to play the game of teach me, show me, let me see what you’re proud of, because everyone’s proud of something in their job. And then I circle back and reinforce it with their boss who … I hope their own boss doesn’t micromanage them, but I do hope that their boss gets to see them and care even more than I do. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. In periods when you’ve either encountered problems on those visits or you’ve sensed that the entire corporate culture is slipping, I think in the book you described it as going sideways, how do you move to correct it? DANNY MEYER: The only things I will correct if I’m visiting a restaurant that doesn’t report directly to me is if I think it’s either dangerous or it’s going to cost us customers that minute. So I’ve walked into Shake Shack … I went into one in Chicago a couple months ago, and I walked in on a Sunday afternoon at about 4:00 when you would not expect the restaurant to be busy, and yet the place was still packed. And I noticed that there was water spilled on the floor, and I noticed that there was ketchup on the condiment station right on the surface. I said to myself, “This doesn’t look right. It doesn’t feel right.” In that case, I asked for the manager, said hello, introduced myself, but I brought what I call a charitable assumption. I didn’t say, “This place doesn’t look clean right now.” I said, “Looks like you’ve had an incredibly busy day today.” So I started the whole conversation with that, and I learned, yeah, there was some big event that day, and they were just playing catch-up. And he said, “I don’t know if you got 15 minutes, but this place is going to look like day one if you got 15 minutes. I’m going to show you that, but we’re just playing catch-up right now.” I’ve had an experience where something in the food didn’t taste right, and I’m not talking about Shake Shack now. I’ve talked about another one of our restaurants, and I said, “Guys, we’ve got to take that off the menu till we figure out what’s going on because that’s not how it’s supposed to taste.” It’s important for me that when I leave there, we center the salt shaker, we go back to doing it the right way, but I also want people to feel proud that they’re on a championship team whose ultimate boss cares deeply about that. And guess what? I then, in every case, I absolutely circle back, whether it’s good news or constructive news, to speak to that person’s boss or write an email or whatever. But we also have a culture where whenever I dine in any of our restaurants, I know that the next morning I’m going to have an email from the chef and the general manager asking me for feedback. They want it. And that’s part of the culture is that they don’t wait for me to say this was good or that could have been better. I want them literally to be saying, give us the goods because I’m on our side. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. So we talked about hiring for hospitality quotient and technical skills and ultimately good judgment. How do you indoctrinate people into the culture so that everyone is on the same page and then also incentivize adherence to it? DANNY MEYER: We talk about this from the minute that we hire people. We tell people what we mean when we say a 100%er. We tell people not everyone gets hired here. We’re really, really selective, and we tell people exactly what we saw in them that made us want to hire them. So right from the get-go, we’re letting people know we hired you because we believe that you either already have or have the potential to be really, really good at the job that we are paying you to do, but that’s not enough. There’s another 51% that made us really want to hire you, and that’s for who you are, and we talk about what the six emotional skills are right there that we’re looking for. We let people know that when you have a performance review, we’re going to be talking about how you’re doing with the 49% and how you’re doing with the 51%. We even … At Union Square Hospitality Group with all of our restaurants, when you work for us, one of the benefits is you have a 51% dining discount whenever you come to any of our places, and it’s just constantly reinforcing what matters. And then not just words on the wall, but we also catch people doing things right, and we’re very, very clear with what you did right that reinforces the culture. And then probably the most important thing, Alison, is that the people that get the promotions as you’re growing have got to be the people that best illustrate, exemplify, embody the behaviors as well as the technical performance you want. And it doesn’t matter how many times Danny talks about what matters to him. If the people getting the promotions and raises are contrary to the words that they hear from my mouth or from my writing, then it’s almost worse than if I had never said those things in the first place because it just makes me look like I didn’t really mean it. And so the most important thing we can do to advance our culture as we grow is to make sure that the people getting the promotions are the exemplars of our hospitality and they are truly the culture carriers. ALISON BEARD: So in any large organization where you have multiple business units and functions, there is a tendency for micro cultures to develop. And so I’m just wondering, especially in an organization like yours, that before the Shake Shack IPO definitely spanned everything from the highest level of fine dining to what you call fine casual but a chain. How did you prevent that from happening or when it did happen, fix it? DANNY MEYER: I think what you’re talking about is the difference between house pride and company pride. And as much as there are commonalities to the culture, or should be, for all of our places, I call it the thumbprint. We love the microcultures. What we don’t love is when it breaks down and sibling revelry turns into sibling rivalry. We don’t like when this restaurant is not on the side of the other restaurant. I don’t mind that they’re competing with each other for excellence. I think that’s not a bad thing at all, but I really mind when they do anything that’s in a destructive way. We’ve even seen sibling rivalry within one restaurant. We’ve seen micro cultures within one restaurant before. And if the question is, what do you do about it? You got to lean in. You got to see it. You got to tell people, “That’s not how we do things around here,” and if people can’t get with that program, then they can’t be on the team anymore. ALISON BEARD: What about the tension between corporate office culture, which maybe is incentivized to prioritize profitability and the on-the-ground culture, whether it’s at Shake Shack or the fine dining restaurants, to really care most about pleasing the customer and the team there? DANNY MEYER: Since the beginning of business, you’ve had- ALISON BEARD: Exactly. DANNY MEYER: … the sales team and the production team, whether it’s a magazine, editorial and publishing, whether it’s a factory, which is manufacturing and sales. In a group like ours, another one could be the home office or the support office and the people who are cooking the food, serving the food and doing the dishes. And it’s my job as the leader of the company, but it’s everybody’s job to realize we are one team, and the reason that our office is a support office is the only reason anyone in that office has a job is for the purpose of helping the people in the field be more successful. And were we always good at it? Absolutely not. I mean, I saw years where someone in the home office would call a chef meeting for 2:00 in the afternoon when the chef is just breaking down lunch service and thinking about dinner service. You can’t do that, and those kind of things became irritants. So, again, it gets back to hiring the right people who understand what their role is. Your role is to help the restaurants, which is where our guest experiences are happening, which is where our revenue is happening. There’s no revenue in the home office. You’re a cost unless you are helping restaurants be more successful. ALISON BEARD: So you write about lots of successes in your business, but also a lot of lows, having to back out of deals and close restaurants, struggling through the 2008 financial crisis and COVID-19 closures and really serious layoffs. So how do you keep the vibe positive and the culture strong during those really trying periods? DANNY MEYER: Well, the culture itself actually helps me stay strong because when I make mistakes and people speak up to me, that means our culture is strong because when people say, “Danny, this is not how we do things around here. We’re a company that puts people first, and you’re putting investors first, as opposed to the investors being the outcome of really great employee and guest and community experiences.” The culture is the one that sets me straight when that happens. The cover of what could possibly go right is an arrow that goes up and then it goes down, and then it goes up and then it goes down. Those downs are just like waves in the ocean. It’s only a matter of timing and size, but there’s always going to be another down. And I think the way we deal with those downs is really what determines whether the next up is going to be a little higher than the last up was. ALISON BEARD: But in a period when you’re having to close restaurants or make layoffs or cut back due to budgetary constraints, how do you sort of keep the trust of everyone and ensure that everyone’s still buying in to the fact that this is a caring organization that prioritizes hospitality for employees and customers above all else? DANNY MEYER: You got to be straight with people, and you got to give them a balanced sense of reality and hope, and it’s worth our while to fight our way through these problems and solve them effectively and creatively and generously because tomorrow could be a better day. ALISON BEARD: Danny, thank you so much for being with me today. DANNY MEYER: Alison, thank you. I’ve really appreciated all your great questions. ALISON BEARD: That was restaurateur Danny Meyer. He’s author of the forthcoming book, What Could Possibly Go Right? The Essential Journey to Scale an Enduring Culture. Next week, Adi speaks with psychologist Martin Seligman about the importance of agency in your career and your organization. If you found this episode helpful, please share it with a colleague, and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive Insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to our team, senior producer Mary Dooe and senior production editor Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new regular episode on Tuesday. I’m Alison Beard.

item.title: What Happens When AI Starts Doing Business with AI?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.48
Summary. As AI agents increasingly interact with one another on commercial platforms, firms need new rules governing what those agents can see, decide, and do. In a controlled AI-to-AI simulation covering In late 2025, Perplexity’s Comet browser began logging into shoppers’ Amazon accounts and buying on their behalf. Amazon treated it as an intruder. It blocked the agent and when Perplexity slipped past the block within a day, Amazon took the dispute to federal court. WeChat drew the line differently. After shutting out ByteDance’s Doubao assistant, which used system-level access to navigate WeChat without permission, Tencent later opened what it describes as an agent-to-agent channel to selected assistants from Huawei, Xiaomi, and others to send messages and place calls. Under this arrangement, an external agent translates a user’s request into a structured instruction and passes it through a Tencent-controlled interface to WeChat, which executes the action inside its own environment. Tencent controls which agents can connect, which functions they can invoke, and what data and execution remain inside WeChat. In other words, one platform shut the door to AI agents outright; the other unlocked it on its own terms.
