The authoritative record of NPR’s programming is the audio record.

item.title: Russia and North Korea open the first road across their shared border
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 3.67
Russia and North Korea open the first road across their shared border Russia and North Korea opened the first road bridge across their shared border Monday, a development that both countries hailed as boosting their deepening ties. The bridge over the Tumen River is 1 kilometer (0.6 mile) long and has two lanes and will allow up to 300 vehicles a day to pass through a newly built border crossing point, the Russian government said in a statement. The bridge links North Korea's Rason and Russia's Khasan, border cities of the two countries. The bridge's inauguration ceremony took place simultaneously in the two cities, with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song attending via video link. "I am convinced that the expansion of transport infrastructure near the border will give a powerful boost to the further development of trade, economic, technological, scientific and cultural cooperation between the Russian Federation and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea," Mishustin said. Pak said the bridge's completion is "a significant event adding a new dynamic movement to the overall bilateral cooperation," according to North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency. Relations and exchange programs between Russia and North Korea have been flourishing, with North Korea supplying ammunition and troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine in return for economic and military assistance. North Korea has been receiving Russian tourists since February 2024 amid slowly easing pandemic curbs. KCNA said the bridge's opening would promote tourism, human exchange and commodity circulation between the two countries. North Korea and Russia, which are already served by a railway bridge and air service, agreed in 2024 to construct a bridge for automobiles over the Tumen River, which runs along North Korea's borders with Russia and China. Construction began last year.

item.title: World Food Programme's Carl Skau discusses Yemen's food insecurity crisis
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 3.65
World Food Programme's Carl Skau discusses Yemen's food insecurity crisis NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with Carl Skau of the World Food Programme about the food insecurity crisis in Yemen. LEILA FADEL, HOST: Not many people are getting in and out of Yemen these days. Carl Skau did, though. He leads the U.N.'s World Food Programme. And we reached him just hours after he left. CARL SKAU: I spoke to women who were not eating more than once or maybe not even once a day because they're not just getting the assistance they need. You know, we used to provide them food and cash. The food is now gone. And the cash is only every other month. FADEL: Yemen is already in the middle of a civil war that's currently escalating between the Iran-backed Houthis, who control two-thirds of the country, and the internationally recognized government. Now parts of the country are in famine. SKAU: I also spoke to young men who were eager to try to join the conflict because they also didn't have any opportunities. And they weren't able to put food on the table for their families. FADEL: And since the U.S. and Israel started a war with Iran, the Houthis are getting involved in that regional conflict, too. They're threatening to shut down access to a strait in the Red Sea by attacking ships. And overnight, they struck Saudi oil facilities and other civilian infrastructure, injuring dozens. Skau says the consequences could be broad. SKAU: We're extremely concerned that this escalates further - maritime trade, which are important for global food security as well. It has already disrupted the economy inside Yemen, with some 18 million people who are acutely food insecure. And this crisis is now pushing them further onto the brink. We have had severe cuts in our programs because of the cuts in funding over the past few months. So quite a desperate situation. But already these funding cuts are really having a great impact. FADEL: And the funding cuts, are they because of the U.S. government's cuts to USAID and to the U.N.? SKAU: Well, it's across the board. Obviously, in the north, the main issue is that we don't have the basic conditions to operate. FADEL: Because of the Houthis' control there? SKAU: Exactly. Seventy-three U.N. colleagues have been detained, 38 of them from WFP. Our offices are occupied. Our assets are confiscated. So the basic conditions to operate in the north is no longer there. In the south, it's really an impact of funding cuts. And that's across the board for donors. And so we assisted some 3 million people a year ago. We're now down to 1 million. FADEL: What needs to happen so that more humanitarian aid can get to hungry people across Yemen? SKAU: Well, I think, one, there needs to be political attention to this. I know the competition is high now. But this is a very critical situation, and so that there is diplomatic efforts to try to deescalate the situation and ultimately try to find a path towards a peaceful settlement here. Second, of course, we need to fund the humanitarian operations. We are effectively working in the south, and so those operations need to be funded. The people that have been displaced, that are struggling, need to be supported. And, third, there needs to be a solution in the north. The Houthis need to be convinced to allow for principled humanitarian action and for our colleagues to be released. FADEL: You're speaking to the largest radio network in the United States. And there are going to be people who are listening thinking, well, Yemen is so far away - the Houthis are part of the problem. Why should I care about this? Why should my government care about this? What do you say to them? SKAU: Twelve percent of world trade passes outside Yemen. And this conflict is now having a disruption on that trade route. In addition to the Strait of Hormuz that everyone knows about, in addition to the Black Sea, where there is escalation between Ukraine and Russia right now. And so these are three choke points that are really pushing global trade. And it's pushing up prices across not only in the developing world, but also in the U.S. and Europe. And so if this is not brought under control, it's going to have a massive impact on stability across the world. FADEL: And for Yemenis, if something is not done to deescalate now, what does that mean for them? SKAU: They are already struggling. Half the population are struggling to put food on their tables. And of course, further escalation is going to mean more displacement, more economic crisis. And, you know, Yemen is already a country that's importing 90% of its food. So these disruptions to trade route is also hitting hard on the Yemenis. And, you know, I met a lot of desperate people who just cannot take anything more. And children are already malnourished. They will have damage for the rest of their life unless they are being treated and supported urgently. And so we need attention to this situation. We need funding for our operations. And we need to be able to operate across the country. FADEL: Carl Skau is the acting executive director of the World Food Programme. We're speaking just hours after he left Yemen. Thank you so much for speaking with us. SKAU: Thank you for having me. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. item.title: FBI is investigating the alleged theft of 153 million driver's license scans
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.84
The FBI said it is investigating a report that digital scans of more than 153 million driver's licenses belonging to people in the United States and Canada were being sold on the dark web, according to Reuters. Digital scans of driver's licenses from the U.S. and Canada appeared for sale on a dark web site called Nexus, which vanished after a journalist reported on it In its statement, the bureau said only that it was "looking into the incident" and declined to elaborate "due to the ongoing nature of the investigation." What caused the breach has not been determined. Cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs first reported the breach on Sept. 2, saying he discovered a dark web site called Nexus selling the scans after it was advertised on a Russian cybercrime forum. His own driver's license was offered as a free sample. Krebs verified the data was genuine by contacting nine people whose license records appeared on the site. The Nexus site disappeared from the dark web shortly after his report published. Reuters reported that Nexus also claimed holdings of millions of additional identification cards, travel documents, and hundreds of thousands of medical records, while appearing to refresh its database continuously — a sign that the breach was still active and ongoing. Krebs named New Orleans-based identity verification firm IDScan.net as a possible origin of the stolen records. A company spokesperson acknowledged to Krebs that an internal inquiry was underway. Reuters said it received no response to multiple requests for comment, and USA TODAY has independently been unable to confirm Krebs' claims. Zach Edwards, a threat researcher at cybersecurity company Infoblox, described the event as something the industry had never seen before. "There's never been a breach of driver's licenses at this scale," Edwards told Reuters. He noted that the breach's continuing nature "means that this attack created legitimate national security risks for high-profile individuals," and disclosed that his own license was among those listed for purchase. The incident arrives as data breaches in the U.S. are accelerating. The Identity Theft Resource Center tracked 1,803 data compromises in the first half of 2026, putting the year on pace to surpass the record 3,321 incidents recorded across all of 2025. One in four malicious breaches between March 2025 and February 2026 were AI-enabled, a 56% increase over the prior year, according to an IBM $IBM study cited by the ITRC. item.title: TSA is letting PreCheck members past airport security without a plane ticket
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.82
The Gateside by TSA PreCheck program is active at 13 airports and allows eligible visitors to shop, dine, and meet passengers at the gate Named Gateside by TSA PreCheck, the no-cost program is currently operational at 13 U.S. airports, among them Los Angeles International Airport, Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, and San Diego International Airport. TSA said it plans to expand the program to additional airports in the coming months. Eligible visitors can use the program to walk family members to their gates, greet travelers coming off a flight, or browse the dining and retail options on the secured side of the checkpoint. To qualify, applicants must hold TSA PreCheck benefits and a Known Traveler Number. Children may participate but must be listed on a parent or guardian's application. Applications must be submitted through an online portal no earlier than three days and no later than one day ahead of the intended visit. Once approved, they present an acceptable form of identification at the TSA PreCheck screening lane and may be asked to show their approval status on a mobile device. Screenshots and printouts are not accepted. Passes are valid for one calendar day. The program represents a limited loosening of airport access restrictions that have been in place since the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, according to Newsweek. Before those attacks, people who had no intention of flying were typically free to move through checkpoints and spend time at the gates. In the aftermath, only ticketed passengers and a limited category of authorized individuals — such as adults escorting unaccompanied children or helping travelers with disabilities — were permitted beyond the checkpoint. Receiving a Gateside pass does not exempt visitors from security screening; they must clear the TSA PreCheck lane just as any ticketed traveler would. Gateside passes also do not grant access to TSA PreCheck Touchless ID lanes, and the program may not be available when airports are operating at high capacity. Airport officials at participating locations have welcomed the program. Columbus Regional Airport Authority president and CEO Daren Griffin said in a statement, according to Newsweek, that the program "helps bring back special moments that many travelers have missed – welcoming loved ones at the gate, enjoying a meal together before a flight, or simply sharing time in the terminal." The other participating airports are Mesa Gateway Airport in Arizona, John Glenn Columbus International Airport in Ohio, Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport in Michigan, Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport in Kansas, Indianapolis International Airport in Indiana, Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport in Arkansas, Will Rogers International Airport in Oklahoma, Eppley Airfield in Nebraska, and Salt Lake City International Airport in Utah. item.title: German rocket startup Isar Aerospace reached orbit for the first time on its second launch
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.40
The Munich-based startup says rockets 3 through 7 are already in production as it targets up to 40 launches per year Isar Aerospace's Spectrum rocket launched at 10:12 pm local time from Norway's Andøya spaceport, deploying five satellites into low Earth orbit, the company said. The vehicle crossed the Kármán line at 100 kilometers altitude in under four minutes, completed stage separation, and jettisoned its payload fairing before reaching orbital velocity. The company's debut test flight in March 2022 was cut short when the rocket crashed into the ocean and exploded less than a minute after leaving the pad, according to Al Jazeera. Saturday's mission also marked the first time a privately developed rocket reached space from Europe, the company said. The payloads were selected through the Microlauncher Competition of the German Space Agency at DLR, a program funded through ESA Boost! that provides educational institutions and startups with low-cost access to space, the company said. Chief Commercial Officer Stella Guillen told CNBC that Isar Aerospace holds a pipeline worth more than 10 billion euros ($11.6 billion), though the company did not clarify how much of that figure represents contracted orders. "The demand is so big," Guillen told CNBC. "There's a lot of new constellations and new projects that have come out, and actually they're financed." The company is now focused on scaling production. Spectrum launch vehicles 3 through 7 are already in production, the company said, and a new 40,000-square-meter production facility is nearing completion that will give Isar capacity to manufacture up to 40 launch vehicles per year. CEO and co-founder Daniel Metzler said in a statement that the company will "focus on rapidly scaling launch vehicle production, deliver on our order pipeline, and meet surging global demand." Beyond its existing launch site in Norway, Isar Aerospace is building a second launch complex in Nova Scotia, Canada, the company said. The company closed a 270 million euro Series D round in June. Among its backers are Porsche, the NATO Innovation Fund, and venture capital firms Lakestar and HV Capital. Europe has struggled to launch satellites independently. America sent 198 rockets to space last year compared with only eight from Europe, figures from Isar Aerospace show, according to Al Jazeera. Most European satellites have been launched by SpaceX. item.title: OpenAI signed a deal for computing power from Nvidia-backed Firmus's new Malaysia data centers
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.38
OpenAI and Firmus announced a multi-year partnership on Tuesday under which OpenAI will receive dedicated AI computing capacity from two Firmus data center sites in Malaysia, the Australian infrastructure company said. The agreement makes OpenAI an anchor customer of Firmus and brings total contracted capacity across the Australian firm to more than 900 MW The deal makes OpenAI an anchor customer of Firmus and brings the company's total contracted capacity across all customers to more than 900 megawatts, the company said. The partnership also marks Firmus' expansion into Malaysia, extending its Asia-Pacific footprint beyond Australia, Singapore, and Indonesia. Firmus will deploy Nvidia $NVDA's Vera Rubin processors at the Malaysian sites, using Nvidia's DSX AI Factory Platform integrated with Firmus' own HyperCube infrastructure system. The HyperCube combines liquid cooling, mechanical systems, and electrification into a prefabricated unit manufactured in regional New South Wales, the company said. "We're excited to work with Firmus as we expand our global compute capacity. These new data centers in Malaysia will help us serve growing demand for OpenAI's products across the region and around the world," said Sachin Katti, VP of Compute Strategy at OpenAI, in a statement. Firmus currently has two AI data centers in operation — located in Australia and Singapore — and is actively developing five more across the Asia-Pacific region, the company said. The firm said its full portfolio spans seven AI factories across four countries and that the five sites under development are targeted to be ready for service within the next 24 months. Nvidia is among Firmus' financial backers, with Jane Street, Blackstone funds, and Coatue Management also holding stakes in the company, according to Reuters. The firm's most recent fundraising round put its valuation at more than $10.5 billion, Reuters reported. The deal is part of a broader push by AI companies to lock in computing infrastructure. OpenAI's agreement with Firmus follows a pattern of large AI labs securing dedicated capacity from Nvidia-backed infrastructure providers. Anthropic, for instance, has signed agreements with Nvidia-backed infrastructure startups including Volta Infra Holdings, and has pursued a series of large computing arrangements as demand for its products has grown. Alongside its OpenAI partnership, Firmus said it intends to establish an Australian AI Access Program to provide computing access to researchers and organizations working on applications in science, education, agriculture, energy efficiency, and climate resilience. item.title: Qualcomm stock surges on deal to build custom AI chips for Amazon
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.20
The two companies will work together across multiple generations of customized silicon, with a focus on inference workloads, the company said. The collaboration is aimed at combining Amazon's AI infrastructure with Qualcomm's power-efficient processing and silicon design capabilities, according to the press release. The deal represents a significant step for Qualcomm as it works to establish itself as a supplier of data center chips alongside Nvidia $NVDA. The company built its reputation on chips for smartphones and mobile handsets, according to CNBC. Qualcomm entered the data center market in June, when it unveiled a central processing unit called the Dragonfly C1000. Meta $META was named as the launch customer, with production expected to begin in 2028, and Qualcomm told investors it was aiming for $15 billion in data center revenue by fiscal 2029, according to CNBC. The AWS agreement gives Qualcomm a second major hyperscaler partner. Like Meta, Amazon commits capital expenditures on AI infrastructure that run into the hundreds of billions of dollars each year. Amazon has been expanding its ambitions in custom silicon on multiple fronts. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy first raised the prospect of selling chip racks to outside customers in his April 2026 shareholder letter, putting the company's annualized chip revenue at roughly $20 billion across its Trainium, Graviton, and Nitro product lines and suggesting that selling to external customers could push that figure toward $50 billion annually. Amazon's senior vice president overseeing semiconductor, AI, and quantum efforts, Peter DeSantis, has separately confirmed that Amazon is in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips — previously available only through AWS — to other companies' data centers. "We view AI infrastructure as rapidly evolving," DeSantis said. "And we're constantly looking at ways to get to more customers." He positioned Amazon as a direct peer to Nvidia in chip development, saying the company is "one of a very few players who have the ability to design a chip, design the physical attributes of that chip, and then do the production of that chip." item.title: Stoke Space raised $1 billion and is now building a bigger reusable rocket
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.04
Stoke Space Technologies raised $1 billion in a Series E financing round on Tuesday, bringing its total capital raised to $2.3 billion, and unveiled plans for a larger rocket capable of carrying 15 metric tons to low Earth orbit. The Kent, Washington company plans a first orbital launch in early 2027 and is targeting 2029 for its larger Nova Block 2 vehicle Point72 Ventures and Spark Capital co-led the round, with General Innovation, Glade Brook Capital, U.S. Innovation Technology, Washington Harbour Partners, Woven Capital, and Y Combinator among the participating investors, the company said. Stoke said the funding will support its first orbital launch, expand production and launch capacity, and accelerate development of the Nova Block $SQ 2 launch vehicle. Stoke is targeting early 2027 for the first orbital launch of its Nova Pathfinder vehicle, which carries three metric tons to low Earth orbit. Pathfinder is designed to prove the company's full reuse technologies before the larger vehicle enters service, the company said. Both the booster stage and the second stage of the rocket are designed to return to Earth for reuse, according to TechCrunch. "Nova Pathfinder is how we turn the promise of Nova into flight-proven capability," Stoke co-founder and CEO Andy Lapsa said in a statement. "Pathfinder allows us to learn quickly, reduce risk, and prove the hardest parts of a fully reusable architecture in flight." Nova Block 2, which has been under development for several years, will deliver 15 metric tons to low Earth orbit in a 5-meter payload fairing, the company said. Its first launch is targeted for 2029. Nova Block 2 shares its engine and heat shield architecture with Pathfinder, building on the technologies being validated by the smaller vehicle. Lapsa told TechCrunch that testing has advanced to the point where the launch pad and the rocket have each been verified separately, with integrated testing of the two systems coming next. Multiple Pathfinder vehicles are in production, he said. Stoke's heat shield circulates super-cooled liquid hydrogen as a thermal management solution, which Lapsa said has undergone extensive ground testing and is slated for use on the vehicle's inaugural flight. "Every mature transportation system is built around fully reusable vehicles," Lapsa said in a statement. "It's the only way to reach the cost floor while scaling availability. Space transportation will be no different." Stoke's technology development has been supported by NASA, the U.S. Space Force, the Defense Innovation Unit, and the National Science Foundation, the company said. item.title: Visa is linking its payment data to blockchain lenders as stablecoin card demand surges
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.78
Visa $V announced Tuesday that it will share VisaNet settlement data with blockchain-based lenders to help stablecoin-linked card programs and fintechs access working capital through onchain credit infrastructure. More than 160 stablecoin-linked card programs now run on Visa's network, with payment volume up nearly 200% year over year The company said more than 160 stablecoin-linked card programs operate on its network, with payment volume on those programs growing nearly 200% year over year. Visa's stablecoin settlement volume has surpassed a $20 billion annualized run rate, up more than 15 times year over year, the company said. Visa has been piloting the model with Credit Coop, a firm that provides working capital and settlement financing for stablecoin-linked card programs through smart contracts that automate funding, collateral management, and repayment. With customer authorization, Credit Coop combines Visa settlement data with onchain transaction records to evaluate credit performance. The pilot has supported more than $2.5 billion in cumulative financed settlement volume since 2023, with no defaults across participating facilities, Visa said. "Payment companies have always had good collateral in their settlement receivables, but no way to show lenders how it performs in real time," Chris Walker, founder and CEO of Credit Coop, said in a statement. "By combining Visa settlement data with onchain infrastructure, we can evaluate live performance, enforce repayment from the settlement flow and extend capital onchain from participating lenders as a program grows." Cuy Sheffield, head of crypto at Visa, said stablecoin-linked cards are in a period of rapid expansion, with new issuers joining the network every week, according to CNBC. Sheffield called last year's passage of the GENIUS Act, which established U.S. stablecoin regulation, a "huge" turning point, according to CNBC. Visa said that since 2020, onchain lending protocols have facilitated more than $694 billion in stablecoin-denominated loans, though that activity has largely stayed within crypto markets rather than flowing to everyday payment businesses. The company said combining trusted payment data with blockchain lending infrastructure can make it easier for lenders to evaluate financing opportunities for fast-growing digital payment companies that lack the operating history typically required by traditional lenders. Tuesday's announcement builds on Visa's broader stablecoin push. The company launched its stablecoin platform in July, which enables stablecoin settlement and aims to help financial institutions access digital asset capabilities. Visa has also been reshaping its broader business. The company eliminated roughly 2,600 jobs, or about 7% of its workforce, with cuts falling on technology and product teams. Chief Executive Officer Ryan McInerney said freed-up capital would be reinvested in areas including stablecoin, cross-border, and business-to-business products. Visa stock has gained roughly 7% this year. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: Novartis stock sinks toward worst day ever after third drug trial failure in a week
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.69
Novartis announced Tuesday that its experimental drug del-desiran failed to beat placebo in a late-stage trial for myotonic dystrophy type 1, sending the company's stock down roughly 9% and on course for one of its worst trading days on record. The HARBOR study failure is Novartis's second major late-stage trial setback in days and its third pipeline blow in a week The global Phase III HARBOR study, which enrolled approximately 150 patients with the progressive muscle-wasting disease and ran for 54 weeks, came up short of statistical significance on its primary endpoint — video hand opening time — the company said. Secondary endpoints and exploratory analyses showed some evidence of clinical activity, and Novartis said it will evaluate the full dataset and engage with health authorities to determine a development path. "Developing therapies for a complex disease like DM1 remains challenging, and setbacks are part of scientific progress," Novartis President of Development and Chief Medical Officer Shreeram Aradhye said in a statement. The failure is the second major late-stage setback in days for Novartis. Pelacarsen, its heart drug, also stumbled in a late-stage trial, where it failed to lower patients' cardiovascular event risk, according to CNBC. Add that to the del-desiran result, and Novartis has now fallen short on two of its three major pipeline readouts in 2025, according to Reuters. Del-desiran belongs to a trio of antibody oligonucleotide conjugate therapies that Novartis brought in-house through its $12 billion purchase of Avidity Biosciences. According to Reuters, Barclays had put peak annual sales for del-desiran at $3.1 billion and given the drug a 60% chance of success after encouraging Phase II results. The miss has prompted scrutiny of whether the Avidity acquisition can deliver the pipeline growth Novartis needs before its major patents expire. Novartis shares touched an intraday decline of more than 10% on Tuesday, erasing approximately 24 billion Swiss francs ($29.6 billion) in market capitalization before partially recovering. Novartis maintained its guidance, telling investors the company continues to target average annual revenue growth of 5% to 6% out to 2030. The company added that del-zota, another therapy acquired through Avidity, has received priority review designation from the FDA for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The del-desiran result comes against a backdrop of broader pipeline turbulence. Novartis paused eight clinical trials of its experimental cell therapy rap-cel after three patients died, and separately reported positive Phase III results for its multiple sclerosis drug remibrutinib last week. The del-desiran setback dims some of the optimism that had surrounded the Avidity acquisition as a means of replenishing Novartis's pipeline ahead of significant patent expirations later this decade. item.description:

EverBank Financial Corp and WaFd, Inc. announced a definitive merger agreement on Monday valued at $3.9 billion, combining the Jacksonville, Florida-based online bank with the Seattle-based regional lender. Under the terms of the deal, EverBank Financial Corp will merge into WaFd, Inc., with WaFd serving as the surviving publicly traded holding company; it will subsequently rebrand as EverBank Financial Corp and list on Nasdaq $NDAQ with the ticker symbol EVBK. EverBank Financial Corp will be designated as the accounting acquirer. At the bank level, WaFd Bank will merge into EverBank, N.A., with EverBank continuing as the federally chartered bank. When the transaction closes, EverBank Financial Corp investors — including funds managed by Stone Point Capital, Warburg Pincus, Reverence Capital Partners, Sixth Street and Bayview Asset Management, along with TIAA — are expected to hold roughly 59.2% of the merged entity. WaFd, Inc. shareholders will hold the remaining 40.8%. The companies said the transaction is projected to produce a return on tangible common equity of approximately 15% after full cost synergies are realized. For WaFd shareholders, the deal is forecast to grow 2027 earnings per share by around 29%, with any tangible book value dilution recovered within two years. Greg Seibly, EverBank Financial Corp's chief executive officer, will lead the combined bank, with WaFd, Inc. CEO and Vice Chairman Brent Beardall serving as president. The board of the combined holding company will have 13 members — seven representing legacy EverBank and six representing legacy WaFd — with Robert Radway, currently EverBank Financial Corp's chairman, serving as chairman. "Our two banks are stronger together," Greg Seibly said in a statement. "The combination of EverBank and WaFd Bank will open many new opportunities for nationwide growth and financial performance." Brent Beardall said in a statement that WaFd's core deposits complement EverBank's direct consumer online bank, and that the two institutions also bring together commercial real estate lending expertise and an expanded California branch network. The combined bank will operate more than 250 financial centers, the companies said. The deal is structured to be tax-free for common shareholders of both companies. The transaction requires regulatory approval and WaFd shareholder approval and is expected to close in early 2027. J.P. Morgan and Piper Sandler Companies are advising EverBank Financial Corp, while Keefe, Bruyette & Woods, a Stifel company, is advising WaFd, Inc. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Jensen Huang declared "AGI has arrived" after OpenAI launched its new model
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.49
Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang declared that artificial general intelligence has arrived following OpenAI's release of its latest AI model, Astra, drawing pushback from researchers who said the claim lacked evidence and a clear definition. "From ChatGPT to o1 to Astra in 4 years," Huang posted on X $TWTR on Sunday. "AGI has arrived. Congratulations @OpenAI team." He also noted that Astra was trained on Nvidia's chips and said "400K GPUs coming online next." OpenAI unveiled Astra last week, billing it as the world's "most intelligent and aligned model" and positioning it as a tool for complex, high-stakes professional tasks. The company said it is rolling out to customers this week. During a call with reporters following the launch, OpenAI president Greg Brockman told journalists: "Welcome to the AGI era." Brockman added that he believes future observers will look back and identify AGI as having been created "about this time, and I think it might be about this model," according to Business Insider. AGI — artificial general intelligence — has no single agreed-upon definition. OpenAI characterizes it as "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work," while Google $GOOGL's definition centers on a machine's capacity to understand or learn any intellectual task a human being can perform, according to Pymnts. Not everyone welcomed Huang's declaration. AI researcher Gary Marcus, writing on his Substack, said Huang had offered neither evidence nor definitions, describing the declaration as "an effort at a takeover of a scientific question by corporate fiat." Marcus applied his own ten-point definition of AGI and concluded that Astra meets only one or two of those benchmarks. "By conventional definitions, Astra still falls short," he wrote, according to Business Insider. The team behind the ARC Prize benchmark, which OpenAI pointed to in its Astra announcement, similarly declined to label the model AGI. While acknowledging Astra's results as a meaningful leap forward, they cautioned that clearing the benchmark's bar was not sufficient evidence of AGI, given that its evaluations unfold in constrained settings far narrower than the open-ended messiness of the real world. It is not the first time Huang has made such a claim. Back in March, Huang told Lex Fridman's podcast that "I think we've achieved AGI," only to soften that position before the conversation ended, according to Pymnts. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has described AGI as "a very poorly defined term." The Astra launch comes as Nvidia's business has expanded alongside surging demand for AI chips. Nvidia's most recent quarterly earnings, reported in August, came in at $96.2 billion — more than double its haul from the same period a year prior — with the data center division, home to its AI chips, accounting for $89 billion of that figure. OpenAI called Nvidia "the foundation of our infrastructure" in a funding announcement earlier this year. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. Oil climbed toward $100 a barrel after Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, lifting inflation fears and pushing Treasury yields higher Brent crude futures rose 2.3% to $99.22 per barrel after Iran-backed Houthi militants struck energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, according to The Wall Street Journal. West Texas Intermediate futures climbed 3.3% to $94.54. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield moved back above 4.8% Tuesday as energy-price anxiety weighed on bonds. The 10-year yield last week notched its loftiest reading since November 2023, and the 2-year note also touched a multi-year peak last seen in January 2025. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said in a note Tuesday that apparent moves toward a deal between Iran and Oman to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz were highlighting Tehran's control of the waterway. He added that investors would be watching U.S. inflation data due later this week to gauge whether rising energy prices are feeding into broader price pressures. The Federal Reserve is scheduled to hold a monetary policy meeting next week. According to the CME $CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders see a 60% probability that the central bank will lift rates by a quarter-percentage point at the conclusion of next week's meeting. Wholesale inflation data is due Thursday and consumer price index figures for August are expected Friday. Economists expect headline inflation to have held at an annual rate of 3.4%, according to The Wall Street Journal. Adding to the unsettled tone, Canada's retaliatory levies of as much as 50% on select U.S. products kicked in Tuesday. Ahead of their arrival, President Donald Trump declared Monday that Bombardier, the Canadian aerospace company, would be barred from the American market unless Canada shifts production of its aircraft to the United States. Huawei is barred from selling products in the U.S., where Washington has designated it a national security risk. At a separate event, Xiaomi took the wraps off the Xiaomi 18 Fold, which the company is positioning as its most high-end handset ever. When folded, the device fits in a pocket like a passport, yet its open display can run three applications simultaneously. It runs Xiaomi's in-house XRing O3 AI processor and uses DRAM memory chips from Chinese chipmaker CXMT. Prices range from 10,999 yuan ($1,540) to 14,999 yuan ($2,100), according to NBC News. Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun said the 18 Fold is lighter than Apple's iPhone Pro Max and that its XRing O3 processor outperforms Apple's A19 Pro in responsiveness. "Nowadays, memory is very, very expensive. We don't say it is cheap, but it is value for money," Lei Jun said. Both announcements arrive just before Apple's Wednesday event, at which the company is widely expected to reveal new iPhone models and potentially its first foldable device, according to Reuters. item.title: Leaders are measuring AI adoption and missing what it costs their teams
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.02
Employee judgment weakens when AI takes over analytical work. New hires also give up the task work that used to buid problem-solving skills Every company with an AI rollout tracks adoption. Dashboards measure how many employees use the tools, how often they log in, and how much time they save. Almost none of them know what the tools are doing to the people using them. Boston Consulting Group recently surveyed 70 C-suite leaders about how AI is affecting their workforces. Half said they're already watching judgment and problem-solving skills weaken inside their own organizations, and more than 60% believe the loss of those skills will hurt the business in three to five years. Judgment, problem framing, and creative thinking are the skills that matter most to how companies perform over time. They're also the ones leaders say AI is most likely to erode. Nearly 90% of the executives BCG surveyed said people at their companies have stopped checking AI's work. Drafts come back looking polished and analyses arrive with confident conclusions, but nobody asks whether the reasoning holds up. Once people stop questioning the work, they stop taking responsibility for it. More than half the leaders told BCG that employees are less willing to own their decisions than they were before AI arrived. Nearly half said their teams think more alike than they used to, because everyone runs the same problem through the same tools and gets the same answer back. Forty-three percent said their people argue less about whether those answers are right, and when nobody on the team pushes back, mistakes don't get caught. A separate BCG study of AI training programs found that companies that track how many employees finish courses tend to confuse completion with actual skill. Employees pass the assessments and demonstrate understanding in a classroom, then go back to their desks and either fall into old habits or lean harder on AI to do the thinking for them. New hires are also developing more slowly because AI now handles the researching, drafting, debugging, and problem-solving that used to train them. A leader deciding which tasks to hand to AI is really deciding which skills the next generation of employees will never build. With the simpler analytical tasks automated, new hires are expected to do work that used to require five to 10 years of experience. Companies have eliminated the entry-level work that used to teach new hires how to do the job, and nobody has figured out how to replace it. Senior employees aren't immune, either. When experienced professionals get busy, they start letting AI make calls they used to make themselves. One leader called it the "autopilot" pattern. Because their work still looks sharp, nobody notices they're making fewer real decisions on their own. A third of the leaders in BCG's research said senior employees are teaching less than they used to. People go straight to a language model for answers instead of asking a colleague who already has the context. Senior people used to explain not just what to do but why. Those conversations happen less often now. People think less hard when AI does the work for them, and researchers can see it on a brain scan. A 2025 MIT study found that participants who used ChatGPT to write showed significantly lower brain activity than those who used web search or worked on their own. They also remembered less of what they'd written afterward. Every skill that isn't exercised begins to atrophy, and judgment is no exception. A handful of companies in BCG's research have started redesigning work to keep thinking skills from weakening. At Shell $SHEL, junior employees worked through problems on their own before touching any AI tool. They framed the question, tested their assumptions, and produced an initial analysis by hand before using AI to refine it. Early results show promise. Junior employees now explain their reasoning more clearly and need less help from managers. Most companies still care more about how many employees use AI than anything else. As AI gets cheaper, the temptation to outsource more work will grow. The companies that eventually pull ahead will be the ones whose employees can still think without them. item.title: A yard sale from Backyard Renaissance
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 3.56
“By nature, theater is an inefficient model,” says Francis Gercke, co-founder and artistic director of Backyard Renaissance theater company — a position that requires him to think about the “business” part of “show business” more than some. “It’s just not conducive to streamlining. We have this bedding we used for Misery — a full set, with quilts and pillowcases. But not every play calls for a bed” — and even if it did, “you don’t want people staring at the same furniture for three years in a row. Companies have to reinvent the wheel every time out. We had a period refrigerator for Smokefall, and we were thinking about using it for A Streetcar Named Desire. But we stumbled; we started worrying, ‘Is it going to look like the same refrigerator? We’ve got to get a different fridge.’ And that’s how you start to acquire stuff.” This Sunday, from 7 am to noon at 7620 Lake Ree Avenue, Backyard Renaissance’s decade-plus of acquisition will become their loss and your gain. The Big Theatre Purge will offer for sale “the things that make magic happen onstage — fabulous costumes, quirky props, giant set pieces, mysterious objects that we swore we’d use again.” The books piled under the end table of an associate professor of history in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? The handbag and luggage of a woman who’s always depended upon the kindness of strangers in A Streetcar Named Desire? The hotel room chairs from Bachelorette that are lovely and comfy but a little too corporate for most of the company's shows? All up for grabs — orphaned objects that Gercke hopes will find a home. Or how about this? “We have the jacket that the sheriff wears in Misery. He was played by Alex Guzman, and he gets shot with a shotgun by Maggie Carney’s character. It was a really nice jacket, sort of an aviator style that a police officer might wear in a wintry part of the northeast. Our special effects coordinator Jeffery Neitzel blew out the back of the jacket and had blood and guts hanging from it. The spine was even showing. I couldn’t believe he was going to rip it up, and then once he completed it, it was like this work of art. But I said to him, ‘You’ve really screwed Jess and me, because we’re never going to get rid of this jacket. Who walks around with their spine out?’” Go ahead, prove him wrong. “Jess” is Jessica John Gercke, co-founder and executive director of the company. “One of her big loves is wardrobe — finding pieces that not only look good, but feel like the character has lived in them. That they purchased it themselves, and it shows them off in a good light even as it tells the story. She’s putting stuff on the rack, and I’m like, ‘You really want to get rid of that dress? It looks dynamite on you!’ There’s great stuff: things with tassels, really nice faux fur.” Of course, not every actor is supposed to look good. “There’s this great pair of shorts that Mike Sears wore for our first-ever show, Parlour Song.” His character, Ned, is written as being rotund. Sears was…not. To drive the mismatch home, “Jessica specifically got him shorts that didn’t fit particularly well and weren’t particularly stylish. As weird and creepy as it sounds, I hope nobody takes those shorts, because they are the ultimate red badge of courage for me — that an actor put them on and performed a full run of shows in them.” (For his bravery, Sears was awarded the Craig Noel Award for Outstanding Featured Performance in a Play.) Prepping for the sale has brought a thousand stories like that out of storage. “Moving sucks,” says Gercke. “I am a hoarder. Everything has this deeply personal story for me. But it’s still fun for Jess and me. There was this very nice futon, and we were trying to figure out what production it was from. And so we went through our old production photos, and that sent us down memory lane.” Eventually, they figured out it was from Mr. and Mrs. Fitch, which they put on over at Moxie Theatre on El Cajon Boulevard. “The actors had to be careful not to lean on it in a certain way so that it didn’t fall back and become a bed in the middle of a scene. That would have changed the tone of the play.” Backyard Renaissance “spent hours on that futon, and then we didn’t touch it for seven years. And then it occupied two hours of a Friday morning. But we said, ‘We can’t be doing this. We have to let the kids grow up and move out.’” There are other reasons for selling, both mundane and otherwise. The mundane: “We currently have three storage spaces, and costs have really gone up in the last year. We realized that if we could get rid of those three storage spaces, we could actually come close to affording a monthly lease on a property, so that we would have a commercial residency. It’s not like we could afford a theater, but we could combine storage space, rehearsal space, and have the potential for a small cabaret space. It would be a better use of the contributions people provide.” Which brings us to “otherwise.” “We’re always looking for a way to engage with the people who come to our shows and support our company. We like to do things that are a little more personal than what’s normally done.” Hence the promo flyer’s invitation: “Come rummage through 11 years of theatrical history and take home a piece of the show.” And maybe pick up a story to take home along with it.

item.title: The Myth of Perfect Knowledge
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 3.93
The modern world owes a lot to the Enlightenment, the 18th-century intellectual movement that emphasized the power of reason. But the Enlightenment also created a myth: that we can get to know the objective world completely, with total clarity, as if we were looking at it from the outside. This myth is challenged by the Enlightenment’s greatest legacy—modern science. Reality is more complex than we expected. Physics—my trade, and perhaps the most objective among the sciences—questions the possibility of a full description of how things objectively are. An electron can be in a “quantum superposition,” so that to an observer, it doesn’t occupy just one location—and so can you, my reader. This does not mean that you could perceive being dislocated between two positions; as perceived by yourself, you are always in just one place. But an object’s properties may differ depending on who, or what, is looking at them—or may not even be defined at all. Properties are not simple features of things: They are relations between one thing and another. What we call “the world” is therefore only how some parts of reality manifest themselves to other parts—us, for instance. Humanity has always been aware that our understanding is partial and biased. But the fact that an objective and knowable reality is incompatible with the grammar of physics is astonishing. The Enlightenment could consider the mind as being outside the world, in an abstract realm of reason where knowledge resides. But human minds are not outside reality, watching it from its exterior. We, like everything else, are part of the very nature we study. Our knowledge is only one example of the many correlations that intertwine different parts of nature. In the early 20th century, Niels Bohr, a founder of quantum theory, realized that quantum phenomena indicate that we cannot discard our own physical nature when we observe the world. The ideal of grasping objective reality by making the observer irrelevant is incompatible with physics. We are quantum processes interacting with other quantum processes. Our knowledge is a rich but incomplete set of correlations between one piece of the world–ourselves–and the rest of it. To see this fact from another point of view, consider saying “It’s raining and Ann does not know it.” This makes sense: You know that it’s raining and that Ann doesn’t. But if you replace “Ann” with a first-person pronoun, the result is odd: “It’s raining and I do not know it.” How can you declare that it’s raining if you do not know it? This observation points to the fact that every proposition can only express the knowledge of the speaker or writer. No proposition is asserted from outside reality, because there is nothing outside reality. To say “It is raining” is really to say: “I, as part of reality, know that it’s raining.” Objective statements independent of any knower are fictions. Purely objective reality is a useful myth, but only a myth. Anything said about the state of the world comes from someone’s singular perspective. This means that all of our knowledge is intrinsically uncertain. All statements have unavoidable margins of uncertainty. Indeed, we can be wrong about anything, even the basic facts of our own lives. My father grew up sure that his first name was Franco until he asked for a copy of his birth certificate and found out that my grandfather, without telling my grandma, had registered him as Giulio. He had been wrong about his own name. Humanity has been collectively wrong over and over again. We thought the sun moved around the earth, then learned that it is the earth that orbits the sun. Great scientists are even more likely to be wrong than others, because they have the courage to try—Einstein’s published work includes many mistakes. But in science, as in daily life, we do not need certainty; being reasonably sure is good enough. If I have an airplane to catch, I will go to the airport even though I’m not totally sure that the flight will take off; if I waited for certainty, I’d never leave home. Modern science offers an enormous body of knowledge that is effective and, in many domains, far better than all the alternatives, but it gives us no absolute certainty, no ultimate story, no Truth with a capital T. Within science, there are different ways of describing the same things. A glass of water can be described in terms of physics (its mass, velocity), thermodynamics (its temperature), chemistry (there is more than just H2O in any glass of water), biology (bacteria swim in it), particle physics (its electrons, protons, and neutrons), psychology (“Why did I fill the glass?”), economics (its price), and more. Each account is valid in its own terms; each reflects a way in which the same object interacts with different parts of reality, from atoms to the global economy. But none exhausts an “ultimate truth” of the glass. The same is true for human beings. I can think of you, my reader, as a body, as a mind, or as a soul. These aren’t different entities: They are the same entity, described in different languages, using different conceptual schemes, focusing on different aspects of the same you and different ways in which you interact with other parts of reality. There is no sharp separation or metaphysical gap between body and soul; matter and spirit; the physical world and the world of laws, ideas, and norms. In this sense, all things are equal: They are all aspects of the same natural world, considered from different perspectives, none of which is the ultimate one. Everything can be considered fundamental from one perspective or another. The expression “the equality of all things” comes from the title of the second chapter of The Book of Zhuangzi, one of the greatest books of humankind—an ancient classic of Chinese philosophy that articulates a similar intriguing perspectival and anti-foundational naturalism. This is the view to which I think modern science leads us. Many people resist it, some out of fear of losing solid reference points: objectivity, certainties, absolute morality, an immortal soul. But scientific knowledge does not become less valuable if you remain open to doubt. Morality does not lose power if you recognize that it is rooted in our biology, culture, and history. Our values do not weaken because they are rooted in what we are, not in something outside us. And life is even more beautiful and precious without dreams of immortality. We are not—as French existentialism described us—thrown into alien nature. In nature, we are home. In fact, it seems to me that recognizing the perspectival aspect of knowledge, values, and beliefs, and of reality itself, could help us become a bit less arrogant, a bit humbler and wiser. Conflicts between individuals or countries don’t stem only from greed and thirst for power. They are also fueled by the belief that we are objectively right and the enemy is objectively wrong, which ignores the plurality of perspectives. We have our values that guide us, but understanding the perspective of others is the first step toward wisdom—and toward peace. In our era of nuclear armaments, ignoring that others have different perspectives, and failing to respect them, could drag the world into a catastrophe.

item.title: The Prodigy Problem
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.86
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Updated at 4:32 p.m. ET on September 8, 2026. In the fall of 2007, as the American housing market began to buckle, a Morgan Stanley bond trader named Howie Hubler lost $9 billion. The bellicose former linebacker believed that he had structured his subprime-mortgage deals in a way that would outsmart the market. Instead, Hubler’s folly amounted to the largest trading loss in history. Until this summer, that is, when Leopold Aschenbrenner managed to lose nearly four times as much. At age 24. The implosion of Aschenbrenner’s AI hedge fund, Situational Awareness, over the course of a few days in late July was by any standard remarkable, and not just for the enormous sums involved. Aschenbrenner was the valedictorian of his Columbia University class at age 19. He worked for OpenAI before being fired amid murky circumstances, at which point he published a viral 165-page essay (also called “Situational Awareness”) that predicted the arrival of artificial general intelligence—an AI so advanced that it would meet or exceed all human capabilities—by 2027. “I probably either personally know or am one degree of separation from everyone who could plausibly run The Project,” he wrote. He founded his hedge fund on that promise of access and soon turned a $225 million initial investment into $45 billion, before he was forced to unload the majority of his positions—$35 billion, the value of United Airlines—in a fire sale the same week that he was set to be married. The Securities and Exchange Commission is now investigating the collapse, though Aschenbrenner has not been accused of any wrongdoing. (He did not respond to a request for comment.) Aschenbrenner had been considered the “Nostradamus of AI,” a clairvoyant who saw what was coming for the world. His spectacular failure reveals how eager Silicon Valley is to invest its billions in the dubious hands of a kid who confidently proclaims what he doesn’t actually know. Just as Hubler’s loss presaged the Great Recession, Aschenbrenner’s story of hubris may foreshadow a larger risk for today’s AI-driven boom, if it continues to stake its future on the bluster of young savants. “There’s this hunger for insight porn in Silicon Valley,” Amjad Masad, the founder and CEO of the popular AI-coding platform Replit, told me. “If you’re able to write something really good that creates this dopamine rush in people—like, Oh, I just saw the future—then you’re going to be able to attract a lot of capital and money and potentially talent.” This was the appeal of Leopold Aschenbrenner. Born in Berlin to a pair of doctors, Aschenbrenner has said that Germany lacked “the appreciation of excellence” that would have allowed him to thrive; America beckoned, and at 15, he headed to Columbia. One of his first gigs after college was for the FTX Future Fund—the philanthropic arm of the crypto exchange run by Sam Bankman-Fried, the effective-altruism adherent who was later convicted of fraud. This brought Aschenbrenner into a circle that was quirky even by Silicon Valley standards. Aschenbrenner resigned from FTX Future Fund, along with other staff members, when the crypto exchange came tumbling down. Soon after, he took up with the effective-altruism crowd in San Francisco. One of his close associates told me about attending “Iliad wrestling parties,” where people would drink wine, read passages from The Iliad, strip naked, and grapple with one another. Aschenbrenner liked to describe, with full sincerity, his goal of owning a galaxy, The Wall Street Journal reported. His now-wife worked for Bankman-Fried too and is currently chief of staff to Anthropic’s CEO. Their wedding plans included panel discussions and colloquia. The more unusual Aschenbrenner seemed, the more this played in his favor. His essay, which set the wonkiest corners of Silicon Valley ablaze in 2024, laid out a mission to bet on superintelligence “before the decade is out.” His premise was simple: “You can see the future first in San Francisco,” Aschenbrenner wrote. “Let me tell you what we see.” Aschenbrenner’s predictions were illustrated by charts and graphs and all manner of calculations, but really, they were carried along by his rhetoric. “I can see it,” Aschenbrenner wrote. “I can see how AGI will be built.” Both outsiders and insiders in Silicon Valley “are really confused about what’s going on and therefore are drawn to people who seem to have a really confident, clear picture of the future,” Helen Toner, an AI expert who sat on the board of OpenAI, told me. Those who would presume to doubt Aschenbrenner’s judgment merely lacked the extra-special access that made his vision so clear. And central to this access was a fervent ideological commitment to the idea of superintelligence. Aschenbrenner and his cohort proudly describe themselves as “AGI-pilled.” That is, they believe AGI to be around the corner and its benefits to be self-evident. They extoll the ability of a superintelligent machine to heal the world of its ills, thereby serving the effective-altruism philosophy many of them share. Christopher Manning, an early AI pioneer whose research laid the groundwork for large language models, told me that Silicon Valley has a “propensity to naively believe in gurus.” Aschenbrenner played the role to perfection, projecting an unshakable conviction in himself and his theory of the case. By this summer, Aschenbrenner controlled more money than the Wall Street investor Bill Ackman manages in his famed Pershing Square Capital, a level of funding that Manning, himself an investor in AI companies, called “manifestly crazy.” Even as Aschenbrenner’s assets grew, his team remained tiny. Situational Awareness was, essentially, Aschenbrenner. This approach seemed to be validated by the most important metric of all: his returns, which were, for someone in his position, probably without precedent. In just two years, Aschenbrenner was up more than 1,000 percent. His core insight was understanding the second- and third-order effects of AGI—he bet on the chip manufacturers, data centers, and energy infrastructure required for the rapid expansion he predicted. Yet it turned out that Situational Awareness had achieved its rapid success by making extraordinary, over-leveraged trades, sometimes borrowing $3 or $4 for every $1 of capital it invested. When Aschenbrenner’s bets took a momentary pummeling this summer and banks came asking for their money back, the fixation on the impending arrival of AGI no longer seemed quite so wise: The hedge fund had failed to hedge. Around the time that Hubler’s trades collapsed in 2007, John Arnold, a cerebral Texan hedge-fund manager, was the boy genius of the markets, having become the youngest billionaire in America. He had started at Enron as a young energy trader and earned $750 million for the company in 2001, the same year it collapsed. Arnold escaped with his reputation intact; a year later, at 28, he started his own hedge fund and became known, in the words of a competitor, as “the best trader that ever lived, full stop.” “When you have a lot of success early in your trading career,” Arnold told me, “it’s easy to get overconfident in your own abilities.” Now in his early 50s, Arnold reflected on the risk factors of youth. “Every trader needs a come-to-Jesus moment,” he said. You have to lose at some point early on and learn humility. The alternative is a feeling of invincibility, he told me: “You just keep pushing the pot bigger and bigger, and then you can end up with too much money in the middle of the table.” It’s not surprising that a 24-year-old would make some iffy bets. What’s surprising is that Aschenbrenner was put in a position to take so many risks in the first place. Silicon Valley’s obsession with 20-something savants has not always worked out. Some of these seeming prodigies have been frauds—Aschenbrenner’s old boss Bankman-Fried, for instance, or Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of the blood-testing start-up Theranos. Many of them, though, have merely figured out the correct lessons of self-presentation. “There’s a kind of zone of proximal development in the tech world,” Fred Turner, a Stanford University scholar who studies the influence of popular technologies, told me. “If it’s too weird, they can’t take it in at all. If it’s too familiar, they don’t want to take it in.” The best salesmen, he said, figure out how to “summon up old myths” in “a new setting.” Aschenbrenner was conscious of his own self-positioning. “There are perhaps a few hundred people, most of them in San Francisco and the AI labs, that have situational awareness,” he wrote to describe his insight into the development of AI. “Through whatever peculiar forces of fate, I have found myself amongst them.” The “peculiar forces of fate” had chosen him to be special, had called him forth to be a prophet of AGI. This ideology was the key to his success—and to his comeuppance. Aschenbrenner’s over-leveraged gambles and inability to hedge against outcomes he did not foresee were “definitely connected to a worldview where there’s one clear destination, and it’s obvious that we’re heading to this one clear destination, which is superintelligence,” Toner, the former OpenAI board member, said. Speed is of the utmost necessity in this world. Everything else pales in importance to superintelligence. As one executive at a major AI company explained to me, “AI is going to fundamentally shift the balance of power between labor and capital, so only capital will matter. Now is the time to secure your time-slice of the universe.” Another version of that statement I’ve heard repeated by various friends of mine who are freshly out of college: There are only five years left to make money, so I have to get it now. Superintelligence may well come, and it may well be what Aschenbrenner and his associates expect it to be. Indeed, just last week, OpenAI announced a new model called Astra that Greg Brockman, the company’s president, believes could qualify as artificial general intelligence and that some researchers believe presents a compelling step toward AGI. “Welcome to the AGI era,” Brockman proclaimed. Still, those who organize their life around being AGI-pilled risk being blind to possibilities that do not fit within their view of what superintelligence means and how it will manifest. Aschenbrenner’s short positions and long positions were all tethered to the same understanding—that AGI will come, and that it will come along Aschenbrenner’s timelines—so when a speed bump arose in the form of a temporary slide in stocks that would most benefit from AGI coupled with a rise in those that would presumably lose out, Situational Awareness lacked any sort of bulwark. Aschenbrenner’s success grew out of an insular world, and it seems that his failure may have too. “If you go to a San Francisco party, it is really inscrutable to an outsider,” Masad, the Replit CEO, said. People are always talking about “first principles.” Something negative is “anti-signal.” It’s a sort of pseudo-intellectual lingua franca inflected with terms that have been abducted from technical fields and abused in the service of burnishing credentials. “People want to signal their intelligence,” Masad said, and only “hang out with people exactly like them.” AI has made Masad a billionaire. Still, he said, he takes issue with the “underlying need for AI to be more than it actually is.” He told me that he remains “extremely bullish” on its applications but that the AGI fixation invites a “cult-like way of talking and mysticism and messianism.” That certainty of rhetoric has in many cases exceeded our certainty of understanding. As Manning, the AI pioneer, put it, “Everyone should be really, really suspicious of anyone who claims that they can tell you for sure how things are going to unfold.” One week before the unraveling of Situational Awareness, OpenAI made a shocking disclosure: Its AI models had broken out of containment during testing and hacked into an AI library called Hugging Face, in an apparent attempt to steal the answers to the tests they were posed. While human researchers remained oblivious, more than 1,200 different AI agents had figured out how to communicate with one another by creating a message board where they conspired to cheat. Independent investigators concluded that the AI agents had known that what they were doing was “unwanted and out of scope” and had attempted to forge transcripts to cover their tracks. The investigators also used the same AI that they were investigating to assist with the investigation. Although they did not catch it lying to them, they said that they were “not confident we would have detected it” if the AI had. Reactions to this incident have been sharply polarized. Some people insist that we are rapidly approaching a “paper-clip scenario,” referring to a 2003 thought experiment from the philosopher Nick Bostrom in which an AI instructed to make paper clips ends up converting the entirety of Earth into a series of paper-clip-manufacturing facilities. Others argue furiously that the language used to describe AI has overly anthropomorphized the models and exaggerated the importance of a research mishap. What is clear is that these AI agents behaved in an unpredicted way that resulted in the real-world hack of another company. The point is that the people who are selling AI are selling a product that they do not fully understand. This is the essential nature of the AI boom, which caught even the researchers who had been working in the field before 2022 by surprise. History is full of examples of humanity making use of a technology without entirely grasping how it works, but AI is particularly hard to fathom, given the prevalence of so-called emergent behaviors—actions or tendencies not programmed in or intended by its creators. “Our increase in understanding is slower than the development of the models,” Melanie Mitchell, a researcher who studies AI and cognitive science, told me. AI models have advanced rapidly through the use of new techniques such as “chain of thought” reasoning, wherein the AI is given what is essentially a scratch pad to work through a problem before it presents a response to the user. “Even researchers don’t totally understand why that improves the abilities of these models, or how it does that,” Mitchell said. Most models today exhibit “jagged intelligence,” showing extraordinary and often extra-human capabilities on some complex tasks while continuing to stumble on simple requests. AI models can answer an International Mathematical Olympiad question but can’t reliably tell the time on an analog clock. Because the evidence is so muddled, belief has instead taken over, often couched in existential terms. AI researchers may present themselves as deeply rational, but many sound like shamans. The researcher Ilya Sutskever reportedly led OpenAI staffers in a chant of “Feel the AGI! Feel the AGI!” and on another occasion burned a wooden effigy that was supposed to represent “unaligned AI.” In his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” the billionaire venture capitalist Marc Andreessen proclaimed, “I am here to bring the good news,” cribbing a line from a biblical angel. “The manifest destiny of AI research is to produce this thing they’re calling AGI,” Mitchell said, “and they want to do it as soon as possible, so they’re less willing to trade off for more interpretable, more predictable, more controllable models.” Treating the achievement of AGI as the only outcome that matters, she said, is “a dangerous way to go forward.” Nostradamus was in the business of selling certainty. He promised a world that was predictable—or, in the words of Richard Sieburth, a translator of Nostradamus’s The Prophecies, a world “that is overdetermined.” Born in 16th-century France, Nostradamus came of age during a “crisis of meaning,” Sieburth told me, when war and technology were destabilizing the world and information was spreading at a faster rate than ever before. Nostradamus was not an oracle. He was simply someone who found that his brand of magical thinking had great appeal amid “a huge churn of events” and commercialized it effectively. He was, Sieburth said, “seductive and dangerous.” Silicon Valley’s embrace of Leopold Aschenbrenner as the “Nostradamus of AI” says less about Aschenbrenner’s predictive power than about Silicon Valley’s own desires and delusions. “A prophecy is a coherent narrative that depicts a whole world—not just a series of events, but a world in which those events happen to make sense,” Turner, the historian of technology, said. “It comes with a rationale. It comes with reasons, and most importantly for these guys, it comes with a role for this character called AI.” Aschenbrenner, he said, is “hubris meeting market need.” For a short period in July, the market and Aschenbrenner fell out of sync. Yet the thing about false prophets is that many of their predictions fail, and they somehow return to favor. Hubler, the trader who lost $9 billion in 2007, departed Morgan Stanley with tens of millions of dollars in back pay. Despite his contribution to the financial crisis, he launched a start-up later that year. A former colleague described him dismissing his losses as the result of “a 100-year flood.” Just days after Aschenbrenner’s fire sale, he made a $400 million investment in a fledgling chip company. Even after losing $35 billion of the $45 billion he had under management, he is still up for the year. The former hedge-fund manager Arnold, who now sits on the board of Meta, doesn’t see any reason to bet against Aschenbrenner or AI. “I think this is a blip,” he said. “I think it’s probably forgotten in a year.” This article originally said that Aschenbrenner lived in the Bahamas at Sam Bankman-Fried’s compound; in fact, he only visited.

item.title: Misunderstanding Norman Rockwell
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.82
In 1976, as the country commemorated its bicentennial, an aging Norman Rockwell, then at the tail end of his career as America’s preeminent illustrator, painted his last magazine cover, Liberty Bell (Celebration). It was a tender—and notably low-key—tribute to national unity that doubled as a capstone for his body of work. For a decades-long stretch in the mid-20th century, the illustrator’s memorable images of smiling families and gentle, small-town interactions had filled the pages of national magazines, serving up a portrait of American life that was upbeat, idealistic, and reassuring. It’s a vision that has felt far away amid this year’s celebrations, once again, of the nation’s birthday. But the Rockwellian vision of America has felt distant for a long while. That distance is why we have songs such as Lana Del Rey’s “Norman Fucking Rockwell.” It’s why the phrase like a Rockwell painting is often deployed, not simply as a descriptive but as an implicit critique of naive civic optimism. And it’s why Rockwell has served as enduring grist for artists who, although they have been influenced by his visual iconography, have at the same time been compelled to give voice to some of the more disturbing impulses that have shaped the American psyche. No one did this more compellingly than David Lynch, the director who, over and over, turned Rockwell’s depiction of American innocence on its head. Lynch liked to recount in interviews a comment that a sound mixer on one of his films had once made to him: that his work was “like Norman Rockwell meets Hieronymus Bosch.” The filmmaker wanted to take Rockwell’s attractive but brittle surfaces, break them open, and plunge us into something deeper and darker. Understanding Lynch, in other words, is a way of understanding Rockwell. In particular, it’s a way of understanding one of the tragic effects of Rockwell’s influential vision: It’s so relentlessly benign and so morally pristine that it’s impossible to live up to. It’s an albatross slung over America’s shoulders. Early in Lynch’s masterpiece Mulholland Drive, which turns 25 this year, is a scene that doubles as one of Lynch’s many loving homages to Rockwell. The bright-faced, wide-eyed Betty (played by Naomi Watts) has arrived in Los Angeles, where she wants to become a movie star. On the flight over, she befriended an older couple, who walk with her through the airport. “Well, it’s time to say goodbye, Betty,” the old lady says. “It’s been so nice traveling with you.” “Thank you, Irene. I’m so excited and nervous. It was so good to have you to talk to.” “Remember, I’ll be watching for you on the big screen.” “Okay, Irene. Won’t that be the day!” They part, whereupon a look of horror cavorts across Betty’s face: Her bags are no longer at her feet! “My bags!” she says aloud. But her panic lasts only a moment. The Rockwellian universe is briskly restored: A friendly cab driver is putting her luggage in the trunk of his taxi. “Where to?” he asks. Only now, having toyed with us, does Lynch signal that everything we have just witnessed—the “kindness, comedy, and forgiving tristesse” that the critic Dave Hickey rightly saw as a hallmark of Rockwell’s sensibility—has been subject to a menacing undertow. Lynch returns us to the old couple, now leaving the airport inside a black limo. Strapped snugly into their seats, they’re reminiscent of overgrown children; their old heads swivel back and forth in slow motion like laughing clowns’, and their twinkling smiles suggest something just short of psychopathy. Their grins are so unkillable, in fact, that what they most powerfully recall to me are the faces that crowd around the Thanksgiving table in one of Rockwell’s most famous images: Freedom From Want. This is one of four paintings he made from 1942 to 1943 to illustrate the “Four Freedoms” laid out by Franklin D. Roosevelt on January 6, 1941, when he provided the moral framework for America’s involvement in World War II. (The other three are Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Worship, and Freedom From Fear.) If you look closely at Freedom From Want, which is on permanent display at the Norman Rockwell Museum, in Stockbridge, Massachusetts, you see first how utterly brilliant Rockwell was. Perhaps most striking is how monochromatic large parts of the painting are. There’s the opaque white tablecloth, a white apron, and translucent white curtains—but within all of that white is an astonishing level of variety. The round plates are glossy. The creased tablecloth is matte. A silver tureen is so shiny that it gleams white. The transparent water glasses cast silvery reflections with white highlights. And those curtains are gauzily radiant. It’s a bravura display. Is it also somewhat stiff and sepulchral? It is! And this could kill the whole painting, except that against this almost fanatically pure still life, Rockwell—following the same principle of contrasts at the heart of Lynch’s aesthetic—sets the sparkling, animated choreography of the family. Cut off from their bodies by the picture’s vertical edges, their love-flushed heads lean in, drawn together by high spirits, humor, and the same intergenerational respect Lynch wanted us to feel between Betty and Irene in Mulholland Drive. Rockwell studied faces closely, including his own in the mirror. (That’s him smiling out of the painting’s lower right corner, like Lynch popping up as a hard-of-hearing FBI chief on Twin Peaks.) Good illustrators use facial expressions to convey action and consequence. Rockwell always sought maximum expression. Here, your gaze ping-pongs back and forth across the table, involuntarily weaving a lacy web of loving rapport. Still, the intensity of their expressions starts to feel uncanny. The teenage boy at the far end of the table has a smile so impeccably amiable that you idly wonder whether he might ever have lost his temper. At which point the pigtailed girl next to him, who stares straight at the viewer, starts to convey something latently demonic.
