Next to her, you notice with a start, is a wrinkled and waxy, almost clawlike hand, which presumably belongs to the venerable paterfamilias who stands at the head of the table, but which is cut off from his body by the platter carrying the turkey. If it’s easy to imagine the whole scene as a movie, slowed down, subtly sinister—like the scene with the grinning retirees in Mulholland Drive—that’s because Lynch’s work so effectively gives the lie to Rockwell’s. In the good-humored and reassuringly rational world that Rockwell constructed, there was no such thing as evil. His portraits of everyday life included pratfalls, minor moral lapses, and some genuine pain, but the arc of history was always bending the right way. In its fundamental integrity, Rockwellian America was as immaculate and charismatic as that Thanksgiving table. What is clear today is that the strain, so many decades on, of trying to make America conform to Rockwell’s softly arcadian image is too great. It’s a burden the nation cannot collectively handle and probably never could—which is why it continually demands forms of cultural release. These, over the years, have come in the form of not just Lynch’s creations but also novels such as Portnoy’s Complaint and American Psycho, and films such as Apocalypse Now. All are explosions of irrationality designed to release us from the whole Rockwellian racket and to renew our connection to darker truths. It’s not that Lynch’s take on America was any more real than Rockwell’s. It’s that his films expressed the absurdity of trying to make actual life match the illustrator’s gorgeous yet finally intolerable image of pleasantness and perfectibility. Since Rockwell’s heyday, this image has loomed over America like an impossibly kind, wise, and accomplished parent—and like a silent rebuke. On your way to the Norman Rockwell Museum, you may pass through the nearby town of Stockbridge, where Rockwell lived for a quarter century. He lovingly rendered its Main Street in a Christmas Eve scene painted in 1967, a year that also saw the Summer of Love, the release of Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, and another 100,000 American troops sent to Vietnam. Fifty years ago, during the nation’s bicentennial celebrations (and two years before Rockwell died), Stockbridge staged a parade of floats with tableaux inspired by the illustrator. The procession, in which 2,000 people participated, was attended by more than 10,000. No other American artist has ever received such a tribute. The most extraordinary room at the Rockwell museum is always the basement gallery, which is festooned with the artist’s Saturday Evening Post covers—more than 300 of them. Rockwell first walked into the offices of the mass-circulation weekly in 1916, carrying a portfolio of his artwork. His timing was excellent: This was near the beginning of a great era in illustration, when advances in printing technology transformed large-scale color illustration into an essential aspect of communication. His talent was quickly rewarded. Within four years, Rockwell had become the Post’s leading illustrator. By 1925, he was known around the nation, and before the Depression was over, he had been all but canonized—America’s leading “Painter-Patriot,” as his biographer Deborah Solomon wrote, its paragon of picture-making. Rockwell achieved his status by painting small-town America. “I do ordinary people in everyday situations, and that’s about all I do,” he said in his 1960 memoir, My Adventures as an Illustrator. He was so successful, and so much better known than just about any other American artist, that people had great sport comparing him with his avant-garde peers in the art world. (This reputation gave rise to some amusing images: Rockwell’s The Connoisseur, from 1962, for instance, shows a portly, fastidious-looking man in a light-gray suit standing in front of a parti-color splatter painting in the manner of Jackson Pollock. When he saw The Connoisseur, Willem de Kooning, Pollock’s friend and rival, quipped that the illustrator had done it better than Pollock.) But Rockwell never pretended to be other than he was: an artist paid to make images in service to stories. Content to be called an illustrator, he was nevertheless unsure about the difference between what he did and fine art. His confusion was legitimate. Illustration, after all, is not inherently better or worse than any other style of art. Rembrandt was, to a large extent, an illustrator, a visual artist involved in the challenge of dramatizing Biblical stories; so was Winslow Homer, and not just in his magazine work. Narrative art is difficult for the obvious reason that it’s hard to show cause and effect (the core engine of narrative) with a single image frozen in time. The illustrator’s art lies in implying both cause and effect, so that a story—with its conventional, if artificial, movement from obscured buildup to crystalline consequence—unfolds in the viewer’s mind even as the image remains static. At this, Rockwell was brilliant. Still, professional illustrators are usually beholden to the directives of those who publish their work. In Rockwell’s case, this meant 47 years following the dictates of the Post, a magazine that sold 2 million copies a week and was avidly read by many more people. For decades, it also had an abhorrent policy (against which Rockwell chafed more and more until he finally severed ties with the magazine) of not depicting Black people except in subservient roles. After he left, Rockwell felt freer to address civil-rights-era issues, especially desegregation, which he did in such celebrated paintings as New Kids in the Neighborhood and The Problem We All Live With, his depiction, for Look magazine, of Ruby Bridges being escorted by federal marshals to her previously all-white school. To see the Post covers gathered together is to discern a cumulative, if highly prejudicial, portrait of America spanning more than four decades. Was it a portrait that helped America understand itself? Despite its cheesiness, and notwithstanding the Post’s appalling racism, I think it did—not just because Rockwell was so good at what he did but also because he was an artist in whom humor, grace, and loving appreciation easily commingled. These attributes were tethered, moreover, to a larger civic-mindedness. His best paintings are not only ingeniously constructed and brilliantly colored—they’re also richly humane. Stories are connected to our curiosity about how the world works, and for Rockwell, this curiosity was rooted in everyday life. “The commonplaces of America are to me the richest subjects in art,” he wrote in 1936. “Boys batting flies on vacant lots; little girls playing jacks on the front steps; old men plodding home at twilight, umbrellas in hand—all of these things arouse feeling in me. Commonplaces never become tiresome. It is we who become tired when we cease to become curious and appreciative.” Rockwell’s portrait of life in America is certainly kitsch. (Kitsch, Milan Kundera wrote, is “the absolute denial of shit, in both the literal and figurative sense of the word”; it “excludes everything from its purview which is essentially unacceptable in human existence.”) Still, his vision has had an enduring afterlife. Inevitably, its narrative potency—in particular its appeal to nostalgia—has been exploited across the political sphere. A Forbes columnist writing in 2012, more than three decades after the illustrator’s death, described the GOP primaries that year as “a process by which the candidate who demonstrates the most willingness to bring back Norman Rockwell’s America wins.” In 2020, shortly after he was elected, President Biden posted on Instagram a Hollywood ad agency’s reimagining of Rockwell’s United Nations mosaic, The Golden Rule, populated (in both the original and the adaptation) by a diverse group of Americans. And last year, President Trump’s Department of Homeland Security posted—without permission, prompting uproar—several of Rockwell’s paintings (including Salute the Flag and Working On the Statue of Liberty) to its social-media account. But it is not just this country’s politicians who are in Rockwell’s thrall. The painter’s affable pictorial rhetoric has cast a spell over holiday celebrations, modes of patriotic display, civic relations, even family relations. He was such a powerful image-maker that he created prototypes—ideals, really—of how life ought to be. And his work leaves a lingering sense that, if you want to be a happy American, you must (consciously or otherwise) reenact Rockwellian rituals. What Rockwell visualized was, of course, suffocatingly narrow. The critic Robert Hughes once called it “a dream world of small-town America.” In this America, Hughes wrote, “kids did not snort angel dust and get one another pregnant; they stole apples and swam in forbidden water holes but said grace before meals. All soldiers were nice boys from next door; all politicians were benevolent or harmlessly bumbling.” Big cities were subject to the roiling forces of unchecked capitalism and the blights of anonymity, rootlessness, and exploitation. Small towns, in Rockwell’s view, provided antidotes to all this. (He died well before the peak of deindustrialization and the first wave of the opioid epidemic.) They offered daily connection, neighborly interdependence, and, always, the lubricant of good humor (qualities that oiled Lynch’s twisted soap opera, Twin Peaks, too). To say that Rockwell’s America never existed is not to say that Rockwellian virtues do not exist; they do, all around us, every day. It’s only to acknowledge that the starched-white fiction these virtues cumulatively illustrate is by now so stained and sullied that just trying to keep up the pretense can trigger a kind of collective hysteria. The psychic pressure of trying to live up to an impossible ideal deeply interested Lynch. It produced his bifurcated visions of Rockwellian naivete and raw malevolence. In Rockwell, a diner is a place where a policeman can buy a runaway boy a milkshake before taking him home to his parents. In Lynch’s Mulholland Drive, Winkie’s Diner is where a tormenting nightmare becomes atrociously real. The night after I returned from Stockbridge, I rewatched Lynch’s Wild at Heart, his bizarre, hilarious, and very disturbing spin on Bonnie and Clyde. A lot of the action takes place in Big Tuna, a kind of anti-Stockbridge in the Texas badlands where evil thrives. The rusty, fish-shaped sign on the edge of town has been defaced with an expletive. The film’s main characters, Sailor and Lula (Nicholas Cage and Laura Dern), are deliberately cartoonlike, avatars of innocence transplanted to a context so malignant that it eats away at their mutual infatuation. When Lula picks up Sailor from prison, she brings him his favorite snakeskin jacket. “Did I ever tell you that this here jacket represents a symbol of my individuality and my belief in personal freedom?” he declares, like a third-grader reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. “About 50,000 times!” answers Lula, with no hint of a rebuke, only adoration. But that Rockwellian earnestness is no match for a setting corrupted by a hit man, a depraved mother, and the sniggering malevolence of Willem Dafoe. When Sailor confesses to having once worked for the man who murdered her father, Lula becomes pensive: “It’s just shocking,” she says, “when things aren’t the way you thought they were.” Rockwell expressed a similar sentiment before he died. It had been his idea to paint the Four Freedoms. He first took the proposal to the United States Office of War Information, where it was rejected, but after the paintings were published in the Post and received a huge response (60,000 letters were sent in by readers), the OWI reversed course and printed 2.5 million posters of the paintings, which the agency used to sell war bonds. In 1977, near the end of his life, Rockwell said: “I really believed that the war against Hitler would bring the Four Freedoms to everyone. But I couldn’t paint that today. I just don’t believe it. I was doing this best-possible-world, Santa-down-the-chimney, lovely-kids-adoring-their-kindly-grandpa sort of thing. And I liked it, but now I’m sick of it.” Lynch saw and loved Rockwell’s America—really loved it, as a child loves their parents—but something compelled him to break its surface and turn it violently inside out. This was a psychic and an artistic reaction, which is very different from a civic or political one. Maybe what America has to do with Norman Rockwell, as all children must eventually do with their parents, is figure out how to love him and leave him at the same time.

item.title: A War of Assassinations
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.54
Sign up for our newsletter about national security here. The latest Iranian assassination threat arrived last month as a video called “Where to Kill Barron Trump,” promising $10 million for the murder of the U.S. president’s youngest child. Less than 24 hours later, on social media, the State Department re-upped its own $10 million bounty for “information” about five leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, including Majid Khademi, the intelligence-office commander. The State Department offer, part of its Rewards for Justice program, first circulated on March 20. A few weeks later, the Israeli government took credit for killing Khademi in an air strike on Tehran, adding an ominous note to the U.S. government’s decision to recirculate the poster. I asked the State Department whether this was deliberate, so soon after Iran’s announcement of a $10 million bounty for the president’s son. An official declined to comment on “internal deliberations” but noted that information obtained through the Rewards for Justice program can be used to “support a range of U.S. government responses to disrupt threats, consistent with U.S. law and policy.” Threats of assassination have, from the start, been dark and disruptive subplots of the U.S.-Iran war. Both sides have made the tactic central to their national strategies, though the executions have been rather one-sided, as President Trump and his Israeli allies have overseen the widespread killing of Iran’s senior leadership. The impact on the American government has nonetheless been profound. “We are aware of ongoing threats from the Iranian regime and its proxies and take them extremely seriously,” the State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told me in a written statement. “We will not hesitate to act to protect U.S. government officials, current and former, and their families.” Iran clearly sees the propaganda value of threatening American officials. Murals in Tehran now depict Trump, members of his family, and other senior U.S. officials in coffins. Hey Terrorist! Get Ready To Die, reads one apparently AI-generated billboard that shows Trump looking skyward on a golf course. Iran’s army chief promised a $30,000 bounty last month to any Iranian man who kills or captures a U.S. service member, without specifying a target location. (Women would be paid twice as much.) In addition to threatening Barron, Iranian outlets have released a “How to Kill Melania” video about the first lady, and published a target list of multiple world leaders and U.S. Cabinet members. “The criminal, disgraceful murderers of the martyred Leader, whose names are fully documented from the highest to the lowest ranks, will carry their dream of a peaceful death in bed to the grave,” Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, the nation’s supreme leader, said in a written statement on July 11. He succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was assassinated by Israeli air strikes on his compound on the first day of the war. But the Iranian campaign is not limited to posturing. Last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that “Iran tried to murder” one of his sons, an apparent reference to 35-year-old Yair Netanyahu. In July, Israeli intelligence described an Iranian plot to use a French resident, Servet Ozkur, to recruit assassins to target senior officials in Israel. Iran has repeatedly sent assassins to kill Trump and other U.S. officials, according to the Justice Department, as punishment for Trump’s 2020 order to assassinate the Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani. About a week after the start of the Iran war this year, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Asif Merchant, the architect of one of two alleged Iranian plots in the United States. Prosecutors claimed that Merchant, a Pakistani national trained by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, had entered the United States with orders to recruit “mafia” hit men. But Merchant ended up speaking with undercover officers, telling them they would receive instructions on the target after he left the country. He was arrested before he made it to the airport and faces a sentence of up to life in prison. Assassination was clearly on Trump’s mind when the elder Khamenei was killed. “I got him before he got me,” Trump told ABC News’s Jonathan Karl in March. “They tried twice. Well, I got him first.” The U.S. presidency has long been a dangerous job. Trump has faced at least three assassination attempts by domestic assailants. Those attacks, along with Iran’s threats, are reshaping the lives of the president and his advisers, and restricting Trump’s ability to interact with the country he governs. Earlier this year, at a summit in Ankara, Trump told reporters that his own chance of dying in office was 5.2 percent, dramatically higher than that of race-car drivers and bull riders. (He did not provide a source for his comparisons. Of the 45 men elected president, four, or about 8.9 percent, have been assassinated in office.) Trump said at the same appearance that “I’m No. 1 on the kill list for Iran.” Then the president turned his traveling press corps and two Cabinet officials into flying decoys when he snuck out a side door of Air Force One as it sat on the tarmac, to avoid a purported Iranian plot to target the plane. After a short ride in a catering truck, he boarded a different plane and flew to his next stop, in England. The logistics of presidential travel are now far more burdensome than they were when Trump first took office. The Secret Service’s personal-protection budget has nearly doubled since 2016. New airspace restrictions have been imposed over Mar-a-Lago. Lafayette Park, just north of the White House, has been closed for months for security; there are plans to install new fencing that would further obstruct public access. The new White House ballroom, the U.S. Army has argued in court, is “essential to ensure uninterrupted command and control” given the new threats of a drone attack. A number of Cabinet officials and top White House aides now live on military bases to protect themselves and their families, in certain cases because of specific foreign threats. Other rank-and-file White House advisers, unnerved by a homegrown assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April, have receded from the city where they live. “People are just more careful about where they go and, frankly, how often they are out in public,” a White House official told me. All of this portends a grim future in which assassination moves from an extreme risk to a more commonplace threat. Perhaps that will lead to a reassessment of its use as both a tool of U.S. foreign policy and a way to menace an enemy’s senior officials. “At some stage, I do wonder whether politicians thinking about themselves actually come to the conclusion that they are signing their own death warrants or essentially undermining their own democracies” by promoting the extrajudicial killing of their enemies, Simon Ball, a professor at the University of Leeds, in England, and the author of Death to Order: A Modern History of Assassination, told me. He added that assassination threats are now such a regular fact of life that to have protection against them confers a macabre prestige. “Elite status is defined by whether you have protection from assassination,” Ball said. “If you do not have protection, you are not important. You are little people.” The assassination threats from Iran have had a big impact on Trump’s life, but administration officials contend that the threats have played no role in Trump’s decision to attack Iran, which he did in June 2025 and again in February, citing the need to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, among other reasons. “He has never equated their threats against him as a reason for doing this,” one senior administration official told me. “He views the threats against him as a part of the job.” But the military has made killing those who allegedly threaten the president part of the campaign. Four days after the conflict began, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth walked into the Pentagon with triumphant news about an Israeli strike the night before. The U.S. and Israel, he announced, had hunted down the “leader of the unit who attempted to assassinate President Trump.” On the one hand, Hegseth suggested that the strike was a personal victory for the president. “Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh,” Hegseth told reporters. On the other hand, he said that Trump had not concerned himself with the strikes. Going after the president’s assassins, Hegseth said, “was not the focus of the effort by any stretch of the imagination, in fact, never raised by the president or anybody else.” Instead, by his account, it seems to have just sort of happened as a favor to the boss. “I ensured, and others ensured, that those who were responsible for that were eventually part of the target list,” Hegseth said. Trump has similarly blurred these lines, sometimes focusing on the threat and at other times dismissing it. After Cole Tomas Allen, a tutor from California, was apprehended while attempting to infiltrate the Correspondents’ Dinner armed with multiple guns and knives, Trump told reporters that “I don’t think about” the prospect of assassination, and “if I did, I wouldn’t be doing a very good job here.” But hours before B-2 bombers struck Iran in June last year, the president told reporters after disembarking Air Force One in New Jersey that they had put themselves in danger just by standing next to him. “Be careful,” he said. Trump has also made clear that any nation that assassinated him would face apocalyptic retaliation. “I’ve left instructions. If they do it, they get obliterated. There won’t be anything left,” he said of Iran two weeks after taking office last year. This July, hours before Mojtaba promised revenge for his father’s death, Trump posted on social media that even an attempted assassination on him would result in a military response: “Orders have already been given, and the U.S. Military is ready, willing, and able, for a one year period of time, subject to extension, to completely decimate and destroy all areas of Iran.” Iranian officials have been ambiguous about how seriously the U.S. should take its threats. Days after the Barron video began circulating on Tebyan.net, an arm of the Iranian government’s propaganda machine, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, called the threats against Barron a lie and dismissed the alleged plot against Trump in Turkey as “false news.” But in the same interview with Lebanon’s Al-Manar TV, Rezaei—whose predecessor was killed by Israeli strikes in March—said Iran would send Netanyahu “to hell.” The claim received scant coverage. World leaders plotting to kill one another has become routine. Jonathan Lemire and Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed reporting.

item.title: The Novel That Looks Death in the Eye
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.48
The human brain has a method for dealing with the intrinsic fear of death. Terror-management theory, which builds on the work of the cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker, explains that the psyche handles this fear in a variety of ways. Many people either escape reality or adopt a belief system that promises immortality: so on the one hand, sex, drugs, or entertainment; on the other, religion, fame, or careerism. Or we might immerse ourselves in family, or culture—something that imbues life with meaning. Otherwise, the theory goes, we would be cognitively immobilized by impending doom. In her gut-twisting third novel, Switzy, Emma Cline does not abide by the tenets of terror management. Instead, she pulls death out from behind the curtain and forces her readers to look it in the eye for more than 300 pages. Switzy follows the final few days in the life of David Hastings, a former high-flying executive who’s been forced into retirement, and obsolescence, by an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. He has taken advantage of Switzerland’s right-to-die laws, paying the fees (a paltry sum for a wealthy man) and filling out the required paperwork. Now he’ll swallow some barbiturates and die in an impersonal room just outside Zurich, far from his family and his home in America. Cline’s approach is merciless—not toward David, for whom she shows tenderness and grace, but toward the reader, who will be nearly flattened by this novel. Or so I sincerely hope, because death ought to flatten us once in a while. Switzy begins mid-flight, as David hurtles across the Atlantic in a friend’s private jet. Accompanied by Cody—a former corporate underling who now functions as David’s caretaker, body man, and secretary—he lands first in London. There, he has dinner with his only child, an emotionally distant daughter who doesn’t know about her father’s decline, let alone his upcoming euthanasia. David tours a museum, visits his grandson, reboards the plane for his final flight, to Zurich; he dazedly lets Cody steer him around as a parent would guide a toddler. The younger man negotiates the intricacies of the world on David’s behalf, buffering him from the demands of day-to-day life—buying a museum ticket, sending a text message, procuring beverages. David needs the help: He is at times absent in his own mind. As rendered by Cline in a wandering, dreamlike style, this becomes a startling and eerie phenomenon—like the moment you realize you’ve been driving for miles but don’t recall anything about the journey. Far from experiencing the blissful ignorance that some people might project onto dementia patients, David is all too aware that his brain has locked away basic memories and social customs. He writes his grandson’s name, Rainer, in a notebook so he can recall it; a clock “in big kindergarten letters” informs him of the date and time each morning; he stares too long at someone in the museum and provokes his annoyance. And he sees each gap, knows that it signals another loss. “Work,” he thinks as he chews a croissant, “everything seemed like work. Even these good things—even this buttered mouthful.” The first half of Switzy crawls by, but it feels achingly necessary. This is time the way David experiences it, slowed down and sometimes skipped over: Alzheimer’s novels are rare, and those told from the patient’s point of view are even rarer. Cline, always a graceful stylist, employs a kind of abbreviated modernism to leap among David’s thoughts. They skitter backwards to memories of his failed marriage and his time at a boys’ boarding school. They run in circles, around catchy sayings—such as a mnemonic about Henry VIII’s abbreviated marriages, “Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived”—that Alzheimer’s hasn’t stolen from him. And they jump ahead to the moment and manner of his death, which inches closer with every turned page. Cline’s last novel, The Guest, also followed a character who hastily approaches a reckoning. Alex, a poor and wily 22-year-old sex worker who has just been kicked out of the home of her most recent catch, Simon, has to make it through five days in the Hamptons, until she can plead to be let back into the high-end milieu of Simon’s Labor Day party. Dead-eyed and mutable, Alex, like David, is trying to put on just enough of a show to pass muster with the people around her. For her, a different kind of death awaits—complete impoverishment, and removal from a perch where she may or may not belong. Switzy raises the stakes on this kind of quest. As the novel’s second half picks up steam, so does the cadence of David’s confrontations with the fact of his looming extinction. When the plane lands in Zurich, an official comes on to inspect their passports. “David smiled to himself. It was obvious, wasn’t it? This man was Death. Why else would he know to come right onboard?” Soon after, he sees Death again as a waiter, a busboy, two restaurant patrons. On his last night, he wakes repeatedly in his hotel, checking the sky’s brightness as a sign of how much time he has left. An Omega watch advertisement catches his eye, and though he doesn’t say it, the meaning is clear: Omega is the last letter in the Greek alphabet, the universal symbol of finality. As long as David cannot stop returning to his ticking clock, neither can you. This kind of sustained attention to the one topic many people spend their lives avoiding is practically subversive—a thrill, really. And it’s possibly a public service too. Studies have repeatedly shown that people who think about death on a regular basis are happier, because contemplating mortality reinforces the idea, as Emily Dickinson put it, “That it will never come again/ Is what makes life so sweet.” I daresay most readers won’t feel much happiness reading Switzy—though it does have glimmers of humor—but they might experience moments of sublime clarity. Death functions here in a way that isn’t common in fiction. Its presence doesn’t make this novel a tearjerker—it’s not, for example, Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet, which beautifully laments the loss of a child. It offers no spectacle akin to Anne Boleyn’s trembling march to the scaffold at the end of Hilary Mantel’s singular historical novel, Bring Up the Bodies. Unlike many 19th-century novels, Switzy doesn’t use death to solve a social problem, à la Anna Karenina (romantic devastation) and Madame Bovary (financial ruin). Nor is death here a handy plot device, as it is in so many works across the past century. Switzy is not about the living who are left behind. Cline’s approach to death marks different territory: It’s about raw, undeniable truth. Dying is a transformative event: People pass from the only reality they’ve ever been able to recognize into something nebulous and ungraspable (even for the most fervent religious believers). And this might sound obvious, but you, reader, will die. So will I. Much of humanity has raised its defenses high against death, perhaps unintentionally, as Ernest Becker proposes. So how will it feel to see a man marching straight toward it—not unflinchingly, or tremulously, but with a perfectly ordinary mixture of confusion and acceptance? In Switzy’s final pages, David becomes a man who cannot help but be alive, even in his last moments. He doesn’t want to eat breakfast, but he feels it’s “better to have something in the stomach.” He feels irritated that he is given a blue pen to sign documents—“blue ink was for grocery lists.” He fumbles over his last words. Cline writes, “His was both the realest life in the room and the most unreal.” The line between everything and nothing is as thin as a breath of air. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: A Wildly Popular Movie Meets the Film World’s Most Revered Label
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 5.31
Updated at 12:30 p.m. ET on Aug. 28, 2026 Over the past year, KPop Demon Hunters seems to have completely overtaken culture. Since premiering on Netflix in June 2025, the animated film has been watched nearly 650 million times and, according to Nielsen, accounted for some 20.5 billion viewing minutes last year. The soundtrack topped Billboard charts that fall; Spirit Halloween instantly sold out of licensed costumes. But even the most ardent fans likely did not anticipate the mega-hit’s next big merch drop: a disc release from the Criterion Collection, home to some of cinema’s most distinguished titles. By some metrics, KPop Demon Hunters may be the most popular movie ever to be added to the collection. (Other new entries include David Lynch’s Wild at Heart and a Ukrainian folk romance from 1965.) It’s almost certainly the first Criterion inclusion to have its own flavor of McFlurry. KPop Demon Hunters is an unlikely candidate for what’s come to be called “the Criterion treatment”: a painstaking transfer to disc, along with a making-of documentary and other special features, and a number printed on the box’s spine. Film buffs see this process as akin to an anointing; the trademark C, tucked into the upper-left corner of a plastic clamshell, signals a movie’s importance. Introducing a new title to the library can be fraught: James Kendrick, a professor of film and digital media at Baylor University, told me, “They’re always sort of risking diluting the power of that sign.” Online, some of the label’s longtime devotees greeted the addition of KPop Demon Hunters with an eye roll, calling the move “substantially off-brand,” and a “cash grab.” The movie is so familiar to the general public that its release seems to go against the grain of Criterion’s reputation, which was built on bringing landmark works of film history to the masses. The company adds some 30 to 60 movies to its catalog annually, most of them lost gems of world cinema, festival-circuit darlings, or old Hollywood hits. In past decades, only one or two very new releases might have made the cut; canonization is usually a retrospective project of sifting through the past to see what art stands the test of time. Now the process seems to be speeding up: This year’s roster includes six movies from 2025 so far, many of them distributed by streaming companies. Criterion has good reason to widen the net: Netflix, Apple, and Amazon make and distribute a significant share of films these days. A title that seems ubiquitous today could vanish tomorrow, evaporating from viewing platforms or even from personal digital libraries without warning. “We’ve lived kind of free and easy for the last couple decades, assuming these corporations would do that work for us,” Amanda D. Lotz, a media scholar at Queensland University of Technology, told me, “and that’s not in their remit, necessarily.” Streaming services, unlike their traditional studio competitors, rarely produce physical media. “I suspect it is unclear that there is a market” for companion discs, Lotz said, despite the fact that, in her estimation, they could be a “nice little business niche.” (Signs are mixed: One by one, electronics companies have stopped manufacturing disc players, but the decline in disc sales seems to have slowed.) With more new films seeming transient—especially those whose rights belong to streaming studios—it makes sense for a label like Criterion to invest more in preserving them. The decision to pick up KPop Demon Hunters also seems less surprising when you consider Criterion’s very early history. Back when the label was putting out movies on LaserDisc, in the 1980s, it was more inclined to pick up very new and popular titles, such as Ghostbusters. Some of that popcorn sensibility lived on in the brand’s DVD era, when it released Armageddon and The Rock, by Michael Bay. Part of co-founder Bob Stein’s vision for the label was for it to distribute some titles that already had mass public appeal; Criterion, by offering a feature-packed disc to explore, could then deepen people’s relationship to those works and to the art form writ large. The brand has long been characterized by a high-low eclecticism: The literature scholars Mark and Deborah Parker told me that when they were working on their book about the history of the DVD, they visited Criterion’s office. Peter Becker, the president of Criterion, pressed a copy of a Japanese gangster flick into their hands; just down the hall, Mark told me, “they were doing the transfer of In the Mood for Love.” The reasoning behind Criterion’s selections remains somewhat mysterious. (The company declined to be interviewed for this story.) Addressing an industry gathering in 2019, Becker said, “We let the movies carry the brand into the market place, so we don’t talk about the company very much.” But he did offer this explanation of what makes a work fit for Criterion: “It should be something we want to talk about, it should be a rich point of entry, but we try not to be snobby about what kinds of films can actually be exemplary.” So what might KPop Demon Hunters exemplify? Its public reception has had a unique arc: a family-friendly fantasy that premiered on Netflix with little fanfare before becoming a word-of-mouth hit, then a critical darling, and finally an awards winner. As for its artistic properties, John Adkins, the lead writer for the newsletter Animation Obsessive, suggested to me that the film is “very tied to anime aesthetics and the slick, bright, Spider-Verse-type visuals that Sony Pictures Animation popularized” and that it could be taken to represent a modern-audience preference for an animation style with “a graphic or illustrative edge.” Tom Sito, a retired Disney animator and a professor emeritus at the University of Southern California, told me that the budding animators in his classes have adopted the movie the way he and his peers once did Yellow Submarine, the surrealist cartoon set to music by the Beatles. That fervor might be enough reason to declare KPop Demon Hunters a contemporary classic and worthy of Criterion status. The revenue that it might bring in, which could then potentially fund more esoteric selections, is another. (Criterion, savvily, is releasing its edition just in time for holiday shopping, positioning it as an arty stocking stuffer.) Adding the film to the collection could be seen as part of a broader strategy to increase the company’s visibility, including through its “Criterion Closet” social video series, its mobile van, and a brick-and-mortar storefront during the Toronto Film Festival. For many young fans of KPop Demon Hunters, who are more likely to pull up the “Golden” video on YouTube than pop a disc into a player, a souped-up Blu-ray might function mostly as a collectible—not so different from a Derpy Tiger plush or a Rumi singing doll. Some, though, may grow attached to the idea of physical media, or could even come to see home video as a vital technology rather than a nostalgia object. Cinema is a relatively young art form; the idea of owning a personal copy of a film is an even more recent invention. KPop Demon Hunter’s latest accolade is a reminder that the canon, too, remains far from fixed. This article has been updated to reflect the nature of Criterion’s physical retailer.

item.title: Why Are So Many People Listening to a Podcast About Living in a Convent?
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 4.31
At a convent in Ann Arbor, Michigan, the bell chimes every day at 5 a.m. Then the 40 or so women who live there year-round—Dominican Sisters of Mary, Mother of the Eucharist—head to the chapel. Their day begins with an hour of prayer, followed by Mass. At 7 a.m., they have breakfast together, in complete silence. Many of them head off afterward to teach at nearby Catholic schools—sisters, unlike nuns, are not cloistered—while the novitiates stay behind to study at “the motherhouse,” as they call the convent. On some days, one of the women—Sister Miriam Holzman, who started living there 20 years ago—turns to a new item on her schedule: podcasting. Back in February, Sister Miriam started hosting Dominican Sisters Open Mic, a weekly show in which she and her fellow sisters discuss topics such as scripture, the saints, and day-to-day convent life. Sister Miriam told me that when the podcast started, she hoped it would encourage listeners to “go deeper in their spiritual life, no matter what their background might be”—Catholic or not, religious or not. The show seems to have resonated outside Catholic circles. Clips of the sisters playing the ukulele and describing an Ultimate Frisbee match have gone viral on TikTok. As of late August, their account on the platform has more than 275,000 followers and more than 8 million likes. The podcast has been featured in The New York Times and on the Today show. Listeners seem to be especially drawn to the sisters’ cheerfulness. They laugh frequently and have an easy way of interacting with one another. “Their laughter seems so stress free,” one commenter observed. Another said, “Sisters, I also want that regulated nervous system laugh.” In a post liked by more than 5,000 people, one listener asked, “Why does being a nun seems so fun even though I’m not religious?” Sister Miriam said that the show’s popularity may be connected to the overall trend of people seeking wellness content online. “People are looking for balance, and so are we,” she told me. “We want wellness too.” Their fixed routine—prayer, study, work, fun—minimizes unnecessary distractions. But the sisters aren’t just offering wellness advice or preaching self-optimization. Their search for balance includes trying to become a particular kind of person in body and soul, and noticing traces of transcendence every day. In one podcast episode, Sister Miriam talked about how, when she struggles to focus or when obligations and to-do lists intrude on her mind, her consistent schedule reminds her that in that moment, she is precisely where God wants her to be. “Which is such a gift,” she said. “I don’t need to be planning the rest of my life.” Resisting the pressure to multitask or worry about the future seems to help the sisters prioritize prayer, a pillar of their Dominican order. At midday, the sisters meditate on the essential Christian belief that the all-powerful God took on human form in the person of Jesus Christ. Later in the afternoon, they recite the Liturgy of the Hours, a set of reflections on the Psalms and Gospels. Many of the sisters have said that after years at the convent, these practices spill over into the rest of their life—when they pray for a passerby at the airport, perhaps, or let out a sudden “Come, Holy Spirit” or “Jesus, I trust in you” at difficult points of the day. Prayer, a sister concluded in one episode, “expands your vision of reality.” It has allowed her to notice “the dew on the grass, or the sunrise on the way to work.” As evening approaches, the sisters return to the motherhouse. They pray the rosary and have dinner together as one of them reads aloud from a recent papal address or a biography of a saint. Then out come the Trivial Pursuit boxes and guitars, the bicycles and Frisbees. As with prayer, recreation time together is fixed in their schedule. It’s not optional. The sisters don’t watch TV during it, nor do they scroll on phones. For all the joy that the sisters display on the podcast, they are also open about the sacrifices involved in convent life. They seldom see their families. Their daily lives downplay individuality: Their sleeping quarters, called “cells,” are designed to be interchangeable and are minimally arranged with a bed, a dresser, a table, an image of the Virgin Mary. Adjusting to the 5 a.m. wake-up call can take years. And like all of us, the sisters are prone to stress and worry. The contentment that the sisters seem to have despite these challenges may be partly explained by the documented benefits of engaging in religious practices. Clay Routledge, a social psychologist who studies sources of meaning in people’s lives, told me that prayer’s “cognitive and motivational power” can make people more attentive. He added, “It focuses your attention on something; it takes you off of these other distractions and worries, and helps you pay attention to what you care about.” In a 2016 study, psychologists at Georgia State University found that prayer motivated very religious students to “invest a greater amount of mental energy in the performance of everyday tasks.” A study from 2012 found that praying for others made participants feel more satisfied about making sacrifices for others—about living, in other words, a less self-oriented life. Starting at 8 p.m., after their evening prayer, the sisters spend the rest of their night in complete silence. Sister Miriam told me that during this time she likes to pray about both the difficulties of the day and the things she’s grateful for. Another sister said that she sometimes walks up a nearby hill, notices the twilight sky, and thinks of her Creator. Then she returns to the motherhouse, ready for the next morning’s bell to chime.

item.title: Why Was This Looney Tunes Movie Almost Shelved for Good?
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 4.03
Perhaps the starkest sign that Coyote vs. Acme isn’t your typical children’s movie is that it’s based on a New Yorker article. Yes, it features many Looney Tunes characters that multiple generations know and love, interacting alongside real-life actors in a style similar to prior big-screen efforts, such as Space Jam or Looney Tunes: Back in Action. But the director Dave Green’s film—which opens August 28, after a protracted saga that almost saw it kept from audiences forever—draws from a slyly funny “Shouts & Murmurs” story from 1990. Written by the humorist Ian Frazier, “Coyote v. Acme” has a wry and self-aware premise: What would happen if Wile E. Coyote, the Looney Tune on a constantly unsuccessful hunt for the ever-chipper Road Runner, filed a lawsuit against the (fictional) Acme Corporation for selling him faulty products? “I thought the baseline idea for the movie was just, like, the funniest thing in the world,” Green told me in a recent interview, reminiscing about when he first signed on to direct the film, back in 2019. He wasn’t the first person in the film industry to be charmed by Frazier’s story. Despite the erudite tone, the simple notion of Wile E. Coyote pursuing legal action was amusing enough to Hollywood producers that various attempts were made to develop it for the screen, dating back to an effort by the producer Scott Rudin in the late 1990s. Warner Bros., which owns Looney Tunes, jump-started the latest version of the project in 2018, and Green completed it in 2022. Coyote vs. Acme was initially scheduled to debut the following summer, but it was taken off the schedule early into production; a new release date was never announced. In the fall of 2023, Warner Bros. told the director that the movie would be shelved entirely. The studio reportedly made the call for a tax write-off—the latest in a series of such decisions, as it dealt with debt issues after the coronavirus pandemic. Three years later, Coyote vs. Acme is finally entering theaters. After years of limbo, it ended up in the hands of Ketchup Entertainment, an independent distributor that has now become its unlikely savior. The company cut a $50 million deal with Warner Bros. for it last March. “I continued to not believe it, up until now, when I still can’t believe it,” Green said. “It’s a completely surreal reality to check into. But it seems to be happening—I think it’s happening,” he added with a laugh. His trepidation is understandable: The path the film took to cinemas reflects Hollywood’s continued post-pandemic instability, even as theatergoing has picked back up. Coyote vs. Acme had reportedly tested well with audiences and featured some of Warner Bros.’ most well-known creations, yet the cancellation suggests the company still expected to lose too much money on the project. The wildest part of the production, Green admitted, was how easy it was at first. When asked by Warner Bros. to pitch ideas for an adaptation of Frazier’s article, the director proposed something along the lines of a true-crime documentary crossed with a legal drama. To his surprise, the studio didn’t immediately turn him down. “It almost felt like everything was a ‘yes,’ and there were no boundaries. So then I got really excited,” Green said. “They were looking for a take and they were looking for something that would help them narrow in. And, as different as my tonal comparisons were, I think they responded to the fact that there was a take in it.” Green’s notion was to take the tropes of underdog courtroom movies—he cited The Insider, Erin Brockovich, and A Few Good Men as inspirations—and place cartoon characters within them. The humans they interact with (played by Will Forte, Lana Condor, and John Cena, among others) would treat Wile E. Coyote’s lawsuit with humdrum seriousness. “That’s the kind of behavior that really comes from Looney Tunes historically,” Green said—winking references to grown-up media that its young audience might not understand. “It’s Bugs Bunny in Casablanca or Elmer Fudd at the opera, poking at high art.” That device has become a hallmark of the franchise, with self-aware comedy making up the bulk of its spin-off Tiny Toon Adventures and of Looney Tunes’ spiritual successor, Animaniacs. The devious extra twist of Coyote vs. Acme, however, comes from watching the Looney Tunes themselves navigate human society, with its mundane rules and morals. The story is set in Albuquerque, and the live-action sequences were shot almost entirely on location, lending the kind of jarring verisimilitude Green was hoping for—the animated elements pop against the dusty backdrop. Wile E. Coyote is still capable of speaking only through hand gestures and written signs, but he’s hoping to get a personal-injury lawyer named Kevin Avery (Forte) to help him sue Acme; the manufacturing company is presented as a corporate juggernaut that sells products to both humans and cartoons, while gleefully cutting corners in the name of profit. The result is explosively zany. It’s also surprisingly sensitive—a quality often lacking from the anarchic Looney Tunes. In bite-size animated form, Wile E. Coyote has a monomaniacal obsession with destroying the Road Runner that’s designed to be a recurring, villainous gag; here, it’s a sad compulsion, a habit he cannot kick. The turn works because it doesn’t feel dark, but rather sweetly relatable. “What if you treated Wile E. like a person and his pain as real?” Green asked. “Then that kind of led to the path of, like, what if it’s about cartoon characters being treated unfairly? That kind of split the whole thing open in a fun way.” Green shot the movie in spring 2022, an experience he describes as entirely pleasant. “There was actually a lot of support from even the very highest-up voices at the studio, and they were really positive in reacting to my initial cut,” he recalled. Yet that summer, Warner Bros. made the surprising decision to shelve Batgirl, a $90 million HBO Max production. “That was really scary to us,” Green said. “But we never thought we were in the same danger.” Batgirl seemed plagued by various other corporate maneuvers: a shift away from movies produced exclusively for streaming, and a general impending reset of the DC Comics cinematic universe. (Analysts also believed that Warner Bros. intended to take a write-down on Batgirl, to help alleviate its multibillion-dollar debt.) Still, the decision alarmed many filmmakers, who now had to worry that studios might choose to just delete their work instead of bothering to release it. Coyote vs. Acme was initially slated to debut July 21, 2023, before Warner Bros. decided to put Barbie in that summer slot. After that, Green remembered, his cast and crew waited for a rescheduled date, which never came. Finally, in November, the studio told him that Coyote vs. Acme would not be released at all. A public outcry from both fans and members of the industry quickly pressured Warner Bros. to shop the movie to other distributors, including Amazon, Apple, and Netflix. The studio’s price tag, however, was reportedly too high for these potential buyers, and Warner Bros. eventually rejected all competing bids to hand it over—an apparent death sentence for Coyote vs. Acme. Green recalled a fellow director comforting him during this period by saying, “You got away with it. You robbed the bank. You made a courtroom drama for kids starring Looney Tunes characters. In so many ways, this movie should not exist.” Still, as Green told it, the thinking behind pulling Coyote vs. Acme was never fully clear to him. Although it is more complex than a typical kids’ film, the good test-viewing scores and positive critical reception suggest there’s an audience for it. Ketchup Entertainment can’t afford the large marketing budget that a more established studio could have; it is likely looking to recoup costs through international sales and at-home rentals. That Warner Bros. abandoned all of this goodwill and earnings potential, to Green, was somewhat baffling. But he feels lucky to have finished the film—which he called an “impossibility” for its blend of classic Looney Tunes absurdity and legal-thriller influences—in the first place. Now it has finally escaped containment; Green, it seems, has successfully rewritten his movie’s real-life ending.

item.title: The Painter Who Shaped Rothko
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 3.64
The evolution of European modern art can be explained as a story of susceptible young people falling under others’ spells and then asking, What can I do with this? How can I convert it to my purposes? What’s remarkable is how often the main chapters of this story have unfolded in coastal or mountain retreats. Think of Claude Monet on the Normandy coast, wrestling with the influence of his mentor Eugène Boudin. Or Henri Matisse staying in Saint-Tropez with his mentor Paul Signac, before breaking with Signac’s neo-impressionist style and co-inventing fauvism. Or Pablo Picasso, goaded into radicalism by the latest bizarre creations of Matisse, retreating to the Spanish mountain village of Gósol and, mere months later, beginning work on his proto-cubist masterpiece, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon. All of these key episodes happened in agreeable resorts, seaside ports, and villages, far from the sophisticated cities assumed to have been the cauldrons of modernism. Modern art in America is no different. Its story can scarcely be told without reference to artists summering on the Atlantic Coast, including Winslow Homer, Marsden Hartley, and Edward Hopper in Maine and Massachusetts and Jackson Pollock, Lee Krasner, and Willem de Kooning on Long Island. Beginning in the early 1930s, three Americans—Milton Avery, Mark Rothko, and Adolph Gottlieb—began spending summers together on Cape Ann, along the coast of northeast Massachusetts. They loved the gritty authenticity of Gloucester, the nation’s oldest fishing port. Cape Ann’s distinctive, undulant geography combined pungent industry and village intensity with Atlantic immensity of sea and sky. The story of the relationships among these artists, in particular between the older Avery and the now–stratospherically famous Rothko, shows us American modernism in its moment of greatest transition. Avery was the mentor figure, the one destined, in the usual telling of this story, to be eclipsed. Whereas Rothko is a regular subject of museum retrospectives in Europe and North America, and his paintings can sell at auction for as much as $98 million, Avery remains relatively unknown outside of the U.S. (The most expensive Avery sold at auction was a little more than $6 million, in 2022.) But are we telling the right story about Avery if we cast him in this role? Certainly, when Rothko and Gottlieb, during World War II, turned to abstraction, they broke from Avery and, in short order, became central figures in a mid-century revolution—one that transformed modern art from a marginal activity to a cultural phenomenon attracting cash, prestige, and international acclaim. Avery wasn’t exactly forgotten in all of this, but he has long been overlooked. He had first come to Gloucester in 1920, returning regularly during the summer until 1945. It’s where he met his wife, a fellow artist named Sally Michel. The fishing port was known as a bustling artists’ colony. In the 19th century, Homer and Fitz Henry Lane had spent productive time there, as had Hopper, Cecilia Beaux, and Stuart Davis in the 20th. So Avery was far from alone as he strolled around the harbor with his sketchbook and retired at night to rudimentary rooms lacking toilets and bathtubs. In 1932, he and Sally, who was pregnant with their only child, were joined on Cape Ann by Rothko—at the time called Markus Rothkowitz; he began using the name Mark Rothko in 1940—and Gottlieb. Avery was in his element in Gloucester. Confident, good-humored, and in the noontime of life, he sat comfortably on his own shadow. Unlike his protégés, he was not especially intellectual. He was a taciturn pragmatist with a gentle sense of humor. He had a dog called Picasso. To those who said modern art was ugly and hard to appreciate, he would answer: “Olives taste ugly, too, until you learn to enjoy them.” The two younger men felt his support, but he didn’t force his ideas on them. According to Eliza Rathbone, the curator of an exhibit about the trio’s seaside summers currently on view at the Cape Ann Museum, Avery “never uttered a word of advice or instruction to any painter other than ‘do another one.’” He set an example: how to be a modern artist, yes. But also: how to be a husband and father, how to carry on. His very reticence was liberating. The three men had become friends in New York, where they would gather in the evenings to sketch and discuss art at the Averys’ Lincoln Square apartment. “I cannot tell you what it meant for us during those early years to be made welcome in those memorable studios,” Rothko would later recall. In Gloucester, they explored the port, with its wharves and warehouses and fish-processing facilities, filling sketchbooks and painting small-scale works in watercolor. A total solar eclipse that August provided fodder for Avery, who made an amusing watercolor showing people on Good Harbor Beach looking at the celestial phenomenon through smoked glasses and colored film. That first summer together was bookended by major life events back in New York. The Depression had flooded the streets with the unemployed. Gottlieb married in June. In October, as memories of summer receded, Sally gave birth to a daughter, and a few weeks later, Rothko married. In those days, Rothko and Gottlieb would study Avery’s paintings and, according to Sally Avery, “take them apart.” On Cape Ann, they watched him treat the beach as a backdrop against which he placed monumental, thick-hipped figures, arranging areas of pattern (umbrellas, beachwear) against flat, colored shapes in compositions with shifting horizon lines. Following Avery’s example, they experimented with gouache and watercolor applied to colored construction paper. The Averys and Gottliebs returned in the summer of 1933, and were joined by the Rothkos in 1934. The Depression was biting hard, but the artists’ life in Gloucester remained simple and uncorrupted. “We saw each other day in and day out,” Sally recalled of those years. “Evenings we’d gather to have a cup of tea and look at our day’s work. There was no talk of selling—only of painting.” “I always thought Avery was a great artist,” Gottlieb would later say. “I always regarded him as a brilliant colorist and draftsman, a solitary figure working against the stream.” Gottlieb was right. Avery was one of the 20th century’s most original colorists. His expansive compositions were influenced by Pierre Bonnard and Matisse as well as by American folk art. Unlike Matisse, who loved bold, blatant colors, he favored unusual, in-between hues—mauves, browns, pale greens—all close in tonal value. He would often unify three or four slightly clashing varieties of the same color with a complementary hue elsewhere in the arrangement. Like spacious minor-key chords given a subtle major-key lift, these color combinations can arouse powerful emotions that are excruciatingly just short of fulfillment. When it came to being influenced by others, Matisse understood what was at stake. But, he said, “I have never avoided the influence of others. I would have considered it cowardice and a lack of sincerity toward myself.” To be open to influence is to risk being dislodged from your former self. It requires you to have the confidence to convert the ensuing upheaval to your own (still unknown) purposes. The process is complicated and rarely goes smoothly. Often, though not always, it involves some kind of betrayal. No one betrays anyone in this story. All three artists remained friends. But the two younger painters, Rothko and Gottlieb, although deeply affected by Avery’s original way of painting, eventually decided that they needed to go further—to change not just the colors, the shapes, or the subjects, but something more fundamental. In 1943, they broke away. Perhaps coincidentally, perhaps not, the breach happened just as Avery was beginning to thrive. He had been choosing larger canvases and distilling his paintings down to a few essential ingredients. The strategy was working. His work was selling. Dealers were fighting to represent him. He had a series of successful shows. The reviews were good. Rothko, meanwhile, experienced a creative crisis and, in 1940, stopped painting for a year. He had been digging into philosophy, reading Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Kierkegaard, as well as the Greek myths and tragedies. Gottlieb, at the same time, made works merging surrealism with imagery inspired by masks and ritual objects from Africa, the Pacific, and Native North American cultures. As the two younger men moved steadily closer to total abstraction, a tension that has in many ways defined American art—between the concreteness of the material world and the amorphousness of the sublime—was coming to a head. Avery, ever loyal to his sketchbook, remained committed to direct observation of particular people and places. His summer companions were about to throw in their lot with the sublime. The push toward abstraction in mid-century American art coincided with a surge of interest in existentialism, which had begun to displace the pragmatism that underlay Avery’s approach. A sense that even the closest ties might be loosened by what T. S. Eliot—who had himself summered for nearly two decades in Gloucester—had described (in a review of James Joyce’s Ulysses) as an “immense panorama of futility and anarchy” was lent gravity by the world wars. But the human predicament, as Albert Camus made clear in The Stranger (1942), went beyond man-made conflict. It was inextricable from all that was inhuman, arbitrary, and immense—from the blinding energy of the sun on an Algerian beach, for instance. On Cape Ann, Rothko and Gottlieb thought a lot about the sun, as well as the sea, the sky, and the smallness of human life. They were no doubt aware of the death-haunted history of Gloucester, where, between 1866 and 1890, more than 2,450 Gloucester men and 380 schooners failed to return from the fishing grounds. They wanted their art to communicate awe, and a sense of the insecurity and brutality of existence. It was as if the Atlantic were pulling them out to sea, away from both the harbor intimacy of Gloucester and the embrace of Milton and Sally Avery. In 1943, Rothko and Gottlieb co-authored a letter and sent it to The New York Times, which published it on June 13. The letter responded to the Times critic Edward Alden Jewell, who, in a review, had misjudged (they felt) paintings by Rothko and Gottlieb. It also doubled as a five-point manifesto: “To us,” they wrote, “art is an adventure into an unknown world, which can be explored only by those willing to take risks.” That was the first point. The fourth point ended: “We are for flat forms because they destroy illusion and reveal truth.” According to the fifth point, “only that subject matter is valid which is tragic and timeless.” A concluding salvo declared that for their work to succeed, “it must insult anyone who is spiritually attuned to interior decoration; pictures of the home; pictures for over the mantle; pictures of the American scene”—the list continues—“prize-winning potboilers; the National Academy; the Whitney Academy,” and so on. Avery could easily have felt personally targeted. He had exhibited, after all, at the first and second Whitney Biennials (in 1933 and 1936); he painted domestic interiors and American landscapes; and his pictures could be called “decorative” (at least in the sense Matisse meant when he described his more ambitious paintings as “decorations”). He was probably too magnanimous—or phlegmatic—to take umbrage, and the summer proceeded pleasantly enough. If the group dynamic had become awkward, it correlated, the art historian Robert Hobbs wrote in his monograph of Avery, “with the way rebellions between initiates and their mentors are frequently enacted: certain brash rejections are cushioned with compliments, and personal assurances attempt to heal the break that has in actual fact been made.” Which it had. Mentor and protégés went separate ways. They wouldn’t summer together again until 1957, when they reconvened in Provincetown on Cape Cod. Sometimes after a clear-cut break, a reciprocity gradually reemerges. Even as the abstract expressionists transformed American art, Avery wasn’t entirely left behind. The period’s most influential critic, Clement Greenberg, cast Avery as a sort of John the Baptist to the artists whom Greenberg had tried to deify. The new crop of abstract painters, he wrote in 1957, “has certain salutary lessons to learn” from Avery “that they cannot learn from any other artist on the scene.” In World War II’s immediate aftermath, Rothko painted abstract, colored shapes, beginning with what he called “multiforms” and shifting, around 1949, to his signature format of floating “lozenges” of soft-edged colors. He liked to layer warm and cool colors, so that in one lozenge a cooler purple might subdue a thin overlay of red while in its neighbor, a warm yellow rises like steam through the same red. The effect can be akin to music, and so intensely affecting that you’re almost willing to accept the artist’s preposterous rhetoric about his work. (“I would like to say to those who think of my pictures as serene,” Rothko once wrote, “that I have imprisoned the most utter violence in every inch of their surface.”) Meanwhile, Avery, working now on larger canvases, let particulars of the observed world dissolve into trembling fields of color. The paintings remained recognizable depictions of sea, land, and sky, but they, too, had as their true subject something closer to music. A gallery in the Cape Ann Museum exhibit (which will travel to the Phillips Collection, in Washington, D.C., in October) allows these late Avery paintings to share space with a sequence of mature Rothkos and similarly spare Gottliebs. The sense the gallery creates is of all three artists tenderly reunited and singing together in unison. If Rothko’s abstract paintings recall the ethereal, spatially ambiguous atmosphere of Caspar David Friedrich’s Monk by the Sea (painted between 1808 and 1810) or certain late works by J. M. W. Turner, they may also evoke the natural environment he observed on Cape Ann. His compositions are oriented vertically, but the lozenges nestled within each painting tend to be horizontal, so it’s tempting to see the thin strips dividing them as swaths of land hovering between sea and sky. Gottlieb, too, favored shapes that suggested the sun and moon—phenomena that he, a passionate sailor, had daily observed while out on the water. Despite all of this concordance, I came away sensing something unresolved about the relationship among these three powerful artists. The late Averys are good, but they’re simply not as strong as the best Rothkos, which hum with colors so richly resonant that they make Avery’s attempts to work on a larger scale look anemic. The Averys also lack the deep, metaphysical suggestiveness of the Gottliebs. Yet when you set aside the late works and consider Avery’s oeuvre, it seems to me that he was the better—more richly poetic, more generative—artist. The problem with the abstract expressionists’ relentless courting of the sublime was that the process of distillation produced too much bombast. And it led them into a cul-de-sac. As a skeptical character in John Updike’s novel Seek My Face put it, referring to the postwar generation of abstract expressionists, “they all still spoke of painting in terms of self-exploration and an agonized authenticity that would revolutionize the world and whatnot, but the results were a little like company logos, everybody working on the scale of 19th-century academic art but each of them having come up with some eye-catching simplification.” After Rothko settled on his signature manner, the level of repetition in his work became oppressive. Gottlieb, too, as he chased the sublime, seemed to shun the finer tendrils of the sensuous world, with results that felt fatally monotonous. To Greenberg, Avery was a prophet, his work a precursor to his younger peers’ more radical experiments. But maybe Avery was actually better than that. Rejecting Greenberg doesn’t mean claiming that abstraction was some kind of aesthetic mistake. But I would argue that, whereas Avery’s paintings continued to be aerated by the beautiful unruliness of the material world, Rothko and Gottlieb, especially later on, were relatively formulaic. True, if forced to choose, I might prefer to look at my favorite single Rothko over my favorite single Avery. But I would rather spend time with a dozen of Avery’s finest works than a dozen of Rothko’s. That’s because Avery understood that a deep canyon separates things in the world from their representations in art. The mystery of painting lies in what takes place in that shadowy, fertile zone, where what you thought was green foliage turns into the strangest dark purple, that body of gray water has flushed vivid turquoise, the blue sky is now flaming orange, and you don’t even know whether these transformations have taken place in life or on the canvas. Avery proved that figurative artists, in trying to represent the observable world, can be as free in their choices as any abstract painter. But their work is less likely to become clichéd, because any stale fixations will always be rinsed and refreshed by the real.

item.title: What to Read to Wake Up Your Brain
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.23
Summer is the ideal season for fun, frothy reads. On languorous weekends or hard-earned vacations, many people skew their literary diet toward lighter fare—fast-paced thrillers, steamy rom-coms—rather than, say, an in-depth history or an experimental novel. But fall is fast approaching. For some, that means a return to school; for many others, it represents the end of the most leisurely time of the year. Whether or not you’re heading back to the classroom, you may soon be tasked with, or else seek out, a more vigorous reading regimen; generally, the autumn months tend to require more from our brain. But it’s useful, as Labor Day approaches, to have an on-ramp—a way of easing into that more intense intellectual mode. These six books can help reacquaint the fall reader with the pleasures and demands of paying serious attention. Although none of them is especially strenuous—most are either brisk, bite-size, or divided into digestible parts—they are undeniably stimulating. Each will give your mind a much-needed burst of energy. The Age of Innocence, by Edith Wharton I came late to Wharton’s 1920 novel about a high-society love triangle in Gilded Age New York City—in fact, I read it only two months ago. I had gotten into my head that the writing would be too ornate for my liking, the settings and dialogue too stuffy. But classics tend to be classics for a reason, and The Age of Innocence snapped me out of my heat-induced inertia. Wharton’s witty, sophisticated sentences require and then amply reward sustained attention. Narrating the follies and frivolities of the city’s elite, she’s sarcastic and allusive, winking even as she dazzles with dialogue that verges on poetry. (The novelist Roxana Robinson once compared Wharton’s diction to a “sword wrapped in satin.”) Yet the universality of the novel makes it a perfect gateway for reengaging with foundational literature: Its core subjects are the timeless tensions between desire and obligation, and between self and society, expressed through a smoldering romance between forbidden lovers. Any Person Is the Only Self, by Elisa Gabbert One of the best entry points to rigorous reading is our own curiosity. Genuine interest is powerful; it can help readers move through the most daunting chapters or grasp even the most complicated ideas. As both a reader and a writer, Gabbert has always been guided by the compass of her inquisitiveness, perhaps never more so than in her wide-ranging third essay collection. The author’s sense of wonder stimulates the reader’s, and her primary subject—literature—may lead one to more invigorating reading. She is as erudite as she is earnest, and as she ponders Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein and Marcel Proust’s Swann’s Way, or the lives and work of Sylvia Plath and Rainier Maria Rilke, her passion becomes contagious. As she suggests in an essay about her classic-literature book club, it’s always worth finding time to have your own “intimate experience” with famous novels. Following the winding pathways of Gabbert’s mind might well show you to your next great read. Enough Is Enuf, by Gabe Henry Few books have made me laugh harder or more frequently than Henry’s exploration of the English language’s nonsensical writing system—one in which the spelling of words tells us precious little about how they’re pronounced—and the centuries of failed attempts to fix it. Enough Is Enuf chronicles some of the staunchest advocates of “simplified spelling” systems (including Teddy Roosevelt, Mark Twain, and the dictionary maker Noah Webster), each of whom attempted to streamline the haphazard rules of written English—a uniquely weird amalgamation of other, older languages. Henry’s book sits at the nexus of linguistics and history—two subjects that can be daunting, in many cases making for dry reading—but it is brisk and entertaining, full of archival images, clarifying examples, and hilarious anecdotes. By its end, you’ll likely feel grateful for the miracle that is your own literacy and eager to read more about quirky characters, both human and lexicographic. Suppose a Sentence, by Brian Dillon Each of the 27 short essays in this collection is inspired by a single sentence that captured Dillon’s imagination. For more than a quarter century, the critic has kept dozens of notebooks in which he copies down striking phrases he’s stumbled across. They vary widely in length, register, and complexity: the cascading clauses of Roland Barthes, a nine-word short-story opener by Susan Sontag, the prince of Denmark’s dying “O, o, o, o” in Hamlet. Each essay is a perfect introduction to its source material, providing both a hook (the sentence) and a primer (Dillon’s reflections) to an eclectic set of authors (who also include Gertrude Stein, James Baldwin, and Hilary Mantel). Dillon’s notebook exercise, I might add, could be just the thing to re-attune one’s brain to the wonders of the written word. Practice, by Rosalind Brown Brown’s trim novel takes place over a single day in the life of Annabel, an Oxford undergrad who’s trying to write an essay about Shakespeare’s sonnets. The paper’s due tomorrow, and it’s not going well: She’s constantly interrupted by roving, unruly thoughts and a very demanding body (she’s hungry, now she’s horny, and now she’s gotta pee). She’d planned to stick to a rigid routine—a 6 a.m. wake-up, a distraction-free morning of work, a break to walk through campus—but is consistently derailed. (Who among us?) Flashes of insight come, but nothing sticks; the poems will not yield to her. As the deadline approaches, we get an intimate glimpse of a mind both at work and at war. Watching Annabel try to push her intellect past new limits may compel a reader to do the same—or perhaps just to read the novel with the same close attention she pays the sonnets. As for whether she finishes her essay on time, I’ll disclose no spoilers here. Guilty Pleasures, by Arielle Zibrak The smutty hockey romance Heated Rivalry is passionately beloved, yet many of its fans admit to being embarrassed by their obsession with the TV series and novels that inspired it. (Ardent and committed lovers of other things—such as, say, hockey teams—tend not to feel the same way.) But Zibrak, an English professor at the University of Wyoming, insists that no novel, film, or show is more shameful, or less worth consuming, than any other is—and that even art dismissed as lowbrow has “much to tell us about ourselves and the world.” In this short, snappy tract, she confidently surveys the landscape of “guilty pleasures”—usually those written by, about, or for women—and unearths newfound complexity. She manages to cover the obscure 1850 best seller The Wide, Wide World as well as Judy Blume’s Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret, along with critical essays from thinkers such as Hilton Als and Saidiya Hartman; each volume mentioned is worth tracking down. So are other volumes in the series this belongs to, NYU Press’s Avidly Reads. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: Our Last Wi-Fi-Less Refuge Is Gone
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Score: 3.30
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Until very recently, airplanes were one of the last places where you couldn’t count on having good Wi-Fi. Even the Amazon’s most remote villages have high-speed internet, but for years, the typical in-flight connectivity experience could have been best summed up by the aviation Reddit thread titled “WiFi horrible?” Now major airlines have started rolling out Wi-Fi that is both free and usable. In June, United announced that by the end of this year, nearly 1,000 of its planes would be getting high-speed Wi-Fi via Starlink, the network of low-Earth-orbit satellites owned by SpaceX. Other major airlines, including Delta, JetBlue, and Alaska, are partnering with either Starlink or its closest competitor, Amazon Leo, to offer better Wi-Fi in the next year or two. This new technology provides almost the same internet experience you’d get on the ground, Seth Miller, an airline-industry analyst, told me. This is not Wi-Fi that’s “good for an airplane.” It’s just … good. As technology conquers this final Wi-Fi frontier, air travel will never be the same. The fickleness that made in-flight Wi-Fi infuriating was also its own kind of luxury: Planes were a bastion of unreachability. And once that luxury is gone, we may miss it. Delivering the internet to a metal tube traveling at 500 miles per hour, 30,000 feet above the Earth, is so difficult because the tube is both far from internet sources and constantly moving. In the early days of plane Wi-Fi, aircraft had what were essentially giant mobile hot spots attached to their bellies, which would connect to cell towers on the ground. (This was Gogo’s in-flight Wi-Fi which, let’s be honest, never really Gogo’d.)
